A visible preview matching a palette is insufficient grounds to delete an arbitrary matching library entry.

The hero computes generated names on demand at the gesture rather than every render, which avoids repeating perceptual naming work during slider movement. Its selection key may be a catalog ID or content signature, while the rendered ramp can be supplied separately from config; payload actions still send config. Bind preview and action payloads to the same committed revision so a live/held approximation is not silently substituted when saving or dragging. This is particularly relevant to the Working pipeline's distinction between live ramp and provisional fitted configuration.

A source search found CanonicalHero used by ImageStage; it did not substantiate the header's historical claim that all current surfaces embed it. Treat shared-component comments as design history until the active caller paths are traced. GradientHoverPreview's generic paint callback is nevertheless a useful way to reuse placement and resource sizing without duplicating palette/easing rendering logic. These observations are source analysis for RFF adoption, not a completed visual or accessibility audit. No screenshots, runtime tests or performance measurements were produced for this batch.

## Preview editing coordinates and distinguish an effect from a pending edit

Full reads of `palette/components/faces/CurvesFace.tsx`, `AdjustFace.tsx` and `palette/components/GeneratorModifierActions.tsx` connect the previously reviewed generator/Working stores to their controls. The RFF opportunity is a shared palette-adjustment editor that can target either the 2D fractal palette or an environment gradient, with the host owning the final apply command. These files establish data flow and command wiring, not a visual or accessibility audit.

**Preview another authoring space without committing a conversion.** CurvesFace keeps a local previewSpace and refits the current live curves into that space for display. While preview tracks exist, onTracksChange is replaced with a no-op, so that callback cannot commit a hover preview. Selecting the space invokes the store's real conversion. This can help an RFF user choose whether a particular palette is easier to edit as RGB components or perceptual lightness/chroma/hue without first altering the document. Keep the working representation and preview recipe separate, and show the approximation associated with an actual conversion.

The coordinate contract must include every overlay. In this caller, shownSpace/shownTracks follow the hovered space, but ghost and ghostPoints are calculated using the committed space and passed alongside them. Whether an incompatible overlay is omitted or drawn depends on ChannelGraphEditor, which remains to be fully inspected. Do not claim the whole graph follows the hovered axes from this caller alone. RFF should derive tracks, ghost values, control-point positions, channel labels and units from the same preview-space revision. Returning from hover should restore the committed view without touching Undo or shader parameters.

The ghost memo also depends on tracks and derived.final while its curves-on branch computes a prospective fit from base. Consequently, ordinary keyframe changes can invalidate and recompute the prospective fit even though its source and fit settings did not change. The separate ghostPoints calculation fits again through prospectiveFitFrames. For RFF, cache the fit result by base revision, detail, smoothing, knot-placement policy and authoring space, then derive both ghost values and point locations from it. This is a concrete CPU-editor optimization candidate, not an established GPU speedup.

**Entering an editor needs a transaction owned by the host.** CurvesFace's mount-only fallback fits when tracks are absent and a base already exists, or enables existing disabled tracks. It does not rerun when an initially missing base arrives later. Its comments explain that the main shell normally does this before mounting so opening the face participates in the host's undo command. A shared editor should not independently guess how to restore state after Undo or asynchronous source loading. RFF should make the host explicitly provide the editable source, enabled state and command ownership, and test entry before image extraction completes as well as entry with a valid palette.

Detail/Smooth callbacks in this face set values and toggle the local ghost-visibility flag; they do not themselves call the parameter-transaction bracket. Any automatic slider bracketing belongs to Slider and surrounding infrastructure, so this file is not sufficient evidence that each gesture produces exactly one Undo entry. Similarly, disabling onTracksChange during a space preview proves only that mutation path is suppressed, not that every editor action is inert. Verify shared-child behavior before adopting the pattern.

**Use separate predicates for effective rendering change and editable-state change.** AdjustFace gates both Apply and Cancel using isIdentityAdjust. That helper checks transform parameters and noise strength, but not noise frequency, target flags or the noise seed. Changing frequency while strength remains zero leaves these buttons disabled even though an editable setting has changed. Conversely, a nonzero parameter does not guarantee a visible difference for every input gradient. RFF should use an effect predicate to avoid unnecessary baking and a draft-dirty predicate to decide whether cancellation can restore changed settings. Define whether Cancel restores entry state or defaults; GMT's resetAdjust uses defaults, not an entry snapshot.

The reseed control is enabled when noise strength is positive, independently of whether any noise target is enabled. Seed changes are a separate part of reproducibility and should be included in a full cancel/restore contract when relevant. Apply is a host callback with no result acknowledgement here; the panel cannot establish successful commit, correct destination or durable save. RFF should execute the destination-bound command against the source revision and clear its draft only after the commit succeeds. Closing a panel and pressing Escape must use the same explicitly chosen transaction semantics rather than relying on labels.

GeneratorModifierActions exposes an older Bake-to-curve action whose tooltip promises an unchanged result and names L/C/h. The inspected generator implementation fits into the active authoring space with an approximation tolerance. Thus that wording is not a precision guarantee, and it can be inaccurate for a different active space. RFF should distinguish exact materialization into a dense ramp from approximate fitting into editable curves, offering an error comparison or retaining the dense result when necessary. Do not use the word unchanged for an unverified lossy conversion.

Both CurvesFace and AdjustFace reuse host-independent controls while the application decides where to bake. That separation is worth adopting, but their state still comes from module-global generator/engine stores. Multiple simultaneous RFF palette or environment editors should receive independent sessions rather than implicitly sharing tracks and adjustment dials. The measured-container layout code here is useful source context, but its historical sizing claims were not remeasured. Suggested verification cases are a space preview with all ghost overlays visible, a source arriving after mount, Undo of opening curves, a frequency-only edit with zero noise strength, an Apply failure and a bake in RGB authoring space. No new runtime tests were executed in this batch.

## Separate curve visibility, selection and document effects

Full reads of `palette/components/ChannelTrackSidebar.tsx`, `palette/components/faces/FaceTabs.tsx` and `palette/components/HeroSlot.tsx`, plus a targeted read of the track-list wiring in ChannelGraphEditor, clarify several supporting contracts for a RFF curve editor. ChannelGraphEditor itself is not credited as fully read by this targeted inspection.

ChannelTrackSidebar is a controlled component: it receives channel definitions, visibility, active channel and selection callbacks. The caller connects hiding to local visible state, changing the active channel to setActiveChannel, and selecting keys to channel-qualified keyframe IDs. Thus hiding a curve in this wiring is a presentation operation, not disabling its contribution to the generated palette. RFF should keep these states separate and describe them accurately. A user should be able to hide a noisy channel plot while its color effect remains active, or disable its effect through a separately named command. This transfers equally to 2D palette curves and environment-gradient authoring.

Per-channel selection builds IDs as channel plus keyframe ID, preventing ordinary identical keyframe IDs in different tracks from referring to the same selection. If RFF uses a string encoding, delimiters must be constrained or escaped; a typed pair is clearer. The All command walks displayTrackIds, while an individual channel's Select keys action directly uses that track. The complete definition of displayTrackIds and subsequent edit filtering still requires the full editor read, so this batch does not establish whether every hidden selection is excluded from editing. Verify hiding a selected track, switching authoring space and applying a multi-channel edit before claiming that selection cannot affect invisible data.

Ghost layers have a separate list with visibility toggles and no key-selection controls. This is useful for comparing an original or prospective fit without making that reference editable. RFF can use the same distinction for source/result overlays, but should bind their channel units and source revisions to the editor's current space as described in the preceding section. The horizontal implementation now wraps full labels despite its older header describing abbreviated labels in a scrolling line; comments alone are not sufficient evidence of current layout behavior.

FaceTabs renders host-supplied choices and reports the clicked face. It does not itself close a panel, bake a draft, cancel an operation or establish an undo boundary. This is a useful architectural separation: RFF's host should own one transition command that resolves the current draft and then changes the active editor. Keep destination selection independent from how the shared tab control is drawn. The custom data attributes provide stable hooks for GMT's tests, but their presence does not prove the lifecycle works or that those tests have run in this audit.

HeroSlot routes one child through a supplied portal target or renders it inline; railOnly renders nothing without a target. This avoids constructing an independently derived duplicate preview, but it is not a guarantee that changing targets preserves component state or avoids rerendering. Its header records that the former mobile provider host was retired. The inspected ImageStage references still use HeroSlot; the source search in the inspected host paths did not find an active HeroPortalProvider registration. Treat the alternate placement as available support code, not proof of a current live application feature. A native RFF implementation should share the underlying preview data/resource while explicitly preserving or recreating editor state when docking changes.

These files do not add a new shader priority. They support a coherent editor around the shader and palette improvements already ranked above. No visual audit, input simulation or runtime test was performed. Acceptance checks for an eventual RFF adaptation are that hiding a curve leaves the image unchanged, selecting keys does not change source data, reference overlays cannot be edited, face switching uses one documented commit/cancel policy, and moving the preview between containers neither loses the draft nor duplicates its renderer.

## Import planning and portable palette-library commands

A full read of `palette/components/FavientsCollectionMenu.tsx` (353 lines) confirms how the previously reviewed readers/writers reach the user-facing commands. RFF can adopt the useful separation between an editable native library, exchange-format export and a visual contact sheet. For 2D palettes and environment-gradient presets, an attractive preview image is not by itself a complete authoring document; preserve editable metadata and clearly distinguish any pixel-based recovery path from exact recipe recovery.

**Decode first, commit synchronously.** Collection and multi-file import await reading/parsing before opening the parameter-history bracket, then apply the batch synchronously as one operation. This avoids leaving an undo transaction open across unrelated user gestures. It is a sound RFF command pattern: produce a validated import plan outside the document transaction, then atomically commit that plan with one Undo entry. The menu requires the reader's document flag for replacement and refuses a lone exchange gradient, reducing accidental whole-library replacement. The actual flag semantics remain those of the shared reader reviewed earlier; this call site does not independently validate every archive member as a collection.

The current command lacks an operation-generation guard or busy state. Two imports can complete in a different order from their initiation, and a replacement can apply after intervening library changes. The import mode is captured at onFile entry, while the target group for ordinary imports is obtained after asynchronous reading. RFF should deliberately choose whether the target means the destination selected when the command started or the destination selected when it completes; bind that choice to an owned request and validate the library revision at commit. Do not let a stale replace overwrite later work merely because decoding finally finished.

Replacement confirmation here occurs before choosing and decoding the file, so it cannot describe the admitted entries or the actual resulting collection. An RFF import plan can show added/matched/skipped entries and the concrete replacement scope after parsing. This is a product-design recommendation for a future implementation, not a request for extra permission in this audit. Keep merge and replacement distinct and preserve Undo or a backup of the prior library.

**Report completion at the boundary actually observed.** Save/export messages are emitted after downloadBlob is invoked; this component does not receive confirmation that a file was durably written. Import messages similarly report the mutation count, not successful persistent storage. Awaited readers/contact-sheet creation have no local try/catch, and the contact-sheet path silently closes when no blob is returned. RFF should distinguish decoding, document mutation, encoding and successful file writing, retaining a useful error when any stage fails. Never mark a document saved solely because an export request was dispatched.

The export capability is supplied by the host through withExport rather than a branch on application identity. Host-owned onImported also handles actions beyond simple library insertion, such as opening a session or revealing a destination. This is a useful seam for RFF's palette and environment editors: share the reader and command result while keeping destination-specific behavior with the owning editor. Define structured outcomes so an unsupported scene/session or a partially admitted batch is not presented as a generic successful palette import.

**Describe format loss using the selected writer's actual contract.** The warning list is computed for collection formats, but its message uses AI_STOP_LIMIT for every selected collection format and describes all warnings as exceeding that stop count. The previously reviewed warning function measures approximation, not just the source stop count, and different writers can have different limits. The sentence about most applications' caps is not substantiated by this source audit. RFF should report the selected format's actual representation, interpolation/alpha/precision losses and measured conversion error, using the same resolved writer options for both warning and output. Per-gradient ZIP exports can also be lossy and should not be excluded merely because they are not a single collection file.

Collection ZIP/file creation and quality-warning evaluation are synchronous in this component; large libraries can therefore require substantial work on the calling thread. Native RFF can snapshot the collection revision, encode on a worker and report cancellation/progress while keeping the snapshot immutable. A contact sheet and a native library should identify the same source revision even if the user continues editing during generation. No file round-trip, failure injection, application compatibility or performance test was run for this batch. Proposed checks are reverse-order import completion, a library edit during replacement parsing, a failed file write, format-specific warnings and an export followed by re-import with authoring metadata compared separately from rendered colors.

## Channel editor: localized tools, immutable preview bases and precise cancellation

The complete 1,412-line `palette/components/ChannelGraphEditor.tsx` has now been read, superseding the earlier targeted-only coverage. It adapts shared animation-graph drawing, selection, inspector and tool hooks through a local GraphDataSource, using palette parameter history rather than the animation timeline's mutation path. For RFF, this suggests a reusable curve-editing core serving 2D palette channels and environment-gradient channels without coupling those edits to animation playback. Reuse mathematics and commands; give each document its own history and ownership.

**Use localized curve tools with a common error budget.** The pencil and smoothing brush receive the active channel's fit epsilon multiplied by the same detail scale as the main fit. Their target includes screen-to-channel conversion, and publication composes with current tracks through a ref. The wave tool samples a chosen span, fits that span and splices it into the original key list, aiming to preserve data outside the edited interval. RFF could offer local lightness shaping, chroma smoothing and periodic color modulation through one precision policy. The shared hook and splice implementation determine the exact seam and smoothing behavior; this component alone does not prove error bounds between samples or preservation of derivative continuity.

The strip under the graph uses the graph's horizontal transform, so panning and zooming keep each palette position aligned with its curve coordinate. This is a useful mechanism for RFF: a local change in the curve should correspond to the same position in the palette preview. The strip always smooths its image, unlike the band-aware GradientStrip, and uses a 256-sample byte representation. Preserve the previously identified common sampling/encoding contract when introducing this view; a graph preview should not conceal a deliberately hard palette boundary.

**Preview from an immutable gesture base.** Arming the wave stores the original channel's keyframes; each update derives from that base rather than the previous preview. At nonpositive strength it returns the original keys directly, avoiding approximation drift from fitting an unchanged curve. Switching channels restores the previous channel's base before taking a new base, and a channel-ownership check prevents the preview effect from writing the old channel into the newly active one. These are particularly useful RFF design details: effect previews must not accumulate, a zero-strength operation must be an exact no-op, and a target switch must not strand an uncommitted edit.

Wave amplitude uses the channel's defined range rather than its current plotted range, so zoom and automatic axis expansion do not change the numerical effect. Remembered wave settings are module-global and carry across editors, while the source snapshot is local. For RFF, persist user preferences separately from an armed document-bound operation. Reseeding uses a random increment and stores the resulting seed in local wave parameters; reproducibility requires retaining the chosen seed or committed output, not replaying the random gesture sequence.

**Bounds described as true are sampled estimates here.** waveExtent evaluates 129 positions over the domain; narrow peaks or high frequencies can fall between them. It is not an analytic extrema guarantee despite the comment's wording. Ordinary trackRanges primarily use key values and ghost samples, so Bezier overshoot between keys is not necessarily included. RFF should compute curve extrema where feasible or conservatively sample/subdivide to a declared tolerance. The extent memo also reads waveBaseRef without including waveBaseTick in its dependencies, unlike the preview-writing effect, so a rebase is not independently represented in its cache key. Tie all preview-derived bounds and handles to the same immutable base revision.

**Cancellation must include every exit path and transaction owner.** Explicit wave cancellation restores original keys before ending the parameter bracket; commit writes the current result and ends it. Escape is registered as a dismissible scope, allowing an inner dropdown to consume one Escape before the tool consumes the next. This is a useful RFF approach to nested editor controls. The unmount cleanup, however, only ends the bracket when waveOn was true; it does not restore the base. Closing/destroying the editor is therefore not intrinsically equivalent to cancelling the wave. Specify whether each host exit commits or cancels and execute that command before teardown.

Ordinary pointer transactions start through the editor root's pointerdown capture and end through window pointerup/pointercancel listeners whenever the editor is interactive and no wave is armed. The end listener is not tied to a pointer ID or to proof that this editor opened the current transaction. Multiple mounted editors can therefore contend for a shared bracket unless the surrounding infrastructure prevents it. The ordinary listener cleanup only removes listeners, whereas the wave has a separate cleanup end. RFF should use owned transaction tokens, pointer capture, explicit cancellation and finally-style teardown, then test focus loss and source replacement during a drag.

**Resolve the previously open hidden-selection question.** displayTrackIds filters hidden channels and drives drawing, hit testing, view fitting, ordinary tool track lists and Select all. However, hiding a channel does not clear its already selected key IDs. deleteSelected groups those IDs directly and can delete from a hidden track; selecting a hidden channel's keys through the sidebar also remains possible. The inspector and selection box receive the full selection. Thus hiding is not a guarantee that the channel cannot be edited. RFF should choose a consistent policy: either keep such selection visibly disclosed, clear it when hiding, or explicitly exclude hidden tracks from destructive commands.

Deletion protects a minimum count of two keys, not the original endpoints. Both bulk deletion and right-click removal can remove an endpoint if enough other keys remain. Double-click insertion rounds/clamps the frame but does not reject another key at the same frame; generated IDs combine frame and current key count, which can collide after deletions and repeated insertions. updateKeyframes sorts touched tracks, while replaceKeyframes trusts the incoming order. RFF should enforce unique IDs, ordering, duplicate-position semantics and any required endpoint anchors centrally, with the same rules for dragging, tools, import and the numeric inspector.

**Controlled publication needs an explicit acceptance contract.** commitTracks updates its ref before calling the parent, correctly allowing two same-tick operations such as copy then transform to compose. The parent callback returns void; if it rejects or ignores an update, the local ref can temporarily diverge. Several discrete add/delete paths instead call onTracksChange directly and read props. For RFF, centralize mutation publication and acknowledge the resulting document revision, particularly while a host is showing a noncommitting color-space preview. Do not let the editor's private working state become command authority after a parent has rejected a write.

**Complete the overlay-space finding.** Ghost drawing indexes arrays by the current space's channel keys and skips missing keys. Therefore a hovered space with different keys can omit the old-space ghost rather than converting it; spaces sharing keys can still pass semantically mismatched values. This confirms that the CurvesFace caller must convert all overlays together. The loop assumes 256 values after only checking for a nonempty array, so validate lengths/finiteness at the data boundary. Ghost extent and points also need the same units and source revision as the live curves.

The interactive flag blocks several canvas and keyboard handlers and hides tools, but the KeyframeInspector and selection box are still rendered with a data source containing mutators. This file alone therefore does not prove a hard read-only boundary; verify those child capabilities or remove mutation authority in read-only mode. The keyboard handler excludes INPUT targets but does not generally exclude textarea or contenteditable descendants. These are command-routing concerns for reuse, not a completed accessibility audit.

No graph interaction, numerical-fit benchmark or visual comparison was executed in this batch; historical test claims in comments were not rerun. RFF acceptance cases should cover exact zero-strength/cancel restoration, nonaccumulating previews, a channel switch mid-wave, close/unmount while armed, hidden selected keys, endpoint deletion, duplicate-frame insertion, two editors sharing history, and overlay alignment across every supported color space. These editor features support shader authoring but do not replace the previously ranked rendering improvements.

## Wave controls must share the preview's original source

Full reads of `palette/components/WaveOverlay.tsx` (457 lines) and `WaveToolHead.tsx` (336 lines), together with the just-reviewed ChannelGraphEditor caller, establish the control-to-preview contract. For RFF, the useful feature is a localized wave modifier with span, feather, phase, amplitude, offset, wavelength and shape controls. It can shape 2D palette channels or an environment gradient; it is not itself geometry displacement or a new fractal formula.

**Publish the original and evaluated result as distinct resources.** WaveOverlay's sampleBase contract says it receives the curve before filtering. It applies applyWaveSample to that base for its invisible hit path and handle positions. ChannelGraphEditor supplies sampleWaveBase, which reads tracksRef.current, while the live preview writes the filtered/fitted result into that same ref. The committed keys are correctly derived from waveBaseRef, but the overlay can evaluate the effect again on an already modified curve. Add and multiply modes make this distinction particularly relevant. This is a verified static connection mismatch, not a measured visual offset. RFF should pass the immutable pre-operation source to analytical handles, or directly sample the evaluated result without applying the modifier a second time. Include source/result revision IDs so drawing, hit testing and commit cannot silently use different generations.

**Separate positional controls from rate controls.** Span and feather movement divide horizontal pointer displacement by the plotted t-axis width, using the same transform that draws their handles. Wavelength instead changes multiplicatively, with four octaves per canvas width and a bounded range. Bias/skew use an exponential response with bounded positive values. This is a useful RFF interaction model: positional handles should track their data coordinate, while scale/rate controls can span a large range smoothly. Vertical amplitude/offset use canvas-height-normalized deltas, not the inverse channel-value transform, so they are sensitivity controls rather than guaranteed pixel-for-pixel tracking of the curve. Document and test that distinction.

The overlay stores pointer-down parameters and computes each move from those originals, preventing parameter accumulation. It does not freeze width, height or coordinate transforms with that snapshot, so resizing or changing the view mid-drag changes how the same displacement is interpreted. Its drag record has no pointer ID and the move handler does not verify ownership; another pointer can replace or drive it. pointercancel uses the same end path as pointerup and does not restore pointer-down parameters. There is no lost-capture or unmount cleanup here. Native RFF should bind each gesture to one pointer/capture owner and define cancellation separately from release.

**Clipping a handle must not clip the authored value.** The crest marker clamps its displayed vertical position while retaining amplitude and showing a direction indicator when the true point is outside the plot. The wavelength gauge similarly caps its drawn width to the span while retaining a larger wavelength value. These techniques let RFF keep an extreme edit adjustable without altering the actual curve to fit the viewport. The crest is found by scanning 97 samples of waveValue in a portion of the span; it is not necessarily the exact maximum of the combined, feathered result. The invisible body hit path uses a finite sample count capped at 480, so fine structure is also approximate. Avoid claiming exact geometric correspondence beyond the sampling and fitting tolerances.

Feather shoulders can overlap up to 99 percent of the span; dragging a shoulder outward beyond zero begins moving the associated span endpoint. This combines edge softness and placement in one gesture, useful for localized palette changes. It also means a feather control can change the affected domain. Make that transition visible and preserve the original outside-span data through the commit operation. The overlay clamps individual interactions but does not validate an arbitrary incoming parameter object; imported/preset values still need a shared validation boundary.

**Generate illustrative icons from the same waveform, but do not label them exact previews.** WaveToolHead traces the shape function for icons at module initialization. Preset icons use their default parameters and a bounded displayed interval; amplitude is normalized and only 41 positions are sampled. They communicate shape rather than the current effect on a source channel, actual strength or an arbitrary reseeded noise realization. RFF can use shared procedural icon generation to prevent a shape definition and its symbol diverging, while reserving the real material/palette preview for judging the result.

Presets are filtered by whether their semantic channel role exists in the active color space. This is a useful distinction for RFF: a lightness preset should not silently target an arbitrary RGB channel. Shape/mode changes, reseeding and Apply/Cancel remain parent callbacks. The Strength control supports bounded pointer updates and left/right keyboard increments, but pointerdown is not restricted to the primary button and pointermove tests button state rather than its captured pointer identity. Treat control metadata as source-level intent; full input/accessibility behavior was not tested here.

No runtime comparison or pointer simulation was executed. Recommended RFF checks are that a nonzero Add/Multiply wave's handles follow the once-filtered displayed result, zero strength preserves the exact source, a second pointer cannot hijack a drag, capture loss has a defined outcome, resizing during a drag is stable, and narrow/high-frequency waves remain selectable within a documented tolerance. These support the palette/environment authoring proposals without changing the provisional ranking of shader improvements.

## Rendering design records: transferable contracts and superseded decisions

Full reads of ADR-0016, ADR-0017, ADR-0018, ADR-0019, ADR-0020 and ADR-0024 add architectural context to the RFF recommendations. These are design-record findings; reading them does not complete the underlying generic engine implementations. In particular, the coverage ledger still marks engine/AdaptiveResolution.ts and engine/AnimationEngine.ts pending and engine/RenderPipeline.ts partial. Runtime behavior, timing gains and frame equivalence remain unverified by this batch.

**Drive exported modulation from frame coordinates.** ADR-0016 specifies integer-frame timing and oscillator time derived from currentFrame/fps for deterministic playback, while dropping an excessive interactive wall-time backlog. RFF can use the distinction when animating palette phase, noise or environment rotation: define each exported frame from its index and the chosen seed, independently of how long previous frames took to render. Dropping elapsed interactive time is a responsiveness policy, not proof that no export frame is skipped. Verify recording separately, including pauses, slow frames and fractional frame rates, before claiming preview/export equivalence.

**Measure GPU progress only when someone needs it.** ADR-0017 describes fence-based asynchronous convergence readback; ADR-0018 enables convergence measurement only for an interested consumer. RFF can apply the general principle to optional quality diagnostics, histograms or convergence indicators: schedule GPU work on demand and retrieve completed results without synchronously stalling each render. Vulkan requires its own resource/barrier/readback implementation, not WebGL calls copied literally. Tag results with the source image revision and expose unknown/pending/stale states rather than presenting a default numeric value as a valid measurement. If multiple windows consume a diagnostic, use scoped subscriptions or reference counts rather than a single boolean one window can clear for all others. A fence alone does not prove the whole readback path is stall-free; staging copies, memory visibility and result consumption still require code review and measurement.

**Use one adaptive policy with independent caller state.** ADR-0024 places the resolution decision in a pure shared module while leaving buffer resize and accumulation reset with each caller. Its selfResized marker distinguishes a caller's own reset from new scene activity, preventing resolution adjustment from repeatedly triggering itself. This is transferable to RFF's interactive preview scheduling: distinguish camera/input changes, resource changes and self-induced renderer resets. Keep full-precision fractal results and restore full-quality output when settled and before export. The document's historical mobile minimum quality is a device policy, not a universal value to import into desktop Vulkan. Adoption requires explicit hysteresis, cancellation and idle restoration checks in the actual implementation; this ADR alone does not establish them.

**Prefer typed shader assembly and validated interfaces.** ADR-0019 explicitly distinguishes the generic free-form section map from GMT's typed live raymarch builder. Therefore a recommendation to copy the free-form map as the mechanism driving GMT's main shader would misattribute the architecture. RFF should favor named, validated composition points with explicit dependencies and report unknown sections rather than silently dropping code. This can support reusable environment, shading and post-processing modules shared where appropriate between 3D-style relief and 2D rendering without assuming all 3D geometry stages are transferable.

ADR-0020 contains a later amendment superseding its original silent uniform-collision handling. A targeted source search confirms that both generic and GMT UniformSchema files contain throwing collision checks, so the old Decision/Consequences text must not be reported as current missing behavior. The useful RFF lesson is to validate shader interfaces before rendering. For Vulkan, name uniqueness is only one part: descriptor set/binding, type, array count, byte layout and push-constant range must match C++ declarations and compiled shaders. Keep cached CPU-derived uniforms tied to their source parameter revisions, and retain safe defaults for optional features. The document does not prove a complete Vulkan-compatible layout scheme.

These records reinforce existing rendering priorities rather than introduce measured speed claims. They also illustrate why later amendments and actual call paths must take precedence over an ADR's original wording. Suggested RFF validation includes deterministic frame-by-frame export, stale diagnostic rejection after a palette/camera change, overlapping diagnostic consumers, idle quality restoration after adaptive resizing, unknown shader-section rejection and a deliberate CPU/GLSL interface mismatch test. No GPU benchmark or animation export was run in this batch.

## Adaptive resolution implementation: predict cost without confusing it with precision

`engine/AdaptiveResolution.ts` has now been read in full, advancing the preceding ADR-only coverage to implementation-level analysis of the decision module. It mutates caller-owned state and returns a downsample factor; it does not resize images, execute shaders or prove that any caller restores full-quality output. RFF can borrow its scheduling ideas for temporary previews while preserving the full-precision iteration/reference data and mandatory final-resolution rendering.

**Seed the first interactive frame from normalized cost.** The module estimates full-resolution frame cost as tick interval multiplied by the square of the current downsample factor, then updates an exponential moving average with weights 0.7/0.3. It seeds scale with the square root of target FPS divided by estimated full-resolution FPS. This follows the assumption that work is proportional to pixel count and avoids restarting every gesture at an obviously expensive full resolution. The first feedback window lasts at least 200 ms and jumps to the computed scale; later windows use at least 500 ms and a 0.3 blend. These are useful starting mechanisms, not universal constants or measured RFF performance recommendations.

The model assumes predominantly pixel-dependent work. RFF can have significant fixed costs, reference-orbit work, CPU/GPU synchronization and content-dependent iteration cost, so scaling by pixel count alone cannot predict all frame times. Prefer separate GPU timings for shading/post-processing and CPU timings for fractal work where available, and associate samples with the actual completed frame and resolution. A late result from a previous resolution or different scene must not train the current model. The module's tick interval is an indirect estimate, not a GPU duration.

**Exclude unrepresentative samples.** Cost samples require explicit interaction or an increasing accumulation count; an optional mode samples only interaction frames to avoid treating cheap progressive bands as full-frame work. Pauses of at least two seconds are ignored. A sample is capped at four times the previous estimate, limiting a one-off stall's influence. Tick intervals at or below 17.5 ms are treated as cadence-limited and allowed only to lower the estimate, apart from initial full-resolution seeding. These guards reduce some feedback errors, but a hardcoded cadence threshold does not cover all pacing regimes or distinguish CPU stalls from GPU work. In RFF, preserve sample provenance and use measured render work rather than assuming a display's refresh interval represents shader cost.

**Engage on declared scene activity and restore quality when idle.** The module supports explicit interaction, inferred accumulation drops, or an always-active policy for simulations. mouseOverCanvas is unused. An inferred reset caused by the caller's own resize can be ignored through selfResized. The flag is consumed once, so reset timing must match the caller contract; a delayed reset can otherwise look external. RFF should use a renderer/source generation and a reset reason rather than relying solely on a one-tick flag. Avoid reducing quality when an unrelated control changes without invalidating the image.

Default grace is 100–2000 ms based on still FPS. An explicit grace can override it; callers with a reliable gesture-end signal need not wait seconds before sharpening. Full-resolution accumulation above a threshold of 8–50 samples suppresses adaptive mode, including during an explicit interaction until the caller invalidates that accumulation. The sample count is meaningful only for the current scene and target. For RFF, a generation change must invalidate old quality protection before the next decision; existing samples must not protect an image that is no longer valid.

**The hold contract is narrower than the header suggests.** holdUntilMs blocks a further downscale only in the feedback-window update. Initial smart-mode seeding assigns scale before that check, and manual-mode assignment bypasses it entirely. Therefore a hold is not a global guarantee that resolution cannot fall. Manual mode also does not use minQuality's smart-mode cap. Decide and test RFF's intended policy for initial engagement, manual downsampling and quality holds separately, and apply a global bound at the final decision boundary if that is the contract.

The suppressed path forces scale 1 and clears active-window bookkeeping, which is appropriate as an export decision. It does not ensure that the caller has resized, discarded obsolete accumulation, rerendered at full quality or completed GPU work. RFF export should explicitly await those transitions before reading pixels. Suppression also runs after cost sampling and retains some historical activity/quality state, so ending suppression is not a complete fresh-state reset. Test export interruption and resumption rather than assuming the toggle handles every lifecycle boundary.

The function trusts numeric inputs. Nonfinite quality/target/time values, negative overrides and contradictory activity flags are not comprehensively rejected. gateOnAccumOnly and ignoreAccumDrop are described as mutually exclusive in practice but are not enforced. Initialize activity explicitly rather than interpreting a default timestamp of zero as recent activity near process start, and define reset behavior on scene replacement or a clock discontinuity. State and feedback windows are per caller; they must not be shared across independent RFF render targets.

The file now provides concrete evidence for the pure-policy/shared-caller-state recommendation. It does not yet establish end-to-end behavior of every worker/main-thread consumer. No timing simulation, Vulkan benchmark or visual convergence test was run in this batch. Proposed checks include a known fixed-plus-per-pixel cost model, a compile stall, progressive idle bands, a hold active during initial engagement, manual versus smart limits, delayed self-resize reset, deep accumulation followed by a scene change, and export immediately after a low-resolution preview. 3D raymarching and 2D fractal shading can share the policy structure, but their cost models and precision constraints require separate calibration.

## Animation implementation: deterministic evaluation is not exhaustive frame playback

`engine/AnimationEngine.ts` has now been read in full. Its local-track evaluation, injected stores, explicit binder registry and pre/post scrub hooks provide useful architecture for animating RFF palette phase, shading controls and a proposed environment rotation. This implementation read supersedes any interpretation of ADR-0016 as proof of exact exported-frame behavior. The export driver and modulation oscillator remain separate dependencies.

**Separate realtime scheduling from frame-complete export.** Deterministic tick accumulates dt, computes an integer number of steps and advances by that amount, then calls scrub once at the destination. It does not evaluate every intervening integer frame despite comments describing multiple emitted frames. If playback starts on a fractional frame, adding integer steps also preserves that fractional offset. At a looping boundary it sets nextFrame to zero rather than retaining the overshoot remainder. These can be deliberate preview policies, but they are not an export iterator. RFF should evaluate a specified frame index directly for export and await rendering/encoding before advancing, while allowing a distinct realtime preview scheduler to drop display frames.

The long-gap implementation also differs from its prose: when dt exceeds 0.25 seconds it clears detAccum, then immediately adds that same dt and converts it to frame steps. Thus it drops the old fractional remainder, not the long gap itself. A resume can still advance substantially. The function lacks comprehensive finite/nonnegative dt, FPS and duration validation, and switching deterministic mode does not explicitly clear its accumulator unless playback is observed stopped. RFF should specify pause/resume, mode-switch, seek and project-replacement clock policies and test them directly rather than inheriting a comment's guarantee.

**Share evaluation semantics, including composite tracks.** scrub checks paired-camera evaluation before ordinary interpolation. Public evaluateTrack calls only interpolate and has no sequence context, so it cannot reproduce paired-track behavior in general. It also does not run scrub hooks, registered binders or a modulation overlay. For RFF, expose one pure scene-at-frame evaluator returning a complete parameter snapshot, with explicit context for coupled coordinates, log zoom and modulation. Use the same evaluator in preview and export, and keep applying the snapshot separate from computing it. This matters particularly for deep-zoom motion; a numeric track sampler alone is not evidence that high-precision camera state is preserved.

Recording modulation evaluates a stored sequence snapshot instead of a live sequence being edited during recording. This avoids feeding newly written keys back into the source evaluation. RFF can use the same immutable-base principle already identified for palette tools: layer recorded modulation over a stable source and materialize it once. Confirm how seeds and oscillator phase are captured in the modulation module before claiming reproducible noisy animation.

**Use typed parameter metadata, not name heuristics.** This engine only applies float tracks; other types are skipped. Rotation behavior is inferred from substrings such as rot, phase and twist, whereas log behavior uses a registry. A substring can misclassify an unrelated parameter, and phase may have units or wrap semantics different from an angle. RFF should declare interpolation domain, units, wrap period and discrete-versus-continuous behavior in its parameter schema. Boolean/enum settings need explicit step semantics if they are to be animated, not float interpolation or silent omission.

Beyond the last key, Continue extrapolates using raw endpoint-value differences or a stored tangent ratio and adds the result directly to the last value. That branch bypasses log/rotation-aware interpolation; for a logarithmic Bezier track a tangent expressed in log units is not an additive value-space slope. OffsetLoop likewise adds raw endpoint differences. RFF should define extrapolation in the same domain as interpolation, validate duplicate key times to avoid division by zero and preserve intentional multiple turns. Frame evaluation assumes ordered, valid key arrays; import validation must establish that contract.

**Binders require lifecycle ownership and validation.** Explicit registered binders are looked up before cached fallbacks, allowing late custom registration to take effect. However, connect replaces store pointers without clearing the fallback cache, and some fallback closures capture setter functions from the old store. Unresolved no-op fallbacks are cached too. RFF should invalidate binding caches when a project/schema/store generation changes, distinguish an unsupported track from a successfully bound one and report the former. Legacy path parsing also assumes fields such as a position axis exist; malformed imported track IDs need validation before binder resolution.

Vector-axis fallback writers clone the current vector before replacing one component, which helps successive axis writes compose. Still, scrub writes tracks individually, and an exception in a hook or binder aborts the remainder without guaranteed post-hook execution or rollback. The pre/post hook mechanism is intended to batch composite camera changes; RFF should generalize this to a validated frame snapshot committed atomically so shader uniforms and high-precision camera fields cannot be observed halfway through a frame update. Keep rendering invalidation to the final publication where possible.

Once-mode reaches duration, scrubs that endpoint and stops. Whether duration denotes a final frame index or a frame count must be agreed with the exporter; this file alone does not settle the off-by-one convention. No playback/export test or numerical interpolation comparison was run in this batch. RFF acceptance cases should cover a long pause, fractional-frame start, loop overshoot, deterministic-mode switching, reconnecting stores after a cached binding, logarithmic Continue, paired-camera evaluation and one failed binder within a multi-parameter frame. These apply to both 2D zoom/color animation and 3D-derived lighting effects without changing the fractal calculation method.

## Render-pipeline adoption: responsive feedback with trustworthy completion

The complete 910-line `engine/RenderPipeline.ts` has now been read, replacing the earlier partial coverage of ping-pong accumulation. The useful RFF transfers are consumer-gated diagnostic passes, retaining a provisional image during resizing, explicit ownership of per-pixel sample counts and region-limited rendering. These support both 2D rendering and 3D-derived material previews. They do not require adopting GMT's temporal accumulation as a replacement for RFF's fractal computation, and they do not establish a measured speed improvement.

**Separate visible change from convergence.** GMT's convergence shader samples two consecutive color buffers, computes the largest absolute RGB difference and writes it into the red channel. The CPU scans a target capped at 256 pixels per axis. This is texture sampling at reduced resolution, not a conservative maximum reduction over every source pixel: isolated changing details can be missed. Differences between successive running averages also tend to shrink with sample count; they are not, by themselves, a statistical uncertainty estimate or a guarantee that the fractal is accurate. RFF should present such a quantity as a change indicator unless a separately justified stopping criterion is implemented. Never use it to shorten precision-sensitive orbit computation or declare all tiles equally resolved. Validate non-finite values explicitly: the current maximum scan ignores NaN because its comparison is false.

**Measure only for a consumer, but finish pending work independently of drawing.** The explicit convergence-needed flag avoids a diagnostic render and readback when no overlay consumes the result. That ownership pattern is useful for RFF. However, GMT's draw method returns on hold or sample-cap completion before reaching its polling code. A measurement launched on the final permitted sample therefore needs an external poll to finish; this class does not supply that scheduler. Disabling the consumer also stops the in-render polling. RFF should give pending transfers their own completion path, tagged with render generation, region, dimensions and sample count. A stopped draw loop must not prevent completion or cleanup, and a stale result must not label a new view as converged.

**A fence after drawing is not an asynchronous transfer.** GMT inserts a fence after the difference pass, checks it with a zero timeout, then calls synchronous `readRenderTargetPixels`. The fence establishes completion of preceding GPU work; this implementation does not first enqueue a pixel-buffer transfer. Consequently, comments describing the entire readback as stall-free are stronger than the code proves. For RFF, use its Vulkan resource model to enqueue a copy into an owned staging slot and consume that slot only after the copy's completion is known. Respect host visibility/coherency requirements and retain resources until completion. Measure actual transfer and CPU costs before claiming a responsiveness gain.

Fence creation returning null leaves GMT's pending flag true while its poll requires a non-null fence. The failed-wait branch returns a previous numeric result without conveying failure or freshness. Reset abandons pending state but defers deletion of the old fence until another measurement starts. These are reasons to use explicit pending/completed/failed/cancelled states and generation ownership in a RFF implementation. This is an adoption requirement derived from local control flow, not a reproduced RFF failure. Synchronous and asynchronous callers also share one convergence target; concurrent use needs serialization or separate slots.

**Keep format, CPU representation and required precision together.** Ordinary pixel readback inspects the actual target type, which is a useful contract. Its half-float converter nevertheless shifts subnormal mantissas without compensating the exponent: for bit pattern 0x0001 the expression returns 2^-14 instead of 2^-24. This counterexample follows directly from the source arithmetic; no GPU experiment was run. RFF should use a verified conversion and check all half-float encodings if conversion is needed. Clearing the public float output does not clear GMT's reused half-float scratch array, and success here means only that no exception was caught, not independent confirmation that new pixels arrived.

The convergence path always allocates Float32Array while its target can use the selected half-float format; unlike ordinary readback, it has no matching conversion branch. Moreover, initConvergenceTools only creates its target once, so a later accumulation precision change does not rebuild that target's type. RFF should validate the complete image-format/transfer/CPU-layout contract and recreate dependent resources together. The exact behavior of the installed Three.js readback implementation was not verified in this batch.

GMT's format chooser can select half precision to obtain linear filtering. That fallback must not be copied into RFF when it reduces required precision. Query the actual Vulkan device's relevant format capabilities and choose a precision-preserving sampling alternative or an explicit unsupported result. GMT's separate-context capability probes, including an informational alpha probe unused by this chooser, are not evidence about RFF's selected device. Keep display filtering choices separate from orbit, field and accumulation accuracy.

**Preserve a preview without treating it as new data.** When supplied a renderer, resize copies the old displayed image into both new ping-pong targets before disposing the old targets, while resetting accumulation counts. This offers a useful continuity pattern for RFF: show the retained image as provisional while fresh pixels arrive. Track validity separately so a rescaled image never becomes a valid sample, an export result or a convergence reference for a changed view. Omitting the renderer deliberately takes a different path; precision changes in this class do so. Sample-budget edits retain existing accumulated content, which likewise avoids discarding valid work unnecessarily.

**Give partial rendering explicit ownership.** The write index denotes the next destination, so output/history access deliberately selects its opposite. Tiled blending delegates sample counts to the band scheduler; a single global draw count cannot describe differently updated pixels. Bucket scissoring is applied after target binding to restrict rasterized work. RFF can adopt these contracts where applicable, while including the neighboring-pixel halo needed by later filters and preserving untouched history correctly. The optional scene/camera arguments allow this method to advance counters and swap targets without issuing a scene draw; a RFF submission API should publish counts only for accepted work. Error paths also need reliable state restoration and deferred resource cleanup. No public disposal method exists in this class, so broader ownership must be checked before copying its lifetime pattern.

Acceptance checks for a RFF implementation should include a one-pixel changing feature, NaN diagnostic input, a measurement at the sample cap, hold/cancel during transfer, a region change while pending, precision changes, half-float subnormals, resize with retained display, and tiled/full-frame agreement. CPU wall time recorded after submission is not proof of GPU completion time. No render comparison, performance benchmark or GPU compatibility test was performed in this batch; the provisional environment-reflection priority remains unchanged.

## Shader parameter contracts: share definitions without sharing mutable state

Full reads of both `engine/UniformSchema.ts` and `engine-gmt/engine/UniformSchema.ts`, plus `engine/UniformNames.ts`, `engine/ConfigDefaults.ts`, `engine/defineEnumParam.ts`, `engine/AccumulationController.ts`, `engine/features/index.ts` and `shaders/chunks/uniforms.ts`, clarify how shader settings become GPU inputs. The register and getUniformDefinitions methods of the common FeatureSystem were also inspected, but that file remains only partially inspected. The RFF opportunity is a consistent parameter contract for new environment, filtering and material controls across interactive rendering and export, not a requirement to replace its Vulkan framework with GMT's registry.

**Validate composition before building a shader.** Both uniform schemas reject feature names that shadow core names and duplicate names across feature definitions. This catches otherwise silent default replacement. The declaration generator then derives GLSL types and array declarations from the schema, skipping backingOnly entries. A single source of interface metadata is useful in RFF, but string-name uniqueness is only one check: Vulkan descriptor bindings, array lengths, offsets, alignment, push-constant ranges and shader-stage visibility must agree with the C++ configurators. Preserve existing binary settings order independently of any in-memory registry order. Adding a shader parameter does not authorize renumbering saved palette recipes or rewriting ConfigIO layout.

The schemas execute feature registration at module evaluation and snapshot the resulting definitions/defaults. The inspected registry permits development replacement of an existing feature object and invalidates its own sorting/dictionary caches, but these already-exported schema arrays are not rebuilt by that operation. New registrations are separately blocked once the registry is frozen. RFF should finalize a validated schema before creating dependent pipelines, or explicitly version and rebuild all affected state. Do not assume late registration automatically updates defaults, descriptors and compiled shaders together. The common and GMT schemas are distinct: GMT adds mat4 support and a derived rotation bank. Their resemblance is not evidence of interchangeable interfaces.

**Separate source settings from derived render values.** The base schemas contain frame/time/camera inputs, export tile coordinates and CPU-derived matrices, environment rotation and pixel-size values. This is a useful division: source settings remain editable/persisted, while derived GPU values are recomputed from one coherent frame snapshot. Moving uniform trigonometry or matrix construction out of per-fragment work can be useful for proposed RFF environment rotation, where the result is constant across pixels. Profile the existing RFF path before claiming savings; preserve its numerical conventions and precision. An environment lookup for 2D relief needs the relevant direction transform, not GMT's entire formula rotation bank or path-tracing CDF infrastructure.

Image-tile origin/size, full-output resolution and pixel origin are separate from the current target resolution. Retaining that distinction helps filters and procedural coordinates agree across preview and tiled export. Identity defaults only make a feature harmless when all dependent values are synchronized: the default full-output resolution of 100 by 100 is not dynamically linked to a later viewport size by this schema. Test actual frame binding and tile seams rather than treating a default comment as proof of equivalence.

**Construct independent defaults deliberately.** createUniforms clones cloneable objects and Float32Array, and maps ordinary arrays one level deep. It does not recursively clone arbitrary nested values; an array containing null also reaches an unguarded v.clone access. This is a limitation of the generic factory, not evidence that the currently declared defaults trigger it. UNIFORM_DEFAULTS itself retains the original default references. ConfigDefaults uses a different policy: cloneable objects are cloned, arrays use JSON round-tripping, and other objects are shallow copied. Nested references and special numeric/object types therefore need explicit contracts before extending these factories.

For RFF, use typed default constructors, immutable asset handles and owned per-render mutable values. A palette/environment editor, export job and live preview should not accidentally edit one another through a shared default object. ConfigDefaults omits composeFrom parameters, leaving derived values to later binding, and does not itself register features. That ordering should be explicit in any adopted construction pattern. Asset persistence, CPU authoring data and GPU resource lifetime are different responsibilities.

**Keep enum identity stable.** defineEnumParam generates numeric option positions and a resolver that floors an input index, returning the configured default for invalid/out-of-range values. It does not validate an empty tuple or an invalid default index. Its extra configuration can override the generated default/options while the resolver retains the original tuple/defaultIndex. RFF should give persistent modes explicit stable IDs, validate defaults and decoded values, and distinguish discrete animation from continuous interpolation. Display ordering must not silently change the meaning of a saved shader mode. This applies to 2D palette mappings and 3D-derived material/environment source choices alike.

**Keep control protocols honest about scope.** AccumulationController provides a reusable pause/cap/reset/count interface, but its generic cap wording is broader than the concrete RenderPipeline behavior just reviewed: that implementation bypasses its viewport cap in bucket and tiled modes. A constant convergenceValue of 1 is permitted for renderers with no estimate, so the scalar alone cannot communicate support or freshness. For RFF, expose which operation a cap affects and use explicit availability/generation metadata for diagnostics. A generic UI should not turn a preview budget into an export-quality limit or present an unsupported estimate as a measurement.

This batch adds interface and initialization evidence, not runtime validation. Useful acceptance cases are independent default instances, duplicate declarations, schema changes after pipeline creation, enum reorder/import, an absent diagnostic producer and matching full-frame/tiled output from the same parameter snapshot. No application source was modified.

## Feature composition: independent invalidation, preset and capability policies

The full 909-line `engine/FeatureSystem.ts` and ADR-0078 have now been read. This supersedes the previous targeted-only coverage of the common registry. The main RFF benefit is a declarative contract for new rendering controls: what data they affect, whether they require a pipeline rebuild, what a preset may overwrite, and what supporting features they require. This is equally applicable to 2D coloring and 3D-derived relief materials. The declarations and ADR establish intended contracts; this batch does not claim that every downstream setter, import path or worker consumer enforces them.

**Treat recalculation and preset ownership as independent decisions.** ParamConfig distinguishes noAccumReset, userScoped and preserveOnApply. The first concerns accumulated rendering data; the second protects device/user preferences on scene loads; the third protects selected content/session values during bulk application. A feature can additionally declare holdsLiveSession, a conditional whole-feature policy for a full scene load. ADR-0078 explains why overloading a single flag previously caused display-only adjustments to be skipped by Reset and look-copy operations. Its cited historical symptoms and tests were not reproduced here.

For RFF, express invalidation in terms of its actual stages: high-precision reference/orbit data, per-pixel fields, material shading and final display processing. A palette or tone adjustment may reuse valid upstream data while still being replaced by a look preset. Environment rotation may invalidate shading without invalidating the fractal field. A formula or camera change has a different dependency footprint. Determine each setting's actual consumers before assigning these policies; GMT's noAccumReset value is not a ready-made RFF invalidation rule. Device preferences should remain independent of artwork presets, while an explicit full-reset command should have a documented scope. Conditional preservation of live audio or modulation sessions must not make their saved configuration permanently unloadable.

**Separate runtime values from compiled structure.** onUpdate distinguishes uniform updates from shader rebuilds, while engineConfig and panelConfig describe compile gates and runtime toggles. This supports responsive edits to environment intensity/orientation and material values while reserving compilation for genuinely structural choices. The estimated compile-time metadata is an estimate, not a measured duration guarantee. For RFF, publish a coherent setting snapshot only with a compatible pipeline and avoid redundant upstream recomputation when a pipeline replacement already performs the necessary invalidation. A UI visibility condition or disabled option is not validation for imported or animated values.

The parameter metadata also supports slider scale, explicit rotation units/order, linked image color-space settings, composed vector fields, dynamic ranges and additional onSet updates. These can keep 2D palette modulation and relief-lighting controls consistent. Preserve parameter identity even when two values share one range widget. Validate composed fields and apply related updates together so a frame cannot observe only half of a dependent setting change. Actual enforcement belongs in setters/binders, not merely in the metadata type.

**Validate required capabilities and dependencies before composition.** FeatureDefinition separates dependsOn ordering from primary/secondary/pair capability requirements and rejection rules; individual compilable sections can override broader requirements. This can let RFF expose a material function only when the necessary field or normal is available, without disabling unrelated controls. The registry itself does not evaluate the capability rules. Its topological sort orders known dependencies, skips absent dependencies, and falls back to registration order on a cycle. Registration-time warnings therefore do not prove a shader can be composed safely. A RFF implementation should reject an invalid required dependency graph before pipeline creation and keep the last valid pipeline available, rather than treating fallback order as successful validation.

The base inject callback accepts any builder because different renderers expose different methods. That interoperability choice sacrifices static checking at the common boundary. In RFF, prefer typed composition interfaces and validated stages for reusable shader features. Post-processing metadata already distinguishes UV changes before texture sampling from color changes before tone mapping; preserve this ordering explicitly when sharing effects between a flat 2D image and relief rendering. Reusing an effect name does not imply equivalent results if color space or execution order differs.

**Treat compact names as persistent format identifiers.** getDictionary checks feature aliases globally and parameter wire keys within a feature, including collisions between an alias and an unaliased sibling name. It memoizes and recursively freezes the constructed dictionary. These are useful techniques for compact share formats, but production collision handling only warns and still returns a dictionary. RFF should require collision-free encoding before publishing a saved/shareable result, preserving old IDs and applying explicit migrations where necessary. Do not infer safety from a shortId convention alone. The code's cited share-link regression tests are references, not tests executed during this audit.

**Freeze definitions as well as registration policy.** Registry freeze blocks new feature IDs, but does not recursively freeze registered definitions. get returns a definition reference and getAll returns its cached array; external mutation could bypass cache invalidation. Development replacement of an existing ID is deliberately allowed even after freeze. RFF should use immutable validated descriptors or explicit versioned replacement, especially where pipeline keys, saved identifiers and GPU bindings depend on them. The dictionary's deep freeze does not make the entire feature graph immutable.

Uniform conversion maps color to vec3, boolean to float and images/gradients to sampler2D, then appends extra uniforms. Other parameter kinds pass through. For example, a future complex parameter directly declaring a uniform would need an explicit GPU representation instead of relying on the unrestricted conversion. Check type validity and value shape before emitting GLSL, as well as the Vulkan layout requirements noted above.

Finally, validateComponentRefs checks viewport and custom-UI references after UI registration, returns missing references and only warns in development. It is intentionally not part of registry freeze and does not validate every parameter relationship. For RFF, distinguish optional panels from required controls and run the appropriate checks after registration is complete. Recommended validation covers a shading-only edit reusing fields, a look preset replacing post-processing while retaining device preferences, missing/cyclic dependencies, alias collisions, invalid parameter mappings and consistent preview/export snapshots. No application code was changed and no runtime or performance test was run in this batch.

## Video adoption: deterministic clocks, bounded queues and explicit output semantics

Full reads of `engine/export/videoEncoder.ts`, `engine/codec/VideoExportTypes.ts`, `engine/codec/halton.ts`, `demo/demoRenderRunner.ts`, `data/constants.ts` and ADR-0045 establish the shared encoder and one concrete caller. MainThreadEncoder is used by the demo and fluid application; it is not GMT's WorkerExporter implementation. GMT also imports its capability probe through renderDialogExtras. WorkerExporter itself remains a separate pending full read, so these observations must not be generalized to its complete export lifecycle.

**Use one timeline clock and a separate output clock.** VideoExportConfig explicitly defines fps as the output rate, with timelineFps/frameStep preserving duration when exporting every Nth timeline frame. The encoder assigns timestamps from the contiguous encoded frame index, which avoids making playback depend on render speed. RFF can apply this principle to palette cycles, environment rotation and procedural shading: evaluate scene state at a requested timeline time, then encode that completed image at its output timestamp.

The demo caller computes timelineFrame=startFrame+i*frameStep but uses time=timelineFrame/cfg.fps for modulation. Under the documented output-fps convention, that time is scaled again when frameStep exceeds one. This is a source-level contract discrepancy, not a reproduced GMT worker-export defect. A RFF export plan should carry timeline rate, sampled frame indices and output rate explicitly, preferably using rational rates and a declared integer timestamp rounding policy. Test nonzero start frames, fractional rates and stepped exports with animated shader effects and audio. Define endpoint inclusion and final-frame duration rather than deriving them independently in several callers.

The demo waits one zero-delay timer after changing animation/modulation state before sampling the canvas. That is not an explicit acknowledgement that a particular GPU frame has finished. It also snapshots playback state without explicitly stopping playback here. RFF should export from an owned frame snapshot with an explicit render-completion dependency; a UI yield or fixed delay is not a substitute. Restore editor state on all outcomes without letting interactive playback mutate the export snapshot. The demo's disk-mode argument is intentionally ignored and it always encodes into memory, so it does not demonstrate scalable streamed export.

**Bound rendering, encoding and file-write queues independently.** MainThreadEncoder copies encoded chunks and serializes packet insertion through a promise chain. Serialization preserves callback order but imposes no queue-length or byte-budget limit, and encodeCanvas provides no waitable backpressure interface. Fast rendering or slow storage can therefore accumulate outstanding frames/chunks. RFF should stop submitting new frames when the relevant queue reaches a defined budget, then resume on completion. Report rendering and finalization as distinct stages. Streaming output alone does not bound all intermediate memory; the MP4 path also requests in-memory fast-start handling, whose actual memory behavior requires library-level verification.

**Make cancellation a session operation.** cancel closes the encoder and clears instance fields, but already queued closures capture output/source objects and can still execute. Starting again has no active-session guard, and callback error state belongs to the mutable instance. finish clears fields in finally, but an exception during flush occurs before its explicit encoder close. An encode exception also skips frame.close in the current straight-line sequence. For RFF, use a session identity, cancellation-aware queue draining/aborting, scoped frame ownership and unconditional cleanup of native resources. Decide explicitly whether a cancelled partial output is deleted, retained as incomplete or finalized. A successful encode callback is not durable file completion.

**Probe the configuration that will actually run.** The shared capability probe rounds odd dimensions down and tests the nominal bitrate, while start uses its supplied dimensions and multiplies bitrate by 2.5. The demo normalizes dimensions first, but other callers must establish their own contract. The constants file calls this a compensation for smooth-gradient content; it is not a generally established quality rule. RFF should validate dimensions, rate, format and bitrate once, present any dimension adjustment, and test the effective encoder configuration. Preserve stable format identity instead of relying on a reorderable array index. Invalid indices fall back in the encoder, whereas the demo later directly indexes format metadata; avoid inconsistent fallback semantics.

Encoded timestamps are shifted by the first callback timestamp. Comments attribute this to a browser-specific leading-latency workaround; this audit has not independently verified that behavior. A RFF implementation should preserve its encoder's documented presentation/decode ordering and validate any offset correction using actual output, rather than universally applying a browser workaround. The shared class contains no audio mux path, explicit HDR metadata configuration or alpha-preservation contract. Its canvas input and format labels do not establish those capabilities.

**Transfer auxiliary passes with meaningful 2D semantics.** VideoExportTypes distinguishes beauty, alpha and depth, including separate files for video passes and combined beauty/alpha for appropriate image sequences. This is useful inspiration for RFF compositing workflows. A 2D iteration field or relief height, however, is not a 3D camera-distance depth pass. Name and document any exported field, range, units and invalid/interior-pixel representation. Keep numerical auxiliary data out of appearance tone mapping and lossy color-video paths when accuracy matters. The leading depth comment names MAX_SKY_DISTANCE while the same interface exposes depthMin/depthMax; the actual worker shader path must resolve that discrepancy before adopting exact normalization behavior.

**Use deterministic sampling without assuming it solves antialiasing alone.** The short Halton helper computes a radical-inverse sequence by repeated remainder/division. It supplies no input validation, centering, dimension selection or temporal reset policy. Callers must provide finite nonnegative integer indices and an integer base greater than one; base one cannot terminate for a positive index. For RFF, define how sample index, pixel/tile coordinate and exported frame determine jitter, preserving consistency across tiles and resumes. A shared low-discrepancy sequence is only one component of filtering and must never reduce orbit precision. Attribution for any adopted named sequence remains subject to NOTICE requirements; no implementation was copied in this batch.

ADR-0045's separation of still-image tile scheduling from fixed-sample video scheduling is useful: reuse shading logic while giving each export mode appropriate resource ownership. Its statements about per-bucket convergence are historical and conflict with the later removal recorded in ADR-0067 and the current RenderPipeline comments already reviewed. Do not treat this older ADR as evidence that current buckets still stop by convergence. Runtime output quality, codec compatibility, memory bounds and cancellation behavior remain untested here.

## GMT worker export: shared frame state and trustworthy multipass delivery

`engine-gmt/engine/worker/WorkerExporter.ts` (986 lines) and `exportFrameNaming.ts` (43 lines) have now been read in full. This closes the exporter-class gap left in the preceding shared-encoder review; the main-thread frame driver and surrounding worker message protocol still require separate coverage. The strongest RFF transfers are a common frame snapshot for multiple outputs, deterministic sample scheduling, a preview drawn from the rendered result and timeline-based image naming. The concerns below are adoption conditions derived from source, not reproduced RFF defects.
