GMT smooths distance increases with `1-exp(-1.2*dt)` while responding immediately to decreases, then scales movement by distance. Rotation uses exponential smoothing too. This is a useful interaction pattern for gently changing sensitivity, but the controller clamps translation/rotation integration time to at most 0.1 seconds while roll's velocity smoothing uses the original delta. It does not validate negative/nonfinite delta locally. The squared joystick movement vector is subsequently normalized, removing analog magnitude for pure movement beyond its dead zone; do not describe that implementation as retaining a squared speed response. Mouse drag deltas are treated as rotation targets and multiplied by frame time later, so input-unit semantics must be checked at the producer before claiming frame-rate-independent mouse displacement.

RFF can apply time-based damping to an optional environment-rotation interaction, without smoothing saved fractal coordinates or modifying mathematical results. Keep deterministic export separate from interactive inertia. For 2D navigation, scale movement from the viewport's mathematical span rather than copying a 3D surface-distance heuristic.

Finally, GMT separates calculation and display scenes and maintains a fallback camera. `updateFallback()` sets FOV/aspect and calls `updateMatrixWorld()`, but does not call `updateProjectionMatrix()` in this file. Any CPU ray construction depending on its projection needs the corresponding update somewhere in the caller chain; this read does not prove whether all callers satisfy it. RFF's screen-to-field transforms should similarly come from the same versioned view state used by rendering, with explicit ownership of transform updates. This is especially important when adding interactive material controls to an already accurate deep-zoom renderer.

## Render-worker pacing: keep new material effects responsive

**Full reads:** [handleRenderTick.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine-gmt/engine/worker/handleRenderTick.ts) and [WorkerProtocol.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine-gmt/engine/worker/WorkerProtocol.ts). RFF's [SwapchainUtils.hpp](../src/vulkan_helper/util/SwapchainUtils.hpp) was read, together with selected `RenderScene.cpp` fence-wait sites. These RFF links identify existing infrastructure; this is not a claim of a new whole-renderer audit.

**Existing RFF baseline:** `SwapchainUtils::begin()` waits for the current frame slot's fence before acquiring an image, and the frame index cycles over the configured maximum frames in flight. `RenderScene::waitFramesInFlight()` explicitly waits for every slot before shared-buffer mutations such as preview seeding. Therefore, proposing a frame-in-flight bound as an entirely missing RFF feature would be inaccurate. The remaining useful question is whether the existing submission depth and state-capture timing give good input latency when more expensive environment/material shaders are enabled. Answer that with measurements; do not arbitrarily force one frame in flight or remove synchronization.

### GMT's concrete pacing mechanism

The live worker polls a fence from the previous frame with a zero timeout before applying the next camera state or computing. If the fence is not signaled, it returns false so the surrounding scheduler can retry. This file describes retries as coalescing to the newest camera, but proving that guarantee requires the scheduler/producer implementation, not merely this function's comment. Bucket/held-frame modes bypass this gate, and active export returns before it. Failed/throwing fence waits release the gate to avoid a permanent live-view freeze. The observed source is not evidence that the historical half-second lag described in comments occurs on the current user's machine.

When a frame is accepted, camera pose and optional virtual-space offset are applied together. Modulation offsets are replaced as a complete dictionary, including an empty dictionary when absent, preventing removed modulation targets from persisting. The smoothing delta is elapsed wall time between accepted frames, capped at 0.1 seconds, rather than always the main thread's offered-frame delta. Export has a separate explicit frame/time message. These are useful contracts for RFF's interactive effect controls: atomic view state, clear replacement-versus-patch semantics, and separate interactive and deterministic-export clocks.

The `RENDER_TICK` protocol carries a timestamp, but this handler does not consume it as an animation clock. Its first accepted frame uses the supplied delta without the later elapsed-time clamp. Module-level fence/time variables have no reset function in this file, so renderer lifetime and reinitialization must be handled deliberately in an adaptation. Do not assume the function alone provides complete context-loss recovery.

### Completion and timing have different meanings

The handler submits display work, calls `flush()`, then inserts a fence. The next poll requests a flush of pending commands. `FRAME_READY` is posted without waiting for that fence and does not mean the frame has been presented to the monitor. RFF diagnostics should similarly separate CPU state acceptance, command submission, GPU completion and presentation. The disabled debug instrumentation measures CPU duration inside `compute()` and wall time from submission until a later polling observation; neither is a direct isolated GPU shader-time query. Use GPU timestamp queries when comparing shader costs, and input-to-visible-update measurements for interaction quality.

Depth/focus readback happens after the display submission and after the posted shadow-state message. Consequently the new depth state appears in a later shadow update. This ordering reduces work before display submission, but it does **not** prove readback cannot affect timing: the synchronous full-frame focus snapshot previously identified can stall the worker, and work appended after the frame fence is outside that fence's completion boundary. Profile auxiliary readback and presentation alongside the main shader. A single frame fence cannot automatically bound all later GPU work.

Held-final-frame mode runs `engine.update()`, reblits its stored result and returns before ordinary compute, depth reads and timing recording. Any RFF reuse of a held material preview should explicitly specify which edits invalidate it and which inspection values remain stale. A retained image alone is not proof that all associated fields match the current view.

### Preview filtering and transport boundaries

While bucket rendering, the handler letterboxes the current tile to preserve its aspect ratio. It sets the display source resolution to the tile dimensions and chooses a box-sampling count from the source-to-preview ratio, capped at eight. This is a bounded preview approximation, not arbitrary-ratio exact area integration; an extreme reduction still needs a stronger minification strategy. RFF already has output resampling, so the transferable requirement is to maintain correct source dimensions and filtering when switching between preview/export resources, rather than adding another generic downsampling feature.

The typed protocol makes camera, offset, render state and modulation data explicit. It also separates HDR buffers from ordinary bitmaps and offers shader-source and uniform-snapshot inspection messages. That inspection pairing is a useful model for a reproducible RFF shader diagnostic: capture the shader variant and the effective parameter state for the same generation, including texture identity, color-space interpretation and dimensions. This protocol's separate requests do not by themselves guarantee that atomic capture.

TypeScript declarations provide no runtime validation. Correlation IDs exist for picking and diagnostic requests, while live frames carry no returned frame/view generation and export completion carries a frame index without a session ID. Validate dimensions, finite values, payload sizes and lifecycle ownership in any adopted transport; reject responses from an old session. Do not infer complete memory backpressure or reliable cancellation from message types alone. For RFF's native implementation, the same contracts can be expressed through typed in-process jobs without introducing a browser worker architecture.

**Adoption priority:** improve diagnostics and verify state freshness alongside any new environment-reflection prototype. Tune queue depth only if latency measurements justify it. These measures protect usability and reliable comparisons; they do not independently improve the rendered material's appearance or justify lowering fractal precision.

## Material lifecycle: consistent environment assets and shader replacement

**Completed full read:** [MaterialController.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine-gmt/engine/MaterialController.ts), upgrading the prior partial audit. This section distinguishes the controller's behavior from guarantees that must be supplied by its compile scheduler or texture-loader callers.

### Environment reflection adoption includes derived data, not only a sampler

GMT's environment image loader enables mip generation and trilinear minification, records the maximum mip level from the image dimensions, installs the image, and rebuilds environment sampling data. `rebuildEnvCDF()` obtains image pixels through a canvas or reads a data texture, then updates the marginal/conditional CDF textures, dimensions, luminance integral, mip bias and solid-angle average color. That average is passed to the environment shader for rough-reflection handling; it is not simply the last rectangular image mip. On extraction failure a 1×1 size and a negative average-color sentinel select fallback behavior. The old CDF textures are not replaced in the stub function itself, so consumers must honor the validity metadata.

**RFF implication:** the proposed gradient/image environment should have one owned resource bundle containing the source, its color interpretation, filtering data and any average-radiance value. Publish a replacement only when the required bundle is ready; retain the previous valid bundle on failure. Separate the needs of deterministic relief reflection from path-tracing importance sampling: RFF does not need a CDF merely to sample an environment in the reflected normal direction. Mip or prefiltered reflection data and a correctly weighted average may be useful independently. Preserve the distinction between an artistic roughness blur and physically integrated GGX lighting described earlier.

This loader does not carry a request generation or an error callback. An earlier image request can therefore install after a newer request if callers permit overlap; clearing a color image disables its use but does not invalidate an in-flight callback here. Clearing an environment through `loadTexture(..., null)` simply returns. These observations motivate generation-tagged loading and explicit clear semantics for RFF, not a claim that all GMT upload routes have these behaviors. The worker's HDR/bitmap routes are separate and must be examined on their own. Do not infer HDR decoding support or color-space correctness solely from this LDR loader.

### Compile only needed variants, publish only current results

The controller keeps Direct and PathTracing materials with shared main uniform objects. A configuration update regenerates the active variant and marks the inactive one dirty for lazy regeneration. It compares a hash of generated fragment source before setting `needsUpdate`; the source is still generated before this comparison. The histogram shader is regenerated and marked for update on every `updateConfig()` call, without the same checksum check. These facts support separating source generation, driver compilation and parameter updates when profiling a proposed RFF variant system.

For two-stage compilation, GMT builds a preview with advanced lighting disabled, then creates a full material for external async compilation and swaps it into its mode slot. The full material shares live uniforms; it is not an immutable parameter snapshot. `swapFullMaterial()` trusts attached mode/checksum metadata, changes the current mode, disposes the old material, and emits the generated source. This method has no generation check itself; freshness belongs to the scheduler. `compilePreview()` returns true after taking the preview path even if its generated source checksum was unchanged, so its return value is not strictly proof that new source was installed. The comment promising a sub-second preview compile is historical and unmeasured in this audit.

**RFF adaptation:** if optional material variants cause noticeable pipeline-creation stalls, cache variants and compile the requested replacement without discarding the last valid pipeline. Publish only a result matching the current shader-layout/configuration generation. Retire old Vulkan objects after all submissions using them complete; a JavaScript material-disposal sequence is not a Vulkan lifetime recipe. An optional simplified lighting preview must leave fractal arithmetic unchanged, remain clearly provisional, and never silently become the final export. Do not introduce two-stage compilation if measured compile latency does not justify the complexity.

A fragment-only hash is adequate only while all other program-defining inputs are fixed by this local contract. RFF's pipeline identity must account for the applicable shader stages, specialization values, descriptor/push-constant layouts, render formats and other relevant pipeline state. Keep an equality or collision strategy rather than treating a short noncryptographic hash as infallible. The distinctive `cyrb53` implementation/constants need original-source and license verification before any copying; the adoption proposal does not require that particular hash.

### Uniform sharing needs explicit type and ownership contracts

GMT shares most main uniform wrappers with display/export materials, while histogram uniforms start from a partial clone. The clone handles Vector2/Vector3/Color/Float32Array and cloneable array elements; other objects, including matrices and standalone Vector4 instances, fall through by reference. A null array element would reach an unchecked `v.clone` access. Therefore this helper is not a general deep snapshot and must not be described as one.

`setUniform()` updates existing entries in four maps and includes plain-object fallbacks for worker-serialized vectors and matrices. Missing keys are skipped, arrays update only existing slots and retain omitted elements, and newly added main keys do not automatically appear in previously constructed post-process maps. Use schema-driven, length-checked updates for any new RFF descriptor or uniform data; distinguish partial patching from complete replacement. A shared wrapper also means iteration over four maps does not necessarily mean four independent objects.

The equality probe uses an absolute 1e-9 threshold, but still assigns the new value. It can therefore report no significant change while altering the shader input. NaN and missing vector components can evade comparisons because comparisons with NaN are false; the update and equality branches also validate components differently. Do not transfer that tolerance to RFF's sensitive deep-zoom inputs. Validate finite typed values first and define invalidation by semantic field: mathematical coordinates require their existing exact/high-precision contract, while explicitly bounded appearance controls may use a documented policy.

Texture replacement disposes previous texture objects from the participating maps, and gradient conversion also disposes the old main texture before propagation. Independent wrappers can reference the same texture, so disposal ownership is not guaranteed unique by this loop. Setting a texture uniform to null goes through the generic assignment path and does not use the replacement-disposal branch. For RFF, centralize resource ownership, update references together and defer destruction until GPU use finishes; avoid having each consumer independently destroy a shared environment asset.

### Gradients and animation ownership

Gradient uploads bake a fixed 256×1 RGBA byte texture with linear filtering and repeat wrapping. This is an LDR sampled ramp, not an HDR illumination representation; a new RFF environment ramp should choose its storage and radiance range explicitly. Repeat wrapping also requires an intentional endpoint policy, especially for a lighting ramp that is not meant to be periodic. `syncConfigUniforms()` rebakes supplied gradient parameters and skips image parameters for their dedicated transfer route. Cache gradient derivation by the actual source/configuration revision where profiling shows repeated uploads; do not alter RFF's frozen palette recipe RNG or saved IDs.

The optional `skipUniforms` list gives live modulation temporary ownership of selected uniforms so a base-config write does not alternate with a modulated value during dragging. Omitted skip lists rebuild the base state and rely on a later modulation tick to restore offsets. For RFF preview and export, resolve base plus modulation from a single frame snapshot before drawing, rather than depending on a visible intermediate correction. The same rule applies to 2D palette controls, environment rotation and relief material properties.

**Priority:** resource consistency, correct color/filter metadata and stable parameter ownership are prerequisites for the environment-reflection proposal. Lazy variants are an optional responsiveness improvement after profiling. Neither requires importing path tracing into RFF, and neither establishes a measured visual or performance gain yet.

## Composable shader stages: state ownership and faithful editor conversions

**Full reads:** [emitWeave.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine-gmt/engine/weave/emitWeave.ts), [types.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine-gmt/engine/weave/types.ts), and [convert.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine-gmt/engine/weave/convert.ts).

### Transfer the composition architecture, not hybrid orbit equations

GMT's weave assembler receives resolved formula slots and a schedule function. It emits each slot's functions, the schedule, and a dispatcher selecting one slot by iteration phase. Shared scalar scratch variables are unioned in first-appearance order and passed as `inout` arguments; each slot receives its own subset. Native slots can instead carry namespaced global state, per-pixel initialization and pre/post-call code. Initialization is assembled once outside the iteration body, while the dispatcher executes inside it.

For RFF, the useful transfer is explicit ownership when composing appearance stages: distinguish read-only shared fields, per-layer parameters, per-pixel scratch and persistent frame resources. Hoist invariant transforms out of repeated per-pixel/per-sample operations when doing so preserves numerical behavior. A future material-stage interface could declare its required normal/field inputs and output channels rather than relying on accidental global names. This complements existing RFF shader layers; it is not evidence that RFF has no layer system.

Do not graft alternating 3D formulas into RFF's Mandelbrot perturbation loop under the label of a shader optimization. Such a feature changes the mathematical orbit and would require compatible reference generation, derivatives, perturbation equations and MPA analysis. Scheduling appearance layers over a completed 2D field is a much more direct transfer. The schedule's recurring pattern is not RFF's MPA periodic structure and must not be conflated with it.

The assembler trusts its resolver: phase IDs, GLSL identifiers, duplicate function definitions, scratch-variable meaning and schedule coverage are not checked locally. Duplicate phases make the first branch win; a phase with no branch performs no slot call. Unioning scratch by name assumes identical semantics for equal names. Slot initializers precede emitted scratch declarations, so they cannot freely reference those later locals. These are interface contracts to enforce in a proposed typed RFF stage builder, not evidence that valid GMT resolvers currently violate them. Syntax validity alone is insufficient to prove the intended effect order or state isolation.

### Editable schedules versus compiled schedules

The type contract separates compiled count schedules from live modulo schedules. Count schedules use a baked iteration lookup table and recompile after structural edits; modulo schedules use runtime parameters for periodic selection and can be animated. Only alternate mode is represented. Negative counts represent silent slots with special escape-count semantics, not ordinary disabled slots.

A comparable distinction can help RFF effect editing: structural changes may require a pipeline variant, while intensity, range and timing values should remain ordinary parameters when practical. Keep stable layer identity independent of row position. Do not promise arbitrary branching, every MB3D combine mode, or precision-preserving orbit conversion from this limited contract.

### Exact conversion requires an explicit proof scope

`convert.ts` translates between a counts-based sequence and a layered rhythm. Rhythm checks layers in order and uses the first matching arithmetic progression, falling back to a designated base row. Sequence-to-rhythm fitting simulates the intro plus two cycles, fits non-base occurrences to arithmetic progressions, and elects a valid base with the smallest remaining endless-layer density. It refuses silent slots and out-of-range patterns. Rhythm-to-sequence computes an eventual period, searches divisors for the minimal tail period, shrinks the intro, then run-length encodes it. Its limits are six rows and 192 baked steps; long rhythms may be valid but intentionally unrepresentable in that editor form.

The shared certificate compares phase functions over `max(intros) + lcm(periods)`, which proves equality of correctly described eventually periodic sequences when the whole window is checked. It caps that window at 4096 and reports a `capped` flag. Both conversion functions inspect `equal` but do not propagate `capped` in their successful result. The header's suggestion of reporting bounded exactness therefore is not implemented by these return types. Whether valid constrained inputs can reach an accepted capped case requires a separate bounds proof; do not assert a reproduced incorrect conversion merely from this observation. A new RFF converter should return full proof, bounded comparison, or refusal distinctly.

More importantly, the certificate compares selected **row IDs**, not complete shader state or rendered pixels. Rhythm-to-sequence expects the caller to duplicate a row when it appears in multiple runs. If duplicated native slots receive independent state while the original rhythm reused one stateful slot, matching row selection alone does not establish orbit equivalence. The resolver/materialization path must prove shared identity where required, or restrict conversion to compatible stateless stages. This matters in RFF too: duplicating an animated or stateful effect is not necessarily equivalent to invoking the same effect twice.

Validation belongs before simulation: these helpers assume finite integer intervals, starts, counts, periods and valid row mappings. `Math.max(1, interval)` does not reject NaN or turn a fraction into an integer; `simulate()` allocates its requested horizon, and rhythm-to-sequence builds an intro-plus-two-period array before applying the baked-length limit. Guard sizes before allocation, preserve input on refusal, and avoid unchecked LCM growth. CPU editor previews and emitted GLSL also need matching integer/rounding semantics; using one CPU phase function for preview and conversion does not independently prove GPU agreement.

**RFF-facing outcome:** borrow explicit stage/state contracts and honest conversion/refusal behavior for 2D material or animation tooling. Verify saved-output equivalence at the level actually promised—parameter values, scheduled stage identity, or final pixels—and preserve palette recipe and configuration format contracts. This is infrastructure for extensibility, not a higher-priority appearance improvement than the proposed environment reflection.

## Independent effect instances: native-slot rewriting and parameter banks

**Full reads:** [nativeSlot.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine-gmt/engine/weave/nativeSlot.ts), [nativeResolver.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine-gmt/engine/weave/nativeResolver.ts), and [nativeSlotCatalog.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine-gmt/engine/weave/nativeSlotCatalog.ts).

**RFF opportunity:** independently configurable instances of a material/pattern effect should have stable instance identities, isolated parameters and declared state. GMT demonstrates the machinery needed when two instances use identical source: prefix helpers and globals per slot, bind each instance's inputs explicitly, and avoid accidentally reading a neighboring instance's parameter slot. This is a transferable architecture for flat 2D coloring and relief materials, not a proposal to rewrite the Mandelbrot perturbation loop.

The native resolver supports three parameter strategies. Bank binding keeps each declared scalar/vector parameter in a slot-specific uniform bank and preserves its descriptor metadata; dense packing allocates shared lanes and can decompose vectors; baking substitutes literals. Undeclared core parameters are backfilled from the formula preset so they cannot accidentally read someone else's lane. Explicit remapping is simultaneous: A→B and B→C do not turn an original A into C. This property matters for generated material code too. In RFF, descriptor layouts and serialized parameter IDs should remain stable even when the visual row order changes.

Bank mode avoids the dense allocator's overflow path for the expected core parameter vocabulary; that is not a guarantee of unlimited GPU uniform capacity or support for arbitrary parameter IDs. The local resolver does not validate the bank index or parameter vocabulary. Dense allocation failure returns `ok: true` with `paramOk: false` and empty code, leaving fallback and allocator ownership to the caller. For a new RFF stage builder, prefer a result type that cannot accidentally publish such a partial success. If an editable parameter must be baked because of resource limits, report the loss of editability and preserve its exact current value rather than silently changing the effect.

The resolver's `num()` turns missing/nonfinite/nonnumeric values into zero, and literals are ordinary JavaScript numbers formatted as GLSL floating-point expressions. This is not a deep-zoom precision strategy. RFF should reject invalid sensitive inputs and retain its high-precision representation; a forgiving appearance-control default must not become a general mathematical fallback.

### State isolation is concrete, and affects conversion semantics

Mutable loop-initialized state listed in `preambleVars` is hoisted into namespace-prefixed globals and assigned during per-pixel initialization. Each slot receives its own temporary `c`, whose fourth component comes from that slot's ParamA binding; the shared orbit's `z.w` remains shared. Because the call uses a temporary copy of `c`, modifications to that temporary are not automatically propagated back to the outer `c`. A compatible formula must satisfy that contract.

Slots declaring shared rotation get per-slot axis/cos/sin snapshots. Initialization saves the shared rotation, runs slot initialization, captures the result, and restores the original. Each dispatcher branch then installs its slot's rotation and restores the prior shared values after the call. It does not capture mutations made to those shared rotation values by the iteration body back into the slot snapshot, so this mechanism assumes precomputed rotation state rather than arbitrary evolving rotation state.

This read strengthens the prior conversion warning: native state really is namespaced by slot index. Duplicating one stateful slot as two rows can therefore create two separate histories. A phase-sequence comparison proves selected row order, not equivalence of stateful formula evolution. Actual duplication/materialization callers still need inspection before declaring a user-visible conversion failure. For RFF effect graphs, distinguish a second reference to one instance from a clone with independent state.

### Text rewriting has a deliberately limited grammar

The rewriter uses word-boundary regular expressions and a brace-depth scan; it is not a GLSL parser. Top-level discovery recognizes a selected list of scalar/vector/matrix types, counts braces without stripping comments, and splits variable declarations using parenthesis depth. Its variable-declaration pattern can also encounter function text despite the explanatory comment claiming function declarations are excluded. Such scanning needs a controlled source grammar and generated-source validation; arbitrary imported shaders are a broader problem.

The loop-call rewrite assumes simple first three arguments and replaces the fourth `c` argument in the expected call shape. Nested comma-containing expressions or multiple calls require a stronger representation. It does not apply the generic uniform map to the entire loop-body string, so extra direct uniform references there need a caller/source contract. Hoisting recognizes selected types and the first matching line-start declaration; arrays, complex multi-declarations and qualifiers are not generally handled. A future RFF generator should use structured stage inputs or token-aware rewriting where feasible, and reject unsupported source forms instead of claiming general translation.

The catalog and resolver both reject self-contained-loop and modular-graph formulas. Their logic matches in the inspected sources, while the catalog's comment about regression tests is not evidence that those tests were run in this audit. The catalog lists registered formulas, groups known categories, and places imported/unclassified entries in a trailing group. Registration establishes availability, not mathematical correctness, licensing clearance or successful compilation for every combination. Keep those distinctions in any RFF extension catalog.

### Derivative detection is a heuristic, not a numerical guarantee

`writesDeriv` scans function, loop-body and initialization text for an assignment to the name `dr`. It can see a comment or initialization without proving a useful derivative, and can miss writes under a different helper parameter name or in a preamble helper not included in the scanned text. Even a genuine assignment is no proof that the derivative is correct for a hybrid orbit. RFF should use declared mathematical capabilities and targeted numerical validation rather than source-text assignment detection when choosing a precision-sensitive computation path.

The resolver also carries the lead formula's custom distance body and a limited generic-estimator settings subset. Carrying one formula's distance policy through composition does not independently establish a conservative or correct hybrid distance estimate. These details reinforce the boundary: reuse the parameter/state architecture for 2D visual effects, while treating any new fractal mathematics as a separate feature with its own derivation and validation.

## Bank-design reconciliation and animation that follows an effect

**Full reads:** [ADR-0089](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/docs/adr/0089-weave-core-unification.md), [ADR-0090](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/docs/adr/0090-weave-slot-banks.md), and [retargetTracks.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine-gmt/animation/retargetTracks.ts). Selected loader/editor references establish the connection to rebuild results, without granting those larger files full-read status.

### Read the later amendments before adopting an architectural conclusion

ADR-0089 contains historical stages subsequently superseded in its own updates: native state shipped as namespaced globals rather than a new struct framework; native parameters moved from shared dense packing to banks; lead-slot custom distance handling was added; interlace and interleaved Hybrid Box were absorbed into the weave path. Later fold changes explicitly narrow an earlier pixel-identical migration claim. These are not all simultaneous current guarantees.

ADR-0090 further extends banks to woven MB3D slots in its July 11 update. Its older body saying that only native slots bank, and that every MB3D scene stays byte-identical, no longer describes that widened design. The update distinguishes standalone MB3D core parameters from multi-slot bank routing and reports pixel-equivalence re-certification rather than unchanged generated text. References in the current loader to `mergeWeaveBanks` and the narrowed `mergeDenseLanes` role are consistent with this amendment; a full emitter/loader review remains necessary to independently verify all behavior. Do not recommend importing the superseded shared-pool limitation into RFF.

The ADR's approximately 2% compile-cost / no-FPS-cost measurement concerns unread uniforms on one documented RTX 2070/ANGLE configuration. It does not establish that arbitrary active Vulkan uniform banks are free. RFF needs actual descriptor/buffer limits, active shader resource use and measured pipeline costs. The document's historical GPU certification claims were not rerun during this reading pass.

### Concrete RFF improvement: preserve animation identity through layer edits

For proposed multi-instance material, reflection or pattern layers, reordering should preserve both current values and every durable animation target. GMT's current retargeting code updates three stores: keyframe tracks, LFO targets and audio/modulation rules. The July 12 ADR update mentions tracks and LFOs; the implementation additionally documents and handles audio rules. Preserving only the obvious timeline can leave an audio link driving a different effect after a reorder.

The code expands each base-parameter rename to vector-axis forms and applies the map simultaneously. An A↔B swap therefore does not cascade into a double rename. It updates track IDs, selected track IDs and selected-keyframe routing prefixes while retaining keyframe values. That is a useful transfer for RFF's 2D palette/material animation as well as relief controls. Prefer persistent instance IDs where the storage design allows them; otherwise generate one authoritative old-to-new mapping and apply it consistently to values, tracks, modulation and selection.

Collision policy is explicit but differs by consumer. A destination track/LFO whose old owner is not itself moving is removed; an audio rule in that position is disabled and retained for manual retargeting. The latter preserves its frequency/envelope/gain settings, and multiple audio rules can legitimately share a destination. The returned `displaced` count combines these actions, so a user-facing migration report should say which items were removed versus disabled.

This function assumes a valid mapping rather than proving a permutation. Duplicate sources overwrite earlier entries, and multiple sources targeting one track ID overwrite according to iteration order. Validate mapping injectivity for track identities before mutating stores. Even with no incoming track present, an existing destination occupant can be displaced because the mapping describes semantic ownership, not just current animations; document that intended policy rather than treating it as an automatic merge.

Undo also has a bounded scope: a timeline snapshot precedes keyframe changes, while LFO and audio-rule edits have no corresponding history here. Thus this is not one atomic, fully undoable transaction across all three stores. For an RFF layer-reorder feature, coordinate value/routing/history changes so undo restores the same semantic configuration, or clearly expose the narrower supported behavior. Sequential store updates also need a frame-boundary publication policy to avoid drawing a transient mixture of old and new routes.

### Orphans and save compatibility

The orphan finder checks only bank-shaped targets against the current definition's exposed parameters, including valid vector axes. It intentionally excludes rhythm and coreMath targets. With an undefined definition its exposed set is empty, so all matching bank targets become candidates; defer destructive cleanup until the owning definition is successfully loaded. The removal function reports requested ID counts, not independently verified removal counts. A stale candidate list should be revalidated before cleanup.

ADR-0090 describes value matching by slot `kind:ref`, with duplicate formulas claimed left-to-right. That is useful compatibility behavior but is not unique persistent instance identity: two identical effects with different settings need special care when reordered. Its rebuild changes are distinct from loading an old saved definition unchanged. RFF must likewise separate structural migration from ordinary loading, preserve stable palette recipe IDs and ConfigIO ordering, and keep a reviewable report when a conversion cannot preserve an animated target.

**Adoption result:** add semantic identity and complete animation-route preservation to any future RFF effect-layer expansion. This is an editing-reliability improvement supporting the shader proposals, not evidence of a currently reproduced RFF reorder defect. Historical GMT migration choices and one-way conversions are not instructions to change RFF's saved formats.

## Shared infrastructure boundaries and independent effect defaults

**Full reads:** GMT `engine/ConfigDefaults.ts`, `NodeRegistry.ts`, the re-export modules `FractalEvents.ts`, `TickRegistry.ts`, `HardwareDetection.ts`, `RenderPipeline.ts`, `UniformNames.ts`, `utils/FullscreenQuad.ts`, and [engine-fork-rules.md](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/docs/policy/engine-fork-rules.md). Here `engine/` refers to `engine-gmt/engine/`; the re-export targets remain distinct audit entries and are not granted new full-read credit through these shims.

The current hardware-detection and fullscreen-pass modules are already re-export shims. Thus K3/K4 in the May architecture document, which propose converting duplicated implementations to shims, are historical work items rather than current missing features. Event and tick modules likewise re-export their core owner, preserving one module identity within a runtime. That does not imply one shared object across separate browser-worker runtimes. The document usefully distinguishes shared implementations from deliberately domain-specific shader builders and feature-registration-dependent schemas; its older line counts and open-issue list are not current-state proof.

**RFF application:** share low-level color/filter/effect operations across preview and export while keeping their coordinate, sampling and resource-ownership contracts explicit. Avoid copying a stateful registry or resource cache into a second subsystem merely to reuse its interface. Conversely, do not merge 2D fractal mathematics with 3D raymarching just because their shader builders share a name. The document is architectural evidence, not a request to refactor RFF into GMT's browser engine layout.

`createDefaultShaderConfig()` seeds GMT-specific root settings and enumerates whichever features are registered at call time. It omits `composeFrom` fields, leaving their values to composition elsewhere. It clones objects exposing `clone()`, serializes/deserializes arrays through JSON, and shallow-copies other objects. The result is not universally deep-independent: nested objects in an ordinary object remain shared, and JSON array cloning does not preserve every possible value/type. Calling the helper before feature registration also produces a different seed. These are source contracts, not a demonstrated current default-editing defect.

For new RFF environment or material settings, use an explicit default factory that owns nested gradient stops, transforms and masks independently. Ensure two fresh effect instances cannot modify each other's defaults. Derive composed values from the canonical components rather than storing conflicting copies. Preserve the existing palette recipe generator and binary configuration layout; introducing a default factory does not authorize changing saved recipes or silently replacing user presets.

`NodeRegistry` maps node IDs to definitions with input metadata and a GLSL-emission callback. Registration overwrites an existing ID without diagnostics. `get()` and `getAll()` expose the definition objects themselves (the latter copies only the array), and grouping follows registration order. Input minima/maxima/steps are metadata; this registry does not enforce ranges or validate generated GLSL. The source comment's fixed node count is not independently checked by this file.

**RFF application:** if optional material-stage registration is introduced, define duplicate-ID policy, validate the schema at registration, and expose immutable definitions to editors. Keep UI ranges distinct from runtime validation and shader capability checks. Reject incompatible stage connections before compiling, while still checking the emitted program and descriptor layout. Stable IDs must be independent of presentation order and remain compatible with serialized effects. A registry is a way to organize extensibility, not by itself a reason to replace RFF's existing layer implementation.

**Verification scope:** this batch establishes module ownership, seed-copy semantics and registry behavior by static reads. It does not establish all registration call order, all current node definitions or cross-path image equivalence. Those require their respective callers and implementations, and remain separate from the completed shim reads.

## One appearance-update plan for preview and export

**Full reads:** [applyTarget.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/features/modulation/applyTarget.ts) and [ADR-0109](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/docs/adr/0109-one-modulation-dispatcher.md).

GMT resolves a modulation target into a plan containing uniform writes, engine-side offsets, a live display value and optional recording values. The plan has no direct store/event/worker writes; the caller delivers it through the appropriate path. It does mutate the explicitly supplied composite accumulator and can invoke an injected recording-base callback, so its useful property is separation of calculation from delivery, not absolute absence of all mutation. The ADR explains that this replaced diverging live/export implementations; its historical target counts and test claims are not fresh test results from this audit.

**RFF transfer:** for animated environment orientation, roughness, palette fields or light controls, calculate effective values once from an immutable frame's base state and modulation, then use that same result for preview and export. Preserve any existing shared RFF evaluation paths rather than adding a second evaluator. Backend-specific submission can differ while parameter semantics stay identical. Distinguish final absolute values from offsets: GMT transmits camera/geometry/light offsets for later composition, whereas ordinary scalar targets often become direct uniform values. Applying both forms to the same parameter would double-apply modulation.

### Compose every vector axis before emitting the vector

A per-frame accumulator groups independent axis targets by their base uniform, starting from a copy of the original vector. Each axis replaces only its own component, and one final flush emits the vector after all targets have been processed. Julia components use nullish fallback, preserving a deliberately modulated zero. This avoids the common error where each axis writes a fresh base vector and the later axis erases the earlier change.

The pattern applies directly to 2D offsets and 3D relief/environment directions. Keep the accumulator local to one frame, flush after all target contributions, and use a defined collision policy when different controls address the same component. GMT keys this accumulation by uniform name, which assumes that aliases sharing a uniform also agree on the underlying base vector. Shader binding metadata supplies the uniform name; reconstructing it from display labels or parameter-name guesses is unnecessary and fragile.

### Recording parity needs its own contract

The shared dispatcher preserves some older recording behavior explicitly acknowledged in ADR-0109. Its generic recording step emits a capture when the offset magnitude exceeds 1e-6, then Julia/light/vector branches can add another capture. Julia uses the current store base; the vector branch records and publishes a clean-base result while assigning `finalVal`, computed from the current store vector, to the shader accumulator. These expressions coincide only when the relevant bases coincide. The eventual recording caller may deduplicate entries or maintain equal bases; this file alone does not prove either condition. Do not describe a shared dispatcher as proof that every recorded playback equals the original live render.

For RFF, compute the resolved value used for drawing and recording from the same declared base snapshot. If recording intentionally captures a different domain, label and test that transformation. Avoid feedback in which a previously recorded modulated value becomes the next frame's base. Apply recording tolerances only to appearance-control capture policy; they are not permission to discard small changes to precision-sensitive fractal coordinates.

Color repeat modulation preserves a scale-to-repeat ratio through `modulated * (scale / base)`, but guards the store's repeat value rather than the potentially replaced recording base. A clean recording base of zero therefore needs a defined policy; the visible guard alone does not establish finite output. Color phase has another deliberate distinction: the displayed live value is composed from phase while the shader offset is composed from a separate offset field. In RFF, document such derived relationships and validate finite results before upload rather than assuming every target is simple base-plus-offset.

### Removal and invalidation remain caller responsibilities

The `isRemoved` option suppresses live-value publication only in selected branches; restoring a removed target relies on callers replaying it with zero offset and maintaining the proper base state. Vector/Julia flushes and several special branches do not carry the scalar branch's `noAccumReset` metadata. Correct accumulation invalidation therefore depends on more than sharing arithmetic. Define one field-level policy for whether an edit changes the sampled scene or only its presentation, and preserve it for compound values too.

This design is a strong supporting pattern for both flat 2D color animation and relief-material animation. Validation should compare effective frame parameters and rendered output across live playback, recording replay and export, including simultaneous axes, exact zero, target removal, aliasing and base edits during modulation. No such new runtime comparison has been executed in this documentation batch, and no current RFF mismatch is asserted.

## Routable effect controls: distinguish discovery from successful application

**Full reads:** [targetRouting.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/features/modulation/targetRouting.ts) and [setFeature.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/features/setFeature.ts).

GMT centralizes both target enumeration and routing classification. The classifier distinguishes direct uniform writes, engine-side offsets, state merged before transport, display-only values and unconsumed targets. Ordinary scalar/vector parameters are resolved through the feature schema, while camera, light-array, Julia and geometry-rotation controls have special branches. This is a useful architectural reference for adding RFF environment/material animation: every offered target needs a documented consumer, including effects whose parameters are computed on the CPU before shader upload.

Enumeration deliberately ignores current formula/scene visibility and synthesizes targets for every possible light slot and camera axis. It is a capability superset, not a list of values successfully applied in the current scene. Lighting classification checks a legal index/property but does not require that light to exist; the previously read dispatcher does require an actual element and can return an empty plan. A coverage check that only accepts a non-`none` sink therefore cannot establish current-scene application. Test routing with valid and absent owners, not only string membership.

The `optics` feature is manually listed as merged into render state. That declaration is a claim about a separate producer, not proof that every field is merged and consumed correctly. RFF should tie such routing to explicit field descriptors or verify the actual producer/consumer pair. A control that moves in the interface but has no shader or CPU consumer should be diagnosed rather than silently offered as an image effect.

### Keep names from substituting for a type contract

Generic vector-axis recognition uses an `_x/_y/_z/_w` naming pattern. A real scalar ending in that pattern is swallowed by the vector branch if no corresponding vector exists; the source says shipped parameters avoid the case, but that claim was not newly verified across all definitions here. Dotted feature resolution initially takes only the first two split components. Camera classification uses broad prefixes whereas dispatch later requires a usable axis suffix. Legacy bare `param...` names can be classified as resolved without confirming a corresponding registered parameter. These are controlled-vocabulary assumptions, not a general parser for arbitrary target strings.

For a proposed RFF effect system, use typed target identities with an explicit component index and consumer kind internally, converting to a stable serialized form only at the boundary. Validate imported/legacy names against the schema. Preserve aliases intentionally rather than letting prefixes imply a valid binding. Validate vector dimensionality and finite values before upload; classification alone does not establish them.

The picker excludes compile-time parameters and `composeFrom` controls, exposing component parameters instead to avoid double application. It also excludes whole tooling/quality/reflections features. Thus the presence of reflection code is not proof that all reflection settings are offered for modulation. For RFF, select animatable environment controls deliberately—orientation and intensity are plausible; structural resource changes need a separate lifecycle. Do not assume a numerical slider is safe to animate simply because it has a range.

### Static typing and runtime readiness solve different problems

`defineFeature()` preserves parameter literal types, allowing `setFeature()` patches and `getFeature()` results to infer scalar/vector shapes. Gradient, image and complex values remain `any`. At runtime the setter is looked up through a generated `set` plus capitalized feature-ID string. If it is missing, production execution performs no update and returns no error; `getFeature()` casts the store value without proving it exists. Therefore these wrappers improve authoring checks but do not validate loaded data, registration order or resource readiness.

The transferable RFF requirement is to bind feature definitions, configuration storage and shader layouts explicitly and validate initialization before exposing controls. Return a meaningful failure when an optional effect is unavailable. Keep default creation independent per instance and distinguish schema validation from descriptor/push-constant compatibility checks. This benefits flat 2D palette/pattern controls and relief/environment materials alike, without requiring a wholesale registry rewrite.

**Recommended verification for an eventual implementation:** enumerate intended animatable controls, resolve them against a real frame snapshot, inspect the resulting update plan and verify the receiving shader/CPU stage uses it. Include missing light/layer instances, malformed axes, aliases, removed targets and preview/export parity. This batch provides static evidence of GMT's mechanism and its assumptions, not an executed end-to-end coverage result or a diagnosed RFF failure.

## Effect runtime ownership and failure reporting

**Full reads:** [appHandles.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/appHandles.ts), [renderPopupRegistry.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/animation/renderPopupRegistry.ts), [createSingleSlot.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/store/createSingleSlot.ts), and [AppErrorBoundary.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/components/AppErrorBoundary.tsx).

GMT's handle factory provides per-purpose mutable state usable by both frame-loop code and components. A revision counter drives subscribed component updates, while purely imperative consumers can read the mutable reference without notifications. For RFF, the transferable distinction is between rapidly changing interaction state and a published render configuration. Do not treat a mutable handle as an immutable export snapshot: readers share the same nested objects, and `notify()` changes the revision without copying those objects.

`reset()` restores the originally supplied object reference, not a pristine clone. If nested state was edited in place, the initial reference already contains those edits. A proposed RFF material/brush runtime should separate resettable parameter defaults from GPU/resource handles, constructing fresh logical state and explicitly releasing or reusing owned resources. Copying arbitrary runtime resources is not a substitute for a lifecycle. Notification callbacks are synchronous without per-listener error isolation; a throwing subscriber can prevent later callbacks in that invocation. Development handle names also overwrite earlier entries in the inspection registry without merging their separate runtime containers.

The render-popup registry is a small host-provided component slot. It does not own export progress, locking or cancellation; those guarantees must be sought in the exporter and callers. Its shared slot factory uses identity equality to suppress redundant notifications. Reusing and mutating the same object does not notify, despite a comment suggesting object values always do. Last-writer-wins registration also has no owner token: a previous owner's unconditional clear could remove a later registration if callers permit overlapping lifetimes. RFF can use explicit capability/provider registration for optional output tools, but should attach ownership and teardown semantics rather than assuming a registry provides them.

The error boundary deliberately depends only on React so a broken feature panel/store does not also prevent its fallback from rendering. It records a diagnostic marker and displays the error message plus stack, preserving the message on browsers whose stack omits it. It accepts a pre-mount error through a constructor property, but has no later property-change handling; this is an initial-state handoff. Its reload action is not recovery of unsaved scene data. The file's historical smoke-test claim is not a test executed in this audit.

**RFF improvement criterion:** an optional shader/effect failure should leave a useful diagnostic and, where feasible, the last valid rendering/configuration available. Keep the reporting path independent of the failed effect's resources. A recovered fallback must still count as a failed validation run rather than a successful render. Capture the effective shader variant and settings together with the error, and preserve user work before offering a reset. Existing RFF error handling must be inventoried before proposing a new mechanism; this batch establishes the GMT pattern, not an absence in RFF.

A React render boundary does not catch all asynchronous worker/GPU failures, event-handler errors or initialization failures, and does not repair a lost graphics device. For RFF, handle these at their actual job/device boundaries. The useful transfer applies equally to flat 2D and relief effects: reliable feature ownership, explicit snapshots and truthful failure reporting support new shaders without changing fractal precision.

## Saveable environment/material assets and trustworthy recovery

**Full reads:** [SceneFileDropZone.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/components/SceneFileDropZone.tsx), [UnsavedWorkGuard.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/components/UnsavedWorkGuard.tsx), [SceneFileClaims.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/plugins/SceneFileClaims.ts), and [safeLocalStorage.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/store/safeLocalStorage.ts).

**RFF-facing requirement:** new image environments, gradients and material masks need a declared save/recovery contract. Distinguish embedded assets from external paths, retain color/filter interpretation, and report missing assets without discarding the remaining scene. This batch inspects orchestration rather than the scene serializer, so it does not establish which GMT assets are embedded. It also does not establish a missing RFF recovery feature; inventory existing RFF save paths before implementation.

GMT separates a previous-session recovery key from the live autosave key. On component mount it copies the previous autosave and its timestamp into recovery storage before arming periodic saves. This is a useful model for protecting a recoverable state from the next editing session. The guard is per component instance, however, and the code copies any nonempty autosave without parsing it or proving it is newer, unsaved or from another session. A true remount can repeat promotion. An old recovery timestamp can remain when the new source has no timestamp.

The low-level storage wrapper returns false on failed writes, including quota/access failure. The guard ignores those return values for both recovery promotion and autosave, and updates timestamps separately. Consequently its recovery notification does not prove the recovery copy landed, and a timestamp can be updated while the corresponding scene write failed. Catching exceptions around a helper that already swallows them does not restore that evidence. For RFF, publish a recoverable snapshot only after successfully writing and validating its payload; pair metadata with the same snapshot/version and preserve the prior valid recovery on failure. Large environment images make capacity and asset ownership especially relevant.

Autosave runs only while enabled and while the store reports dirty, with a nominal minimum interval of five seconds. The component delegates dirtiness entirely to the store; its comment excluding camera-only moves is not independently established by this file. Before adopting a similar policy for 2D RFF, decide whether view center/zoom and environment orientation are user work to preserve—3D navigation exclusions should not automatically apply to a 2D composition. Browser unload prompting is separate from autosave and does not prove successful recovery or protect an in-app scene replacement.

### File routing should have one owner and a clear commit point

The drop handler snapshots the operating-system file list before awaiting work, avoids handling drops already claimed by an inner target, then offers files to registered content-based handlers before the ordinary scene loader. Each handler sees remaining files in registration order. Returned objects are intersected with the offered objects in original order, preventing handlers from substituting new files. On handler failure the same files remain available to later handlers. A handler that already performed a side effect before throwing can therefore cause a second operation; content detection and parsing should precede the state-changing commit.

For RFF, a shared file entry point could distinguish scene, palette and environment assets by explicit formats/content markers, with a transactional apply step. Do not infer that any PNG is a restorable scene or that every image should replace the current environment. GMT's generic scene path considers only the first remaining file, filters by extension, and reports success immediately after calling `loadScene()` without awaiting compilation/render completion. That message means the load call returned, not that the eventual shader or output succeeded. Multiple remaining files and concurrent drops need a specified policy; this component has no operation-generation check to prevent a slower older load from applying after a newer one.

The claimed-file extension mechanism is independent of export ownership and unsaved-work replacement policy. Neither the drop handler nor the claim chain itself proves those policies are enforced; callers/store paths may provide them. In a prospective RFF integration, stage parsed settings, validate referenced assets and shader requirements, then replace the active scene while retaining undo/recovery as appropriate. Keep the existing binary formats stable and implement any new compatibility independently under the project's provenance rules.

These reliability requirements apply to both flat 2D palettes/images and relief materials. They support the environment-reflection proposal by making an appearance reproducible after reopening; they do not add visual quality by themselves. No new runtime load/recovery test was performed in this documentation batch.

## Save-frame consistency: current settings are not necessarily the displayed frame

**Full read:** [SceneIO.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/plugins/SceneIO.tsx).

GMT centralizes text save, embedded-scene PNG save, autosave serialization and file parsing behind app-supplied serializers/parsers. It offers a synchronous `onBeforeSerialize` callback to flush state that otherwise reaches the store only after a debounce, such as the live camera. `getPreset()` requests scene and document data consistently in these save paths. This is a useful RFF pattern: capture the actual authored view, material and environment state through one snapshot entry point rather than having each output path select a different subset.

However, flushing logical state does not wait for a matching rendered frame. PNG save obtains a canvas, flushes settings, captures a preset and awaits the snapshot encoder. This file neither pins a frame generation nor waits for the GPU to display those flushed settings. Whether `snapshotSceneToPng` provides additional coordination must be checked in that implementation. For RFF's prospective image-embedded settings or a sidecar scene file, define whether the payload describes the pixels shown or the newest requested scene; for a reproducible snapshot, capture matching image/settings generations. Preserve high-precision 2D center and zoom without converting them to an ordinary floating-point camera representation.

PNG completion calls `markSceneSaved()` after asynchronous encoding without passing the captured revision. The user may have edited the scene in the interim; correct dirty-state behavior therefore requires a revision-aware contract elsewhere, which this call does not establish. Associate completion with the saved snapshot's revision and do not clear newer edits. The same principle applies to new environment assets whose loading/filter preprocessing is asynchronous.

Text and PNG saves invoke a download helper, mark the scene saved and remove the live autosave. This file receives no confirmed durable-file-write result from that invocation. A browser download request is not proof that a user retained a file; RFF's native file writer can use a stronger contract, acknowledging a successfully completed write before changing its saved marker. Retain recovery data where write completion is unknown or fails. JPEG deliberately carries no scene metadata and does not mark the scene saved here, correctly separating an image output from a restorable scene.

Recovery parses the protected text, calls `loadScene()` and removes the recovery keys immediately after that call returns. It does not await a successful compiled render. Keep recovery until the required restore stage is acknowledged, with errors distinguishing parsing, asset resolution, compilation and display. This is a source-level sequencing observation, not a reproduced GMT recovery loss. Previously examined drop loading has a catch path, while this file's menu handler starts an async load without a surrounding catch; a shared loading service should give every entrance consistent error and cancellation semantics.

The loader captures the chosen parser before awaiting file decoding. Its comment calls it a pure decoder, but the documented GMT parser may register embedded formula definitions; returning a preset does not imply the whole operation is free of side effects. For RFF, stage validation/registration explicitly before applying a loaded scene. Format compatibility and embedded code provenance remain separate obligations; a file extension alone grants neither compatibility nor permission to copy code.

Install options are captured before the already-installed guard, so reinstall can update some callbacks while menu labels and canvas-dependent actions remain from the first registration. Missing options do not clear previous callbacks. The uninstall path removes the whole File menu, including any app items installed in that menu by other providers. These are lifecycle assumptions for one app owner; they should not be copied into independently loadable RFF extensions without ownership-aware teardown.

**RFF-facing priority:** pair serialized settings with a concrete revision and, where appropriate, a completed image; preserve newer edits and the last recoverable snapshot. This supports reproducibility of both flat 2D coloring and relief/environment effects. This read does not prove the serialized payload embeds every image or fully restores every custom formula, and the source's blanket round-trip statement is not treated as independent validation.

## Additional 2D shader family: logarithmic fields and temporal accumulation

**Full reads:** [gradientSample.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/fractal/shaders/gradientSample.ts), [fractalDisplay.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/fractal/shaders/fractalDisplay.ts), and [tsaaBlend.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/fractal/shaders/tsaaBlend.ts). These belong to the shared 2D fractal/Gradient Explorer family, not the previously inventoried `engine-gmt/shaders` raymarcher. Completion of that earlier shader subset must not be presented as completion of every shader in the repository.

### Pixel-relative distance coloring without forming tiny distances

The newer distance-estimate mapping computes a logarithmic pixel distance:

`ln(DE_pixels) = ln(0.5) + ln(|z|) + ln(ln(|z|)) - ln(|dz|) - ln(pixel_spacing)`.

It then chooses either a saturating exterior response, `1-exp(-DE_pixels)`, or logarithmic contour bands, approximately `log10(DE_pixels)`, followed by sign-symmetric gamma. Calculating the log ratio avoids separately forming a tiny world distance and tiny pixel spacing in single precision. This is a concrete reference for a possible RFF boundary-distance coloring or mask mode: the control could express visual widths in pixels, useful for stable-looking boundary accents in flat 2D as well as relief masks. It is an appearance mapping, not a replacement for perturbation arithmetic or proof that a distance estimate remains accurate.

The inspected shader actually subtracts stored `ln(1+|dz|)` as an approximation to `ln|dz|`. If all other terms were exact, this substitutes `|dz|+1` in the denominator, giving the ratio `|dz|/(|dz|+1)` relative to the stated formula. That is close only for sufficiently large derivatives. The kernel and texture format determine whether those stored values are usable at deep zoom; this snippet alone cannot prove that. RFF should derive the required log magnitude from its validated derivative representation and preserve precision, rather than copy this approximation blindly. Shader clamps bound the final visual mapping but do not repair invalid upstream derivatives.

Pixel-relative coloring deliberately depends on pixel spacing: the same mathematical point may change color when zoom or output resolution changes. It is therefore a different option from world-anchored coloring. Define preview/export behavior explicitly—fixed output-pixel widths, viewport-equivalent widths, or world-unit contours—and keep global pixel spacing across tiles. Check existing RFF distance/field modes before adding a duplicate feature.

### Absolute iteration fields versus view-dependent fitting

The v2 iteration branch uses `log(1+max(iteration,0))`, optional offset/scale from a fit-to-view operation, and sign-symmetric gamma. It does not divide this branch by the iteration cap, despite the older normalization summary above it. Holding offset/scale fixed preserves a point's mapping when its computed smooth iteration remains the same; changing fit parameters or escape computation can still change it. RFF already contains logarithmic iteration mapping, so the new consideration is explicit anchoring semantics and reversible fit controls, not claiming logarithmic coloring is absent.

Angle mode adds a log-iteration term to the final orbit angle. This yields twisted angular bands without recomputing the orbit when final angle and count are available. Magnitude and potential become aliases in v2 and use escape-radius-normalized overshoot with a logarithmic rate control; that overshoot alone is not a proof of globally continuous coloring across changes in escape iteration. Hard bands still normalize by the iteration cap, and trap iteration is documented as already normalized upstream. Consequently the entire family should not be summarized as uniformly depth-independent.

Orbit-trap branches logarithmically remap the minimum dynamical-plane distance, clamped to [1e-8,1], with shape-specific scales. This can retain contrast over a wider range than a linear remap, but saturates below the floor and above one. More iterations can discover a smaller trap distance even at the same coordinate. RFF adoption would require generating those orbit fields correctly through any iteration-skipping path; a post-process cannot recover an unrecorded minimum. Preserve MPA's distinct algorithm and evaluate orbit-statistic support separately.

All mappings finally wrap the gradient coordinate with `fract`. High repeats, angular seams and hard bands can alias. The ordinary texture lookup here does not itself prove footprint-aware filtering of the nonlinear source field. The earlier RFF filtering proposal still applies; do not treat this 2D shader as an already complete antialiasing solution.

### Color-domain and history contracts

The included OKLab matrices are attributed in comments to Björn Ottosson, but the helper does not decode sRGB before applying the linear-RGB transform and clamps negative LMS values before cube roots. Its own comments acknowledge an artistic display-space approximation. Do not transplant it as a standards-correct sRGB/OKLab conversion or assume it preserves out-of-gamut values. Use RFF's declared color domain and verify original licensing/provenance before adapting distinctive constants.

The standalone display shader blits already display-space RGB, applies the shared dither tail, and writes alpha one. It adds neither tone mapping nor gamma conversion. That path therefore cannot be reused unchanged for RFF's linear/HDR environment lighting. Its static-dither/no-shimmer statement is not a new measured result; the dither implementation and temporal behavior need their own evidence.

The temporal blend shader explicitly bypasses history for sample index <=1, avoiding undefined/NaN history contaminating the initial sample. Later frames use an incremental `1/N` average for every channel of both attachments. This is valid for compatible accumulated samples, but does not establish history invalidation, reprojection, correct color-space averaging or sufficient history precision. The subsequently completed fractalKernel.ts review resolves the producer: it converts each orbit evaluation to color, distance/potential/stripe fields and mask gates before writing these attachments. It does not store averaged raw orbit coordinates here. Those averaged derived fields still do not reconstruct a single exact orbit for picking or other numerical queries; see the later shared-kernel section. For RFF, accumulate quantities with declared semantics, reset on the right state changes, and retain exact underlying fractal fields where needed.

**Priority:** pixel-distance masks and angle/iteration mixing are useful additional 2D appearance candidates, conditional on existing RFF fields and precision. They have not been implemented or benchmarked here and do not yet displace environment reflection as the leading relief-material proposal.

## 2D host contracts: gradient revisions, iteration budgets and numerical range

**Full reads:** [GradientLutManager.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/fractal/GradientLutManager.ts), [iterationPolicy.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/fractal/iterationPolicy.ts), [dd.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/fractal/deepZoom/dd.ts), [HDRFloat.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/fractal/deepZoom/HDRFloat.ts), and [index.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/fractal/index.ts).

### Gradient changes are rendering dependencies

The LUT manager owns three 256×1 RGBA-byte textures: main, collision and interior. Its older introductory text mentions only two. Each upload increments one shared version so histories that bake color can invalidate after a gradient edit. It lazily supplies opaque grayscale defaults for main/interior and an opaque black collision mask, uses linear filtering and horizontal repeat, and explicitly deletes owned textures on disposal.

For RFF, include palette/environment resource revisions in the dependencies of any cached colored output. If the underlying field is retained separately, a palette edit can recolor that field without recalculating the fractal; if color is baked into temporal history, retaining that history mixes different palettes. Distinguish those cases rather than resetting every cache indiscriminately. Per-resource revisions can avoid unrelated invalidation where useful.

The manager only warns on an incorrect byte count and still attempts upload, then increments the version without checking GL success. It also changes active texture/binding state without restoring it. An adopted Vulkan implementation should validate the buffer and publish a new resource revision only after successful preparation and the required synchronization. The grayscale ramp uses repeating endpoints, so it is not a seamless periodic ramp unless that boundary transition is intended. RGBA8 LUT storage also does not support HDR environment radiance; choose that representation separately and preserve RFF's existing recipe stability.

### Reference length and pixel iteration cap are separate quantities

The shallow policy grows a base iteration count with zoom depth, clamps that base to 200..2000, then multiplies it. Consequently 2000 is not the final cap when the multiplier exceeds one. The deep build policy scales a 2000..20000 base and caps the result at 200000. Zero multiplier is deliberately allowed for an artistic dissolve-to-interior effect. These policies are heuristics, not proofs that every pixel is resolved. Do not copy their constants into RFF as a mathematical correctness criterion.

For periodic references, `deepGpuCap()` selects the full build budget rather than the short period length. That avoids confusing a reusable orbit period with a maximum escape count. For nonperiodic references it returns the maximum of the actual orbit length and a multiplier-scaled floor. Despite the comment claiming the cap stays within the orbit, the function alone does not guarantee it: `orbitLen=10`, `period=0`, `mul=1` returns 200. Valid caller construction may prevent that combination, but the invariant must be checked at the caller/buffer boundary. The helper does not itself validate finite zoom, length or multiplier values.

RFF's transferable requirement is explicit consistency between reference availability, periodic reuse, requested iteration budget and actual shader access. Retain existing FPG/MPA semantics; this policy is not MPA and should not be labeled BLA. A periodic nucleus and a compressed reference require their own accuracy/validity proof. Exposing an artistic iteration dissolve would be a separate user-selected effect, never an automatic precision reduction disguised as optimization.

### More exponent range is not more mantissa precision

The double-double helper keeps high/low JavaScript-number components and uses two-sum for compensated addition and subtraction. It is a bounded precision representation, not arbitrary precision, and its approximate 106-bit description is not a guarantee for every operation or every center magnitude. Its tiny-zoom navigation claims need the consuming coordinate path to preserve both components. RFF already uses GMP/high-precision references; this is not a reason to replace them with a fixed pair.
