The HDR helper packs a number as mantissa times a power of two so a shader can operate outside ordinary float exponent range. This preserves range only if shader operations maintain the pair; uploading the mantissa as a float does not retain a double's significand precision, and converting an already underflowed input cannot recover it. Nonfinite inputs are converted to zero, which is a permissive fallback rather than appropriate validation for RFF coordinates. Negative values have negative mantissas despite the header's unsigned interval description. At floating-point exponent boundaries, logarithm-based normalization and reconstruction require boundary tests rather than assuming a perfectly normalized pair for every finite input.

For RFF appearance shaders that need a logarithmic pixel scale or normalized local offset, derive those values from the authoritative high-precision state and document the intentional precision of the visual quantity. Keep reference-orbit arithmetic, navigation coordinates and shader presentation values separate. Verify host/shader component order explicitly; the complex packing here is `(real mantissa, real exponent, imaginary mantissa, imaginary exponent)`.

Finally, the `engine/fractal/index.ts` comment still describes a shallow-only library, while the same tree contains the deep-zoom helpers just read. It exports the renderer and LUT manager but does not establish the renderer's active deep paths. Use the actual renderer/controller/kernel reads to determine functionality rather than taking that historical summary as authoritative. Those substantial files remain separate pending work after this batch.

## Deep-zoom GPU handoff: publish one compatible resource generation

**Full read:** [DeepZoomController.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/fractal/DeepZoomController.ts). This controller binds existing orbit/approximation data; it does not build or prove the approximations.

GMT stores the reference orbit in a nearest-filtered RGBA32F texture with width 2048 and its LA table in a width-1024 texture with three texels per node. Equal-height updates reuse allocation through subimage upload; row-count changes reallocate. Clearing disables logical counts while retaining textures for reuse. The design provides an explicit version for histories to notice data replacement, and fallback textures keep sampler bindings valid when data is absent.

**RFF transfer:** bundle reference identity, compatible approximation tables, geometry metadata and shader-visible counts under one generation. Prepare and validate a replacement before publishing it, then retire old resources after in-flight work completes. GMT exposes separate orbit/LA/AT setters and stores no shared generation ID here; replacing an orbit does not itself clear the old LA/AT data. Whether a mixed combination can actually be rendered depends on callers. RFF should make compatibility explicit rather than rely on undocumented setter ordering. This proposal concerns resource publication, not adoption of GMT's LA/AT mathematics or replacement of RFF's compressed MPA tables.

The controller copies the reference center pairs, but retains the stage array and AT payload by reference. External mutation can change later uniform uploads without a version increment. `setLAEnabled()` also changes its flag without incrementing this version, so a caller must include that toggle in its own invalidation dependency. The file's broad statement that the version changes on every state change is therefore narrower in practice. Use immutable published payloads or explicit update APIs for RFF cache identity; do not assume a counter notices aliased edits.

### Uploaded lengths must agree with shader limits

Upload paths pad short arrays with zero and truncate to complete texture rows. Padding is appropriate for unused tail texels, but no local validation proves that the caller supplied every logical orbit/node record. Validate finite nonnegative counts, required element lengths, texture/device limits and reference period before upload. An allocation/upload failure must not publish metadata as though the new resource were usable. The fixed texture widths and full-row staging copies also have costs; RFF's much larger compressed references should retain their existing compression rather than adopt a dense texture layout merely for convenience.

Stage entries arrive as pairs and are repacked into vec4 uniforms on every bind. Only 64 entries are uploaded, but `uLAStageCount` is set to the uncapped `stages.length / 2`. A safe implementation needs both metadata and upload to describe the same supported count, plus validation of an even element count and valid stage indices. The downstream shader may impose its own bound; this controller read alone does not prove an out-of-range access. Caching the packed immutable stage buffer until its generation changes is a straightforward allocation-saving candidate, conditional on profiling, with no change to arithmetic.

Clear operations intentionally retain storage, and disposal deletes textures without clearing every metadata field. This favors a single-use lifecycle contract; reusing a disposed object requires deliberate reinitialization. Binding helper behavior also assumes a usable fallback: if both the real texture and fallback are null it skips binding. A Vulkan adaptation must supply valid descriptors or a supported null-descriptor policy, rather than translating this implicit texture-unit convention literally.

### Local-coordinate accuracy must survive every conversion

The controller subtracts high/low center pairs before collapsing the small difference to one JavaScript number, then packs that difference and zoom as mantissa/exponent pairs for float uniforms. Subtracting before collapse avoids losing a tiny local displacement in a much larger absolute center. It still does not preserve arbitrary precision: the resulting local value is rounded again when sent as a float mantissa. RFF should derive screen-local offsets from its authoritative high-precision center and enforce an error bound in pixels, while retaining its established coordinate and perturbation precision.

AT scalar/complex coefficients use ordinary float uniforms in this controller; they do not all share the extended-range packing used by zoom and center offsets. Periodic reuse is enabled by a supplied positive period, with a comment asserting exact wrap at a nucleus. This file validates neither nucleus accuracy nor coefficient range. Those claims require the worker, reference builder and kernel audit. Preserve a distinction between an approximate finite-precision nucleus, a periodic-indexing convention and a proved safe reference.

**RFF outcome:** prioritize atomic compatible resource updates, truthful cache invalidation, validated shader-visible sizes and cached invariant packing. These are relevant to accurate 2D rendering and to any derived fields feeding relief shaders. No speedup or precision improvement has been measured, and this controller is not evidence that GMT's approximation system is equivalent to RFF's MPA.

## Reference-worker generation: cancellation, validation and packed precision

**Full read:** [deepZoomWorker.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/fractal/deepZoom/deepZoomWorker.ts).

The worker builds a reference orbit, optionally builds/calibrates LA data, optionally derives AT data, and returns the results with one request ID and the actual reference center/period. Transferable buffers avoid copying during message transfer, but the worker first allocates and copies the used orbit into a fresh buffer; this is not a zero-copy pipeline end to end. The builder's original orbit remains available for LA construction, increasing transient memory. RFF's compressed-reference design should not be replaced by this dense staging approach; profile and budget any new auxiliary shader-field uploads independently.

One response groups compatible orbit and acceleration results, which is a useful basis for the generation publication proposed in the preceding section. It does not by itself prove that callers replace or clear every controller resource together. A response without LA/AT must explicitly invalidate stale optional data from an earlier reference. Request IDs also only identify results; the receiving side must reject a superseded ID before publication.

### Cancellation must interrupt work, not merely identify it

Despite the introductory claim of cancellation checks, the current `cancel` branch simply returns. Orbit construction, calibration and table generation run synchronously inside one message handler. A normal cancel message cannot be processed during that handler, and no progress message is emitted from this file. Its response union contains only final orbit/error messages. Historical comments about short orbit-only builds and later LA support do not describe the current full workload or measured timings here.

For RFF, keep obsolete-result rejection separate from computational cancellation. A canceled job should check a cancellation token in bounded work intervals, or use the existing worker/thread interruption mechanism without publishing partial results. Avoid serially finishing many obsolete views before servicing the newest one. Report phase progress from completed work and retain a coherent previous preview while a replacement is prepared. These are responsiveness requirements, not grounds to shorten references or reduce precision.

### Validate the algorithm actually executed on the GPU

LA construction is skipped for a reference marked unsafe for an exterior-dominated view. Otherwise, nonperiodic references may be calibrated against a CPU perturbation walk. Periodic references bypass that calibration because the comments acknowledge a mismatch between the calibrator's nonperiodic rebasing and the shader's periodic wrap; they use the fixed threshold instead. The statement that a periodic nucleus makes the loose threshold glitch-free is not proven by this dispatcher. Periodicity alone does not eliminate approximation or float-packing error.

RFF should compare any proposed accelerated shader path against a matching baseline with the same reference traversal, escape rule, derivative/orbit statistics and precision domain. A CPU checker implementing a different traversal cannot certify the GPU path. Statistical view samples also need a declared scope; the detailed calibration algorithm remains a separate file to audit. None of this makes GMT LA/AT equivalent to RFF's period-based MPA.

Phoenix requests document that callers must disable LA and AT, but the build condition here only checks `buildLA`, reference length and `laUnsafe`; it does not independently reject Phoenix, Julia or nonquadratic powers. Those capabilities must be verified upstream and/or enforced at this boundary. Typed request comments are not runtime mathematical validation. For RFF's existing formula path, retain its supported-equation contract; any expansion requires deriving compatible approximation rules rather than accepting an arbitrary formula flag.

AT is intentionally disabled for periodic references because its front-loaded iteration advancement has no verified interaction with modulo reference indexing. That is an example of withholding an optimization when its combined semantics are unproven. `screenSqrRadius` is an ordinary number; squaring a very small zoom can underflow before this worker sees it, making the optional branch inactive. This is a capability/performance limit, not proof of incorrect base perturbation output. An extended-range radius representation would require corresponding builder and shader support rather than just changing one field.

### Packed data needs post-packing validation

The worker packs coefficients, thresholds, step lengths and next-stage indices into Float32 arrays. Integer indices are exactly representable only within the float integer range, and numerical thresholds/coefficients may underflow, overflow or round during this conversion. There is no local post-pack finite/range or conservative-threshold check. A calibration performed before packing does not automatically validate the shader's rounded table. RFF must preserve its precision requirements and memory compression; any GPU acceleration table should be checked in its actual uploaded representation.

Timing fields also have specific boundaries: `buildMs` measures reference construction; `laBuildMs` measures LA construction/calibration before table packing and AT construction. Neither is total request latency. `laEpsilonLog2` is set only on the calibration path, despite an interface comment implying it accompanies every built LA table. Diagnostics should explicitly distinguish fixed versus calibrated policies and include packing/transfer/upload costs when assessing user-visible performance.

**RFF-facing outcome:** generation-tagged complete responses, effective cancellation, precise timing boundaries and CPU/GPU-equivalent validation are useful improvements to evaluate around new shader-derived fields. Actual worker/controller call-site atomicity and numerical validity remain unproven until the builders, runtime and kernel are examined; this batch records the orchestration, not a benchmark or a replacement algorithm.

## Calibration scope: sampled agreement is not a whole-view accuracy proof

**Full read:** [epsilonCalibration.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/fractal/deepZoom/epsilonCalibration.ts). Names and historical numerical claims in this source describe GMT's LA path; they do not describe or rename RFF's MPA.

The calibrator samples a fixed 3×3 grid spanning the view, evaluates an ordinary perturbation baseline and an LA-plus-perturbation path, and searches threshold exponents between -53 and -24. If the loose bound passes it returns immediately; otherwise it performs six binary-search steps. Evaluation is capped at `min(maxIter, max(2*orbitLen, 4000))`, rather than always reaching the requested render budget. Both paths use a fixed squared escape radius of 1024 and JavaScript-number arithmetic over the uploaded Float32 reference samples.

The transferable idea is automated comparison of accelerated and baseline results before accepting a configuration. For RFF, this can support diagnostics or regression testing of a proposed GPU implementation, but it must not become permission to loosen precision until a handful of probes happen to pass. The baseline here is not an independent arbitrary-precision oracle, and sharing the same tail can hide a common error. GPU precision, packing and periodic traversal differ from this CPU evaluator, as the worker review already identified.

### What the comparison actually checks

An escape-status disagreement fails immediately. For escaped points, the comparison checks only smooth-iteration relative error below 1e-5, normalized by at least one; it does not compare final angle, derivative, trap minimum or stripe data. For still-bounded points it compares the final reconstructed `z`, with a relative threshold of 1e-3 and a 1e-12 denominator floor. Despite one comment calling this a perturbation-z comparison, the evaluator returns reconstructed orbit coordinates, not just delta-z.

A relative smooth-count tolerance is not a uniform visual tolerance: at a count near 100000, an absolute difference approaching one iteration can satisfy the stated relative bound, while a tightly repeated palette can amplify much smaller differences. Conversely, identical smooth counts need not produce identical angle-based coloring. A cap-limited bounded comparison cannot prove eventual escape behavior or correct interior classification at a larger requested cap. A 3×3 grid can miss small filaments and localized artifacts between samples. Therefore the source's phrases about accuracy being proven for the view exceed what this checker establishes.

For RFF shader adoption, select comparison observables from the actual effect: count and escape status for iteration color, final angle for angular mapping, derivative/log-distance for boundary masks, and orbit statistics for traps. Use independent high-precision spot checks and rendered-image comparisons at sensitive locations. Distinguish a sampling diagnostic from a mathematical validity bound, and preserve the latter where the existing MPA algorithm relies on it.

### Failed calibration needs an explicit safe result

The strict-bound table is compared, but only its passed count is retained; a failed strict check does not cause rejection. `best` starts as that table and is returned if no midpoint passes. The worker previously read uses the returned table and exponent but does not consume `passed`/`testPoints`. Thus an unsuccessful calibration can be treated as usable if the table separately reports structural validity. This is a verified control-flow observation, not a reproduced rendering artifact.

A prospective RFF validator should return explicit success/failure and fall back to the existing validated calculation when no candidate passes. Never infer safety merely because a threshold is very small. Binary search also assumes passing behavior is monotonic in the threshold, and six steps approximate a boundary rather than finding an exact largest passing scale. Changes in table construction or traversal can require verifying that assumption. Record probe coverage, the chosen threshold, packed representation and rejection reason with the result.

Additional evaluator limits include a 2^21 ordinary-loop bound, 64 stage steps and 4096 LA steps per stage. Exceeding an internal loop budget must be distinguishable from mathematical boundedness or ordinary completion. These helpers do not independently validate all array lengths, indices and finite values. Do not use their friendly default-input behavior as an unrestricted public numerical contract.

**RFF-facing outcome:** use calibrated comparisons as evidence with a stated scope, retain a trustworthy fallback, and validate all fields needed by 2D coloring or relief shaders. This mechanism is worth learning from as a verification workflow; copying its thresholds, sparse grid or 'ground truth' label would not satisfy RFF's precision requirements. No new runtime accuracy experiment was executed in this batch.

## Deep-job API: every accepted request needs a terminal outcome

**Full reads:** [laRuntime.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/fractal/deepZoom/laRuntime.ts) and [laParameters.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/fractal/deepZoom/laParameters.ts). Despite its name, `laRuntime.ts` is a main-thread worker wrapper, not the numerical LA traversal.

The wrapper lazily creates one worker, assigns increasing IDs, maps each ID to promise resolve/reject functions, and reconstructs typed-array views over transferred buffers. A normal response removes its pending entry and resolves or rejects it. A worker error rejects all pending requests, clears them and terminates the worker so a later call can create another. This is a useful RFF model for a reference-generation job service, especially when shader-derived fields are built asynchronously.

Cancellation has a different contract: `cancel(id)` posts the cancel message and deletes the pending entry without resolving or rejecting its promise. Disposal terminates the worker and clears all entries without settling their promises. The worker read in the previous batch ignores cancellation messages, so an actual calculation can continue while its result is discarded and its caller remains waiting. Furthermore, `computeReferenceOrbit()` returns only the promise, not the ID or a cancellation handle. These are direct API/control-flow observations; callers may avoid those methods or impose their own timeouts, which requires separate inspection.

**RFF adoption:** return a job handle with an explicit cancellation token and terminal status, or use the existing equivalent facility. Every accepted request should settle as completed, canceled or failed, including shutdown and submission failure. Discarding obsolete output is separate from interrupting its computation and separate again from notifying the consumer. Bound or coalesce queued view requests so stale reference builds do not delay the newest interaction indefinitely. Do not implement this by reducing mathematical precision or reference coverage.

A synchronous `postMessage()` exception rejects the promise through the executor, but the pending entry inserted immediately beforehand is not removed locally. Worker construction occurs before the promise is constructed and can throw directly. The wrapper has no `messageerror` handler, timeout, progress/liveness protocol or payload validation. Response conversion removes the pending entry before constructing all typed views; a malformed payload that throws during conversion could leave the original promise unsettled. An RFF job abstraction should give these failure paths the same explicit cleanup/settlement contract rather than relying on happy-path typing.

### Capability claims must match the worker

The wrapper comment says the worker skips LA for nonquadratic powers, but the inspected worker's LA branch does not directly check power. Its gate depends on request flags and reference-result metadata. Proving safe behavior therefore needs the reference builder and actual request producers; the wrapper's comment is not an enforcement mechanism. Phoenix support similarly relies on callers disabling incompatible acceleration options. Prefer a shared supported-formula capability check at request construction and again at execution, with an explicit baseline fallback.

The result preserves the actual relocated reference center and period. That metadata must travel with the orbit all the way to the shader; using the originally requested center would describe a different perturbation problem. Missing LA buffers and default zero counts must clear previous optional resources when results are installed. The promise correlator provides no atomic installation by itself.

### Defaults are algorithm-specific, not RFF tuning recommendations

`defaultLAParameters()` constructs a fresh scalar settings object with separate delta-z and delta-c threshold scales, two period-detection families and a method selector. All four detection ratios default to 0.03, and both validity scales to 2^-24. Comments attribute the defaults to FractalShark, but this read does not verify the original source/license or establish optimality. Do not copy these constants into RFF's MPA: the algorithms, validity derivations and precision contracts must be evaluated independently.

Keeping delta-z and delta-c validity conditions distinct is a useful conceptual reminder for approximation validation, but neither the settings type nor its comments prove how table size or detected periods change when those values change. Those relationships belong to the builder/runtime analysis. This batch adds job-lifecycle evidence and parameter-schema evidence only; it does not yet establish numerical correctness or a performance gain.

## Approximation-node mechanics and transformed iteration: adoption boundaries

**Full reads:** [LAInfoDeep.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/fractal/deepZoom/LAInfoDeep.ts) and [atBuilder.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/fractal/deepZoom/atBuilder.ts). Both explicitly attribute ported mathematics to FractalShark; original-source and licensing verification is still required before adapting distinctive implementation details. Their claims of bit-for-bit fidelity or sufficient precision are not established by a local source read.

### How the nodes compose

A node contains a starting reference value, complex Z/C coefficients, separate validity thresholds, a step length and a finer-stage index. `stepLA()` multiplies each coefficient by twice the next reference value, adds one to the C coefficient, and tightens thresholds using Chebyshev magnitudes. `compositeLA()` introduces a bridge through twice the second node's reference, multiplies by its Z coefficient, and adds its C coefficient. The missing `+1` in the bridge is an explicit indexing convention; replacing this with ordinary affine-map composition without understanding that convention would change the algorithm.

The header's simple `A*dz+B*dc` description is incomplete when read in isolation: the previously inspected evaluator first forms `dz*(2*Ref+dz)` before applying these coefficients. Likewise, the initializer's A=B=1 is not the identity map of two independent inputs in the elementary affine sense. RFF review should follow the complete producer/consumer convention, including iteration numbering and nonlinear boundary steps, rather than adopting a formula from its short comment.

Detection method 2 watches threshold collapse; method 1 tracks a running minimum magnitude. `stepLA()` and `detectPeriod()` use the general method-1 threshold field, while the separately declared stage-0 method-1 field is not read in these functions. The method-2 step and standalone check use different stage/general fields. Defaults happen to agree, so the distinction matters when tuning. These are GMT's segmentation rules; RFF's MPA derives its levels from its own periodic structure and is not interchangeable with this implementation.

`StepLength` and next-stage indices are left for the builder to finalize. Reference objects are shared by assignment, not deeply frozen, and the arithmetic does not locally reject nonfinite results. Exact-zero predicates check exact zero despite wording about being close to zero. Caller aliasing matters too: some detection comparisons refer back to the input after writing output, so arbitrary in-place input/output aliasing is not guaranteed equivalent. A port must document ownership and validate finite coefficients and conservative thresholds after the actual GPU packing.

### What AT adds, and what its selection test does not establish

AT reinterprets a stage in transformed coordinates so a quadratic iteration can cover several original iterations with no per-step reference texture lookup. It derives `ccoeff = ZCoeff*CCoeff`, `refC = next.Ref*ZCoeff`, an inverse Z coefficient, an escape radius and a delta-c threshold. The selector walks stages from outermost inward and returns the first candidate meeting its usability test, relying on builder ordering rather than explicitly maximizing step length.

The actual usability inequality is `|ccoeff|² * screenRadius² * 2^32 > |refC|²`, together with an escape radius greater than four. It does not compare the screen radius against `thresholdC`. Thus its description as covering the screen must not be interpreted as proof that every pixel is inside the per-pixel validity region. The shader must still enforce its validity conditions and reconstruct the correct continuation state. Reference relocation also means a view-centered radius and a reference-centered maximum offset are different quantities; the caller must provide the intended one.

The coefficient guard uses a component-magnitude limit of 1e4 for Z/C coefficients, their product and transformed reference C. The inverse only receives a JavaScript finiteness check; that is not a complete float-upload representability test. The reciprocal helper returns zero for zero/nonfinite squared denominator. Other radius checks reject some degenerate cases, but the policy is not a comprehensive proof of stable transformed iteration. The source's digit-headroom rationale is a heuristic, and its 'massive speedup' description is not a measured RFF result.

**RFF decision:** do not prioritize replacing MPA with this AT/LA path. The useful lesson for any new GPU acceleration is to evaluate round-trip coordinate error in pixels, validate the actual packed arithmetic, preserve continuation indices, and fall back without compromising precision. Derivative, final-angle and orbit-trap fields needed by 2D coloring or relief masks require their own propagation; these node/AT builders do not alone provide those statistics across skipped iterations. Test those observables before allowing an accelerated path to feed a new shader effect. Table construction and kernel execution remain separate audit work.

## Reference construction and approximation tables: preserve the fields that shaders display

**Scope:** full source reads of [laBuilder.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/fractal/deepZoom/laBuilder.ts), [HighPrecComplex.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/fractal/deepZoom/HighPrecComplex.ts), [nucleus.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/fractal/deepZoom/nucleus.ts), and [referenceOrbit.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/fractal/deepZoom/referenceOrbit.ts). These are CPU producers for GPU fractal data, not new lighting effects. Their transferable value is an explicit contract between reference generation, acceleration and the fields consumed by coloring and relief. RFF already has high-precision references, compression and MPA; this review does not propose replacing those with GMT's LA implementation. MPA is not BLA. Source comments naming FractalShark or other programs are provenance leads, not independently verified licensing or equivalence claims.

### Table structure and fallback have to survive the GPU handoff

Stage zero greedily extends nodes while scanning the reference. A detected period anchors subsequent windows; when no period is found over a long orbit, or the detected period is long, the builder instead uses a length-derived partition. Higher stages compose lower-stage nodes, carrying original iteration lengths and indices into the preceding stage. Thus the table's organization is not exclusively determined by detected periodic structure, and must not be described as RFF's MPA. Each stage ends with a zero-length sentinel whose reference is the last supplied orbit sample; `macroItCount` excludes that sentinel. Leaf links address reference iterations, while higher links address lower-stage nodes relative to their stage. A GPU port needs to preserve these distinct index domains.

The builder permits up to 1,024 stages. The previously reviewed upload path has its own smaller stage-packing capacity, so table production and GPU capacity require one shared contract; the builder's limit alone does not establish safe upload. The public entry point also assumes orbit storage matches the declared sample count. RFF should validate logical counts, storage capacity and integer representability before publication, including zero/one/two-sample boundaries and the terminal sample required for each skip.

The `valid` flag is not simply proof of completed construction: a small orbit with no detected period can leave a complete single-node stage plus sentinel while returning false, disabling its use. Conversely, success does not certify numerical accuracy. The coefficient pass keeps a contiguous prefix of stages whose Z/C coefficient components are finite and at most 1e10. It does not validate reference values, thresholds, all intermediate arithmetic or actual per-pixel errors. Trimming stops at the first unsafe stage; unused nodes remain in the flat array. This happens after all stages have been constructed, so it does not save the corresponding construction work. The source's small memory estimate is not an accounting of JavaScript object overhead or the worker's three-RGBA-texel packing (48 bytes per packed node).

**RFF adoption boundary:** explicit fallback to a smaller skip or ordinary perturbation is useful, but a magnitude cap is not a precision certificate. Preserve compressed representations and distinguish unavailable acceleration from invalid fractal data. Validate after actual GPU packing, and include derivative, angle and orbit-trap observables in comparisons whenever a shader effect depends on them. Do not assume matching escape counts establishes matching relief or material masks.

### Fixed-point arithmetic retains input precision; it cannot create missing coordinates

GMT represents each real value by a BigInt mantissa divided by a shared power of two. Addition is integer addition; multiplication shifts the integer product. The chosen precision is `max(64, ceil(-log2(zoom)) + ceil(log2(maxIter)) + 32)`. This is a working heuristic, not a proved universal bound on error amplification along every orbit. Operands must have the same scale, but the arithmetic methods do not enforce that precondition. Negative multiplication uses an arithmetic right shift, while division truncates toward zero; rounding behavior is therefore not uniform. Nonfinite number inputs and division by zero return zero, which callers must not interpret as a successful numerical result.

`fromDoubleDouble` adds the high and low words separately at the working precision, avoiding premature loss of the low word. However, the incoming center still has only the information carried by those two doubles. Increasing the BigInt precision does not extend the precision of that input. `toNumber` takes the leading 53 bits without a round-to-nearest step; small absolute magnitude does not make an arbitrary high-precision value exactly representable. `toDoubleDouble` constructs a residual around that truncated high word, despite its comment describing the high word as nearest. The method named `toFloat32Pair` itself returns JavaScript numbers; the later Float32Array store performs float32 rounding.

**RFF implication:** retain GMP-quality coordinates through reference selection and offset calculation. For any proposed GPU path, budget separately for center representation, orbit calculation, stored reference samples, offset transport and shader arithmetic. A wider exponent range is not a replacement for mantissa precision. Conversion tests should cover cancellation, negative values, very small residuals and actual pixel spacing, rather than only ordinary values near the origin.

### Better references are a search heuristic, not a proof about every pixel

GMT first builds the view-center reference. When it escapes, eligible modes search a 9-by-9 grid excluding the center, in normalized center-outward order, followed by up to two 5-by-5 refinements. Candidate offsets are retained explicitly to avoid subtracting nearly identical centers during refinement. The refinement span is divided by four each pass, despite the earlier constant comment describing halving. Search stops at the first candidate surviving the iteration cap; that means bounded within the tested budget, not mathematically proven interior. Coarse normalized ordering also differs from physical distance ordering in a non-square view, and refinement points are not clamped back into the original viewport.

A candidate is adopted when it passes either the relative improvement threshold or the absolute one, since rejection requires failing both. Candidate ranking may use ordinary doubles under a zoom/iteration heuristic; the chosen candidate is rebuilt at high precision. This is a useful separation of ranking from final reference calculation, but neither a finite grid nor the double-ranking gate proves the reference outlasts every pixel. Do not inherit the source's stronger wording as a guarantee. Actual eligibility includes Phoenix Mandelbrot and Phoenix Julia relocation, despite older comments saying Phoenix relocation is disabled; plain Julia does not use this relocation path.

The eight-point exterior classification is centered on the selected reference, which may differ from the view center. Five escaping probes disable LA. It is an empirical accelerator-selection policy, not a proof of approximation safety across the image. Preserve a correctness fallback independent of this vote. For RFF, any reference-selection enhancement should first demonstrate benefit over the existing locator/reference logic and should not reduce requested pixel iteration budgets merely because a sampled reference was short.

The stored reference builder allocates `maxIter` texels, yet an escape on the final loop step attempts to store one further sample and reports a logical length one greater than that capacity; the returned subarray cannot extend the allocation. This is a source-level boundary case, not a reproduced RFF defect. Its adoption lesson is to specify whether a count includes the initial and terminal samples and verify the actual buffer length against it before building or uploading tables. Probes count completed steps, while stored orbit lengths include the initial sample, another distinction to preserve when comparing candidates.

### A finite-precision nucleus does not make periodic wrapping automatically exact

Period detection updates the parameter derivative before the orbit and compares the fixed-point Chebyshev norm with `2 * radius * derivativeNorm`, rejecting escaped orbits. Newton refinement solves the period equation using that derivative. The refinement function returns a candidate when the correction stops decreasing or becomes zero, and also returns the last candidate when the step budget is exhausted. A nondecreasing correction alone does not prove convergence; the caller's verification is essential. It checks a zero derivative directly, while fixed-point division can also produce a zero result when a squared denominator quantizes to zero.

The caller adds 32 precision bits, limits candidate periods to 20,000 and requires the period to be shorter than 90 percent of the fallback orbit. It builds P+1 samples, checks non-escape and a terminal residual, then stores only samples 0 through P-1 for modulo wrapping. However, the residual test reads the float32-packed terminal sample and accepts `|z_P| < max(radius * 1e-3, 1e-18)`. The absolute floor relaxes the pixel-relative requirement for sufficiently small views; it does not by itself reject deeper views as the comment suggests. Float32 conversion can also hide a smaller nonzero residual. The test uses an approximate 1,000-pixel scale rather than actual output dimensions, and is not a bound on error after repeated wraps.

The nucleus orbit is calculated from the full fixed-point center, but the published center is reduced to a double-double pair. Its conversion error therefore also matters for reconstructing the pixel offset. The location gate allows a nucleus within eight view half-diagonals, rather than requiring it inside the visible rectangle. Returned `precisionBits` remains the base precision even when the adopted orbit used the extra 32 bits. These are reasons to make numerical metadata precise, not reasons to duplicate GMT's implementation in RFF.

**RFF-facing recommendation:** if periodic reference reuse is extended, preserve the actual high-precision reference center, test terminal residuals before lossy packing, and relate the accepted error to full-output pixel spacing and repeated-use amplification. Compare the resulting shader inputs as well as final colors against the existing trusted path. No speedup or visual benefit has been measured here, and no RFF source code changes are proposed by this batch. Environment reflection remains the leading provisional appearance improvement; these numerical contracts protect the accuracy of any 2D fields used to drive it or other material effects.


## Shared 2D kernel: shade each sample, stabilize interior fields, preserve acceleration semantics

**Scope:** complete reads of [fractalKernel.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/fractal/shaders/fractalKernel.ts) and [FractalColorRenderer.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/fractal/FractalColorRenderer.ts). The renderer's introductory shallow-only description is outdated: it imports and actively drives the deep worker/controller. The shader's older stage-zero-only, Mandelbrot-only and Phoenix-shallow-only comments likewise do not describe all current branches. Findings below follow executed source paths; historical speed and visual-equivalence claims were not reproduced.

### Transferable appearance mechanisms

**Evaluate nonlinear appearance before averaging.** Each jittered evaluation returns final orbit state, trap/stripe statistics, a derivative-based direction and an interior scalar. The caller maps that evaluation through its palette, chooses interior versus exterior color, applies optional lighting, and derives masks before accumulating it. Final MRT outputs are `(mapped DE, normalized smooth iteration, stripe average, injection gate)` and `(composited RGB, collision mask)`. Thus a boundary pixel averages interior and exterior colors rather than using an averaged orbit state as a fictional new orbit. This resolves the earlier uncertainty from reading the temporal blend alone.

For RFF, this is a useful rule for antialiasing new environment reflections, material masks and nonlinear palette mappings. Shade compatible subpixel data before integrating final appearance; do not assume lighting an averaged normal equals averaging the individual reflections. This does not establish that RFF lacks appropriate supersampling, nor does it require re-running the expensive fractal calculation for every palette edit if adequate sample data is already retained. GMT bakes palette and lighting into history, so their changes restart accumulation. A RFF cache should explicitly distinguish reusable numerical fields from baked appearance. Choose the color domain deliberately: averaging GMT's display-space RGB is not automatically linear-light radiance integration.

**A separate interior palette with a fixed observation window.** The kernel can drive an interior gradient from minimum modulus, mean modulus, the modulus or angle at a fixed terminal iteration, mean angular stripes, or minimum distance to a trap. Modulus values use an exponential remap; angle and stripes provide bounded coordinates; the result receives an independent repeat and phase. Crucially, the accumulation window is `uInteriorIter`, separate from the zoom-dependent escape budget, so changing that budget need not change the sampled cycle phase. This is a concrete 2D expression technique, useful for revealing structure in regions otherwise assigned one solid color. The reviewed standalone renderer does not expose or bind these interior-mode controls, so kernel support is not proof that this host offers them.

A RFF implementation would need to preserve the chosen window, sampling convention and accumulated statistics through MPA, or calculate them through an explicitly compatible path. Minimums, averages and endpoint phases cannot all be reconstructed from the final escape count. A finite-budget non-escape is also not a proof of mathematical membership. The fixed window stabilizes the statistic for a fixed point; it does not guarantee that classification remains unchanged when the escape budget changes. Existing saved maps need additional channels or recomputation if they do not contain the required orbit information.

**One scalar can author several independent masks.** GMT reuses the active color-mapping scalar for a second LUT with its own repeat and phase. It converts that LUT's RGB to a bounded scalar and gates it to exterior samples. Separately, the main gradient's alpha controls dye injection. RFF could adapt the separation of source field, remapping curve and destination property to author roughness, coating strength or emission masks without changing palette colors. This complements the earlier material-mask proposal; the collision/dye destinations themselves are fluid-specific. Define the grayscale/color-space interpretation and scalar range explicitly, and do not change existing palette recipe semantics to add the feature.

**Analytic direction as an alternative relief input.** GMT normalizes the complex ratio `z / derivative`, computes an azimuthal dot product, adds a height factor, clamps, applies an ambient floor and mixes with unlit color. This is a cheap directional relief cue, not a full geometric normal, shadow solution or replacement for RFF's existing GGX/clearcoat pipeline. The reviewed RFF studio surface already supports substantially richer material lighting. An analytically derived direction is only a candidate additional input if it supplies detail or stability unavailable from the existing height/normal path.

Do not copy GMT's derivative tracker as a general implementation: it always applies `2*z*dz + 1` from an initial value of one. This fits the usual quadratic Mandelbrot parameter derivative after its first zero-z step, but does not implement the Julia initial-position derivative, the general-power factor, or Phoenix's history derivative. The same tracker feeds distance and lighting. Complex division clamps the denominator, and float derivative overflow is not repaired by subsequently taking a logarithm. RFF needs the correct derivative for its actual formula and a stable representation. Named techniques and the embedded hash constants also require verified original provenance before code adaptation.

### Actual numerical and sampling limits

The deep path unpacks the supplied mantissa/exponent scale and offsets straight back into ordinary float values. Its perturbation state and LA/AT arithmetic then remain float32; the HDR helpers are present but are not the hot-path representation. Therefore an HDR uniform format and a host zoom limit of 1e-100 do not establish distinguishable pixels at that depth. RFF should preserve its existing numerical precision, not inherit this apparent depth capability. The binomial expansion for higher-power perturbation avoids subtracting two large powers, a useful algebraic principle, but the fixed arrays assume powers within the supported range and require matching host validation.

The kernel explicitly disables LA and AT whenever trap/stripe, derivative or interior trackers are requested. The standalone host enables derivative tracking for lighting as well as DE/derivative color modes, so enabling lighting can change the computation cost substantially. This is direct evidence of the acceleration/statistics tradeoff, not a free shader-only effect. The distance motion field is emitted regardless of whether derivative tracking was requested; it should not be treated as a universally valid DE by a downstream consumer without checking those flags. The standalone display consumes the baked color, so this observation alone does not imply an error in every displayed mode.

The ordinary/perturbation loop has a hard limit of 65,536 iterations, while host budgets can reach 200,000. If skips are disabled by the selected appearance mode, reaching that loop limit leaves the non-escape state without a separate incomplete-result marker. Phoenix additionally stops when its reference is exhausted. RFF should distinguish completed, escaped and budget-limited evaluations, and verify that every advertised iteration setting is achievable on the selected field path. Smooth escape coloring also uses a quadratic log2 formula for all powers here; formula-general coloring requires its own convention.

AT rolls back one transformed step when its escape test fires, making space for ordinary perturbation to resolve the crossing. That test occurs before the next AT update; termination at the step/loop cap is a separate path. AT updates the total iteration and perturbation but does not advance `ref`, while the following LA walk begins at its first node. This composition needs an explicit continuation-state proof before adaptation. LA does track reference advances and resets during its own walk, descends through up to 64 stages, and prepares `dz*(2*Ref+dz)` before applying coefficients. Its visible per-node test checks the transformed perturbation threshold; the initial delta-c gate reads the first leaf threshold rather than rechecking every node's delta-c threshold. These are adoption verification points, not a claim that all rendered GMT scenes are wrong. The previously documented CPU table and periodic-reference limitations still apply.

Grid sampling spreads cells over frames and adds deterministic per-pixel subcell offsets after the first round. The implementation computes frames per round with integer division. Its claim of visiting every cell once therefore needs compatible grid/K combinations: grid nine with K four visits only eight cells per round, whereas the inspected renderer's grid sixteen/K one combination is compatible. Jitter hashes and blue-noise lookups use local `gl_FragCoord`; the UV tile remap does not by itself provide full-image sample identities. For RFF exports, seed samples with global output coordinates and preserve sample weights so tile layout or batch size does not change the result. Progressive sampling reduces sampling noise; it does not recover numerical information lost earlier.

### Host contracts for a usable RFF feature

The standalone host renders one sample per frame up to 128 frames, then redisplays the accumulated result. Its parameter hash includes palette version, lighting, mapping, coordinates and deep-resource version; a changed hash resets accumulation, and the blend's first frame bypasses old history. Resolution changes also reset it. This is a useful explicit invalidation pattern. A resize caps the long edge at 1,600 pixels, so the cap and temporal refinement should not be advertised as native-resolution output at every display size.

Format probing prefers RGBA16F, then RGBA32F, then RGBA8. The probe tests a small single attachment, while the actual pass uses two linearly sampled attachments; complete MRT and filtering support are separate requirements. RFF should choose field/history formats from their precision needs and validate actual usages. An RGBA8 fallback can quantize accumulated fields; a successful allocation is not a visual-accuracy test. The final dither is applied after accumulation and does not repair upstream field quantization.

Async builds use a sequence number to reject superseded results, upload the builder's actual relocated center, and clear absent LA/AT resources on accepted results. Those are useful host-side guarantees beyond the controller alone. Uploads occur sequentially in one synchronous continuation, but there is no rollback if one upload fails. A request sequence is incremented by another rebuild, disabling through the dedicated method, or disposal; ordinary parameter changes and context loss do not themselves increment it. The host must initiate rebuilds and restore the relevant parameters/resources. Context restoration creates a new controller but relies on the external restoration callback to supply the missing state. RFF should key an accepted resource bundle to both numerical settings and device generation, retaining a valid displayed frame while replacement work is pending.

Finally, cursor zoom computes an offset correction before adding it to the double-double center, avoiding subtraction of two nearly equal absolute coordinates. This is the transferable navigation principle. The separate `canvasToFractal` helper returns ordinary doubles and omits the low words, so it is not an equivalent deep-coordinate query. Keep RFF's high-precision navigation and picking contract consistent with whatever fields the new shader actually renders.

**Priority:** the strongest additions from this read are fixed-window interior coloring, independently authored material masks, and a precise per-sample appearance contract. They complement the existing environment-reflection recommendation. Their implementation cost varies sharply with required orbit statistics; none has been benchmarked or implemented in RFF during this audit.

## Appearance export: isolate rendering, report actual dimensions, control the final quantization

**Scope:** full reads of [FullscreenCompositor.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/gradient-explorer/fullscreen/FullscreenCompositor.ts), [exportRender.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/gradient-explorer/fullscreen/exportRender.ts), and [exportSize.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/gradient-explorer/fullscreen/exportSize.ts). The previously reviewed `engine/fractal/fitIterationRange.ts` was reread against the now-verified derived-field MRT layout; that reread is not additional file coverage.

**One output plan, with measured results.** GMT separates pure size planning from rendering. It orients the requested dimensions, applies both an edge and a pixel budget, and independently decides whether a two-times render fits the larger intermediate budget. A plan reports output dimensions, intermediate dimensions, whether clamping occurred and whether requested supersampling was dropped. Export subsequently reads the PNG signature and IHDR dimensions to report the file's actual size rather than trusting a renderer request. This is a useful RFF contract for new appearance effects whose resources or export path impose limits: show the effective dimensions and sampling policy, and verify the encoded result. Do not copy GMT's fixed 4K cap into RFF or treat it as a GPU capability limit. Its CPU-only supersampling policy is also an application choice; GPU rendering at the target size does not eliminate aliasing by itself.

The plan uses floor after a common scale, but enforcing a minimum edge can change extreme aspect ratios. Very large finite inputs can overflow the width-times-height intermediate before scaling. The PNG reader is lightweight dimension inspection, not a complete integrity validator: it does not check CRC or the full file. Historical size-test and mutation-test claims in comments were not rerun. These distinctions matter when describing what a plan or completed PNG actually proves.

**Keep preview and export resources separate, with one appearance snapshot.** Compositor modes export through a detached canvas and a separate compositor, disposed in a `finally` block. Modes owning their own canvas delegate to a different `renderAt` interface, outside this function. The separate surface prevents a size change from disturbing the visible preview. However, source ramp/LUT/parameter objects are read after an asynchronous noise wait without being cloned here, so this function alone does not freeze the requested artwork. RFF should capture the effective palette, environment, mask controls, orientation and asset revisions before export begins, and keep that snapshot through rendering and encoding. This complements existing RFF export infrastructure rather than proposing a second independent shading implementation.

The exporter waits up to 1.5 seconds for the noise asset when the GL dither tail needs it, then proceeds even if it is not ready. Thus cold-asset and warm-asset exports can differ. Constructor failure is outside the `try/finally`, and an unavailable 2D downsample context returns the larger source canvas. Actual-size inspection helps describe that result but does not make it the requested output. RFF should make required asset readiness and fallback quality explicit, and retain resource cleanup through partial initialization and failed exports.

**Dither once, at the relevant quantization boundary.** The compositor has three distinct routes. Byte raster input is uploaded and optionally receives the shader dither tail; continuous CPU field input is sampled and error-diffused before upload, then bypasses the shader dither; GL modes execute their fragment body followed by the shared tail. The CPU field route can preserve its already-applied dither even under the Canvas-2D fallback, whereas GL modes have no equivalent fallback rendering. The shared-tail architecture is useful for consistent preview and export, but the CPU and GPU dither algorithms are intentionally different. A mode-ID-only shader cache also assumes each ID's shader and uniform contract remain immutable.

For supersampled CPU exports, GMT renders and dithers at the larger size, then asks Canvas-2D to shrink the byte image. The browser's `imageSmoothingQuality = 'high'` flag is not an explicit area-overlap algorithm in this source, despite its comments describing a guaranteed box/area average. Resizing after dither changes its spectrum and amplitude, and earlier byte quantization cannot be undone by a later noise tail. RFF already has final-image resampling; retain a declared processing order for linear/HDR shading, filtering, tone/color conversion and final output quantization. Compare smooth gradients and bright environment reflections at actual export size. Do not import the comment's claims of superior or exact error-diffusion results without measurement.

**Fit-to-view should be an explicit, persistent color anchor.** The reread histogram helper performs a synchronous full-frame RGBA readback, extracts the averaged normalized-iteration channel, takes approximate 2nd/98th percentiles and converts them to a fixed logarithmic offset/scale. The useful product idea is a one-shot fit followed by stable color mapping, not automatic re-fitting every frame of a pan or video. The helper itself does not verify convergence or bind the readback to the matching image generation and iteration cap.

Its selection of values strictly between 1e-4 and 0.999 is a heuristic for exterior samples; the MRT contains subpixel averages, so a mixed boundary value is not an exact escaped-orbit record. Uniform-valued views also return null, not only all-interior views. The 256-bin helper returns a bin center, despite the comment calling it linear interpolation. It asks for the implementation read type but treats every non-FLOAT type as HALF_FLOAT, so a byte-format fallback needs a separate compatible read path. For RFF, consider fitting from existing precise iteration data or a deliberate reduction rather than blocking on an entire image readback. Preserve an explicit anchor in the appropriate saved settings without altering palette recipe regeneration.

**RFF-facing outcome:** these files strengthen the export and color-stability requirements for environment reflection, material masks and interior palettes. They do not change the provisional appearance ranking or establish measured performance gains. No renderer source was modified in this documentation batch.

## Procedural gradient fields: reusable mask geometry and explicit mode contracts

**Scope:** full reads of [geometryFrag.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/gradient-explorer/fullscreen/modes/geometryFrag.ts), [geometryModes.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/gradient-explorer/fullscreen/modes/geometryModes.tsx), [modeRegistry.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/gradient-explorer/fullscreen/modeRegistry.ts), [modes/index.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/gradient-explorer/fullscreen/modes/index.ts), and [fractalHandoff.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/gradient-explorer/fractalHandoff.ts). The relevant CPU geometry expressions in `palette/core/rampGeometry.ts` were also compared; this selective comparison adds no new full-file coverage credit.

### Three useful scalar fields, independent of the palette

The geometry layer separates a floating-point ramp position from coverage, then applies a gradient. Linear mode projects centered coordinates onto a rotated axis and normalizes using the rectangle's extreme projection, keeping the visible gradient angle consistent across aspect ratios. Radial mode measures distance from a movable center and divides by a corner-normalized reach. An angular sine modulates that reach as `scale * (1 + amplitude * sin(frequency * angle))`, producing petal-like contours without shifting the center. Conic mode maps angle to turns, adds `twist * log(1 + radius)`, wraps, and optionally splits the cycle into rising and falling arcs with independent bias.

The common bias is a symmetric power curve whose exponent is `exp(1.6 * bias)`, with an exact identity branch at zero. These mechanisms offer RFF compact procedural sources for roughness, coating, emission or image-layer blend masks. They can also help author an environment gradient, but an environment must evaluate a chosen directional parameterization: replacing a screen-space field with a spherical map is not automatic. Preserve the distinction between image-position masks, fractal-field masks and reflection-direction inputs so an effect does not move unexpectedly during zoom or rotation.

Coordinates are divided by half the shorter pixel extent, preserving circles under aspect changes. Nevertheless, radial normalization also depends on the frame corner distance: changing aspect can change the falloff's meaning. For a RFF export, decide whether the source is anchored to the full image, a fixed scene domain or the fractal, and use full-image dimensions/origin when rendering tiles. The source's `twist` description as turns at unit radius is imprecise: the implemented offset there is `twist * ln(2)`. Show controls in units matching the actual mapping.

### Seams and CPU/GPU equivalence need targeted checks

Continuous angular frequency is intentionally permitted for radial waves. Fractional frequency can leave a cut at the angular wrap; this is an artistic option, not a seamless periodic field. Conic mirroring returns the ramp towards its starting value and can remove a color discontinuity, but does not necessarily match derivatives across the join. Near a center, angle is singular; near tightly wound contours, one pixel covers a rapidly varying gradient coordinate. A RFF implementation needs an explicit center convention and footprint-aware filtering, rather than relying on a smooth-looking analytic expression alone. The denominator floor in the radial reach avoids division by zero but changes the shape where a petal pinches.

The CPU implementation has a legacy-default conic branch that omits wrapping, while the GPU expression always wraps. At the positive angular endpoint, these conventions can select opposite ends of a non-cyclic ramp. This is a source-level boundary difference requiring focused parity checks, not a reproduced screenshot defect. Shared default lookup reduces parameter drift, but does not prove identical arithmetic, orientation, endpoint sampling or color interpolation. The GPU mode uses a linearly filtered byte LUT; the settled CPU field follows its own ramp sampling and error-diffusion route. The source's old timing and smoothness measurements were not rerun and are not RFF benchmarks.

**RFF adoption:** if an interactive approximation is introduced, compare the represented scalar field separately from the final dithered image, especially at seams, defaults, extreme bias, non-square output and tile boundaries. Keep the existing precision of the underlying fractal calculation. A cheaper preview of an artistic mask is a different contract from reducing fractal numerical precision.

### A mode registry is useful only with enforceable capabilities

The registry distinguishes CPU fields, byte rasters, shared fragment programs and modes owning a canvas. It supplies common appearance inputs and lifecycle callbacks, with optional export and control interfaces. This offers a pattern for adding new RFF gradient/mask sources without duplicating all rendering and export plumbing. The actual registration entry point lists Linear, Radial, Conic, Spline, Fractal, Liquify and Gradient map; the registry header's Arched and Parallax list is not the current list registered by that entry point.

The implementation stores mutable mode objects in a Map, replaces duplicate IDs, and preserves insertion ordering. The TypeScript interface makes kind-specific callbacks optional rather than enforcing a discriminated union. Purity, input-source ownership and reserved-uniform rules are documented assumptions; registration does not validate them. Its comments explicitly say the existing pure geometry tests do not cover arbitrary registered callbacks. For RFF, persist stable source identifiers, validate required callbacks/capabilities and keep each render/export dependent on an explicit appearance snapshot. A reused mode ID must not leave a stale compiled shader in an ID-only program cache.

The field contract has separate position and coverage arrays, but these three current geometries set coverage to one throughout. Do not infer shaped transparency or antialiased coverage from the interface alone. Similarly, `ownCanvas` offers `renderAt` as optional and permits a smaller result; a common export button does not prove uniform resolution or rendering capability across modes. Controls and annotations live outside the exported canvas, a useful separation for RFF's on-image material handles.

### Scene handoff must preserve the appearance being promised

The handoff helper builds a limited Fluid Toy preset carrying kind, Julia constant, center high/low words, zoom, clamped iteration setting, power, basic palette mapping/repeat/phase, optional gradient and the deep-enable flag. It does not carry the full reviewed renderer's appearance state, such as lighting controls, v2 normalization/fit anchor, escape radius, interior color or the individual acceleration preferences. Its iteration value is clamped to 16..512. Therefore this payload is a starting view transfer, not evidence of pixel-identical appearance or numerical-budget transfer. PNG embedding and destination loading are described by comments but are not executed by this helper.

Live handoff writes one shared local-storage key and opens another tab. The returned success flag from `safeLocalSet` is ignored; there is no request identifier or acknowledgement in this helper. Repeated handoffs can compete for the same slot, and opening a tab does not prove the destination loaded the scene. For RFF, an image-with-settings or cross-view handoff should state which appearance controls and precision it preserves, snapshot mutable gradient data, and distinguish a successful write from a successful load. Keep RFF's existing configuration and palette recipe compatibility rules intact.

**Priority:** procedural mask geometry is an optional creative extension that complements environment reflection and field-driven material controls. Its visual value and interaction cost still need RFF comparisons. This batch changes documentation and audit coverage only.

## Image-derived palette and material masks: cache the source field, define its sampling semantics

**Scope:** full read of [gradientMapMode.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/gradient-explorer/fullscreen/modes/gradientMapMode.tsx), with rereads of the already-covered `palette/core/gradientMapChannels.ts` and `palette/core/img2grad/decode.ts`. This is a CPU image-to-gradient path, not GMT's 3D lighting shader. Its separation of source analysis from appearance editing is transferable to a RFF image-layer or material-mask extension; it does not establish that RFF currently lacks every related operation.

**Extract once, recolor repeatedly.** GMT caches source pixels by the display canvas's object identity, then caches one Float32 scalar field by that source object and the selected channel. Palette, mapping strength and output-size changes reuse the field. At full mapping strength it skips the three source-RGB interpolations because the original image contributes no color. This is a concrete optimization for interactive palette edits: expensive perceptual conversion depends on the image and channel, not the selected gradient. In RFF, key reusable image-derived fields to image content/revision, channel definition, color interpretation and any preprocessing; do not confuse an unchanged texture object with unchanged pixels. An in-place modification of the same canvas would not invalidate GMT's identity-only source cache.

The seven drivers are encoded-byte luma, individual RGB channels and OKLab-derived hue, chroma and lightness. Luma uses 0.2126/0.7152/0.0722 on encoded values; it is not linear-light luminance. Chroma is divided by 0.4 and clamped, an artistic normalization rather than a universal chroma ceiling. Hue uses the wrapped angle of OKLab a/b, with near-neutral values assigned zero. The comment's description of the wrap as being exactly on red should not be treated as an exact colorimetric statement: the implemented seam is the positive a axis. Claims about matching a particular commercial editor were not independently verified.

**Choose what gets filtered.** The renderer cover-fits and center-crops the source, computes source coordinates at output pixel centers, and bilinearly samples the cached field. For encoded luma/RGB, extraction and interpolation commute in ideal arithmetic; Float32 caching and operation order mean the source's stronger bit-identical claim does not follow automatically. For nonlinear hue/chroma/lightness, extracting before filtering deliberately defines a different operation from extracting a channel from filtered RGB. A RFF implementation should choose the intended meaning: filtering a material parameter field and filtering final colored radiance are different operations.

Hue interpolation shifts each tap by integer turns toward the first tap, blends and wraps. This avoids the obvious 0.99/0.01 midpoint error, but is a locally chosen angular branch, not a universal circular average. Widely separated or antipodal hues, changes in the anchor tap, and neutral pixels mapped to zero need explicit behavior. A non-cyclic palette still has a visible endpoint seam even with wrap-aware hue interpolation. For a RFF hue-driven mask, define neutral handling and test seam crossings before treating hue as an ordinary scalar texture. A vector representation of angle is a possible alternative, with its own low-magnitude ambiguity; it is not an automatically equivalent replacement.

Only four taps are used regardless of reduction ratio. Consequently this path is not footprint-aware minification of either source detail or a rapidly changing mapped palette. The earlier RFF mip/filtering proposal remains applicable. Mapping a filtered scalar through a sharp palette can still alias because nonlinear lookup and area integration do not commute. The gradient is sampled continuously between entries, then blended toward the original encoded RGB and written to bytes. A dither tail added after this byte buffer cannot recover information already quantized. Preserve higher-precision intermediate data when the new RFF effect requires it, and apply the declared color-space/filtering/quantization order consistently.

**Transparency and source fidelity are separate contracts.** The channel extractor and original-color interpolation ignore source alpha, and every output pixel receives alpha 255. Thus mapping strength zero preserves sampled RGB under the selected crop, not the original image's transparency or dimensions. RFF should explicitly choose whether alpha masks the effect, survives export, or is composited against a chosen background; hidden RGB in transparent pixels should not silently influence visible material fields. Use appropriate premultiplication when filtering color with coverage.

The decoder confirms that this mode reads a display canvas limited to a 1,920-pixel longest edge. Exporting a larger file increases output dimensions but cannot recover discarded source detail. RFF should retain or reload the full-resolution source for final output when appropriate, rather than deriving export quality from a preview cache. The raster callback obtains the current image from a global store instead of its render context, so an appearance snapshot containing only ramp and parameters does not freeze the image used by an asynchronous export. Bind the source revision together with the rest of the export state.

Readback failures are treated as no-image rendering, while the stage hint only tests whether a thumbnail object exists. That separates a visible placeholder from a successful image conversion; RFF should surface a usable-source state rather than letting a valid-looking background stand in for a failed conversion. The current module's timing claims were not rerun. The optimization opportunity is supported by the dependency structure, but its actual RFF benefit requires profiling.

**RFF-facing outcome:** an image-channel-to-curve/LUT stage can support duotone recoloring and independently authored roughness, emission or coating masks while reusing cached source analysis. This remains a candidate creative extension, secondary to the provisional environment-reflection priority. It requires no reduction in perturbation precision and must preserve existing palette recipe identifiers and regeneration behavior. This audit batch modifies documentation only.

## Deformable gradient layers: separate authored shape, animation and rendering resolution

**Scope:** complete reads of [LiquifyRenderer.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/gradient-explorer/fullscreen/modes/liquify/LiquifyRenderer.ts), [catmullRom.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/gradient-explorer/fullscreen/modes/liquify/catmullRom.ts), [LiquifyMesh.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/gradient-explorer/fullscreen/modes/liquify/LiquifyMesh.ts), and [liquifyStore.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/gradient-explorer/fullscreen/modes/liquify/liquifyStore.ts). The owning mode's interaction/export wiring remains separate audit work. The mode registry marks the feature unfinished; these implementation mechanisms should not be treated as a finished RFF feature specification.

**Useful 2D transfer: deform appearance without changing fractal mathematics.** Each vertex carries a fixed scalar gradient coordinate derived from its original horizontal position. Brushes and handles move the geometry while that coordinate remains attached to the material. The fragment shader interpolates the coordinate across triangles, samples a clamped gradient LUT and applies the shared output dither. For RFF, this could provide a deformable decorative gradient or mask layer, with palette edits independent of the authored deformation. Extending it to an image would require two texture coordinates, appropriate alpha and footprint filtering; this renderer currently samples only a one-dimensional gradient. Keep such an artistic layer distinct from fractal-coordinate computation, so it does not silently redefine deep-zoom navigation or reduce perturbation precision.

**Preserve the user's shape as the rest state.** GMT maintains original coordinates, a handle-deformed base, additive brush displacement, their combined sculpted shape and separate live simulated positions. Turning physics off copies the sculpted shape into the live positions and clears velocity; it does not flatten the artwork. Restore decays only the brush displacement, retaining the handle deformation, whereas reset removes user handles and brush displacement. This layered state model is more useful to RFF than the particular physics constants: an optional animated material deformation should settle towards the authored mask, and reset/restore should have explicit scopes.

The handle solver computes a locally weighted rigid rotation and translation from rest/current handles, with inverse-distance weights regularized by 1e-8. It recomputes over every vertex and handle after handle edits. The regularizer means exact handle interpolation is not established by the algebra alone. New handles use the supplied position as both original anchor and current position; inserting a handle on an already deformed sheet needs an inverse-coordinate convention in the owning interaction code. The core move method rejects corner handles but does not reject user handles marked fixed, so pin immobility also depends on that caller. Source comments cite named MLS, smoothing and position-based methods; verify original sources and licenses before adapting distinctive implementation details.

Brush falloff is measured in screen pixels, and offsets are converted back per axis. This keeps twirl/radial brush footprints circular on a rectangular canvas. The renderer's actual fit is `[1,1]`, filling the canvas despite older vertex comments about square letterboxing. Other distances, including handle weights and pin radii, remain in normalized mesh coordinates and therefore need not be screen-isotropic. Brush application scans the full grid, even though only vertices within the brush receive updates. Push uses pointer displacement and falloff without applying the strength value; other brushes apply strength in their own gains. These are distinct parameter semantics to resolve before offering a common RFF brush-strength control.

**Smooth geometry is not automatically an invertible warp.** Rendering separates the coarse control grid from a finer grid obtained by separable uniform Catmull-Rom interpolation with clamped edge neighborhoods. Its static LUT-coordinate and triangle-index buffers are regenerated only when subdivision changes; positions are uploaded per draw. The global level avoids T-junctions, but costs refinement across the whole grid when one edge is stretched. At the high-density 128-side setting and subdivision four, the render grid is 509 by 509: 259,081 vertices and 516,128 triangles. This is a meaningful cost bound for evaluating a RFF implementation, not a measured bottleneck.

The level is rounded from the largest horizontal/vertical coarse-edge length divided by 12 pixels, capped at four. It is not a guaranteed twelve-pixel maximum, a curvature criterion or a bound on the diagonal edges. Even an undeformed high-resolution image can request subdivision because the criterion measures absolute screen length. Resolution changes can change the sampled approximation; no hysteresis is present. The underlying cubic interpolation can be smooth across interior patch boundaries, but the final GPU surface remains a finite piecewise-linear triangle mesh. Therefore the comment's unconditional 'no facets' claim is too strong.

Catmull-Rom can overshoot between control points. Neither the inspected interpolation nor the mesh constraints enforce positive triangle area, non-overlap or a one-to-one inverse map. A gradient can consequently fold, and triangle drawing order determines overlap appearance in this opaque, depth-free pass. Smoothing or denser tessellation does not prove those folds absent. For RFF, choose whether folds are an intended artistic effect or something to constrain; define uncovered areas and alpha. If the desired operation is a stable image warp, consider an inverse sampling representation with explicit validity and filtering rather than assuming a forward mesh is interchangeable.
