**Animation and smoothing need honest timing semantics.** The local smooth brush uses four positive/negative Laplacian pairs on the brush displacement with a fixed boundary. Global smoothing instead uses one positive Laplacian step; it is not the continuous Taubin process described by the store's older comment. A fixed outer boundary can still allow an interior displacement to decay towards its harmonic extension, so 'does not erase the deformation' is not a universal consequence. Pins affect simulated inverse mass, not protection of the authored brush displacement.

The optional simulation uses four substeps, fixed per-substep positional pulls towards the sculpt and its edge lengths, damping and a velocity cap. Despite XPBD labels, these files do not implement an accumulated constraint multiplier and time-scaled compliance formulation. Damping and correction strengths are per call/substep; the method caps elapsed time but does not make the animation invariant to frame rate. A zero or invalid dt is not guarded locally before velocity division. Likewise, brush and smoothing effects are per invocation unless the owning mode supplies a time/stroke policy. RFF video export would need a deterministic timebase and captured authored/simulation state, not a reliance on preview frame timing.

**Lifecycle and persistence:** density tiers are 64/96/128 and UI state is explicitly session-only. Setters clamp ordinary numeric values but do not reject NaN; runtime validation remains necessary for imported data. Renderer context restoration rebuilds GPU objects and delegates LUT restoration to the owner. The renderer does not retain the LUT bytes or authored mesh for that purpose. Required saved deformation, undo, export snapshots and density-change preservation cannot be inferred from these files alone. This is an optional creative extension with substantially more scope than replacing an environment sampler; it does not displace environment reflection as the provisional leading appearance improvement.

## Deformation host follow-through: preserve artwork across quality changes and exports

**Scope:** complete read of [liquifyMode.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/gradient-explorer/fullscreen/modes/liquifyMode.tsx), resolving the caller questions left by the preceding mesh/renderer review. This is a source-level adoption assessment; interaction and export behavior were not exercised in a browser.

**Quality changes must not become artwork changes.** The host rebuilds a fresh `LiquifyMesh` and renderer when density changes. It preserves dither/subdivision settings and reloads the current LUT, but does not transfer handles, brush displacement or live simulation state. Leaving and remounting this mode likewise creates a fresh mesh. No undo or sculpt serialization is supplied in this module. For a RFF deformation or material-mask editor, mesh density should either resample the authored representation or be presented as an explicit reset operation. Store the authored deformation independently of transient render buffers so changing output quality, reopening the editor or recovering resources can preserve it. This is a prerequisite for an adoptable feature, not a suggestion to change RFF's binary formats casually.

**Gesture ownership and coordinates need one definition.** Pointer capture is used, and both pointer-up and pointer-cancel finish the gesture. However, the host keeps one shared drag/paint state without tracking an owning pointer ID, and does not listen for lost capture here. Multiple pointers or a capture-loss path therefore need separate validation. Grab selection includes fixed user pins and forwards them to the core's permissive move method; the earlier uncertainty is resolved: this host does not enforce pin immobility when grabbing. New handles are inserted directly at the pointer's current normalized coordinates, with no inverse mapping through the existing deformation.

The visible grab ring uses a pixel radius based on the shorter canvas side, while nearest-handle selection uses a circular radius in normalized mesh space. These regions differ on a rectangular canvas. RFF should use the same screen-space distance for hit testing and the displayed handle affordance, while retaining an explicit rest-space coordinate for deformation constraints. Pointer cancellation should end a stroke without leaving painting active, and a multi-pointer policy should avoid one pointer finishing another's stroke.

**Input frequency is part of the effect.** A radial brush applies once on press, then once per pointer-move event. Push consumes event-to-event displacement; other brush types use a fixed operation per call. There is no stroke resampling or elapsed-time scaling here, so equivalent physical drags delivered at different event rates can produce different twirls, pulls or smoothing. Global smoothing runs once per animation frame. The host clamps elapsed time for physics, but that does not change the per-call brush/smoothing semantics identified in the core. For RFF, define strokes by a reproducible distance/time policy if saved edits or video replay are expected to match. The Restore tooltip says 'toward flat', while the core retains handle deformation; label it according to the actual brush-only restoration scope.

**Idle work can be separated from visible animation.** The host schedules frames continuously. With physics off it still copies the sculpt into live positions, clears velocity, uploads/draws the mesh and redraws overlay handles each frame. The solver's settled early-out does not stop those other costs. A RFF implementation could use geometry, palette, size, cursor-overlay and asset-readiness revisions to redraw only what changed, keeping continuous ticks for active simulation or deliberate continuous smoothing. This is a dependency-based optimization opportunity, not a measured GMT or RFF speedup. Keep the editable state independent of this scheduling choice.

**Freezing the simulation is only part of an export snapshot.** `renderAt` sets a boolean that makes the animation loop skip simulation and drawing, resizes the visible GL backing store, draws current positions, encodes a PNG, and restores size and drawing in `finally`. It resets the last-frame timestamp to avoid treating the export pause as a large physics step. These are useful mechanisms. Yet pointer handlers, store subscriptions, resize callbacks, palette updates and disposal remain enabled while encoding is awaited. They can mutate mesh state, rebuild the renderer or change dimensions; overlapping exports are not serialized by the boolean itself. Cleanup refers to the current mutable renderer/canvas variables rather than a captured export instance.

For RFF, capture the mesh/appearance revision and use an isolated export target, or protect the full export transaction and restore its exact owned resources. Merely freezing an animation loop does not guarantee an unchanged artwork snapshot. The immediate `exportCanvas` path draws `mesh.pos` without first syncing newly authored changes; between an input event and the next animation tick that can be the previous live shape. Decide whether an export captures the displayed image or the latest accepted edit, and synchronize accordingly. The separate overlay canvas keeps handles out of exported pixels, a pattern worth retaining.

**Recovery and readiness have narrower meanings.** The restoration callback reuploads the LUT and subdivision setting, confirming that those resources are restored by this host. CPU mesh state remains outside the renderer, so ordinary GL context restoration need not recreate the sculpt. Density rebuilding is different and currently resets it. Initial readiness is signaled after the first draw call, without waiting for noise readiness or measured presentation. Errors during the initial renderer construction are reported, but later density rebuilds do not use that same local error handler. A production RFF feature should define readiness, recoverable rebuild failure and retained authored state explicitly.

**RFF decision:** retain the separation of authored shape, optional motion and clean export pixels, while designing persistence, deterministic strokes and export ownership before implementation. These supporting requirements make deformation a larger optional feature than environment reflection; they do not justify changing the current provisional priority.

## Curve-guided gradient fields: a controllable source for material masks

**Scope:** complete read of [splineMode.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/gradient-explorer/fullscreen/modes/splineMode.tsx), including tessellation, the fragment shader, data-texture caching and editing/export integration. This is a gradient-coordinate field, not a physical light, a solved diffusion equation or a demonstrated implementation of another product's freeform-gradient algorithm. Historical visual and portability claims in comments were not rerun.

**How the field is built.** The CPU tessellates control points with centripetal Catmull-Rom and constructs a normalized polyline arc coordinate. Each RGBA32F texel stores position, arc coordinate and forward segment length. For every output pixel, the shader visits up to 63 segments, projects onto each finite segment and obtains its nearest distance and interpolated arc coordinate. It averages those coordinates with weight `segmentLength / (distanceSquared + core)`, then performs one gradient lookup. Spread sets the positive core through a squared control, moving from locally concentrated influence toward a broad wash. Depth adds nearest-path distance to the lookup coordinate; it no longer darkens or brightens RGB directly, despite older introductory and tooltip descriptions.

For RFF, a curve-guided scalar could author a sweeping roughness/coating mask, a colored decorative layer, or an emissive stripe with separate intensity. It could also help design an environment texture, but its screen-space metric must first be replaced or interpreted in a declared directional domain. The shader blends coordinates before lookup, not the corresponding colors. With a nonlinear or cyclic palette those are different results; choose the intended effect explicitly. A true luminous strip would additionally need a distance-to-coverage falloff and the appropriate HDR/emission path. Calling the present Depth control a glow would misdescribe its operation.

**Length weighting improves consistency but is not exact integration.** Weighting by segment length reduces sensitivity to how many samples describe a region. However, each segment is represented using the distance and coordinate at its closest point, not an integral of a spatially varying kernel over that segment. Splitting a long segment can change its contribution. Therefore the source's claim that only path shape matters, independent of sampling, is too strong. Nonzero core also means even a point on the curve receives other segments' contributions; exact interpolation of its arc coordinate is not guaranteed. RFF should compare simple straight lines, close parallel arms, crossings and highly curved sections while increasing tessellation, and specify the approximation tolerance rather than promising exact diffusion.

The shader computes distances after scaling x by output aspect, while CPU arc and segment lengths use unscaled normalized UV. Those are distinct metrics. If the intended source is uniform per unit screen length, its stored weights and arc coordinate need the same metric as the distance calculation. If UV-length coloring is intentional, preserve that definition across preview and export instead of silently changing it. Thin bands, nearby arms and sharp LUT transitions also need pixel-footprint filtering; a soft distance kernel alone is not antialiasing of the final lookup.

**Extension carries endpoint coordinates.** Positive extension adds straight segments at both ends along the sampled terminal directions. The head carries coordinate zero, the tail coordinate one, while the original curve retains its zero-to-one range. It does not renormalize the entire extended path as an older function comment says. Extension points are denser near the joins; the original curve is resampled to make space within the 64-point budget. This is a useful way to keep end colors extending outward, but changing extension still changes field contributions and can change the curve's polygonal approximation. It is not complete independence from Spread or from shape sampling.

**Budget boundaries are part of the visual contract.** Base tessellation allocates at least three subdivisions to each control interval while silently ignoring pushed vertices beyond 64. With 23 controls this requests 67 vertices; with 24 it requests 70, exceeding the buffer even though the editor allows 24 controls. Consequently the last part of the requested path can be omitted. The exported setter accepts any list with at least two points, without that editor maximum or finite-coordinate validation. A RFF port should fit the entire curve into a checked budget, preserve endpoints, and use curvature/error-aware allocation or a clearly stated limit. Do not inherit the comments' blanket no-overshoot/no-self-intersection claim: this function neither checks global crossings nor proves that every control configuration stays inside its control polygon.

**Cache exactly the state being rendered.** The base tessellation uses a point revision; extension caches round its value to four decimal places. Sub-four-decimal changes can therefore reuse the earlier geometry, even though an arbitrary numeric value may reach the API. The per-context texture cache uses the same rounded key and does not explicitly delete the texture or track context-restoration generations in this module. A WeakMap controls JavaScript reachability, not validity of a restored GPU resource. For RFF, give the curve field explicit ownership, full parameter revisions and device-generation invalidation. A cached curve field or rasterized mask could amortize the up-to-63-segment per-pixel work when only the palette changes, provided its precision and export-scale filtering remain sufficient.

**Editing and reproducibility.** Points live in a module-level session store that survives mode switches but is not saved document state. Scalars are resolved from the shared parameter context, while shader upload reads the live point store. Thus the generic export snapshot does not independently capture the curve. The visible editor also overlays a second compositor, sharing the resolved palette and shader but owning separate GPU resources; shared source alone does not prove byte-identical output if sizes, asset readiness or state revisions differ. Preserve a single effective curve/appearance snapshot for RFF preview, saved settings and export.

The editor picks handles and the path in screen pixels, uses pointer capture and finishes on cancel. It does not track an owning pointer ID or handle lost capture here. At the point limit, insertion returns an existing selection (or zero), which the drag handler then treats as the point to move; that is not a clean insertion refusal. Path insertion metadata can also select index zero near the first sampled endpoint even though the user clicked the first segment. These boundary cases belong in an eventual RFF editing contract, along with undo and finite-value validation, rather than being copied with the shader.

**RFF-facing decision:** curve-authored masks are a useful optional complement to environment reflection and procedural gradient fields. Start from the mathematical behavior desired by the user, preserve the full curve under resource limits, and verify licensing of named spline/weighting implementations before adapting code. No visual benefit or speedup has been measured in RFF, and this batch changes documentation only.

## Fractal-mode host: stable appearance controls and reproducible export timing

**Scope:** complete reads of [fractalStore.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/gradient-explorer/fullscreen/modes/fractal/fractalStore.ts) and [fractalMode.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/gradient-explorer/fullscreen/modes/fractalMode.tsx), following the already-reviewed shared renderer and kernel. These files establish which shader features this host actually exposes, how updates trigger reference builds, and what an export captures.

**Separate useful control defaults from persistent artistic choices.** The picker exposes six modes: iteration, bands, angle, potential, stripe and distance. Kernel support for additional traps or interior modes does not mean those features are available in this toolbar. Changing mapping automatically resets density to a per-mode legacy default or one under normalized coloring. Enabling normalization also resets density, while disabling it keeps the new value rather than restoring the former legacy setting. This gives a usable starting point but does not preserve a user's per-mode tuning. For RFF, consider retaining independent field/mapping settings when switching modes, while keeping an explicit reset-to-default action. Do not alter stable palette recipes to implement these viewing controls.

The fit anchor remains an explicit offset/scale, reset to zero and 0.125, despite older comments naming scale one as identity. The actual rate floor is 0.001 and bailout floor is one, not the different values in some comments. Angle setters accept finite radians without wrapping, and the mapping setter coerces to an integer without validating the supported set. Phase lacks the finite guard used by most other numeric setters; fit scale is finite-checked but may be nonpositive. These are reasons to define one validated setting contract across UI, renderer and imported state, rather than treating slider limits as validation.

Lighting remains enabled in stored/rendered parameters when normalization is switched off, even though its controls disappear. The same distinction applies to hidden bailout controls. For RFF material controls, hiding a dependent editor must have a defined relationship to whether the effect remains active. The one-shot Fit button ignores its returned success/failure boolean and does not wait for a matching converged image here. A useful fit action should describe the image generation it analyzed and give feedback when no usable range exists.

**Reuse configuration wiring, but distinguish image readiness.** One `colourParams` mapping is shared by initialization, live subscription and context restoration, reducing divergent settings across those paths. The restore callback explicitly rebuilds the deep reference after reapplying size/LUT/state; this resolves the earlier renderer-only uncertainty about its owner. Initial `onReady`, however, fires after the first render call, not after the asynchronous reference is accepted or temporal sampling converges. A RFF preview can be responsive while work continues, but should distinguish a valid final-quality frame from an initial fallback when that difference matters.

Navigation tracks pointer IDs, uses the first two pointers for pinch, and reseeds when gestures change between one and two fingers. Reference builds are debounced after wheel/pinch updates and requested when the last pointer releases. Single-pointer moves do not schedule intermediate builds. This demonstrates a concrete interaction-versus-reference-build separation; it does not establish that an old reference remains valid for arbitrarily long drags. The handler normalizes wheel delta units, but does not locally prevent default scrolling or handle lost pointer capture. Preserve RFF's existing high-precision offset navigation and define gesture cancellation plus reference validity independently of a debounce timer.

**Drive animation from time, not render count.** Palette cycling adds 1/480 of a turn per animation callback. Its nominal eight-second cycle is therefore specific to 60 callbacks per second. The local phase accumulator is initialized once at mount, not reseeded from the latest manually edited phase when cycling begins. When cycling stops, the local value is committed to the store. In the reviewed renderer, phase participates in the accumulation hash; changing it each frame resets temporal accumulation, so cycling does not receive the same converged antialiasing as a stationary frame. For RFF palette or environment animation, evaluate phase/orientation from the explicit preview/export time and reuse numerical fields where possible. Rendering more frames for quality must not advance animation time.

**An export burst is not a full export-quality guarantee.** The host resizes the visible renderer, calls render 24 times, awaits PNG encoding, restores the current container size and renders once more. There is no `finally` around restoration, no explicit animation freeze and no wait for pending reference builds. While the synchronous burst does not yield to animation callbacks, the asynchronous encoding interval allows other callbacks, gestures, settings and resize operations to proceed. Concurrent exports are not serialized here. A source-level transaction is therefore weaker than the comments' claim that the visible view survives verbatim in every case.

The renderer's normal convergence cap is 128 frames; 24 is a chosen export budget, not evidence of equivalent convergence. With its sixteen-cell grid and one sample per frame, a fresh 24-frame burst covers one complete initial round and only half the next, so cell coverage is unequal at that stopping point. If the requested size does not change the backing store, accumulation is not necessarily reset and the starting sample count can differ. Report actual sample/quality conditions rather than just the number of render calls. The historical sub-second/visually-noiseless export statement was not reproduced.

Changing export aspect also changes the visible region, while the existing reference selection and its view-dependent calibration are not rebuilt by this function. That requires validity checks, not an assumption that an unchanged center and zoom make every reference-derived resource suitable. The intended 1,600-pixel renderer cap remains a separate limitation from the output request. RFF should use a captured appearance/view state, an export-specific target and sampling budget, and the corresponding numerical validity region. Restore or retain the preview even on failure.

**Saved appearance requires more than coordinates.** The host's handoff includes high/low center words and basic palette mapping, but its `maxIter` is the renderer's parameter value rather than the computed effective automatic/deep cap. This confirms that the earlier limited handoff cannot promise the same numerical budget. Its diagnostic coordinate JSON also omits several lighting/normalization/bailout settings. Keep diagnostic snapshots distinct from reproducible scene recipes; a RFF scene or image embed should capture the actual appearance state needed to reproduce the output while preserving existing format compatibility.

**RFF-facing outcome:** the most useful host-level lessons are shared configuration mapping, explicit color-fit anchors, time-based animation, reuse of expensive numerical fields and isolated export snapshots. They support the previously proposed shader improvements; they are not evidence that GMT's shallow/deep arithmetic should replace RFF's MPA and precision strategy. This batch changes documentation and coverage only.

## Rendering-design reconciliation: consistent reflection, sample accounting and shader variants

**Scope:** full reads of [ADR-0100](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/docs/adr/0100-navigation-renders-same-integrand-as-final.md), [ADR-0067](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/docs/adr/0067-bucket-render-equal-spp-no-convergence.md), [ADR-0079](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/docs/adr/0079-shader-compiler-profile-seam.md), and [ADR-0043](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/docs/adr/0043-17-position-shader-assembly.md). Selected current-source checks were made in the already-reviewed ray, reflection, volumetric, shader builder/factory and bucket-runner implementations. Documented historical tests, timings and visual sign-offs were not rerun.

**Keep the reflection model stable through interaction.** ADR-0100 explains that using a sharp mirror for the first/navigation sample and a rough glossy model for subsequent samples mixed different shading models into one running mean. Its chosen response is to retain the glossy sampling model while freezing the noise source during the first/navigation phase. Current reflection code indeed branches on roughness for glossy sampling, with the blend-factor test choosing stable versus animated noise. Ray generation still uses that blend-factor test, including for primary jitter; it is not a direct measurement of user interaction. A stationary first sample also satisfies it.

For RFF's proposed environment reflection, preserve the same roughness, environment orientation, BRDF approximation and color domain during interaction and final rendering. Reduce sample count or update frequency under an explicit preview policy rather than silently substituting a sharp mirror and accumulating it as equivalent glossy radiance. If a deliberately different preview is useful, start a fresh compatible final history. A single incompatible seed contributes a finite-sample error proportional to its weight; it does not establish a permanent asymptotic bias if all later samples are valid and its weight tends to zero. Conversely, a deterministic center sample is not automatically an unbiased random estimator of a pixel-area integral merely because it uses the same shading function. Keep shading-model consistency and sampling-distribution correctness separate.

The current volumetric chunk retains a reduced gate probability in the first/navigation phase and multiplies accepted contributions by its reciprocal. That is the intended probability-compensation mechanism documented by the ADR. It supports the idea of trading variance for work, but the reciprocal alone does not prove that the full random sequence, correlations and estimator are unbiased. RFF's deterministic environment lookup does not need to acquire a volumetric or path-tracing subsystem to benefit from the interaction policy.

**Equal sample counts are one seam condition.** ADR-0067 removes convergence-based per-bucket stopping and retains a fixed sample cap. Current runner code computes completed samples as `bucketFrameCount - 1` before deciding whether to composite, matching the documented submission-order rationale. The document also correctly distinguishes a shrinking difference between consecutive running means from a direct quality estimate: that difference can become small as the sample count grows even while visible noise remains.

For RFF, matched sample count is a useful baseline when validating tiled reflection, masks and other stochastic effects. It is not, by itself, proof of seamless output. Global pixel coordinates, sample identities and weights, compatible field/normal evaluation, asset LOD, postprocessing neighborhoods and completed GPU work must also match. ADR-0067 itself leaves multi-image-tile postprocessing seams unresolved. Its historical claim of bit-identical matched-SPP buckets applies to the cited experiment, not every future effect or tile implementation. Preserve RFF's own output-quality controls; do not import the document's suggested sample-count knee as a measured RFF optimum.

**Separate shader mechanism from artistic presets.** ADR-0079 consolidates compile-time feature bundles around the same parameter metadata used by manual controls, with application-specific profiles registered before store construction. Its important transferable idea is one definition of which settings change a compiled variant and which merely update runtime values. For RFF, adding environment source types or optional material fields should have explicit pipeline/descriptor compatibility and invalidation rules. A quality preset must not silently change precision-sensitive fractal math or overwrite artistic choices without an intentional policy.

The ADR's estimator sums annotated costs over state and uses the same mechanism for preset estimates. Sharing a formula can reconcile displayed estimates, but does not turn them into measured compile durations or a universal cost model. Registration order and late-profile behavior are part of the initialization contract. This document reconciles historical duplicate systems; it is not evidence that RFF needs a new user-facing shader compiler panel.

**Verify every shader variant's actual order.** ADR-0043 describes seventeen ordered assembly positions and always invoking feature injection so disabled features can provide compatible entry points. Current ShaderFactory still invokes `inject` in its feature loop, and the builder has explicit stage storage. This is a useful extension pattern: optional effects should keep call signatures and resource declarations coherent across enabled/disabled combinations. Textual chunk deduplication is not symbol-level dependency resolution or a proof against duplicate definitions.

The current ShaderBuilder header is more precise than the historical ADR: Physics keeps positions through nine plus a simplified trace, and Physics/Histogram place headers after coloring rather than at the Main variant's position. The main sequence therefore cannot be treated as an identical universal ordering. Existing preprocessor-only headers may tolerate this, while future declarations can introduce variant-specific dependencies. For RFF, compile or otherwise validate the actual graphics/compute/export variants affected by a new shared shader helper, including disabled paths, and match GLSL interfaces to the C++ pipeline configuration. Do not copy an arbitrary seventeen-stage architecture merely because GMT uses it.

**RFF-facing outcome:** these documents reinforce stable roughness-aware reflection during interaction, explicit history compatibility, consistent full-image sampling and coherent shader interfaces. They add implementation conditions to the environment-reflection proposal without claiming runtime validation or changing its provisional priority.

## Deep-zoom design documents: distinguish intended guarantees from measured evidence

**Scope:** full reads of [ADR-0065](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/docs/adr/0065-deep-zoom-auto-reference-glitch-fix.md) and [ADR-0066](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/docs/adr/0066-deep-zoom-nucleus-reference.md), reconciled against the previously fully reviewed reference builder, worker, calibration and kernel. Their named reference-renderer comparisons and historical screenshots/timings are document claims, not independent results produced by this audit.

These documents explain why shader appearance and acceleration must be reviewed together: skipped orbit intervals can omit the statistics used by stripes, traps, distance and lighting. The following qualifications prevent transferring stronger guarantees to RFF than the implementation supports.

| Documented intention | Current-source evidence and limit | RFF adoption decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Find a reference that outlasts every visible pixel. | The finite coarse/refined candidate search chooses among tested points and can stop at the first one surviving its cap. It is not an exhaustive whole-view bound. | Evaluate reference selection as a performance heuristic; retain correctness detection/fallback independent of candidate ranking. Do not cap requested pixel work solely from an assumed deepest sample. |
| Build a cheap one-period reference before the fallback work. | The public builder first creates the ordinary orbit, may relocate/rebuild it, and only then attempts a nucleus. Adoption reduces the retained orbit and subsequent table size; it does not erase the already-paid long-orbit construction. | Measure end-to-end preparation latency and peak memory separately from final reference size before prioritizing a change to RFF's compressed reference machinery. |
| Adopt an exact nucleus inside the view, with unlimited exact wrapping. | Verification reads a packed terminal residual with an absolute tolerance floor, exports a double-double center and allows a location within eight half-diagonals. Finite-precision generation/packing and repeated-wrap errors remain. | Preserve the actual high-precision center and establish an error budget relative to output pixel spacing; mathematical exact periodicity is not a certificate for its numerical representation. |
| Nucleus adoption makes the exterior-ring LA exclusion unnecessary for those views. | The current `laUnsafe` classification still runs after adoption whenever its mode/non-escape conditions hold; it does not require `period == 0`. | Use current eligibility checks rather than the historical narrative when comparing accelerator coverage. Do not propose a redundant or incorrectly scoped RFF shortcut. |
| Calibration finds the largest safe threshold against ground truth. | It compares a finite sample grid against a related CPU perturbation baseline; periodic references bypass it because the CPU walk differs, and the worker disables AT for periodic results. | Treat calibration as diagnostic evidence with stated coverage. Use an independent precision-preserving reference for acceptance; a shared numerical error can pass an agreement test. |
| Per-iteration color modes become correct by bypassing skips. | The current gate also includes interior tracking. It avoids omitted statistics, but still inherits derivative-formula, float-range and hard-loop-cap limitations documented in the kernel review. | Validate each displayed observable and the actual completed iteration budget. Bypassing acceleration is not a proof of all remaining arithmetic and is not automatically acceptable production performance. |

**Rebasing is not the same operation as periodic wrapping.** Both ADRs use wording that risks treating any restart at reference index zero as valid only for a periodic reference. An ordinary perturbation rebase changes the delta to the current pixel state relative to the new reference origin; periodic wrapping instead reuses an orbit segment at its period boundary without the same delta reset. Their correctness conditions and finite-precision errors must be derived from the actual recurrence and continuation state. Do not use this historical shorthand as a reason to replace or restrict RFF's existing MPA/perturbation logic. In particular, RFF's MPA is not BLA and is not identified with GMT's LA table by these documents.

The cited central-color-distribution comparisons can detect large blocks in selected scenes but do not certify individual pixel escape counts, derivatives, trap minima, thin filaments or every zoom depth. Likewise, a cursor-anchoring test at one range cannot establish unlimited double-double coordinate resolution. Reuse the supplied scenes as candidate regression inputs, then add independent numerical/field comparisons and representative output resolutions before claiming a RFF improvement. No historical timings or visual tests were rerun here.

**RFF-facing conclusion:** these ADRs strengthen the requirement that any new orbit-driven shader feature preserve its statistics across accelerated intervals. They do not support replacing RFF's mature precision/compression strategy with the inspected float32 path. Environment reflection based on existing relief normals remains a more direct appearance extension because it does not inherently require collecting additional per-iteration orbit history.

## Live palette updates: defer fitting without freezing the shader input

The complete read of [ADR-0117](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/docs/adr/0117-one-sort-per-render-not-one-per-texel.md), reconciled with selected current sections of `utils/colorUtils.ts`, `components/AdvancedGradientEditor.tsx`, `components/gradient/rampMode.ts` and `palette/store/workingStore.ts`, supplies a useful host-side companion to the shader proposals. This is an interaction/preparation optimization, not evidence that a GPU shader becomes faster.

**Separate authoritative appearance from editable approximation.** A processed gradient already has an output ramp. Fitting that ramp to editable stops, then resampling those stops to display the result, adds both work and approximation. GMT's current strip path can paint the supplied ramp directly; authored stop gradients retain their stop-sampling route. During interaction, the working store holds the prior fit when either its parameter bracket or the engine interaction flag is active, while the output ramp continues to update. Merely recoloring fixed stop positions was an intermediate design: it cannot reproduce a narrow feature that moves between those positions. The document's section 6 supersedes section 5 as the source for painting the output bar.

**RFF application:** for future environment-gradient or material-mask editors, keep the evaluated appearance resource separate from the handles used to edit or approximate it. Rebuild/upload the current appearance when its dependencies change, defer expensive handle fitting until release, and make preview and export consume the same committed evaluation. This is an adoption requirement, not a claim that RFF currently performs GMT's redundant fit. RFF already has palette upload preparation in [PaletteBandLine.hpp](../src/rff2/vulkan/PaletteBandLine.hpp), including distinct lined and unlined uses; a shared resource must preserve those consumer semantics rather than treating every palette buffer as interchangeable. Do not convert existing recipe storage to a fitted or quantized gradient as part of this optimization.

**Move preparation outside repeated sampling.** GMT exports the same sampling core as `sampleSortedStops`, placing the ascending-position precondition on the caller. The strip sorts once, then samples each output column. General-purpose unsorted-input handling remains useful at external boundaries. For a RFF implementation, prefer an explicitly prepared immutable stop representation, including parsed colors and interpolation state, when many samples share it. The optimization should preserve empty-gradient behavior, duplicate-position ordering, hard edges, interpolation/color-space conventions and exact authored recipe generation.

**Reconcile the cache with current code.** The ADR describes a cache bounded by distinct color literals, but current `colorUtils.ts` additionally enforces `HEX_CACHE_CAP = 4096` and clears the map before inserting a new miss at the cap. It caches packed values, including invalid parses, and returns a fresh RGB object to callers. Thus an unbounded-cache warning based solely on the historical document would be incorrect. Whole-cache eviction is bounded but may generate repeated misses under a large changing working set; no evidence here establishes that RFF needs this specific string cache. Preparing numeric colors once per resource is the more relevant native-code design.

**Preview fidelity has a declared resolution.** The strip's ramp path selects nearest texels; a 256-entry source spans six columns per texel at width 1536. This preserves that discrete ramp's edges but does not prove faithful reconstruction of a continuous gradient, nor does it imply that channel quantization and spatial sampling resolution are the same quantity. The current source-selection helper also gives a local stop-reduction preview precedence over the host ramp, extending the ADR's older ordering. A RFF editor should identify whether it displays authored stops, a candidate edit, or the actual sampled shader resource. Do not apply this nearest-neighbor editor rule indiscriminately to environment minification or roughness filtering.

**Acceptance evidence:** during a drag, assert both that the output changes and that it matches the current evaluated resource; agreement between two frozen previews is insufficient. Include moving narrow bands, hard transitions, changes in interpolation, empty inputs, release/cancel, and every input route that opens an interaction. Verify final preview/export agreement after fitting settles. Profile preparation, fitting, transfer and GPU rendering separately. The ADR's approximately 47% scripting reduction and reported frame rates are historical GMT observations, not reproduced measurements or RFF speedup estimates. No runtime tests were run in this documentation pass.

## Portable appearance assets: distinguish editable data from a recoverable preview

The complete reads of [ADR-0123](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/docs/adr/0123-the-gradient-file-is-a-png.md) and [installGradientFileClaim.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/palette/installGradientFileClaim.ts), with selected reconciliation of the previously reviewed PNG writer/reader and import router, refine the proposed environment-gradient and material-mask workflows. The transferable feature is an asset that carries an immediately visible preview and its versioned editable definition together.

**Two recovery levels, not one fidelity promise.** GMT embeds a gradients document in PNG text metadata. That document carries gradient configuration, names and optional grouping/provenance. The image independently represents 256 RGB8 samples per gradient in repeated opaque columns. A supported metadata-preserving load can recover configuration; a metadata-stripped load recognizes exact repeated pixel bands and recovers sampled ramps. The latter does not reconstruct authored stop positions, interpolation, bias, names or grouping. It also cannot recover scene-linear HDR intensities, transparency or sub-texel features that were absent from those display samples. Treat the ADR's phrase “exact colours” as exact recovery of the encoded ramp bytes under its reader constraints, not mathematical identity to every evaluation of the original gradient.

For RFF, a portable environment/material preset could carry a display thumbnail plus its original gradient definition, source color interpretation, intensity, orientation and filtering policy in versioned data. An HDR panorama requires its original radiance asset or an explicit dependency; an RGB8 thumbnail is not a replacement. Preserve existing `{presetId, seed}` recipe semantics and generator order. A new portable asset format should not silently replace stable recipe storage or alter the ordered ConfigIO stream.

**Pixel fallback is deliberately constrained.** The writer snaps a single gradient's width to a multiple of 256 within 256..4096 and repeats samples rather than interpolating them. The reader checks uniform column blocks and identical rows, with an opaque-alpha requirement when applicable. Resizing, resampling, color conversion, lossy sharing or added labels can invalidate that fallback or change recovered bytes. Fewest-band recognition is inherently ambiguous: two identical adjacent gradients can resemble one taller band after metadata removal. Large collections may carry more entries in metadata than the image's first 2,048 bands. Therefore the UI should describe the fallback as sampled appearance recovery, with count and metadata loss reported, rather than promise an unconditional collection round trip through arbitrary image editors.

**One parsing core still needs explicit entry-point policy.** The scene-file claim first filters supported filenames, asynchronously reads them, selects recognized gradient content, then imports within one synchronous undo bracket and returns unclaimed files to the scene loader. Current app startup registers it, and the inspected filtered-scene loader calls the claim before proceeding. This is useful separation: slow file reads need not keep an edit transaction open. It does not establish that every possible loading surface uses the claim; the installer explicitly excludes the pre-boot loading screen. Nor is the scene claim purely content-based: filename eligibility and stronger JSON-shape restrictions apply to avoid claiming scene documents.

The scene-claim guard rejects a PNG with a scene metadata key even if it also contains gradients. In contrast, the standalone gradient PNG reader tries usable gradient metadata before checking scene keys. This is an intentional distinction in the inspected routes, not a single universal priority rule. For RFF, define how conflicting embedded payloads are handled per entry point, and retain the original file until its intended destination is resolved. A compatible filename or a recognizable strip alone is not proof of asset provenance.

**Make successful import visible and reversible.** GMT imports recognized files into its gradient collection, summarizes imported/skipped outcomes, and reveals the destination panel when the result identifies one. The current installer also supplies a drop hint for gradient files, superseding the ADR update's older statement that the overlay only mentions scenes. For RFF, show the imported environment or mask in its destination and provide one undoable import action; a success message alone can leave the asset effectively undiscoverable. Keep unknown, failed and partially accepted files distinguishable, especially when an archive contains mixed content.

**Validation before adoption:** test editable-definition equality with metadata, sampled-byte equality without it, altered image dimensions, identical neighboring bands, over-cap collections, conflicting scene/gradient payloads, malformed or newer versions, partial archive imports and every registered picker/drop route. Confirm that a thumbnail cannot overwrite HDR radiance or authoring precision during recovery. No image round-trip, OS drag, browser test or RFF format change was performed in this documentation pass; historical test claims remain source-reported evidence.

## Render-scale controls: bind the visible setting to the actual rendering policy

Full reads of [ADR-0026](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/docs/adr/0026-render-scale-source-pluggable.md), [Viewport.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/plugins/Viewport.tsx), [ViewportModeControls.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/plugins/viewport/ViewportModeControls.tsx) and [resolutionPresets.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/data/resolutionPresets.ts) establish the host-facing contracts. The selected current app registration confirms that GMT's visible multiplier reads `aaLevel` and writes through `setAALevel`, while other hosts may use the generic `renderScale`. This avoids a control that updates a field its renderer never consumes.

**RFF adoption is coordination, not adding an absent draft concept.** [RenderScene.hpp](../src/rff2/ui/RenderScene.hpp) already declares `recomputeThreaded(..., bool lowResolution)` and tracks smooth-zoom draft/full-quality state. These declarations establish existing machinery, not its complete runtime policy. Tie any future environment-reflection quality control into that machinery using explicit dependencies: output dimensions, user sampling preference, temporary interaction scale and effect-specific filtering are different values. Reducing display resolution must not reduce perturbation precision or silently change the requested iteration semantics. On interaction end, the final generation must rebuild the required resources and replace the draft before it is presented as complete.

**The plugin's timing channels have different meanings.** `frameTick` delegates to the store's FPS reporting, while `reportRenderFps` is explicitly the delivered worker-frame readout and does not drive adaptive resolution through this API. A responsive interface can therefore coexist with slow rendered-frame delivery. For RFF, profile actual scene/shader completion separately from interface refresh and reference preparation; do not infer GPU headroom from an idle or fast UI loop. This review does not establish that changing a feedback source alone improves performance.

**Temporary hold and export suppression are different contracts.** The plugin delegates `holdAdaptive` as a temporary downscale hold and `suppressAdaptive` as the full-quality export mechanism. Its immediate interaction subscription only acts in manual mode, when enabled and not suppressed; smart mode leaves its decision to the adaptive tick. The comments additionally warn that the hold does not cover the algorithm's re-engagement seed. For RFF, specify which transitions a hold covers and use a separate, scoped export policy that restores prior state even after failure. Full spatial scale alone does not prove complete temporal sampling, completed reference work or adequate reflection filtering.

**Current implementation narrows historical guarantees.** ADR-0026 describes choosing the default/custom control once at boot. The implementation reads a mutable module-level source on each render; the setter neither freezes registration nor triggers a render, and uninstalling the viewport subscription does not clear the custom source. Separate components avoid conditional calls between the default and custom paths, but replacing one custom hook implementation with another at runtime still needs an explicit lifecycle policy. A native RFF adapter should similarly have a clear owner and avoid settings whose meaning changes while a dialog is open. This is a source-level contract observation, not a reproduced GMT runtime failure.

**Labels must describe dimensions rather than guarantee cost.** The current tooltip equates a 2× multiplier with 4× cost. Doubling both image dimensions gives approximately four times as many pixels before rounding, but total render time also includes fixed costs, reference preparation, memory traffic and scene-dependent work. The shared preset catalog usefully centralizes aspect ratios and sizes across viewport and export, but a “Skybox” aspect does not implement a panorama projection and a print-size label does not prove an encoder writes DPI metadata. Preserve the distinction when reusing preset ideas in RFF. The multiplier control is displayed only in Fixed mode here; that placement is a UI choice, not proof that scaling has no effect in another mode.

**Verification for a RFF change:** inspect the actual produced image/resource dimensions after each setting change, check that all controls share the same effective value, compare a settled preview with exported output, and test restoration after cancellation or export errors. Compare equal output quality when measuring reflection/filter costs. Keep precision and existing recipe/config contracts unchanged. This pass inspected source and documents only; no timing, rendering or adaptive-policy tests were run.

## Adaptive-quality state: restore exact final quality outside the resize deadband

A complete read of [viewportSlice.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/store/slices/viewportSlice.ts), followed by selected checks of the already reviewed adaptive algorithm and the suppression setter in `renderControlSlice.ts`, resolves implementation details behind the preceding viewport proposal. These findings define safeguards for a RFF adoption; they are not a proposal to prioritize repairs in GMT.

**Apply hysteresis to intermediate quality, not to completion.** The slice converts the algorithm's divisor to `targetQuality = 1 / result.scale`, but updates the exposed quality only when its relative change exceeds 5%. That test also applies when the algorithm returns exactly 1 for a settled or suppressed render. For example, an exposed quality of 0.96 differs from 1 by about 4.17% relative to the current value, so this function retains 0.96 even though its internal controller now says full resolution. The separately inspected suppression setter only changes its boolean; it does not directly set quality. This demonstrates a source-level limitation of this slice's contract, not a claim that GMT's worker/export path necessarily consumes this stale value.

For RFF, an interactive controller can use a deadband to avoid repeated image reallocations, but settling, export entry and explicit full-quality requests should force the exact target and await its completed resource generation. Validate actual allocated/rendered dimensions, not just the controller's ideal scale. Keep a distinction between requested, allocated and completed quality so a resize cannot be counted as a full-quality sample before it has taken effect.

**Report the timing that the controller actually consumes.** `reportFps(rawFps)` accepts a supplied rate and uses it for HUD fields, but does not pass that numeric rate into `tickAdaptiveResolution`. The algorithm receives `now` and infers cost/window rate from invocation timing; changing only the supplied number therefore does not substitute a different render timing source. The slice keeps a two-second timestamp window for its own computed display rate, and throttles ordinary HUD writes to 500 ms while allowing immediate quality changes. In RFF, wire a control loop to completed relevant rendering work or an explicitly defined timing source. GPU pass timing, CPU reference preparation and UI callback cadence must remain distinguishable.

**Keep controller state aligned with what was rendered.** The pure algorithm estimates full-resolution cost as tick time multiplied by its internal downsample divisor squared. In the slice, a small divisor change can be withheld from consumers by the 5% deadband. Consequently internal scale and applied scale need not agree, and neither invocation time nor that normalized estimate is automatically a measurement of GPU work at the allocated dimensions. The mechanism is a useful heuristic for pixel-dominated workloads, with saturation/stall guards, but RFF's reference preparation and mixed post-processing costs do not all scale with pixel count. Feed applied scale back to any estimator and invalidate stale estimates after material/filter changes when appropriate.

**Ownership and reset matter.** The adaptive state, timestamp list, hold deadline and HUD throttle timestamp are module-level variables, shared by slice instances in that module. Creating a fresh store does not itself reset them. A RFF controller should belong to its renderer/view lifetime, with defined reset behavior on scene replacement, device/resource recreation, and independent export contexts. A configuration setter here merges values without validating finiteness, and the generic render-scale clamp does not reject NaN; validate persistent or external inputs at the boundary rather than expecting clamping alone to make them valid.

**Do not infer knob wiring from names.** `activityGraceMs` supplies the default temporary-hold duration in this slice, but is not passed as the algorithm's `graceMs`; the adaptive tick uses its own default grace unless another caller supplies an override. The slice maps `engageOnAccumOnly` to `gateOnAccumOnly`, and converts interaction quality fraction to its reciprocal divisor. These conversions should be explicit in any RFF adapter. An identically named setting in a shared panel is not evidence that different render paths implement the same timing policy.

**Verification targets:** include a near-full quality such as 0.96 followed by settle/export, a delayed allocation, unchanged callback cadence with different supplied FPS values, a second controller instance, invalid numeric settings, and a long pause followed by renewed interaction. The expected RFF behavior is exact final dimensions and independent controller ownership without lowering fractal arithmetic precision. No runtime reproduction or performance measurement was conducted in this source-review pass.

## Shader configuration: batch structural edits and associate completion with a revision

Complete reads of [ShaderCompilerPanel.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine-gmt/components/panels/ShaderCompilerPanel.tsx) and [ShaderNode.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine-gmt/components/panels/flow/ShaderNode.tsx), with selected checks of the previously reviewed compile estimator and worker event transport, refine the host-side requirements for adding RFF materials and environment sources.

**Separate live values from structural changes.** The panel queues a parameter when its metadata says `onUpdate: 'compile'`, or when it is a compile-mode master toggle; other values go directly to the feature setter. It displays a merged candidate state and groups pending values by feature when Apply is pressed. This can avoid expensive rebuilds for each intermediate edit. For RFF, rotation, intensity and already-supported material parameters should normally update existing resources/constants, while genuine shader-layout or pipeline-variant changes require a deliberate rebuild path. Texture preprocessing is a third kind of work: changing an environment image or convolution policy is not automatically a shader compilation. Determine the actual Vulkan binding/layout requirements before assigning a control to a category.

The panel calls feature setters sequentially and clears its pending map immediately; it does not itself supply a single transactional compiler request or wait for the corresponding successful pipeline. Coalescing, failure recovery and activation belong to the scheduler/renderer. A RFF implementation should capture a coherent settings revision, prepare the necessary pipeline/resources, and activate the matching set only when ready. Newer edits must remain distinguishable from the revision currently compiling; failure must leave a usable prior result and the attempted settings available for correction. These are integration requirements, not evidence that this panel alone provides rollback.

**An estimate is neither a measurement nor a progress percentage.** Here the estimate uses the current scalability subsystem selection and render mode. The inspected estimator builds synthetic feature defaults plus tier overrides; the panel does not pass its merged pending parameter map. Therefore the displayed number is not necessarily an estimate of the exact candidate configuration being applied. The separate `compile_time` event reports a duration, and the panel clears its local compiling flag on that event. It also listens to `is_compiling`; the worker protocol permits a boolean or message, which the panel reduces to a boolean. For RFF, label estimates as estimates, key measurements to the relevant variant/device/cache state, and distinguish compilation, resource preparation and first displayed frame. An elapsed compile duration cannot establish that a matching rendered image has appeared.

**Persist meaningful state outside a temporary panel.** Pending edits are local React state, and the external `engine_queue` listener exists only while this component is mounted. Completion feedback is cleared by an uncancelled three-second timer with no job identity, so overlapping completion messages can affect the lifetime of newer feedback. A RFF design should own pending structural edits and job status in the renderer/document controller when they must survive closing a settings panel. Use revision-specific completion/failure records rather than making a transient panel the authority. No claim is made here about every actual panel-mount path or a reproduced lost edit.

**A visual node is not a typed shader contract.** The reviewed node component exposes two input handles only when the registry category string equals `Combiners (CSG)`; other nodes receive one. It delegates parameter edits, bindings and interaction start/end to shared actions and supplies enabled/disabled state. The displayed terminal labels are Input (Z) and Output (Distance), reflecting the current 3D formula workflow. This is not a ready-made 2D material graph. A future RFF graph for scalar masks, color, roughness or emission should derive ports and allowed connections from explicit value types, not category labels, and validate cycles/bindings in the compiler rather than relying on visible handles. Reusing the separation between node presentation, definitions and actions is useful without adopting a full graph editor as a prerequisite for environment reflection.

**Validation before a RFF implementation:** change several structural settings together and verify one coherent activation; edit again while work is pending; force a preparation failure; close/reopen the panel; and confirm that reported completion names the revision actually used by the next frame. For typed material channels, reject invalid connections before pipeline creation. Preserve descriptor/push-constant compatibility and existing precision. These files were read, not executed; no RFF compilation-time improvement or requirement for a dedicated compiler panel is established by this review.

## Shader inspection tools: preserve configuration evidence before comparing optimizations

Complete reads of GMT's `debug/dump-default-shader.mts`, `dump-direct-shader.mts`, `dump-pt-shader.mts`, `dump-cp-shader.mts` and `dump-est7-shader.mts` establish what these diagnostics can actually demonstrate. They are useful source-inspection aids, not performance benchmarks. None was executed in this pass.

**Capture reproducible variants.** The default dumper registers features/formulas, constructs a default configuration and writes generated Direct GLSL, with optional PathTracing output. Its all-features switch enables registered master toggles and keys ending in `Compiled`; it does not enumerate every option combination or establish a worst-case reachable program. The PT copy changes render mode but does not independently prove every PT feature is enabled. For RFF, archive the exact settings, source/compiled-module hashes, specialization values, descriptor layout, device/driver and pipeline-cache condition alongside a shader comparison. The environment-reflection proposal particularly needs separate legacy, gradient, image, roughness-filtered and clearcoat cases; one large shader does not represent every useful configuration.

**Source size is a triage signal.** The default script calls JavaScript string length “bytes” and counts selected declarations/calls with regular expressions. These counts can include inactive code or prototypes, omit other GLSL return types and texture operations, and do not represent the number of executed samples, driver-inlined instructions or live registers. Even an accurate source-line reduction is not a GPU-time measurement. In RFF, use such counts to locate duplicated work, then inspect compiled results and measure relevant GPU passes at equal image quality. Do not reduce precision or filter quality merely to improve a source-size statistic.

**A live dump needs a revision handshake.** The Direct/PT browser scripts first wait for a booted compiled program, apply feature changes, then poll for compilation to start and finish within bounded time windows. Those inner waits stop on timeout without throwing, and the final acceptance check only requires a stored generated fragment string longer than 1,000 characters. The selected WorkerProxy assignment confirms that `_lastGeneratedFrag` receives generated-code messages; it is not itself a successful-pipeline certificate. Consequently these scripts alone do not prove that the dumped source belongs to the newly requested successful variant. For a RFF diagnostic, associate request, generated module, pipeline creation and first rendered frame with one configuration revision, and fail explicitly if that revision never completes.

**Backend-specific evidence remains backend-specific.** The live scripts request Chrome with ANGLE/D3D11, a 1280×720 browser viewport and a running GMT development server. Their port check probes localhost using a simple port extraction even if a different host is supplied. They neither time the output shader nor capture image-equivalence evidence. A result from that environment must not be reported as a Vulkan speedup for RFF. Any future executable diagnostic should use explicit task-local output paths and cleanup on failure rather than inherit the scripts' machine-specific `h:/tmp` defaults. These scripts were only read here, so no browser/server or external output file was created.

**Presence checks are weaker than compilation and numerical correctness.** The cutting-plane script generates estimator 5, prints a brace-counted `getDist` body and lists selected references. It does not assert that the body exists or invoke a GPU compiler. The numerical-DE script generates estimator 7 for one fused sample scene, prints PRESENT/MISSING for several strings, and extracts text only up to the first closing brace. Missing symbols are reported but do not make the script fail; the “compiled” wording in its leading comment describes generated source too strongly. Neither script establishes conservative distance bounds, correct normals or preserved thin geometry. For RFF's 2D work, these 3D estimator paths are not substitutes for its perturbation/MPA math. Reuse the diagnostic practice of exposing a fully assembled program, not the unsupported implication that a generated function name proves an improvement.

**RFF acceptance sequence:** first verify the requested variant and successful Vulkan pipeline, then compare rendered output with the reference appearance across representative zooms and resolutions, and only then measure repeated GPU timings with warm/cold preparation separated. For environment filtering, include bright narrow strips, seams, increasing roughness and independent clearcoat response. Keep generated-code checks as quick structural guards; pair them with image/numerical checks appropriate to the actual effect. No new effectiveness score follows from reading these inspection tools.

## Shadow design reconciliation: share expensive work without changing visibility semantics

Full reads of [ADR-0074](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/docs/adr/0074-area-light-shadow-single-march.md), [ADR-0093](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/docs/adr/0093-zoom-normalized-shadow-march.md) and `debug/dump-shadow-shaders.mts`, reconciled against the current shadow implementation and the path tracer's shadow-selection block, distinguish useful mechanisms from obsolete implementation claims.

**One expensive traversal, with parameters selected first.** ADR-0074 historically replaced a separate hard sphere-light shadow call with a near-binary soft march at hardness 2000. The current path tracer instead generates one binary `GetHardShadow` call for the selected jitter-capability variant; optional runtime jitter changes the direction/distance before that call, and sphere lights restore the actual sampled target. The historical near-binary approximation is therefore not the current PT recommendation. Accumulating visibility toward samples on an area source produces soft boundaries; applying an additional analytic softness model is not automatically an equivalent estimator. The ADR itself left sphere-light visual confirmation outstanding, and its compiler-time numbers were not rerun here.

For RFF, the transferable pattern is to resolve material/mask/source choices before a shared expensive evaluation where the semantics permit it. Avoid duplicating an entire filtering or relief-evaluation path merely to select a few inputs. Do not assume that fewer source call sites guarantee faster Vulkan code: branch coherence, specialization, register pressure and compiler behavior require measurement. Adding a 3D shadow marcher is not a prerequisite for the proposed 2D environment reflection.

**Screen-footprint units make a more portable tolerance policy.** ADR-0093 scales shadow origins, starts, hit tolerances and minimum steps from the primary surface footprint, instead of fixed world distances. Current soft and hard shadow code uses `max(0.1 * surfEps, surfEps + epsRate * t)` and a compile ceiling of 512 iterations with a runtime step limit. The broad lesson for a future RFF height-field/contact-shadow effect is to define bias and sampling radius in units related to output resolution and the height field's coordinate system. A screen-space 2D relief implementation needs its own derivation; a 3D distance estimator and its step rules cannot be applied to an arbitrary iteration-value texture as though it were a conservative distance field.

The ADR's exactness wording needs qualification: the derivative of `|p + rd*t|` uses the direction of the current position. A fixed `epsRate` computed at the origin and then multiplied by travel is generally a local linear approximation to radial-distance growth, not its exact value along an arbitrary finite ray. It can be exact for an appropriately defined linear projected-depth model, but those models must not be conflated. Likewise, footprint scaling alone does not guarantee visibility at every zoom: finite precision, non-conservative fields, minimum steps and exhausted iteration limits remain relevant. The inspected hard march returns visible after its loop budget is exhausted; a RFF visibility design should distinguish a resolved clear ray from an unresolved one and choose a documented fallback.

**Hold scene state explicitly in comparisons.** The shadow dump script improves comparability by loading a formula preset once and capturing six configurations in one browser session, rather than reinitializing the camera for each run. However, not writing the camera again does not freeze simulation, time, adaptive size, accumulation or every uniform. Its quiet-window helper returns false on timeout and callers ignore that return. Shader and uniform snapshots are requested separately in parallel without an explicit common revision in the output. The script does not assert equality of supposedly invariant uniforms across files or render/timestamp them itself. Its hard/lite/robust tags also describe older configuration gates; current soft-shadow quality is selected with `uShadowQuality`, so labels alone do not prove distinct intended paths were exercised.

For RFF, capture one immutable reference scene and compare snapshots field by field, allowing only the deliberately varied effect settings. Record actual dimensions, sample state, resource identities and completed pipeline revision. Reject timeout or mismatched captures before timing. Include both image comparisons and pass timings, and distinguish preparation/compile savings from per-frame savings. Any reuse of distinctive named shadow formulas or MB3D-derived constants also requires verifying the original source/license and maintaining NOTICE; historical source-path references are not license evidence. No shadow benchmark or visual test was executed in this pass.

## Shadow throughput measurements: verify the workload before interpreting a speedup

Complete reads of [bench-shadow-fps.mts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/debug/bench-shadow-fps.mts) and [renderControlSlice.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/store/slices/renderControlSlice.ts) extend the preceding benchmark review. They offer a useful distinction between UI refresh and progressive rendering throughput, but do not establish any measured benefit for RFF.

**Measure completed useful work, with its unit stated.** The script measures the change in the worker proxy's accumulation count over an elapsed window, raises the sample cap to avoid convergence halting the run, and attempts to wait for samples before starting. This is accumulated samples per second, including scheduling and delivery effects; it is not a timestamp measurement of one shadow shader invocation. A reset during the interval is hidden by clamping a negative count difference to zero, and a pre-roll that never observes progress still proceeds after its timeout. A RFF benchmark should mark such windows invalid, track the generation of counted work and state whether the metric is completed image samples, completed frames or GPU pass duration.

**A requested resolution is insufficient evidence of equal work.** The script suppresses adaptive resolution and repeatedly requests Fixed dimensions, but sets the generic `renderScale`. The current GMT app registration inspected earlier uses `setAALevel`; the fully read render-control slice confirms that this setter updates `dpr` in Always/Auto AA modes. The script therefore does not prove that its logged supersampling multiplier reached GMT's actual drawing buffers. Its assumption of fixed pixel count needs an assertion of rendered dimensions and effective sampling policy. RFF already has optional GPU pass timing in [RenderSceneRenderer.hpp](../src/rff2/ui/RenderSceneRenderer.hpp); extend the comparison records around that existing facility rather than proposing that timing be added from scratch. Associate those measurements with actual dimensions and resource generations.

**The best repeat is not a typical result.** By default each configuration is measured twice and only the maximum rate is retained. That can reduce visible interruption effects but is an optimistic order statistic, not a median or variability estimate. The configurations also run in a fixed order. For RFF, retain individual samples, use paired/interleaved comparisons after a stated warm-up, report a central estimate and spread, and record thermal/cache conditions where they materially affect interpretation. Do not replace invalid intervals with zero or silently select only favorable runs.

**An unchanged shader does not imply unchanged ray cost.** The script expects nearly zero PT jitter cost because both cases use a hard-shadow routine. Jitter changes directions, which can change hit rates, traversal lengths and branch behavior even when the same compiled routine executes. Likewise, a faster stochastic configuration may have different variance; equal sample counts do not automatically provide equal image quality. For a prospective RFF relief-shadow effect, compare the error or visible stability as well as samples per second. For deterministic environment reflection, compare filtering quality and pass duration instead of importing a Monte Carlo sample-rate metric that does not apply.

**Treat the controls as state, not completed side effects.** The render-control slice exposes requested export, pause, sample-cap and region state; renderer-specific subscriptions own their consequences. In particular `setSampleCap` is a plain mutation despite the nearby comment that capping resets accumulation, and `setRenderMode` does not itself compile a pipeline. The benchmark's compile detection polls a boolean, ignores a false result from its quiet-window helper, and does not verify successful completion for the requested revision. A brief compile can also occur between polls. Runtime-toggle claims require a build/revision counter or authoritative completion event, not failure to observe a transient flag.

**RFF-facing result:** evaluate new environment or material features against an immutable baseline with equal effective resolution, known completed settings and an appropriate image-quality target. Separate setup/compile time, CPU work, GPU pass time and presentation throughput. Preserve all measured repeats and reject reset/timeout windows. The source's historical Hard/Lite/Robust configuration labels remain subject to the current shader-gate reconciliation described above. This pass ran no browser benchmark, GPU timing or rendering test.

## Renderer integration: separate interaction, animation and diagnostic overhead

Complete reads of `engine-gmt/renderer/bindings.ts`, `install.ts`, `renderInteractionState.ts` and `perfProbe.ts`, plus selected current tick-driver/engine consumers, add concrete integration requirements for RFF appearance features.

**Keep three activity states distinct.** GMT's pure interaction adapter carries general gesture activity, autonomous animation and the narrower subset of gestures used to hold accumulation. Playback is combined with enabled modulation sources, while the hold subset comes separately from the caller. The current engine explicitly excludes animated scenes from progressive tiling: repeatedly invalidating the image would otherwise restart the band schedule before the rest of the frame updates. This consumer is active despite the adapter's older phase comments saying the fields are unused. For RFF's animated environment rotation or material masks, distinguish a changing appearance from camera movement and from a static image awaiting refinement. A live color edit must update the whole required image rather than inherit a camera-specific hold that freezes its preview.

The modulation predicate checks enabled LFO entries and enabled audio-sourced rules with their master gates. It does not prove that values numerically change on each frame, that audio currently has a nonzero signal, or that every enabled source affects a visible parameter. Treat it as an activity eligibility policy. A RFF scheduler should preserve responsiveness while allowing genuinely static outputs to settle; deriving that from actual appearance revisions can be more precise than a permanent enabled flag.

**Initialize resources after their consumer exists.** GMT installation explicitly pushes pause and sample-cap state when the worker reports booted, because change-only subscriptions do not deliver initial values and earlier messages may precede engine creation. The renderer binding layer translates generic settings into MSAA configuration, lighting mode and region uniforms. For RFF, replay the complete relevant appearance state after device/pipeline recreation: environment texture selection, preprocessing generation, orientation and strengths must agree before presenting a recovered frame. Installing a change listener alone does not establish initial synchronization.

The binding function's header calls it idempotent, but the function itself creates subscriptions on every call; the normal installer supplies the one-time guard and discards the returned disposer. Repeated installer calls also retain the first callbacks. Distinguish those ownership layers when adopting the pattern. Region minimum/maximum are emitted as two events, whereas effective MSAA is one config payload; the binding alone does not prove atomic application of a pair of region updates. RFF's renderer should apply a coherent revision of coupled values, including descriptor resources and matching shader constants.
