## Configuration diffs: preserve source precision and explicit change semantics

Full reads of `engine/managers/ConfigManager.ts`, `engine/FractalEvents.ts` and `engine/features/types.ts` refine the shared-engine integration advice. This generic manager is distinct from GMT's richer `engine-gmt` manager reviewed earlier; its behavior must not be attributed automatically to every GMT application path.

**Use per-parameter invalidation rules with immutable source values.** The manager maps parameter metadata to compilation and accumulation-reset decisions, and deliberately refuses to write a derived gradient buffer back as source configuration. This is useful for RFF environment gradients: keep editable stops/source assets separate from derived GPU textures and filtering tables. Its constructor only shallow-copies the initial configuration and equality accepts identical object references immediately, so in-place mutation of a shared nested object can evade change detection. Prefer immutable edits or explicit source revisions, particularly for arrays of stops and image-resource descriptors.

**An equality tolerance is part of rendering behavior.** Scalar/vector/color comparisons use an absolute 1e-6 threshold; arrays instead use exact JSON serialization. The manager still merges incoming values and sets `uniformUpdate` for any present feature patch even when its values compare equal. Thus it can distinguish 'upload values' from 'restart accumulation' using a tolerance. Do not transfer that generic epsilon to RFF's sensitive view or fractal parameters. Define change semantics per field, preserve required numerical precision, and ensure any threshold that permits a changed shader value without recomputation is justified by the downstream cache/accumulation contract. Ordinary serialization is also not a substitute for validating finite numeric inputs.

**Resolve defaults without mutating caller-owned patches.** `update` inserts hardware/render-mode defaults into its input object before diffing. Unknown parameter keys are skipped during classification but are included by the subsequent feature-object merge. The uniform-to-parameter map also uses last-wins insertion for duplicate uniform names and requires explicit rebuilding after registration changes. RFF should validate a normalized patch against a closed parameter schema, return an explicit update plan, and reject ambiguous bindings. Keeping that plan independent of mutable caller data makes preview/export replay and failure handling easier to reason about.

**Typed event names do not provide transactional completion.** The shared event bus invokes listeners synchronously without error isolation or acknowledgement. A throwing listener prevents subsequent callbacks from running; payloads are shared references rather than immutable snapshots. `CONFIG_DONE` carries no transaction ID, and compile/texture events do not carry a resource generation in this event map. For RFF, keep authoritative render-state application transactional and revision-tagged; UI notifications can follow the committed state. A notification that a save/download was triggered is not evidence of completed durable output. Subscription cleanup should be owned by the component or renderer lifetime so reinitialization does not multiply actions.

The feature-state map is a type-level extension mechanism; its presence alone does not register a functioning renderer feature. These findings support reliable integration of proposed appearance controls and do not establish additional visual features or measured speedups. No executable tests were run in this pass.

## Interaction lifetime: recover final quality without confusing gestures with rendering

Full reads of `engine/InteractionSessionMachine.ts` and `engine/hooks/useInteractionDrag.ts` show a reusable boundary for RFF's proposed interactive material/environment controls. The hook's historical comment that no consumer reads the session is superseded by the current renderer paths already inspected.

**Separate gesture lifetime from render dirtiness.** The pure machine ref-counts named sources, records activity timestamps and exposes both hard-active state and a short post-activity tail. Discrete wheel/key activity can refresh the tail without opening a gesture. A RFF environment-rotation control can use this to request a responsive preview, but a texture upload finishing after the gesture still needs to invalidate the image independently. Likewise animation is a separate activity axis. Neither an idle gesture machine nor an unchanged pointer proves that rendering is complete.

**Own the release path once.** The hook holds one outstanding begin per mount, collapses duplicate release events, and releases on pointer-up, pointer-cancel, lost capture and unmount. This avoids a cancelled slider leaving adaptive preview permanently active. In native RFF, apply the same ownership principle to capture loss, window deactivation, control destruction and explicit cancellation, using the platform's actual event model. The hook does not itself acquire pointer capture, match pointer IDs or refresh movement activity; those obligations remain with the event producer. Its single boolean is not a complete multi-pointer gesture recognizer.

**A watchdog is a fallback, not an interaction protocol.** The machine clears all active counts after eight seconds without any global activity refresh. Activity from another source can therefore keep a stranded source alive, while a motionless held drag can expire. A later poke updates timestamps but does not restore the hard-active count. RFF should first guarantee balanced acquisition/release, then define explicitly whether a held stationary control is considered active and how movement resumes after fallback cleanup. If independent controls can overlap, a per-gesture lifetime token can distinguish the source being released instead of relying only on shared source counts.

**Use one monotonic timeline and distinguish the two grace periods.** The machine takes time as an argument and keeps its default 200 ms tail separate from the adaptive controller's quality-restoration grace. This permits deterministic transition tests, but does not require RFF to inherit either delay. Choose the combined delay based on visible responsiveness, and ensure final-quality/export requests bypass temporary interaction policy. Filtered consumers can consider camera gestures differently from material sliders without freezing live material updates.

Validation should include overlapping controls, duplicate release events, capture loss, a stationary hold, window deactivation, movement after watchdog cleanup and a late environment-upload completion. No runtime interaction test was executed in this pass.

## Direct appearance controls: align handles with the displayed image

Full reads of `engine/overlay/OverlayProjection.ts` and `engine/components/gizmo/SinglePositionGizmo.tsx` identify a practical 3D-to-2D transfer: direct handles for light direction, environment orientation or image-layer placement. The position gizmo only displays handles and emits a drag-start callback; it does not itself implement constrained movement, undo, capture or field updates.

**Project against the displayed view, with a matching inverse transform.** The helper obtains a display camera and pre-transform canvas client dimensions. That is appropriate when the overlay shares the same parent transform as the image; pointer coordinates arriving in screen space must be mapped back through that transform. In RFF, use the displayed view revision and distinguish window coordinates, viewport presentation scale, shading resolution and fractal coordinates. A handle tied to a newer requested view can drift from a still-displayed older image during expensive rendering. Pair projection with the image actually presented, and verify alignment during resize, DPI changes, preview scaling and export-region inspection.

**Adapt the control to the quantity being edited.** GMT offers XYZ axes, plane constraints and a center handle. A flat RFF image layer generally needs translation/rotation/scale in its own 2D coordinate system, whereas a relief light or environment reflection needs direction/orientation. Reusing the projection and drag-ownership pattern is useful; copying every 3D positional axis would add controls without corresponding 2D meaning. Keep authored appearance coordinates independent of fractal orbit computation.

**Preserve precision before reducing coordinates to display values.** `preciseToWorld` subtracts high and low components separately before combining them, while `storeToWorld` subtracts an already-summed split offset from an ordinary position. The former reduces avoidable cancellation in its intended representation but is not a general arbitrary-precision subtraction guarantee. For RFF deep zoom, retain the application's high-precision coordinate representation through relative-coordinate calculation, then convert the small viewport-relative result for display. Do not transplant the helper's fixed near-depth and 50,000-pixel clamps into fractal numerical logic.

**Validate projections and size handles in display space.** `projectWorldToScreen` checks view depth and extreme coordinates but has no explicit finite-value check; NaN bypasses ordinary greater-than comparisons. `projectWorldToXY` uses projected z greater than one as its behind flag, which is not the same test as signed view-space depth. The gizmo scales its axes by Euclidean camera distance, so screen size can still vary with FOV and off-axis position. RFF should validate finite transforms, use a consistent visibility rule where 3D relief controls require it, and choose handle size from desired screen dimensions. The transparent wider axis hit region is independent of the thin visible line, a useful control mechanism without altering rendered image content.

The projection helpers reuse temporary vectors but return new result objects, and the gizmo allocates axis vectors on update; the comments' zero-allocation language does not describe the entire path. Optimize only if profiling justifies it. No interactive alignment or allocation benchmark was executed in this pass.

## Rotation controls: share the visible basis with the edited parameter

A full read of `engine/components/gizmo/RotationGizmo.tsx` extends the direct-control proposal. This component draws a screen-anchored rotation indicator and reports pointer-down parts; the caller owns drag inversion, units, rotation composition, capture and undo. Its rendering alone does not establish correct parameter editing.

**Use a directional control for environment orientation.** GMT supplies per-ring frames so each Euler component's ring can be drawn in the basis in which that component rotates. Front/back strokes and mild foreshortening make the orientation legible, while a wider transparent stroke handles selection. For RFF relief lighting or an image environment, the useful contract is that dragging the displayed ring changes the corresponding rotation in the same basis and sign convention. A flat image layer only needs its relevant 2D rotation control. Preserve authored angle units and order across preview, save/load and video evaluation rather than inferring them from the drawing.

**Handle directional poles explicitly.** The direction arrow uses angular distance from the view axis: `phi = acos(z)` and radial distance `R * phi / (pi/2)`, with azimuth from the normalized x/y projection. This maps the front hemisphere inside the ring and the back hemisphere outside. The component describes it as fully invertible, but the exact opposite-view pole has undefined azimuth; its small-x/y fallback sets both direction components to zero, placing the displayed tip at the center despite the nominal radius being 2R. A RFF adaptation needs an explicit pole convention, retained azimuth or another interaction chart, with a stable fallback for a zero/invalid direction. Verify continuity near both poles instead of treating the formula as globally one-to-one.

**Keep a compact indicator separate from the complete parameter value.** The angle arc caps its displayed sweep at one revolution and hides very small angles. That is a visualization convention, not evidence that the parameter is clamped or preserves multiple turns. RFF animation may require continuous unwrapped angles; store and evaluate those independently of a wrapped dial, and provide a numeric value when the compact indicator cannot represent the full state. The miniature camera view should follow the displayed orientation, while moving the indicator itself must not alter the environment.

No rotation implementation was copied, and no pointer/animation test was run. This is a supporting control mechanism for the proposed reflection feature, not a higher-priority shader effect.

## Preset evolution and time ownership for new appearance features

Full reads of `engine/migrations.ts`, `engine/plugins/RenderLoop.tsx` and `engine/utils/refs.ts` add two integration requirements for RFF's proposed appearance controls.

**Make migration success transactional.** GMT registers migrations by ID, sorts by numeric version and applies those newer than the preset's `_migrationVersion` (not the `version` field described in the opening example). The implementation catches errors but still advances the version, and an in-place mutation before a throw is not rolled back. Its nullish fallback preserves the old object only for null/undefined, rather than all falsy returns as the comment says. For RFF, normalize a copy, validate the resulting appearance settings, and commit the new migration marker only after required transformations succeed. Preserve the original input when conversion fails so the user can recover it.

**Specify conflicts and keep binary compatibility rules authoritative.** `renameSlice` keeps destination values, whereas `moveField` and `renameField` overwrite the destination. Those differing policies matter when an imported file already contains both old and new fields. Reject ambiguous transforms or declare which value wins, including same-source/destination cases. RFF's existing ConfigIO remains append-only for additive settings with guarded trailing reads; do not import GMT's object-migration version scheme into that stream. Preserve recipe IDs, seeds and regeneration order. A future structured environment-preset format can use its own explicit schema and tested migration chain.

**Separate live frame time from export time.** The default loop updates its timestamp even while paused, so ordinary pause time is not accumulated into the next tick. However, a suspended frame callback can still produce a large delta, and the driver applies no bound itself. It schedules the next callback after the pause predicate and tick dispatch, so an uncaught exception before that point stops this loop. RFF should define resume behavior for animated environment rotation/material parameters, keep one owner of the live clock, and evaluate export frames from deterministic frame times. Do not clamp or reinterpret numerical fractal calculations as a side effect of handling presentation timing.

The small `mergeRefs` helper forwards an element/null to each callback or object ref; it neither owns the attached subsystem lifetime nor makes callback failures independent. It adds no shader feature and needs no direct transplant into native RFF. No migration or animation tests were executed in this pass.

## View bookmarks: adapt state shape without losing deep-zoom precision

Full reads of `engine/plugins/Camera.ts` and `engine/plugins/camera/presetField.ts` show an adapter-based view-bookmark mechanism that works with different 2D/3D camera representations. RFF already has location persistence (`src/rff2/io/RFFLocationBinary.cpp`, and decimal-string centers in `ConfigIO.cpp`); this is a possible quick-recall workflow extension, not a claim that RFF cannot save locations.

**Separate navigation bookmarks from appearance presets.** GMT's adapter captures and restores an opaque camera object through nine numbered slots. For RFF, a bookmark could recall the exact location and view independently of the palette/material/environment, making it easier to compare a lighting setup across views. A separate full-appearance preset can deliberately include those settings. Do not silently make a camera-only recall replace materials, or treat a 3D camera-shaped JSON object as a universal representation for 2D deep zoom.

**Snapshot values, not live references.** The plugin stores the object returned by `captureState` without cloning or validating it and passes the stored object directly to `applyState`. `getAllSlots` also exposes the stored array, while deserialization checks only that the outer value is an array. The adapter must therefore supply the ownership and shape guarantees. RFF should save immutable snapshots, preserve high-precision centers in its established lossless representation, validate indices and loaded values, and restore the view atomically. The generic slot bounds checks do not reject fractional or NaN indices, reinforcing the need for boundary validation rather than relying on intended shortcut inputs.

**Make persistence registration explicit.** Camera-slot serialization is registered by a separate early-import module, before construction freezes the preset-field registry. Installing the visible camera plugin alone does not make slots persist. RFF should make any new saved fields part of its declared serialization contract and test a cold save/load round trip, while respecting ConfigIO's append-only extension rules. Successful recall from memory does not prove persistence. The GMT plugin supplies no animation tracks; a view slot should not be described as a camera-animation implementation.

Verify that repeated recalls reproduce the same deep-zoom center, zoom and projection, and that camera-only recalls retain appearance settings. No bookmark interaction or persistence test was executed in this pass.

## Appearance editing: explicit undo scope and command ownership

Full reads of `engine/plugins/Undo.tsx` and `engine/plugins/Shortcuts.ts` clarify the command-routing layer around experiments with materials, gradients and animation. These files do not implement the history snapshots themselves, so this read does not prove complete state restoration.

**Make the undo target consistent across entry points.** GMT's toolbar buttons and global undo route to parameter history, while timeline-hover shortcuts invoke the animation store's separate history. The opening description's unified-stack wording does not establish unified animation history; the current handlers explicitly use separate stores. For RFF, state whether an action undoes the material edit, view movement or keyframe edit, and keep the action label and keyboard routing consistent. An environment edit that changes source and filtering settings should be one coherent transaction whose restoration invalidates the appropriate GPU resource revision.

**Define whether an unavailable scoped command blocks fallback.** The shortcut resolver chooses one winner by scope/priority first; only afterward does the dispatcher test that winner's input guard and `when` condition. If it is ineligible, no lower-ranked candidate is tried. The score combines scope depth times 10,000 with an unrestricted priority, so sufficiently large priorities can cross nominal scope boundaries. RFF can use a deterministic command registry, but should explicitly choose blocking versus fallback behavior and compare scope/priority as separate ordering keys if scope precedence must be absolute. Text editing, including composition input, should retain its native undo behavior; this dispatcher has no explicit composition or key-repeat gate.

**Own registrations and teardown.** Same-ID shortcut registration replaces the handler, while a component's cleanup unregisters by ID without checking that it still owns the current registration. Duplicate owners can therefore remove each other's command. Clearing the shortcut registry also does not reset the undo plugin's independent installed flag. RFF should bind command registration to owner lifetimes and ensure a recreated editor restores its commands exactly once. A false history result should not silently consume a key unless that is the intended scope policy.

This is integration guidance for predictable appearance experimentation, not a new shader effect. No undo, keyboard or history-restoration test was run in this pass.

## Backend identity: distinguish compatibility stubs from rendering support

A full read of `engine/worker/WorkerProxy.ts` confirms that this shared-engine class is an intentional compatibility stub, unlike the real `engine-gmt/engine/worker/WorkerProxy.ts` reviewed earlier. Its shader, texture and render commands are no-ops; diagnostic methods return empty/null data; export methods reject. `bootWithConfig` can nevertheless mark it booted and invoke its callback synchronously. Method availability and a boot flag therefore do not prove that a shader feature is implemented.

**Expose capabilities and readiness independently.** RFF should use explicit supported operations and renderer/resource readiness for proposed environment reflection, region preview and image capture. An unsupported backend should report that state rather than silently accept settings or return a success-like lifecycle callback. The stub's default true half-float capability is a placeholder, not a device probe. An adapter contract should distinguish unknown, supported and unsupported when resource-format choice depends on that answer.

**Resolve the current backend through a stable owner.** `setProxy` replaces the registry reference, but cannot update a previously captured object. Targeted current-source searches confirm module-scope `getProxy()` captures in `store/engineStore.ts` and `store/slices/historySlice.ts`. The stub includes historical runtime observations about those captures; their user-visible consequences were not reproduced here. For RFF, use an explicit renderer owner or a stable forwarding facade whose implementation can change, and ensure commands after restart reach the new generation. Backend replacement must also retire subscriptions and settle pending operations as described in the earlier worker review.

**Test the effect, not only the facade call.** A test observing an undo callback or a texture-setting method can pass against a no-op adapter. RFF verification should confirm that the restored material/resource revision is actually used by a completed image, and that unsupported export fails clearly. Conversely, a historical dead reset call does not establish stale pixels when another valid invalidation path exists; identify the actual dependency before changing it. This keeps the adoption report focused on reliable RFF integration rather than treating compatibility scaffolding as a missing GMT renderer.

No new shader technique is provided by this file. Its value is clarifying the boundary between portable interfaces and functioning backend implementations. No runtime adapter/restart test was run.

## Modulation controls: distinguish waveform illustration from rendered behavior

Full reads of the four files in `engine/components/modulation/` (`LfoList.tsx`, `WaveformPreview.tsx`, `lfoListConfig.ts`, `index.ts`) refine the earlier animation recommendations. They provide controls and registration, not the complete modulation evaluator.

**Keep authored values separate from a live offset.** The list seeds a base value when adding an oscillator or changing its target and exposes minimum/maximum relative strengths. For RFF environment orientation, reflection intensity or material properties, define units and combination rules explicitly, including multiple drivers on one target, bounded roughness and cyclic angles. Disabling modulation should restore the authored value. Installing the panel alone does not install the evaluation tick, and an enabled row with no valid target is not evidence of a changing shader parameter.

**Do not present an illustrative noise curve as an exact preview.** `WaveformPreview` plots five seconds with 120 intervals. It omits strength, base value and smoothing by design, and its noise uses a random per-mount offset rather than the oscillator's actual seed. Noise sampling does not use the phase value even though phase changes redraw the canvas. Therefore the plotted curve is a shape illustration, not the exact evaluated material trajectory. An RFF preview intended to predict appearance should share the runtime evaluator, saved seed and time convention, showing final parameter values or clearly identifying a shape-only diagram.

**Sample discontinuities and high frequencies deliberately.** A fixed 120-interval, five-second plot can alias short-period oscillation; connecting adjacent samples draws ramps across pulse/sawtooth jumps. This is a graph limitation, not proof of a runtime signal defect. Use frequency-aware sampling and explicit jump segments if precise prediction is needed. Validate finite positive periods and normalize phase consistently at load boundaries; the waveform code only clamps the noise denominator, while other shapes divide by the supplied period directly.

**Validate target resolution and cost policy.** The default base-value resolver supports scalar and vector-axis names, despite older prose suggesting vector axes require an override. Numeric coercion can still admit Infinity, and invalid targets fall back to zero. RFF should validate supported targets and finite values rather than silently treat missing data as an authored zero. The configurable oscillator count limits UI additions, not necessarily imported state, and the claim that per-oscillator cost is trivial excludes downstream consequences such as repeated scene invalidation or resource preprocessing. Prefer continuous uniform-driven appearance targets; measure any target that triggers deeper recomputation. No waveform/runtime parity or animation test was run in this pass.

## Audio-driven appearance controls: expose the signal that actually drives the material

**Sources read in full:** `engine/features/audioMod/AudioLinkControls.tsx` (228 lines) and `engine/features/audioMod/AudioSpectrum.tsx` (513 lines). These are control and visualization components; reading them does not establish DSP correctness, capture latency, or offline export equivalence. This extends the earlier analysis-engine and modulation findings without promoting audio modulation above environment reflection or footprint-aware filtering.

**Transfer to RFF.** An optional frequency-band envelope could drive environment intensity, emission strength, palette position, or a bounded roughness range. This applies to both 3D-style relief shading of a 2D fractal and flat 2D coloring. Keep the authored base value separate from the evaluated value, restore the base when a link is disabled, and resolve multiple links using an explicit composition order. Prefer appearance parameters that reuse existing fractal fields; changing the fractal computation itself is a different, potentially expensive operation. GMT's add actions here default to `coreMath.paramA`, which is not an appropriate default to copy into RFF.

**Share frequency coordinates with analysis.** The spectrum renders one bar per `filterBank` band using `filterBank.normalized`, and maps rule boundaries from stored Hz using the same bands-per-octave spacing. Its inverse screen mapping clamps to Nyquist and deliberately snaps the leftmost 1.5% to zero. Thus the complete mapping is not globally invertible. The selection uses a minimum frequency ratio of 1.02 instead of a fixed Hz width, preserving fine low-frequency selections on a logarithmic display. Bands marked `resolutionLimited` are drawn dimmer. For RFF, retain Hz in saved rules and distinguish display density from actual analysis resolution; more displayed bands do not prove that nearby frequencies can be independently resolved.

**Show separate stages of the response.** The controls distinguish level and transient modes and expose attack, decay, smoothing, gain, offset, and thresholds. A transient response should not be described as a beat/tempo detector merely because it responds to attacks. The controls alone do not establish the time units or frame-rate independence of the envelopes. The spectrum additionally reads `modulationEngine.getRuleValue(rule.id)` for a meter, but that rule-level quantity is not necessarily the final target value after base-value composition, other rules, and parameter constraints. A useful RFF inspector would label band level, processed envelope, and final material value separately. Preserve deterministic evaluation against output-frame time for video; do not sample whichever live audio value happens to be available when a slow frame finishes rendering.

**Validate at the parameter boundary.** Quick-band buttons write low/high Hz directly; the link component does not use its sampled `sampleRate` variable to validate them. This is a local observation, not evidence that validation is absent elsewhere. Gain and offset knobs explicitly allow unconstrained input, while spectrum gain dragging clamps to 0..10. For RFF, different input methods should share a finite-value and target-specific domain policy. A reflectance-like bounded parameter and an HDR light intensity require different domains; do not indiscriminately clamp all material values to 0..1. Populate oscillator choices from actual registered sources instead of copying this component's fixed `lfo-1` through `lfo-3` options. Target changes should explicitly establish which base value is used; this component only sends the new target, so its behavior cannot be inferred without the update/evaluation layer.

**Do not confuse monitoring cost with rendering cost.** The spectrum requests a 2D context with `willReadFrequently`, checks intersection visibility, and limits draws to roughly 30 Hz. These are mechanisms and hints, not proof of a particular browser raster backend or an exact frame-rate improvement. The historical performance claims in comments were not reproduced. Both components subscribe to the whole store, and the spectrum creates a fresh filtered rules array on render; because that array is an effect dependency, unrelated store updates can restart the drawing effect and reset its timing state. A RFF implementation should measure monitor overhead separately, update meters at a modest rate, and avoid rebuilding renderer resources for monitor-only changes.

**Preserve selection identity and gesture semantics.** Double-click creation schedules a callback that edits the last rule in the then-current array rather than the returned identity of the created rule. RFF should create the rule with its full initial band in one operation, or retain its explicit ID. The left-edge inverse can return zero, while this creation path sets the low endpoint to at least `BANK_MIN_HZ` and computes the high endpoint from that zero; validate ordered endpoints at this boundary. Mouse leave ends a drag in this component; adopting native pointer capture would require an explicit release/cancel contract rather than assuming dragging continues outside the panel. These observations inform RFF design and are not a request to modify GMT.

**Verification before adoption:** test silence, sustained tones, short attacks, sample-rate changes, bands near zero/Nyquist, disabled links, multiple links, target switching, nonfinite imported values, and repeated source changes. Compare the same audio and frame timestamps across live preview and video export, with a material-value trace as well as images. Confirm that optional audio monitoring leaves fractal precision, reference data, and MPA unchanged. No application code, audio capture, runtime benchmark, or rendered-image comparison was performed in this pass.

## Audio panel integration: keep source readiness and analysis state independent of the editor

**Source read in full:** `engine/features/audioMod/AudioPanel.tsx` (757 lines). Follow-through reads covered the relevant transport delegation, track-info, and peak-meter paths in `AudioAnalysisEngine.ts`, `AudioTransport.ts`, `WorkletAnalysis.ts`, and `dsp/bandAnalyser.ts`; these follow-through files were already recorded as fully read in earlier passes. This is a source-level integration assessment, not a device or playback test.

**RFF feature shape.** For optional audio-driven 2D palette and relief-material animation, separate three responsibilities: source playback/capture, analysis settings, and material links. GMT's panel presents file decks and live input separately from frequency resolution and link editing. Retain this separation in the runtime too. A lighting preset should describe the intended modulation settings without depending on whether its editor panel happens to be mounted. The engine-enable action must remain reachable when analysis is disabled. Keep monitoring volume distinct from the signal used to drive appearance, and define whether switching to a file source replaces or mixes with a live source; the inspected GMT transport releases its live input when loading a deck.

**Readiness is an event, not elapsed time.** `AudioDeck` calls `loadTrack`, then schedules `play` and optimistic `isPlaying=true` after 100 ms. Its status polling runs only when the locally held `status.hasTrack` is already true; the file handler does not refresh that field. Consequently, the local component does not establish a reliable transition from an initially empty deck to an engine-confirmed ready state. Other rendering activity does not by itself update that local state. RFF should consume explicit loaded/ready/playing/error notifications, associate them with a source revision, and cancel pending actions when a source is replaced or a deck is closed. The existing GMT facade exposes `waitForMetadata`, but metadata readiness alone still does not prove successful playback. Avoid inferring successful playback from the icon state.

**Apply settings outside panel lifetime.** The panel applies master/input gains in a mount-only effect and FFT size and dB range in dependency-based effects; gain and smoothing handlers also call the engine directly. These local paths demonstrate why a RFF settings-to-runtime adapter should own synchronization independently of the editor. This observation does not establish that GMT has no additional writers elsewhere. Verify loading a preset with the panel closed, then opening it, against loading the same preset with the panel open. Preserve zero-valued settings: this panel passes `smoothing || 0.8` to the Response slider, so a stored zero is displayed as 0.8; a RFF control must distinguish missing values from legitimate zero.

**Label measured quantities accurately.** The live meter quantizes `getPeakLevel()` to hundredths, updates at about 20 Hz, and warns above 0.98. Following the value through the worklet-analysis mirror to `BandAnalyser` shows that it is the maximum spectral-bin dB value mapped through the configurable floor/ceiling range. It is not a direct time-domain sample peak or independent proof of hardware clipping. The panel comment referring to an 8-bit FFT must not substitute for this current implementation evidence. In RFF, label analysis saturation separately from audio-input clipping, and use an appropriate independent sample-domain measurement if a clipping diagnostic is offered. Quantization also changes the effective threshold compared with testing the raw value; compute alarm state from the intended measurement before rounding the displayed number if that distinction matters.

**Explain analysis resolution using current parameters.** The panel computes window duration from FFT size and the actual sample rate, and exposes a resolution-limited-band hint from the filter bank. Its option labels, however, contain fixed approximate bin widths (23/12/6 Hz). RFF should derive both bin spacing and analysis-window duration from the current source, rather than presenting sample-rate-specific labels as universal. Separate FFT detail, logarithmic band density, fixed spectral tilt, adaptive per-band normalization, and input automatic gain: these affect different parts of the response. A fixed tilt is conceptually different from adaptive gain, but its downstream range mapping can still saturate; do not promise unchanged output dynamics merely from the word 'fixed'.

**Surface failures where they occur.** Connection errors are stored by the input component, but its message region is rendered only while a live input is running. A first connection failure can therefore lack a message in that region. Analysis failure text is inside the collapsible analysis controls and reads a singleton property during React rendering. For RFF, provide an engine-owned status notification and a visible summary for unavailable analysis, failed source opening, disconnected devices, and missing assets. Do not infer signal failure from a quiet meter alone. No input device was opened in this audit.

**Adoption priority and validation.** This remains an optional creative extension, below the current environment-reflection and image-footprint proposals for immediate visual benefit. Validate initial file loading, failed loading, rapid replacement, deck removal before delayed completion, device disconnect, zero smoothing, source-rate changes, preset loading with controls closed, and silent passages. Check the resulting shader parameter values against fixed output timestamps, not the panel's refresh cadence. Preserve RFF's high-precision fractal fields and MPA computation; audio should normally update appearance uniforms without regenerating the reference orbit. No RFF source code or persistence format was changed, and no latency or performance improvement is claimed.

## Rendering evidence: exercise the production path and assert the intended improvement

**Read in full:** `docs/history/gmt/27_Shader_Testing_Suite.md` (310 lines) and `debug/render-harness.ts` (975 lines). The historical document references `debug/render-cases.ts`, which is absent at that exact path in this checkout; its commands, corpus sizes, timings, and past passing counts are not current execution evidence. The current harness was inspected, not run. This extends the earlier validator assessment with the actual full-engine and bucket-test implementation.

**Useful mechanism for RFF.** GMT's harness constructs the real `FractalEngine`, registers its renderer and camera, builds defaults plus formula presets, hydrates render state, and attaches compile completion before boot/config emission. Listening first matters when an unchanged configuration can complete synchronously. For RFF, exercise the actual Vulkan pipeline configurators, descriptor bindings, precision modes, appearance fields, and output conversion instead of validating an isolated lookalike shader. A compile-only gate remains valuable but cannot establish the visual or numerical benefit of a proposed environment or filtering change. The harness here runs without the production worker; sharing the engine is stronger evidence than a standalone scaffold, but does not prove worker-message, asset-readiness, or export scheduling parity.

**Separate execution success from image assertions.** `runOne` sets `ok=true` after capture and analysis succeeds. It records channel standard deviation, nonblack fraction, and an orange-pixel heuristic; it does not apply those metrics as pass/fail thresholds in this function. A caller may add assertions, but none should be presumed from this return value. The historical document itself later qualifies varied thumbnails as weak evidence and states that interlace's hard gate is compilation despite an earlier reference to numerical breakage. An orange material can trigger the sentinel heuristic, and tone mapping can change a diagnostic color. RFF should use a separate finite-value/status diagnostic and explicit expected-image assertions rather than equating orange pixels with NaNs or image variance with correctness.

**Measure the workload that was actually rendered.** Adaptive warmup measures engine work plus an awaited animation frame, whereas measured frames include camera/state update, compute submission, and synchronous one-pixel readback without that frame wait. The reported timings therefore have different boundaries. `samplesPerSec` is calculated as 1000 divided by median measured-loop duration; it does not count completed samples per output pixel. A readback provides synchronization overhead, not an isolated shader timestamp. Single-image mode forces full-frame scheduling and renders 12 direct-mode or 32 path-tracing iterations; performance mode does not impose that same full-frame policy. For RFF comparisons, record output dimensions, effective render scale, fields recomputed, actual completed work, CPU elapsed time, and GPU timing separately. Stable frame intervals alone do not establish converged images or fixed work per iteration.

**Version assets and serialize test state.** Fresh configuration starts from defaults, but the documented 'deep merge' uses `Object.assign` at feature level; nested values are replaced rather than recursively merged. Imported and raw formulas are registered only if their ID is absent, so reusing an ID with changed source can keep the earlier shader. Key test assets by source revision and record the resulting effective configuration. The shared `inflight` pattern waits on the current promise and then installs another, but multiple callers already waiting on the same promise can resume together; it is not a general multi-caller queue. A RFF harness should have a real serialized job queue and revision-specific completion. The advertised test timeout is passed to compilation, not enforced as one overall deadline for warmup, measurement, image decoding, and capture; give each stage a bounded completion and cancellation contract.

**Use exported pixels without assuming export equivalence.** The bucket path captures production readback pixels by intercepting the runner's save operation, records accumulation counts at composition, and stitches bottom-origin tile positions into a top-down image. These are valuable diagnostics for 2D as well as 3D rendering. However, the harness also skips compute on bucket-transition frames, and its interface comment about an spp+1 cap is superseded by the implementation passing the requested count directly. Verify actual production scheduling against the measured counts rather than copying the old comment. The test returns success after stitching without asserting complete nonoverlapping coverage, expected tile count, or uniform requested sample counts. Four settling frames are also not an asset-ready acknowledgment. RFF should explicitly assert coverage, output orientation, sample count, current asset revision, and parity between normal and tiled export.

**Concrete acceptance cases for the priority RFF proposals:**

- **Gradient/image environment:** use a constant-radiance source, a labeled directional source, and a narrow bright stripe. Check axes, periodic seam, rotation, independent base/clearcoat roughness, and zero-intensity/legacy behavior. Compare scene-linear values before tone mapping as well as the delivered image; an attractive display image alone does not establish HDR preservation.
- **Footprint-aware image sampling:** use high-frequency grids and directional stripes under scale, angular wrapping, and nonuniform field warps. Compare with a sufficiently sampled reference at matching final dimensions; include a short deterministic motion sequence because a still image cannot establish reduced temporal shimmer. Check tile boundaries and fragment/compute output consistency.
- **Field-driven material masks:** inspect the source scalar field and mask separately, then test constant zero/one and threshold crossings. Verify that material-only changes preserve iteration data and MPA/reference behavior, rather than only comparing the final colored image.
- **Shader replacement:** request successive variants while a prior build is pending, and record the revision used in the displayed frame. Successful compilation of each source does not establish that the newest requested variant is the one displayed.

These are proposed acceptance checks, not tests claimed to have passed. No GPU benchmark, shader compilation, runtime screenshot, or numerical result was produced in this pass. The priority remains improving RFF's output and workflow; limitations in the GMT test setup are recorded only to prevent overstating the evidence available for adoption.

## Render-dialog contracts: freeze the effective appearance job before export

**Sources read in full:** `engine/plugins/RenderDialog/types.ts` (159 lines), `ConfigForm.tsx` (257), `index.tsx` (297), and `RenderingView.tsx` (111). These files provide a reusable dialog shell and an application-supplied runner contract. They do not implement the per-frame renderer or encoder; the observations below are local contract evidence, not claims that every GMT runner lacks its own safeguards.

**RFF-facing opportunity.** Extend RFF's existing video/export workflow with an explicit, immutable job description whenever new environment sources, filtering modes, or field masks are introduced. Include the effective dimensions, frame sequence, appearance settings, resource revisions, and color/output conversion. The same principle applies to 3D-style relief and flat 2D coloring. GMT separates generic export controls from application-specific fields through a runner and extension slots; the transferable idea is a shared job contract, not a second rendering implementation. The export summary should describe the actual accepted job rather than current editor preferences.

**Capability results need configuration identity.** The shell suppresses late results from superseded `canEncode` requests with a stale flag, which is useful. However, support initially defaults to true and is not set to a pending state when dimensions, format, or bitrate change. Until the new promise resolves, the preceding result can still enable Start. Rejections are not handled locally, and the start handler itself does not revalidate support. For RFF, distinguish pending/supported/unsupported/error, associate the result with the exact requested configuration, and atomically validate that configuration when accepting the job. Detecting a save-picker function indicates API availability, not successful selection, file opening, or durable completion. A runner may add those checks; the dialog alone does not prove them.

**Snapshot settings and own the job lifecycle.** The shell passes `cfg` and `extra` to `options.runner` and leaves the runner responsible for setting `isRendering`, catching errors, and finalizing output; it neither awaits nor catches the returned promise locally. There is no shell-owned synchronous single-job guard. RFF should accept the job once, clone or otherwise freeze mutable nested appearance data, assign a job ID, and settle every terminal path. Settings shown while rendering should come from that job. In this shell, timeline-duration and FPS effects can replace current form state while the runner retains the originally passed configuration, potentially separating the displayed summary from the running job. The mount effect also pauses timeline playback, but this file does not restore prior playback on close; define the desired RFF behavior explicitly.

**Distinguish stopping from stopped.** Interrupt sets a requested-stop ref and immediately switches the view to Resume/Finish/Discard controls. The shell has no acknowledgment that the renderer has reached a safe boundary. Finish and Discard set different flags, leaving their operational meaning to the runner. RFF should represent requested stop, stopped-at-boundary, finalizing a partial output, discarding, completed, and failed separately. An in-flight GPU frame or encoder operation must settle before resources are reused. Report the actual last completed frame and output disposition; a successful finalization of a shortened video should not be described as completion of the original full range.

**Make timeline semantics explicit.** The form counts an inclusive frame range with `floor((end-start)/max(1,step))+1` and displays output duration as count/FPS. This is a statement about encoded frame count, not necessarily the duration of the selected source timeline interval when step exceeds one. A RFF job should define whether skipping source frames accelerates playback or preserves source-time spacing. Evaluate animated reflection rotation, noise, masks, and audio against those declared timestamps. Form controls constrain ordinary edits but the configuration types and shallow patch operations do not establish validation for nonfinite, invalid, or programmatically supplied values. Check finite positive dimensions/FPS, valid format identity, ordered integer frame ranges, and a positive step before allocating resources.

**Keep recommendations distinct from authored choices.** The resolution-dependent bitrate effect runs on initial mount as well as later size changes, so it can overwrite an explicit default immediately despite the comment promising to retain it until resize. It can also produce values above the visible slider's nominal range. For RFF, keep an explicit automatic/manual bitrate policy, show the effective value, and let the encoder's actual constraints determine validity. Likewise, the FPS effect has no 'user touched' flag despite the comment claiming that behavior; it follows store FPS changes whenever no default FPS was supplied. These are reasons to specify ownership of each setting rather than reproduce incidental component behavior.

**Report progress and quality honestly.** The status adapter converts fractional progress to percent, while `RenderingView` estimates total time as elapsed/progress and renders an ETA range supplied by the runner. The calculation is not proof of a calibrated estimate, especially when shader preparation, heavy frames, encoding, and finalization have different costs. The displayed samples-per-frame value is configured effort, not measured convergence; deterministic 2D paths may not use it at all, as the public contract acknowledges. The declared `renderingViewExtra` option is not passed through by this shell, although the view has an `extraSummary` slot. Verify actual connection of any RFF summary extension rather than relying on its type declaration. This matters if an export must show an environment source, output transfer, or material-pass selection.

**Validation before implementation:** change output settings during a delayed capability probe; reject a probe; attempt duplicate starts; modify the timeline during rendering; interrupt during GPU work and encoder finalization; finish a partial range; discard; and reopen after failure. Compare preview and video appearance at the same accepted timestamps and resource revision. Keep native fractal precision and MPA unchanged. No runtime export, encoder probe, application code change, or measured performance claim was made in this pass.

## High-resolution region preview: inspect appearance at the final pixel scale

**Sources read in full:** `engine/plugins/topbar/BucketRenderController.ts` (53 lines), `installBucketRender.tsx` (122), and `BucketRenderPanel.tsx` (758). These are the controller interface and its generic UI integration; underlying rendering and worker paths were examined in earlier sections. No region preview or tiled export was executed in this pass.

**High-value transfer to RFF.** A selectable region preview at final output pixel density would let users inspect environment-reflection detail, image-layer filtering, relief normals, and field masks before committing a large image. This is equally useful for flat 2D output: a reduced viewport can conceal narrow bands and texture aliasing. GMT separates viewport refinement, region inspection, and file export. Adopt that distinction with an explicit full-image coordinate system and resource revision. Reuse RFF's high-precision fractal data where valid, without reducing precision or treating MPA as another approximation algorithm.

**Tie the preview to the output contract.** The panel clears an active region when output dimensions change and resends the region when its sample cap changes. Those are useful invalidation rules. It computes displayed region dimensions by rounding normalized extent times output dimensions and polls a shared accumulation counter every 100 ms. Neither operation proves the renderer used those exact bounds or that the count belongs to the current region/material revision. The controller interface carries no job or revision ID, readiness acknowledgment, or explicit units/origin for its four region coordinates. For RFF, return accepted integer pixel bounds, revision, completed sample count, and state; derive the display from that acknowledgment. Keep samples-per-pixel distinct from convergence quality.

**Preserve framing without cumulative resize drift.** The panel snapshots the pre-swap physical viewport dimensions, fits subsequent output-aspect changes against that original size, and tracks whether it actually changed resolution before restoring on close. This avoids using a repeatedly shrinking viewport as the next fit input. However, independently snapping fitted width and height to multiples of eight and clamping each to at least 64 can change the exact aspect, especially for extreme ratios. A RFF region preview should define the full output projection/mapping independently of the presentation widget's rounded dimensions, and map pointer selections through the actual displayed image rectangle. An output label alone cannot establish matching pixel footprints.

**Own temporary state explicitly.** The installer avoids dismissing the popover on canvas clicks while rendering, picking, or holding a region, but its toggle button can still close it. Panel unmount stops the render, exits region selection, clears the region, restores a saved resolution when applicable, and releases adaptive suppression that it previously applied. This couples job lifetime to editor lifetime. Decide deliberately whether RFF jobs survive panel closure; if they do, move their ownership out of the panel. Use scoped ownership for shared adaptive suppression rather than clearing a global boolean that another operation may still need. The local interaction wrapper calls begin/action/end without a finally block, so a throwing action can bypass its end call; an RFF wrapper should guarantee cleanup. The global installer guard allows only one installation even though the option comment discusses multiple IDs; do not infer support for multiple independent controllers from that option alone.

**Estimate memory from actual allocations.** The panel estimates image-tile memory using fixed RGBA32F composite and double pipeline targets, a viewport-or-tile bloom allowance, and an RGBA8 readback target. This is an approximate model, not a device capacity query or allocation guarantee. Its tile dimensions use floor division while the comment says the last row/column absorbs the remainder, so the displayed base tile can be smaller than the largest actual tile. For RFF, derive peak memory from the concrete render plan, including maximum edge-tile dimensions, temporary buffers, mip chains, precision formats, and in-flight readbacks. Distinguish the exported file grid from the GPU work-bucket size. Changing bucket size does not automatically reduce every allocation, and larger buckets are not unconditionally faster.

**Make filtering continuous across partitions.** GMT displays a warning that bloom and chromatic aberration may seam across image-file tiles; this is a UI warning, not a runtime seam measurement. For the non-bloom RFF priorities, include the actual neighborhood required by normal reconstruction, image filtering, warps, and any screen-space effect. Evaluate footprint and environment directions in full-image coordinates, render the necessary border, and crop after filtering. A fixed arbitrary border does not establish correctness for every filter radius or displacement. Test both internal GPU buckets and separately exported image tiles against an untiled reference, including nondivisible dimensions and regions crossing periodic seams.

**Progress and metadata are job data.** Local elapsed time starts when this panel observes rendering and can restart on remount; bucket status events are not filtered by job ID here. RFF should report engine-owned elapsed time and progress for the accepted job. The include-scene-data checkbox forwards an option but does not prove metadata was embedded successfully. Treat image completion and editable-state embedding as separately verifiable results, preserving RFF's existing file-format contracts. No performance gain, seamless output, or successful embedding is claimed from this source read.

## Performance readouts: identify the work behind FPS and sample counts

**Sources read in full:** `engine/plugins/topbar/FpsCounter.tsx` (131 lines) and `PauseControls.tsx` (153). These components consume telemetry and control state; they do not themselves establish GPU timing or acknowledge completion of queued GPU work.

**Transfer to RFF.** Separate displayed-image update rate, UI refresh rate, and completed rendering work when comparing environment reflection or image filtering. GMT provides selectable render FPS, accumulation throughput, and an advanced UI-refresh metric. This distinction is useful for 2D too: fast UI refresh can coexist with a slowly recomputed fractal image, and recoloring cached fields is a different workload from regenerating them. Record resolution, effective quality, changed fields, and job revision alongside timing rather than promising a shader speedup from an FPS increase alone.

**Fallback must preserve metric identity.** When render FPS is negative, this component substitutes UI FPS while retaining the 'FPS' unit and the tooltip claiming actual fractal frame rate. RFF should label unavailable render telemetry and any UI-rate fallback explicitly. Paused styling reads the pause preference, not a renderer acknowledgment; a color or tooltip is not proof that GPU work has stopped. Zero rates display as dashes, which does not distinguish idle, converged, paused, missing telemetry, and stalled rendering. Provide a separate state label where the distinction matters.

**Accumulation throughput requires epochs.** The executable SPS logic subscribes to accumulation-count changes, computes count delta divided by time between notifications, smooths the result, and uses a 250 ms timer to decay the displayed value. It differs from the introductory description of a fixed 500 ms measurement timer. A decrease is treated as a reset, but an unreported reset followed by enough new work can still produce an increased count: an earlier count of 10 followed by a new epoch at 12 yields delta 2 even though 12 new samples were accumulated. Multiple resets also cannot be reconstructed from one shared count. RFF should publish a cumulative completed-work counter or explicit epoch/job IDs and timestamps, and report samples per pixel only when that is the actual unit. Deterministic 2D shading should not inherit path-tracing terminology for ordinary redraws.

**Display decay is a heuristic.** The timer caps shown SPS by the reciprocal of time since the last count notification. Absence of a notification does not prove absence of GPU samples when reporting is batched; this is not a mathematically valid upper bound on true throughput in that case. Keep such smoothing confined to the live display and retain raw timestamped measurements for comparisons. Switching away from SPS removes the subscription; switching back initializes new count/time references but does not immediately clear the old displayed SPS state. A RFF display should reset or mark its warmup interval rather than present a prior measurement as current.

**Sample budgets belong to a render owner.** `PauseControls` chooses a positive active-render cap ahead of the viewport cap, avoiding comparison of export samples with an unrelated viewport budget. That is a useful mechanism. The counter still needs the same owner/revision as the cap, and a null/nonpositive active cap falls back to the viewport setting. RFF should represent unlimited, unavailable, and finite budgets explicitly rather than overloading zero/null. Reaching a sample cap means the requested work budget was reached, not that a numerical error target or visual convergence was verified.

**Requested pause and effective pause differ.** The pause button considers camera interaction, global interaction, and timeline scrubbing when choosing its effective paused appearance, while its click toggles the stored pause preference. RFF can allow temporary preview updates while paused, but should document the state transition and show the renderer's actual state. The viewport sample slider remains distinct from the active export cap, as the component's explanatory text correctly notes. Do not allow an appearance-preview control to silently alter an export's accepted workload.

**Checks before adoption:** publish batched counters, reset accumulation between reports, switch render owners, enter/leave a paused interaction, reach a finite cap, use unlimited mode, and lose render telemetry. Compare any live rate with completed frame/work records at fixed dimensions and quality. No runtime performance measurement was performed; these findings refine how future RFF shader improvements should be evaluated, without changing the current visual-priority ranking.

## Saved appearance and view states: distinguish snapshots from reusable assets

**Source read in full:** `engine/store/createStateLibrarySlice.ts` (440 lines). This factory manages session state; it explicitly delegates persistence and undo to its host. A successful local save notification is not evidence of a durable file write.

**RFF transfer.** Named snapshots can help compare complete lighting setups or return to a 2D deep-zoom view after experimenting with reflection and material masks. The factory's stated single-active-state scope is appropriate for a view or whole appearance setup. It is not a general shared material/gradient asset pool: reusable assets need stable identities, target selection, versioned dependencies, and deliberate copy-versus-reference semantics. RFF should preserve that distinction instead of making a palette, an environment image, and a complete view all behave like camera slots.

**Capture immutable, domain-correct data.** The factory stores the direct result of `capture()` and passes saved state directly to `apply()`. It does not enforce a deep immutable snapshot. Its duplicate action uses JSON serialization, then selects and applies the duplicate; duplication is therefore also a visible state change. For RFF, define a typed serializer/clone for high-precision locations and appearance parameters, preserve arbitrary-precision coordinates in the established representation, and reference image resources by stable asset identity. Do not route deep-zoom coordinates through ordinary floating-point JSON numbers or assume generic JSON cloning preserves every state type. Keep existing palette recipe IDs and generation order unchanged, and extend existing persistence only according to RFF's file-format contracts.

**A thumbnail must identify the saved revision.** Add writes the snapshot first and later patches its thumbnail by ID against the current array, avoiding a simple stale-array overwrite for that path. Overwrite/update and overwrite-slot paths instead retain the original array across awaited thumbnail capture and write it back afterward. Intervening additions, deletion, reordering, or another save can therefore be replaced by that older array. RFF should commit the captured state atomically, then attach an asynchronously generated thumbnail only if both snapshot ID and revision still match. Render the thumbnail from the captured state or an acknowledged matching frame; calling a live viewport capture after saving does not by itself establish the image describes the saved parameters. Thumbnail failure should not silently redefine whether the underlying snapshot was saved.

**Apply and identity need explicit guarantees.** Selection and duplication write the active ID before calling the host apply operation. If apply throws, the selected marker alone does not prove the renderer has accepted the state. Use an accepted-state revision or rollback policy in RFF. The factory permits a partial snapshot patch, including identity fields, without reconciling the active ID. Reordering checks bounds but not integer/finite indices; slot saving checks only the upper gap and assumes valid nonnegative integers. Validate these domain rules at the action boundary, not just in keyboard/UI callers. Default labels use array length plus one, which can repeat after deletion despite the uniqueness claim in the comment; treat the internal ID as identity and labels as editable descriptions.

**Registration and history remain host responsibilities.** The installer checks repeated array keys and action-name collisions across its own registry, but this is not a complete schema-level namespace check for every active-ID, transient, existing-store, or within-install field. RFF can avoid that class of coupling with typed library instances. The optional `isModified` callback is declared here but not invoked by this factory, so a modified marker requires a consumer; likewise, durable save and undo cannot be inferred from the bookkeeping actions. Record whether recalling a lighting snapshot joins one undo step and whether duplicating it also applies it. For a shared gradient asset, keep editing history separate from saved recipe identity as described in the earlier gradient-library section.

**Acceptance checks:** save while changing appearance, delete or reorder while thumbnail capture is pending, overwrite twice with reversed completion order, fail an apply operation, duplicate an inactive view, reload saved data, and revisit an extreme deep-zoom location. Confirm exact state recovery separately from thumbnail similarity. This pass adds design requirements for RFF; it does not modify GMT or RFF code, run persistence tests, or claim that a new preset system is already implemented.

## Snapshot recall integration: one command model for menus, keys, and feedback

**Read in full:** `engine/store/installStateLibrary.ts` (292 lines), `engine/components/StateLibraryToast.tsx` (60), `docs/adr/0031-installstatelibrary-two-explicit-keys.md` (31), and `docs/adr/0056-camera-manager-consumer-of-installstatelibrary.md` (84). The ADRs explain historical decisions; their old line numbers and statements about remaining work are not substituted for current implementation evidence.

**RFF application.** Quick recall of whole lighting setups or 2D views could make side-by-side experimentation with the proposed environment reflection practical. Keep one typed command surface for save, recall, reset, and duplicate, and have menu entries and shortcuts invoke it. GMT's wrapper centralizes these bindings and reads the current action/state at invocation time rather than capturing a stale snapshot at installation. The feedback component reads the same derived toast key as the save logic. These mechanisms reduce wiring duplication, but neither the menu nor toast verifies that the rendering or durable saving operation succeeded.

**Retain semantic differences deliberately.** A populated slot recalls its state in both the keyboard and menu paths. An empty numbered keyboard slot does nothing, whereas clicking an empty menu slot attempts to save; the menu title still primarily describes recall. For RFF, make saving and recalling distinct visible commands, or explicitly label the empty-slot action. Array position defines the slot, so reordering changes what each number recalls. Do not accidentally make a stable preset shortcut change meaning when sorting a library; choose either numbered positions or independently assigned stable shortcuts and document the behavior. Shortcut categories describe commands but do not supply a separate key namespace: installing two libraries with the default numeric bindings needs an explicit scope or distinct key scheme.

**Validate registration as one operation.** The wrapper always proceeds to shortcut/menu registration after calling `installStateLibrarySlice`, even if that function declines an installation. A return value indicating accepted/already-present/rejected would let a RFF equivalent avoid partially installed controls. Shared `resolveSlotCount` correctly aligns menu and key counts and preserves zero, but accepts arbitrary numeric counts without a finite/integer/range check. Values beyond the single-digit key scheme require deliberate mappings rather than constructing labels such as '10' and assuming they correspond to one key event. Installation should also supply cleanup if a library can be removed or replaced during a session.

**Use the current scope, not an older generalization.** ADR-0031 records a collision-guard improvement as outstanding; the current factory inspected in the previous pass already has module registries. ADR-0056 suggests materials/effects as generic consumers, while the current factory documentation explicitly excludes shared asset pools. For RFF, whole appearance snapshots remain a suitable single-active-state use; a material reused by multiple layers needs an asset model with target and reference semantics. The two explicit store keys solve naming flexibility, not every collision or type-safety issue. Preserve the earlier recommendation for typed identity and high-precision payload capture.

**Keep reset and completion unambiguous.** ADR-0056 describes distinct reset paths, one additionally restoring optics. Treat that as a historical design distinction until verifying the current consumer; do not silently reproduce two differently scoped 'Reset' commands in RFF. Name reset targets such as view, lighting setup, or complete appearance. The toast component is a transient, pointer-ignoring rendering of a message and slot number, with no internal persistence logic or renderer acknowledgment. An RFF notice should identify session snapshot saved, file saved, or view applied according to the actual completed operation. A misspelled string key can otherwise leave feedback absent without an exception; typed library handles avoid that coupling.

**Verification:** exercise menu and keyboard recall after reorder, an empty slot, zero slots, duplicate installation, a rejected installation, two active libraries, failed state application, and asynchronous thumbnail completion. Verify the resulting RFF appearance and exact 2D location separately from the feedback text. This is a source-read adoption analysis; no shortcuts were registered, no UI was operated, and no application code was changed.

## Parameter transport and editor state: keep authored values, live values, and UI colors separate

**Read in full:** `engine/typedSlices.ts` (241 lines), `engine/store/colorSchemeStore.ts` (373), and `engine/store/toastStore.ts` (56). This pass examines state mechanisms, not a visual/accessibility audit of the application.

**RFF shader integration.** The typed-slice helper is a useful example of separating authored settings from live animation/modulation overrides. `applyLiveMod` replaces scalar numeric fields and x/y/z/w axes before renderer synchronization; vector indicators can separately compose base and live values, including an additive camera convention. For new RFF environment rotation, intensity, roughness, and masks, specify the same evaluated-value contract for both the widget and shader upload. An animated indicator is not evidence that the render path received the animated value. Keep the source settings available for persistence and editing rather than overwriting them every frame.

**Know the helper's actual coverage.** Type declarations map float/int, boolean, vectors, color, and gradients, but unknown parameter types fall back to `any`. Runtime getters use assertions and do not verify installation or payload shape; a missing setter warns and returns without an application acknowledgment. `applyLiveMod` handles numeric scalars and vector-shaped objects only: RGB color objects, booleans, arrays, gradient structures, and image assets are not equivalent cases. It accepts numeric NaN/infinity because it checks `typeof`, not finiteness, and integer-typed settings receive no rounding here. RFF should use typed, validated field descriptors and explicit per-type evaluation, then preserve exact C++/GLSL layout agreement. Do not claim TypeScript-level typing would validate runtime assets or GPU interface layout.

**Preserve reference and ownership semantics.** When no overrides apply, the helper returns the original slice; when an override exists, it shallow-copies the slice and affected vector even if the supplied value equals the base. It also allocates temporary copies while searching, so same-reference return is not proof of zero allocation. A whole-slice subscription remains whole-slice even when a component subsequently reads one property. For RFF, compare effective values and resource revisions at the synchronization boundary to avoid unnecessary pipeline work while ensuring a newly evaluated appearance reaches the renderer. Do not alter numerical tolerances on fractal coordinates merely to reduce update traffic.

**Editor theme is independent of rendered color.** The theme store generates CSS channel values from brightness, tint, contrast, and accent axes, caches them for startup, and invalidates a separate cache used by canvas-based editor tools. This suggests keeping RFF's histogram, curve editor, and material inspector legible under a shared editor theme without changing palette, environment radiance, tone mapping, or saved image values. Theme cache invalidation should repaint editor graphics, not regenerate the reference orbit. The brightness interpolation operates on display channel values; its HSL tint preserves the selected HSL lightness, not a proven physical or perceptual brightness. The hard text/status regime switch at brightness 50 and fixed accent foreground do not establish contrast across every hue and background. No accessibility or color-calibration claim is made from these formulas.

**Validate theme inputs and notifications without coupling them to render success.** Persisted numeric theme reads reject nonfinite values, while runtime setters and preset application do not all provide the same validation. Theme application calls subscribers before committing the new store axes/revision; a subscriber reading store state at that moment can still see old values even though CSS has changed. Use coherent notifications if adapting this pattern. The toast helper always pushes an entry and schedules dismissal, even with no host mounted; its header's 'no-op' description means no visible feedback, not no state/timer work. It has no bounded queue or durable operation record. For RFF, transient notices can report completed actions, but failure details and export outcomes should remain available independently of a short-lived message. A toast must follow the actual accepted shader/persistence result, not substitute for it.

**Validation before adoption:** animate one vector axis while preserving the others; test zero overrides, absent overrides, invalid numeric input, integer/discrete targets, color/gradient targets, and missing resource revisions. Confirm widget values and uploaded values agree for both 3D-style relief and flat 2D coloring. Change the editor theme and verify saved/rendered pixels remain identical. These are proposed checks; no application source change, shader execution, UI contrast test, or performance measurement was performed in this pass.

## Appearance-panel composition: expose one parameter through multiple useful views

**Source read in full:** `engine/PanelManifest.ts` (521 lines). This is a declaration/registration layer; its component-rendering and visibility consumers must not be inferred solely from its type comments.

**RFF opportunity.** Keep shader-feature definitions separate from the organization of their controls. GMT's manifest can compose selected parameters, custom widgets, section headers, help topics, and compile/runtime sections into one panel. For RFF, an environment editor could show a gradient, rotation, intensity, base roughness, and clearcoat roughness together while retaining one canonical setting for each. A field-inspection panel could reuse the same mask controls as the material editor. This works for 2D coloring and relief shading without duplicating settings or adding a second shader implementation. Preserve stable panel/parameter IDs when changing visible labels so existing layouts and recipes retain their meaning.

**A panel is not a capability declaration.** Visibility accepts a dotted state path or predicate; missing paths become false and function exceptions are not handled here. Hiding a control does not disable its shader effect or prove that a formula supports the required field. RFF should retain separate capability validation, feature enable state, and presentation visibility. Keep a route to re-enable a disabled feature instead of hiding its only activation control. The manifest supports compile-gated and runtime-only controls, but cannot itself prove that changing a control rebuilds the right Vulkan pipeline or uploads the right uniform. Use the actual field-update contract to choose the control behavior.

**Registration needs one authoritative collection.** The header says the latest manifest wins, while the implementation merges previously registered IDs and preserves older entries. For an existing ID, `applyPanelManifest` replaces the map entry but does not replace the corresponding object already stored in the manifest array. Consequently, consumers of `getPanelDefinition` and `getPanelManifest` can receive different versions after a repeated definition. Both getters expose live objects rather than an immutable snapshot. A RFF registry should define replacement versus merge explicitly, validate duplicate identities, and expose a coherent version to every consumer. Do not assume a layout-mode switch removes panels merely because a new declaration omits them.

**Keep layout state separate from initial defaults.** Applying the manifest rebuilds panel location/order from definitions and preserves only the prior `isOpen` field in the reconstructed entry. Active selection does not evaluate visibility and accepts a current ID if it exists anywhere in the registry, without checking that it still belongs to the requested dock. `addPanel` treats every non-left dock as right for active-tab updates, although floating panels are also a declared possibility. These local semantics are reasons for RFF to distinguish default placement from user layout, validate active membership against visible panels in the correct region, and handle floating windows separately. They are not runtime UI failures reproduced in this audit.

**Boot ordering matters to shader availability.** The module uses a non-instantiating store peek because initializing the store too early can freeze feature registration. Pre-boot additions are held until a later manifest application synchronizes them.
