The final mouse-up position is not appended by the hook; the committed shape is based on recorded down/move events. RFF should define how reverse strokes and repeated times are resolved, preserve the intended endpoints, and decide explicitly whether subframe authoring is supported.

The hook delegates replacement and seam healing to `spliceSpan`. Retaining keys outside a span does not by itself prove that their connecting curve segments are unchanged. Check continuity and neighboring handles when that implementation is audited. A revision check is also needed before applying a stroke if another operation changes the source track during the gesture; retaining a source array alone does not prevent overwriting concurrent edits.

### Bound work and own the gesture lifecycle

The pencil stores every move point and redraws the full stroke. With preview enabled it also sorts points, rasterizes the integer-frame span and refits on each move. Cost grows with both pointer-event count and duration. For RFF, coalesce preview work to display updates, cap sample work, and retain an accurate final commit. The brush evaluator in this hook explicitly supplies false for both rotation and logarithmic evaluation, so it must receive the shared domain-aware evaluator before being used for phase or logarithmic tracks.

The inspected hook installs window mouse listeners and removes them on mouse-up; it has no unmount or cancellation cleanup path. Provide one owned gesture with cleanup on cancellation, focus loss and editor destruction, plus restoration of any previewed state. The timeline's global keyboard handler ignores INPUT elements only; scope curve-edit commands to the active editor and respect other text editors, including textarea and editable content, before borrowing its shortcuts.

### Fit the visible curve, not merely its keys

The view-bounds helper measures key positions only, excluding Bezier extrema and handles. Normalized ranges likewise come from key values. A fit command can therefore omit an overshoot between keys. Use evaluated or analytical curve extrema when the command promises to show the entire curve. Keep finite positive view scales for small editor dimensions. The host's selected-only filter changes drawing and hit-testing, while several tools and fit operations still receive the original track list; define operation scope explicitly so a display filter does not imply an unsupported editing restriction.

**Proposed checks:** log-positive and mixed-sign tracks, reverse strokes, duplicate sample times, fractional endpoints, two keys with large Bezier overshoot, a long-duration stroke, resizing during editing, source changes during a gesture, cancellation after live preview, and shortcuts while another text editor has focus. No runtime tests or RFF code changes are claimed; this section records source-supported adoption requirements.

## Curve-tool host follow-up: identify the actual operation before adopting it

The full 373-line [useGraphTools.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/hooks/useGraphTools.ts) closes an important caller-level question from the preceding sections. Its positive Smooth gesture calls `calculateConstrainedSmoothing`, not the positive Gaussian branch of `calculateSmoothingUpdates`. The latter utility's Gaussian analysis remains correct for that function, but must not be presented as the timeline toolbar's active positive-smoothing algorithm. The constrained solver was reread in [ConstrainedSmoothing.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/utils/ConstrainedSmoothing.ts).

**RFF opportunity:** borrow the idea of a reversible strength gesture for cleaning palette, material or light animation, with one original source snapshot and lightweight playback during editing. The host starts a history snapshot and an interaction interval, clones the source sequence, and derives successive operations from that source. Implement the corresponding lifecycle using RFF's own state model, without JSON-based copying of high-precision or non-JSON data.

### What the active smooth operation guarantees

The constrained algorithm partitions selected keys into contiguous blocks, holds unselected neighboring values fixed, and solves a tridiagonal system with rows of the form `-s*previous + (1+2s)*current - s*next = original`. Track ends use reflected-neighbor conditions. It works in key-index space, does not incorporate actual frame spacing, and produces value-only patches. Its source comments mention C0/C1 continuity, but fixed neighboring values and this system alone do not establish derivative continuity of the final Bezier curve. For RFF, specify the intended continuity and update or constrain handles accordingly; do not promise C1 continuity from this code alone.

The optional `smoothBakes` path first expands the selected interval by one key on either side and samples integer frames; the timeline host previously inspected leaves this option at its false default. This path omits the log evaluator flag too. Uniform baking can change the spacing problem, but is not evidence that all callers smooth in uniform time or preserve fractional endpoints.

### Make selection scope visible and preserve excluded keys

Bake uses the tracks containing selected keys, then replaces each entire target track. Euler repair likewise operates on entire target tracks. Simplification takes the earliest and latest selected key in each track, passes only selected keys to the fitter, and retains original keys only before or after that interval. An unselected key between two selected keys is therefore not explicitly retained by this host. This is a concrete reason for RFF to distinguish “selected keys,” “selected interval,” and “whole track” commands. Either preserve intervening excluded keys or clearly preview the replacement interval before committing.

The Euler-needed indicator scans a different scope from the action when no keys are selected: it can inspect visible tracks although the action requires selected tracks. Use the same resolved operation scope for availability, preview and execution. Display filters alone must not change or obscure that contract.

### Complete the gesture, including a return to the initial value

Window listeners retain the handlers registered at gesture start. Comparisons against React state such as `bakeStep` and `simplifyStrength` therefore use that render's values, rather than necessarily the latest preview. For example, an initial bake step of 1 can suppress resampling when the pointer returns to step 1 after previewing a larger step. The source establishes this captured-state risk; no interactive reproduction is claimed. Use a gesture-owned current value and always restore the baseline when the control returns to neutral.

The smoothing restore helper can also receive the sequence captured before live changes, so equality checks against that captured sequence are not sufficient to undo the current preview. An empty patch list means “nothing emitted,” not “baseline restored.” Restore from the full original state explicitly. Add pointer-ID ownership, cancel/lost-capture/unmount cleanup and balanced interaction end calls; this host registers pointer-up/move handlers without those cancellation paths.

The toolbar bake gesture clamps its step to an integer of at least 1. This narrows the earlier helper-level concern: ordinary finite pointer movement through this caller does not supply zero or negative steps. Keep validation in a reusable RFF helper anyway, and bound output size. Positive step validation does not resolve endpoint loss or domain mismatches.

Finally, create-key hit testing samples the curve at the unsnapped mouse frame but inserts the sampled value at the rounded frame, and omits the log flag. In RFF, first resolve the insertion time, evaluate the actual playback curve there, and split its segment if shape preservation is promised. Adding a Bezier key with a sampled value alone is not proof of shape-preserving insertion.

**Validation targets:** return each gesture to its initial setting, cancel after a live update, sparse selections containing excluded middle keys, hidden selected tracks, uneven times, logarithmic tracks, whole-track versus interval baking, and insertion near a half-frame boundary. This is an authoring-layer addition to the RFF adoption report, applicable to both 2D and relief; no new shader implementation or runtime verification is claimed.

## Group curve transformations: reuse motion while preserving its meaning

**RFF application.** Group movement, time scaling, reversal, duplication and bias could make palette sweeps, lighting changes and emission envelopes easier to reuse. These authoring operations transfer equally to flat 2D coloring and relief materials; they are not additional lighting algorithms. The complete [GraphSelectionBBox.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/components/graph/GraphSelectionBBox.tsx) was inspected for the concrete mechanism and its limits.

GMT captures selected keys and their handles at gesture start. Time scaling anchors to the opposite edge, or the center with Alt. A negative ratio swaps incoming/outgoing tangent slots and scales tangent X by that ratio. This is the useful core of reversing a Bezier segment in time. However, actual frame coordinates are rounded and clamped to zero while tangent X uses the unrounded ratio. Keys can collide or lose their affine spacing, and the patch does not reassign segment interpolation types. Therefore the implementation is not proof of exact reversal for mixed Step/Linear/Bezier segments or selections crossing time zero. RFF should transform segment semantics as well as keys, specify a collision policy, and preserve subframe times where exact retiming is required.

Duplication is deferred until the first movement, creates unique per-track IDs, clones handles and selects the copies. This avoids creating duplicates from a stationary modifier-click. The helper inserts copies at their original times before the transform patch, so duplicate and transform should become one atomic RFF command to avoid exposing temporary coincident keys to playback. If duplication is unavailable, GMT falls back to transforming originals; a RFF control promising a copy should instead be disabled or report that limitation. Returning the pointer to its start does not itself remove already created copies.

Value scaling operates through screen coordinates and the host's inverse mapping. The listener reads the latest inverse mapping and view, although starting pixels and values were captured earlier. A normalized range that changes during editing can therefore change the mapping used for the same pointer displacement. Anchor subtraction preserves zero displacement but does not generally freeze nonzero displacement. Use a frozen transformation domain for the gesture. For log-interpolated tracks, transform log values and their log-unit handles consistently; do not assume ordinary additive value translation preserves the log curve. Bounded roughness, periodic phase and unrestricted intensity must retain their distinct domain policies.

Bias maps normalized selected time/value positions through a power curve, with exponent changing exponentially with drag distance. This redistributes intermediate points while retaining ideal span endpoints before frame rounding. It is useful for compressing changes toward the beginning/end of a palette or lighting sequence. The inspected value bias uses raw values and calls `reTangentBezier` without a track-domain argument. RFF should apply bias in the declared interpolation domain, bound extreme exponents, and explain whether manually shaped tangents are retained or regenerated. Neighboring unselected keys can still constrain the resulting curve; moving selected keys across them needs an explicit rule.

The component removes its global mouse listeners on unmount, but that cleanup does not end an active scrub interval or restore an unfinished transformation. Mouse-up performs the end calls. Use shared gesture finalization for completion, cancellation, focus loss and destruction. The handles also accept mouse-down without a left-button guard, and the component receives selected IDs without its own visible-track filter. Define active-button and visible-selection policies in RFF rather than relying on the appearance of the bounding box.

**Proposed verification:** mixed interpolation types under time reversal; negative-time clamping; coincident keys; a single missing tangent; duplicate then return to origin; normalized/logarithmic value changes; changing view scale mid-gesture; sparse selections crossing unselected keys; and destruction during an active scrub. These are source-derived integration requirements, not executed tests or a claim that RFF lacks every listed authoring capability.

## Track organization: distinguish curve visibility from animation state

**RFF opportunity.** Group animated palette, texture, environment, material and light parameters, with separate controls for selecting keys, showing curves and enabling evaluation. This would help manage the proposed shader extensions in both flat 2D and relief workflows. The full [GraphSidebar](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/components/graph/GraphSidebar.tsx), [groupTracks](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/utils/groupTracks.ts), [dopeSheetTrackFlags](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/utils/dopeSheetTrackFlags.ts) and [useSidebarResize](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/hooks/useSidebarResize.ts) were inspected.

GMT's eye control changes the list of curves displayed in the graph; it is not an animation mute. Selecting a hidden curve reveals it additively. Group collapse is shared with the dope sheet, and shift-range selection follows the expanded row order. Preserve these distinctions in RFF, including a clear partially visible group state. Do not interpret hiding a curve as disabling its shader contribution or removing its keys. If animation mute is added, it needs a separate evaluated-value and persistence contract.

Grouping is determined by track-ID rules into Camera, Formula, Optics, Lighting and Shading; all unmatched IDs fall into Shading and the standalone array is always empty. The rules explicitly recognize some 2D Julia camera fields. For RFF, use parameter metadata to group palette/image/material/environment controls, rather than copying GMT's prefixes or classifying every future parameter as shading. Keep stable saved parameter identifiers separate from display names and group labels.

The sidebar's per-row live-value loop calls `getLiveValue`, which returns zero during playback in the implementation already inspected. This connects the earlier helper limitation to an actual displayed value: the sidebar cannot be treated as verified playback-value inspection. RFF should show the resolved value used by the current rendered frame, with explicit unavailable/stale status, and share one update mechanism across visible rows rather than creating a polling loop for each row. A source value and an animated evaluated value should be distinguishable when both are useful.

The “flat” classifier compares key values only, using an absolute tolerance of 1e-6. Equal endpoints with nonzero Bezier handles can still animate; a fixed absolute tolerance can also obscure meaningful changes in small-scale parameters. Its current use dims rows, so this is a presentation heuristic, not evidence that evaluation may be skipped. In RFF, determine inactivity from interpolation and extrapolation as well as keys, with a domain-appropriate tolerance; never use this heuristic to bypass fractal or shader updates.

Group key selection loops over tracks and calls the visibility setter repeatedly using the same captured visible-ID list. Several initially hidden tracks need one union update, otherwise later replacements can discard earlier additions. RFF should apply group selection and visibility changes atomically. Likewise, curve colors based on positions in a changing visible list can change when other curves are hidden; use a stable per-track color mapping consistently in sidebar and graph.

Post-behavior choices include Hold, Loop, Ping-Pong, Continue and Offset Loop. Their availability in this menu is authoring evidence, not proof that every preview, baking and export path evaluates them identically. Reuse the same resolved track evaluator across those paths before exposing equivalent RFF options. Group deletion should remain undoable and use stable track references rather than group labels as identity.

The resize helper delegates width constraints to the store and cleans listeners/cursor on mouse-up only. Its caller's resize element is inside a fixed-height header, despite a comment describing a full-height handle. Define the actual hit area and cancellation cleanup from the rendered structure when implementing a RFF equivalent; source comments alone do not prove either. This is a code-level integration review, not a screenshot-based interface audit.

**Proposed checks:** hide versus mute, partially visible groups, group selection with several hidden curves, curve colors after filtering, live values during playback, equal-value keys with curved handles, very small parameter changes, extrapolation consistency and sidebar destruction during resize. No application changes or runtime tests were performed for this section.

## Timeline composition: share time without losing editing context

The complete [Timeline.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/components/Timeline.tsx) and [KeyframeContextMenu.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/components/timeline/KeyframeContextMenu.tsx), 510 inventory lines together, were inspected. A useful RFF transfer is a shared time axis for a key overview and detailed curves, with independent graph visibility and a persistent key inspector. This supports coordinated palette, image mapping, environment and light animation in both flat 2D and relief rendering. It is an authoring proposal, not evidence that GMT's exact panel arrangement is required.

GMT shares horizontal scale and scroll between its two modes, but mounts different containers. Its ResizeObserver is attached once on mount, while the referenced container changes with the mode. RFF should observe the currently mounted viewport and re-establish observation when switching views. Otherwise stored width can cease to represent the displayed editor. The GraphEditor also receives a height derived from a fixed toolbar allowance; use actual available content dimensions when variable controls or scaling affect layout.

The graph initially chooses selected tracks or all non-hidden tracks when its visible list is empty. The same effect can run on later track changes while that list remains empty, so an explicit Hide All is not represented separately from an uninitialized view. Preserve that distinction in RFF and prune obsolete visible IDs when tracks are deleted. Remember the user's chosen view without interpreting deliberate emptiness as missing initialization.

“Fit Duration” routes through a zoom function clamped to at least one pixel per frame. For a sufficiently long animation this cannot show the complete duration in a smaller viewport. RFF should allow a fitting scale appropriate to the duration, with separately chosen editing limits and readable tick spacing. Shared view state should have one validation contract; GMT's graph can call the raw scale setter while the navigator uses a clamped setter.

The key menu represents the clicked key's interpolation even when the resulting operation targets multiple selected keys. It has no mixed-selection state. Its tangent signature accepts broken/auto flags but not `tangentMode`; consequently it cannot accurately identify Unified separately from Aligned, despite offering both actions. In RFF, summarize selected states explicitly and present the actual selected-key count and scope. Capture or resolve one target set consistently when a menu command runs: the inspected host captures selected IDs for interpolation but delegates other actions to store commands that may consult current selection.

Interpolation changes here patch the interpolation type only. Whether valid Bezier handles are created depends on downstream store behavior, which this menu cannot prove. A RFF command should establish the full interpolation invariant atomically. The “Duplicate Selection Here” background command composes copy and paste, which also replaces the clipboard; if RFF promises a duplicate operation, implement it independently when preserving the user's clipboard is intended. Loop labels request additional copies (for example x2 passes one additional repetition), a useful distinction to keep explicit in a saved operation contract.

The timeline clears hover and scrubbing flags on unmount, which partially mitigates child teardown concerns recorded earlier. That parent cleanup alone does not prove that every child interaction interval is ended or that preview changes are rolled back. Centralize owned gesture cleanup rather than relying only on boolean resets. Undo routing is activated by hover in this host; an RFF equivalent should also define keyboard focus and modal-editor behavior so animation edits reach the intended undo history.

**Verification proposed:** switch modes then resize; long-duration fit; intentionally hide all then add/edit tracks; delete displayed tracks; mixed interpolation/tangent selections; change selection while a menu is open; duplicate without losing an existing clipboard; and close the timeline during an active edit. Source benchmark comments were not adopted as current measured performance results. No RFF application code was changed.

## Transport controls: make timing and grouped capture explicit

The complete 520-line [TimelineToolbar.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/components/timeline/TimelineToolbar.tsx) was inspected, with a follow-up reread of [cameraKeyRegistry.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/animation/cameraKeyRegistry.ts). Useful RFF transfers are explicit FPS-change semantics, grouped capture of related parameters, and separate auto-key, modulation-record and export actions. These support both flat 2D palette animation and relief/environment motion; a 3D camera is not a prerequisite.

**FPS policy.** GMT exposes “Keep frames” and “Match time” when changing FPS, passing the chosen policy to the store. The first preserves key indices; the second requests preservation of their time in seconds. The preference is local toolbar state and resets on remount. For RFF, expose the consequence before applying a change and use one project timebase for keys, tangent time offsets, duration, audio and export. The toolbar alone does not establish how the store handles collisions or fractional frames. Its controls use integral FPS and frame displays; do not treat that as support for fractional-rate timebases. A “Deterministic Playback” toggle is likewise an invocation of store behavior, not independent proof of frame-for-frame image equality with export. That requires consistent simulation, random seeds, shader time and render completion.

**Grouped capture.** The toolbar gets camera track IDs and the capture function through a registry rather than hardcoding a particular scene representation. Adapt this pattern to a RFF “capture material/light setup” action with a defined set of related channels. The default registry resolves finite scalar values first and creates one undo snapshot, then writes tracks/keys sequentially. One undo entry is useful but is not the same as an atomic evaluated-state update. Missing channels are skipped. RFF should validate the required group and publish the accepted state together; preserve its own high-precision camera/location storage rather than copying scalar path walking. The default capture does not apply its optional interpolation override; a shared RFF capture contract should either honor the option or declare it unsupported.

**Status must describe the whole group.** GMT marks the camera group keyed when any registered track has a nearby key, rather than requiring every channel. It checks differences with an absolute 0.001 threshold and uses the generic live-value helper plus an evaluator call without the log flag for non-key frames. This can be insufficient for small-magnitude values, paired precision components or logarithmic interpolation. RFF should distinguish complete, partial, changed and unavailable group states, using the same domain-aware values that are captured and played back. A display tolerance must not silently prevent a requested save. Group deletion should apply the same exact frame-matching policy as capture and selection.

**Seek and recording boundaries.** The frame control's final change calls both store seek and engine scrub, while its intermediate change calls store seek alone. Verify the resulting preview contract through the store before borrowing this wiring. Separate auto-key of manual changes from recording generated modulation, and define what happens to armed recording when playback stops, loops, seeks or the panel closes. The existence of the toolbar buttons proves discoverable controls, not those downstream recording guarantees.

**Export extension boundary.** Render and additional export dialogs are registered capabilities; the main Render button is hidden when unavailable. This is a useful way to keep RFF's editor independent of a particular export backend. Additional dialogs survive closing the overflow menu because they are mounted separately. Give such actions stable identifiers and a defined lifecycle if their provider disappears. The overflow menu uses a fixed height estimate despite variable registered content, so measure/clamp its actual bounds if adopting this extension pattern.

**Proposed verification:** keep-frame versus keep-time FPS changes; capture with one channel missing; complete versus partial keyed status; tiny values and logarithmic tracks; grouped undo and evaluated-state consistency; seek while recording; loop boundaries; and preview/export at identical timestamps. This source audit adds no RFF code and makes no new runtime-performance or determinism claim.

## Time navigation: use the accepted viewport transform everywhere

**RFF transfer.** An overview bar with draggable visible-range edges can make long palette, lighting and material sequences easier to navigate. Pair it with a ruler that draws only the visible time interval. The full [TimeNavigator.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/components/timeline/TimeNavigator.tsx) and [TimelineRuler.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/components/timeline/TimelineRuler.tsx), 426 inventory lines, were inspected. These are editing improvements for both 2D and relief videos, not shader speedups.

The navigator derives its thumb from viewport width, content width and scroll. Its displayed thumb has a minimum width of 5%, while scroll calculations use the unclamped viewport ratio. Resizing starts from the displayed thumb, introducing a different geometric basis at small visible fractions. A RFF overview should keep the true range mapping separate from an enlarged hit target. Clicking the track may center the range, but dragging the thumb should retain its initial grab offset; GMT centers immediately even when the thumb itself is pressed.

Resize converts thumb geometry back into frame scale using a fixed sidebar width of 220, although the actual sidebar is resizable. It then requests a zoom and computes scroll from the requested total width before the parent clamps that zoom. Use current sidebar dimensions and derive both scroll and scale from one accepted transform. Otherwise the requested opposite-edge anchor need not remain fixed. Apply the same content-end clamping in the graph's state-based scrolling and the dope sheet's browser scrolling; relying on the browser to clamp one path does not constrain the other.

The wheel factor is linear in raw deltaY and does not normalize deltaMode. Large negative deltas can make the requested factor non-positive; the inspected parent clamps the resulting scale, so this is an abrupt navigation concern rather than proof of invalid stored scale through that caller. RFF should normalize input units and use a positive bounded zoom factor with a declared anchor. Guard zero-sized navigation bars and invalid dimensions before divisions. Navigator drag listeners have mouse-up cleanup but no unmount/cancellation path in this component.

The ruler draws a viewport-sized, device-pixel-scaled canvas and limits tick generation to the visible interval. This is preferable to allocating a canvas for the entire duration. However, its draw effect includes currentFrame, so it redraws static ticks, the end-region pattern and the playhead together on each frame update. If profiling justifies it, RFF can separate static ruler content from the moving playhead and cache the small hatch pattern. This is a source-derived optimization candidate, not a measured bottleneck. Device-pixel-ratio changes also need an invalidation trigger; reading the ratio inside an effect alone does not subscribe to monitor changes.

Ruler scrubbing captures the rectangle, scroll and scale at mouse-down, rounds to an integer frame and clamps only the lower bound locally. Seek/store behavior must establish the final duration bound. Middle-button movement calls seek without the explicit engine scrub call; other buttons take the ordinary scrub path, with no right-button exclusion here. Define these modes deliberately in RFF and reconcile pointer coordinates if auto-scroll or layout changes during a drag. The shared interaction hook may own interaction cleanup, but the local window move/up listeners are not removed by this component's unmount effect; those are separate responsibilities.

**Proposed checks:** resized sidebar, a visible fraction below 5%, thumb-edge grab without a jump, zoom clamping at either limit, high-resolution and line-mode wheel input, hidden/zero-width layout, graph versus dope-sheet end scrolling, monitor DPI changes, duration-end scrubbing, and closing during a drag. No runtime test or RFF implementation is claimed.

## Key inspector: make units and multi-selection edits explicit

**RFF transfer.** A shared numeric inspector for timeline keys and palette-channel curves can provide precise control of timing, value and Bezier handles without duplicating editing logic. The complete 502-line [KeyframeInspector.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/components/timeline/KeyframeInspector.tsx) was inspected. Its injected data-source interface and capability-dependent actions are useful patterns for both 2D palette work and relief material/light animation. This review does not establish which equivalent inspector features RFF already has.

The inspector converts displayed values to degrees only when every selected track ID contains `rotation`. A mixed rotation/nonrotation selection instead edits raw stored values with one common input. For RFF, obtain units from parameter metadata and disable or partition incompatible batch edits. Support explicit “set all to this value” and relative adjustment where appropriate; do not infer either from a mixed selection. The current same-value threshold is absolute 1e-5 and same-frame threshold is 0.001. Keys differing within those thresholds appear as one editable value and the edit assigns the exact same value/frame to all. Presentation similarity should not silently authorize collapsing meaningful small differences.

Frame editing rounds and clamps to zero, but does not explicitly transform tangents or resolve key collisions in this component. Value editing likewise patches values directly. Preserve or recompute the intended curve through a shared command layer, and make overwrite, relative shift and collision policies explicit. Do not reuse this ordinary-number editor for high-precision RFF locations without a precision-preserving adapter.

Tangent “Angle” is calculated from handle Y versus frame X, and “Weight” is the absolute horizontal extent as a percentage of the neighboring frame interval. These are curve-coordinate quantities, not an invariant screen angle or Euclidean length. They change meaning with units and logarithmic interpolation. RFF should label that convention and transform handles in their actual interpolation domain. Unequal neighboring intervals mean equal percentages do not imply equal handle lengths.

The inspector presents only Unified/Broken, although the wider system also distinguishes Aligned from Unified. Its numeric angle edits link the opposite angle when handles are unbroken, but length edits change one side independently and leave tangentMode unchanged. Thus the component alone does not enforce the advertised Unified length invariant. Use one explicit tangent-mode model and one constraint function for numeric edits, graph drags and saved data. Show mixed modes rather than displaying a default-looking Unified state for a mixed selection.

Tangent controls are shown based on the first key's interpolation and display its handle statistics, while their updates target all selected keys. The interpolation selector itself does have a Mixed option. Extend that mixed-selection treatment to tangent controls; do not suggest a common handle value when only the first selected key supplied it. Define whether non-Bezier keys participate in a tangent edit.

Quick actions become global when no keys are selected, which the panel explains. Preserve a conspicuous scope indicator in RFF. Selected Auto/Ease conversion may first patch interpolation and then invoke another action; an injected data source must make the subsequent operation read the converted state and avoid duplicate history entries. Numeric changes call an optional post-mutation refresh, whereas several interpolation actions do not call it here. Centralize the accepted-state refresh contract so palette preview and timeline playback cannot depend on which control performed an equivalent edit.

The component can be used with an external data source or a store fallback, but the fallback hook is called conditionally via null-coalescing. Its source assumes that choice never changes during a mounted instance. An equivalent reusable editor should keep provider lifetime explicit rather than relying on undocumented call-site stability. Controlled collapse and a full-width mode are useful integration capabilities, but this source read is not a visual-layout verification.

**Proposed checks:** mixed units; nearly equal but distinct values; logarithmic tangent units; Aligned versus Unified length changes; mixed interpolation selections; collisions after frame assignment; one-step undo for Auto/Ease; identical preview refresh across editing paths; and switching provider or layout during an edit. No RFF code or runtime tests were added.

## Dense key overview: batch drawing while bounding the surface and edit scope

**RFF opportunity.** For large palette, image and lighting animations, a batched key overview with group summary markers can reduce per-key interface objects while retaining a separate moving playhead. Full reads of [DopeSheet.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/components/timeline/DopeSheet.tsx) and [DopeSheetCanvas.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/components/timeline/DopeSheetCanvas.tsx) cover 754 inventory lines. The renderer and interaction-hook internals are separate evidence boundaries; historical benchmark comments are not current measurements.

GMT builds a shared row layout for track rows, group summaries and a root summary across non-hidden tracks. The canvas draws keys while ordinary elements retain sidebar controls. Drawing and picking receive the same row list, tracks and frame scale, a useful way to prevent independent layout formulas from drifting. The playhead subscribes to current time separately from the key overview. Reuse these principles in RFF's native rendering framework if profiling shows interface-object overhead.

The host passes a canvas width equal to the entire timeline content width minus the sidebar, and a height spanning all expanded rows. The wrapper uses panX=0 and browser scrolling rather than a viewport-sized surface. For long durations, high zoom or many rows, surface allocation can grow substantially even when most keys are offscreen. In RFF, bound the drawing surface to the viewport, cull both time and rows, and use the same viewport transform for picking. Cached row imagery is not by itself a bound on canvas memory. Inspect the renderer's allocation and cache limits before claiming a measured improvement.

Hover changes repaint the back, selection and hover passes; movement within the same picked marker avoids a state update, but still performs picking. Retain this distinction when profiling. A static-layer cache can help, but it does not prove that every mouse move is constant-time. Invalidate hover when its track/key disappears or the layout moves without a mouse event. Pixel scaling and cache behavior remain renderer responsibilities, not established by the wrapper's CSS dimensions.

**Selection semantics.** A row header selects tracks without automatically selecting all their keys, a useful separation to preserve. Summary-key lookup, however, uses the first key within 0.001 of the summary frame in each track. Coincident keys are not all collected by this host. Define exact aggregation and selection rules for RFF, especially after rounded retiming. A root summary represents all non-hidden tracks even when groups are collapsed; make that scope clear before batch edits.

Individual multi-click calls the selection action and then constructs a drag list from the pre-click selection. Whether that matches a toggle or additive selection depends on the store contract. RFF should compute one accepted selected-ID set and use it for both highlighting and dragging, rather than separately reconstructing it. Global key handlers exclude INPUT and TEXTAREA but are not scoped to editor focus and do not exclude editable content. Preserve other editors' shortcuts and modifier combinations when adopting keyboard selection.

**Adding and context actions.** Double-click avoids adding on an already picked marker and adds only on track rows. Its value comes from `getLiveValue` at the requested frame, but that helper reads current live state rather than evaluating that target time. For RFF, distinguish “capture current appearance here” from “insert a shape-preserving key here.” These are different useful operations and should not share an ambiguous default.

The canvas opens a key menu through right-button mouse-down and again through its context-menu handler. Background context handling does not stop bubbling, so the parent background handler can also run with a separately derived frame coordinate. The parent uses the content rectangle plus scroll offset, whereas the canvas uses its own scrolled rectangle. RFF should route each context request once through one coordinate conversion. Verify the actual selected frame after horizontal scrolling before claiming correctness; this source read does not include an interactive reproduction.

The TRACK_FOCUS event collapses other predefined groups but does not itself select the target or scroll its row into view. A RFF “show animated parameter” command should explicitly resolve reveal, selection and viewport movement, preserving the user's other context where practical.

**Proposed verification:** long duration at maximum zoom, many expanded rows, viewport memory bounds, coincident summary keys, multi-click followed by drag, collapsed-group summary edits, double-click capture versus insertion, background menus after scrolling, and key deletion while hovered. These are RFF adoption conditions for 2D and relief authoring; no shader implementation or runtime speed claim is added.

## Key renderer completion: cache pixels with a complete validity contract

Six complete reads close the renderer-side boundary from the preceding dope-sheet section: [DopeSheetRenderer](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/utils/DopeSheetRenderer.ts), [builder](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/utils/DopeSheetRendererBuilder.ts), [cache wrappers](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/utils/DopeSheetRendererCache.ts), [TrackRow](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/components/timeline/TrackRow.tsx), [TrackGroup](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/components/timeline/TrackGroup.tsx), and [SelectionTransformBar](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/components/timeline/SelectionTransformBar.tsx). The interaction hook remains a separate pending read.

**Mechanism worth adopting for RFF.** Each track's static markers are drawn into one row image, with Step squares, Bezier circles and Linear diamonds. Groups build a sorted union of exact frame values and draw summary diamonds. Selection and hover are separate drawing passes, and selected-key lookup constructs an ID map per selected track instead of searching its key array for every selected ID. This is a concrete batched-rendering pattern for large 2D palette or relief-lighting timelines. It does not imply a measured shader-rendering benefit.

Track cache validity uses key-array identity plus rounded scale/pan, row height and flatness. Group validity compares child key-array references, copying the reference list when storing it. This prevents later mutation of the list itself from corrupting the stored token, but still requires immutable key arrays/objects for reliable invalidation. The caller does not sort those tokens, despite wrapper comments describing a sorted list; membership-order changes can cause a harmless rebuild.

Canvas width is absent from both view keys, and the previously inspected shared cache lookup does not compare stored dimensions. A wider timeline with unchanged key arrays and scale can therefore reuse a narrower row bitmap. Runtime group-color overrides are also omitted from the key. Theme changes do explicitly clear both caches, so the conclusion is not that themes are wholly unhandled. For RFF, include every pixel-affecting input—dimensions, device scale, theme or explicit colors, layout and source revision—or use deliberate invalidation at the owning boundary. Rounded transform keys require a bounded screen-space error policy.

The renderer walks every supplied row, composites its full-width image, and evicts entries absent from that row set. The host supplies expanded rows, not a vertically clipped viewport set. Consequently this eviction is membership-based, not actual scroll-based culling. Builders scan all keys and merely skip those outside the canvas; sorted group frames do not cause an early loop exit. Bound the viewport surface and cache byte budget, then use sorted frame-range queries and visible-row ranges where profiling warrants them. Module-level caches are shared across mounts; give independent editor instances clear ownership to avoid eviction interference. Neither the wrapper nor these drawing functions establishes a device-pixel-scaled backing surface; unlike the ruler, this path renders at the supplied CSS-sized dimensions.

**Picking contract.** The picker scans rows, binary-searches each relevant sorted track's time window, then selects the nearest key within eight horizontal pixels. It accepts the entire row height, not the exact marker shape. Dense windows still require scanning their candidate keys, and group picking repeats the search for every child. RFF should choose a deliberate hit region and tie-break rule, preserve sorted data, and expose coincident keys without silently hiding their identities. Group aggregation uses exact frame equality, while the host's group-selection lookup uses a tolerance; align those semantics before claiming summary markers select precisely what they represent.

Selection rings are only drawn for track rows, so a collapsed group's selected keys do not receive an aggregated selection ring in this renderer. A RFF summary should distinguish none/some/all selected when collapsed. Group transform bars use group-local bounds but forward the common callback without a group-specific key list; the source comments say it affects all selected keys. Verify the pending interaction hook, and ensure the displayed bounds match the actual transformed set before adopting that behavior.

Track-row live values are a literal `--` placeholder, distinct from the graph sidebar's live-value loop. Do not describe them as implemented value inspection. Track/group row heights are hardcoded here while the canvas layout uses shared constants; keep one metric source in RFF. The decorative row regions pass pointer events through to the canvas, while transform handles re-enable them—preserve that interaction ownership when changing visual stacking or opacity.

**Proposed verification:** width-only changes with a warm cache, immutable versus in-place edits, color overrides, multiple editors, DPI changes, many offscreen rows, dense/coincident keys, collapsed selected groups, and group-local handles with selection in another group. No benchmark, screenshot test or RFF implementation is claimed.

## Key movement completion: transform the intended set from one original curve

The full 560-line [useDopeSheetInteraction.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/hooks/useDopeSheetInteraction.ts) confirms that a group-local transform bar captures **all selected key IDs**, using the min/max bounds supplied by that bar. Thus the earlier scope concern is established at the implementation level: selecting keys in several groups and dragging one group's scale handle can transform other groups around that group's bounds. For RFF, either restrict the operation to the represented group or show bounds for the complete affected selection. Coordinated material/light retiming is useful, but its scope must be explicit.

**One retiming command for both editors.** Ordinary key dragging and transform-bar movement follow different handle policies. The bar moves frame positions without changing handles; direct key dragging scales handles using initial handle values and neighboring positions taken from the changing sequence. The helper scales both X and Y to retain handle angle, while bar time-scaling changes only X. These represent different intentions: slope preservation versus affine retiming. Define the intended policy for RFF palette and lighting curves and use it consistently across graph and overview editors. Translating a whole segment in time should preserve its internal shape, while retiming only an endpoint needs a stated boundary policy.

The direct-drag neighbor collection also has a concrete limitation: when one unselected key lies between two dragged keys, the first insertion stores only one of its handle snapshots. Encountering it from the other side adds the reference-key ID without adding the other handle snapshot. Its later update requires both the reference and stored handle, so both adjacent handles are not necessarily adjusted. Build complete affected-segment records once at gesture start, keyed by track and key ID, then derive every preview from those records. The dragged-position map here uses key ID alone even though other identities are composite; RFF should retain track identity throughout unless global uniqueness is an enforced invariant.

Direct dragging repeatedly sorts the same track for individual dragged keys and re-reads current neighbors. Crossing keys can change those neighbors while the source handles remain from the start. Cache sorted track/index data for the gesture and resolve all new positions together before applying handle rules. Do not adopt the source comment's unmeasured “99%” assurance. Guard collisions and crossings explicitly rather than allowing incidental array order to determine segment ownership.

The dope-sheet scale ratio stays positive with a minimum span of one frame, unlike the graph box's negative-ratio mirror. Both round or clamp resulting frames. Treat reversal as a separate explicit capability if the overview does not support it, and verify graph/overview equivalence for ordinary positive retiming. Apply any zero-bound translation limit to the whole selected set when preserving spacing is intended; individually clamping keys can collapse their relative timing.

**Marquee selection.** Mouse-up calculates the actual summary-row position from element rectangles, a useful improvement over assuming a fixed audio-strip height. Yet mouse-down still contains a forced-Y shortcut for the region immediately beneath the ruler, and mouse-up reconstructs group/track rows independently of the renderer's row layout. RFF should use the same layout snapshot for drawing, picking and marquee selection, including optional audio rows. The start path recognizes Meta as additive, while completion only checks Shift/Ctrl. Keep modifier policy stable for the gesture and derive selection from the final pointer position, not only the last rendered selection-box state.

The hook cleans its global listeners when its effect is disposed, and mouse-up ends the scrub gesture. Those facts narrow earlier concerns about missing listener cleanup in other components; they do not establish cancellation rollback or complete teardown of this hook's editing state. Its live previews immediately update keys and scrub the current frame. A RFF equivalent needs one transaction with explicit completion/cancel semantics and final accepted-state rendering. Freeze or re-anchor view scale if it changes during a drag; this implementation divides the full drag distance by the latest scale.

**Proposed verification:** selection across groups with a local scale handle; whole-block translation; one unselected key between two selected keys; repeated drag previews and return to origin; crossing/coincident keys; keys at time zero; graph/overview retiming agreement; optional audio rows; Meta selection; and cancellation during live rendering. These are source-supported authoring requirements for 2D and relief animation, not implemented RFF fixes or executed tests.

## Audio timeline support: preserve source time before driving shader animation

**RFF opportunity.** An audio strip can help align palette sweeps, emission pulses and lighting transitions to sound. The full [AudioStrip.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/components/timeline/AudioStrip.tsx) and [audioWaveform.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/utils/audioWaveform.ts), 354 inventory lines, were inspected; [audioFileCache.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine/animation/audioFileCache.ts) was reread for source lifetime. This establishes clip authoring and waveform mechanisms, not an end-to-end audio-reactive shader or export guarantee.

GMT separates playback duration from the decoded waveform's covered duration. The strip maps peaks using their own duration and leaves uncovered audio time blank rather than stretching a partial decode. Retain that distinction in RFF, and describe missing waveform coverage explicitly. Waveform peaks are maximum absolute sample amplitudes across all channels, not loudness, frequency-band energy or a modulation envelope. Do not route them directly to shader controls under those names; audio analysis and parameter mapping need their own time and filtering contract.

**Accept asynchronous results by clip identity.** Loading creates an optimistic 60-second clip, starts playback loading, awaits metadata separately and decodes waveform peaks. Both completion paths update by deck index without checking the original clip ID. A removed/replaced clip or a user trim made while decoding can therefore be affected by a late update; both completions write trimEndSec. RFF should accept results only for the current source generation, keep metadata initialization separate from user-edited trim, and reject stale completions after removal. Represent pending, failed, partial and ready states separately: this strip catches decode failure but its no-peaks display still says “Decoding…”. Metadata rejection also needs a handled terminal state.

**Waveform coverage and cost.** The peak builder uses a floor-sized bucket for every output entry. When sample count is not divisible by bucket count, trailing samples are omitted, although the returned duration describes the entire decoded buffer. Partition with exact proportional boundaries so the final bucket reaches the last sample. The function loads the entire file and decoded channels before reduction; short-lived context cleanup does not make peak memory independent of file length. Its comment mentions OfflineAudioContext, but the implementation constructs AudioContext. Use explicit decode size limits or a streaming/chunked strategy for large sources, and move expensive reduction off the interactive path where practical.

The strip linearly interpolates neighboring peak buckets for each CSS pixel. At far zoom-out this is not a max-over-pixel-interval reduction and can miss a narrow transient between samples. A multiresolution peak hierarchy provides a better overview while preserving sharp attacks. The drawing loop covers full clip width, not just the viewport. Its intended 16384 backing-width cap is weakened by a minimum DPR of 0.25: above 65536 CSS pixels, the resulting buffer can exceed the named cap. Bound allocation directly and render only visible time. Verify detail before claiming that resolution loss is imperceptible.

**Clip time and persistence.** Position is stored in frames and trims in seconds. Left trim shifts the frame position to preserve the right edge, but rounding and zero-clamping mean that preservation is not exact at all boundaries. Define the timebase and snap policy, minimum length for very short clips, and behavior under FPS changes. The drag code has listener cleanup but no explicit snapshot/cancel transaction in this component; inspect the store before claiming audio edits are undoable as one gesture.

The source-file cache is a page-lifetime map for two decks; metadata and waveform peaks alone do not recreate audio after reopening. For RFF, define project asset references or packaging, missing-file relinking, and source identity used by both playback analysis and export. Removal should invalidate pending work as well as clear the asset reference. The inspected group renders an Audio header even with no clips; if only deck B is populated, it offers no empty deck-A slot through this component. Expose available capacity independently of deck order if adopting multi-source audio authoring.

**Proposed verification:** replace/remove during decode; trim before metadata arrives; failed and partial decode; a transient in the final sample remainder; long files at high zoom; short clips; FPS changes; reopen with missing source; and identical source-time mapping for preview and export. These requirements apply to 2D and relief shader animation. No RFF implementation or runtime audio test is claimed.

## Shared curve-editing adapter: unify commands as well as controls

The full [GraphDataSource.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/utils/GraphDataSource.ts) and its [unification plan/history](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/plans/graph-editor-unification.md), 382 inventory lines together, were inspected. The useful RFF architecture is one curve-editing core with adapters for palette channels and time-varying shader parameters. Keep application-specific precision, persistence and rendering in the adapter. Shared drawing and gestures can prevent separate editors from acquiring different interpolation or tangent behavior, but a shared interface alone does not prove behavioral equivalence.

GMT's interface separates patching existing keys from replacing complete arrays, and exposes optional capture, selection, history and scrub capabilities. The timeline adapter forwards store actions, while complete replacement directly updates the sequence with new track objects. This immutable replacement correctly gives subscribers new identities. However, it stores the supplied arrays as-is: it neither sorts nor clones their contents, validates finite values/unique IDs, normalizes tangents, reconciles selection, takes a history snapshot, nor invokes its separate post-mutation callback. Callers therefore own several important invariants. For RFF, put those guarantees in a common command boundary so baking, fitting, drawing and ordinary edits cannot bypass them accidentally.

Use an explicit edit transaction with begin, preview, commit and cancel semantics. Return an accepted revision or structured rejection when the source changed or a channel is unavailable. Publish keys and selection consistently, request one render of the accepted state, and keep the history boundary independent of display refresh. Optional methods should correspond to discoverable capabilities; silently invoking an absent replacement action must not leave a changed selection without changed keys. Preserve append-only settings and existing recipe stability if new editor preferences or animation parameters are persisted.

The adapter returns a new outer object and nested scrub object each render, even though individual action functions are stable. Consumers that depend on whole-object identity can still recreate callbacks. This is not inherently a fault, but the lifecycle contract should state whether a gesture uses captured state, current state or a revisioned source. The previously inspected tool hook and selection box use different approaches. A RFF core should freeze mathematical input for a gesture while obtaining the current accepted destination through an explicit API, rather than relying on incidental callback identity.

The accompanying document is a mixture of initial plan, completion notes and later follow-ups. It records removal of duplicate interaction/tool components and describes historical tests; these are project history, not tests executed in this audit. Some draft interface fields differ from current code, and stable-reference guidance differs between its main completion section and final follow-up. Use current implementation to resolve what is actually wired. In particular, its claim that smoothing is equivalent because every move overwrites the same keys does not establish restoration when an operation emits no patches; the return-to-neutral concern documented above remains relevant. Likewise its description of logarithmic dragging as a linear-span approximation is a limit to inspect, not proof of log-domain correctness.

**RFF adoption checks:** apply the same curve edit through palette and timeline adapters; compare accepted samples, tangent modes and undo behavior; replace arrays containing unsorted or coincident times; cancel after preview; remove a target channel mid-edit; and verify one accepted-state refresh after each command. The generic graph-interaction hook remains pending, so complete end-to-end equivalence is not claimed. These findings apply to flat 2D color curves and relief material/light animation; no RFF code was changed.

## Graph interaction completion: transform values and handles in their declared domains

The complete 920-line [useGraphInteraction.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/hooks/useGraphInteraction.ts) was read in two contiguous, nontruncated parts. This closes the pending generic-interaction boundary from the shared-adapter section. RFF can reuse the design ideas of multi-key editing, soft selection, coordinated tangent adjustment and explicit active/passive scrubbing for 2D palette curves and relief lighting. The concrete implementation needs the domain and transaction conditions below; shared code is not a guarantee of correct behavior in every value space.

**Logarithmic movement.** In normalized mode, key dragging multiplies a pixel-derived delta by the track span, then adds it to the original raw value. The inspected host stores positive log-track ranges in logarithmic units. Adding that log-unit delta to a raw magnitude is not the inverse of the displayed log mapping and can produce non-positive values. Use a shared forward/inverse domain transform: transform the starting value, apply the gesture delta there, then invert. Freeze the transformation basis for the gesture, including range and view scale. The hook currently reads the latest range and scale while retaining original key values.

Handle picking likewise uses `key.value + tangent.y` and linear range normalization instead of a log-domain handle mapping. Handle dragging starts from the displayed key and produces a span-scaled Y delta; that can represent log units when the range is logarithmic, but it does not make the separate picking formula correct. Give rendering, hit-testing, dragging, numeric inspection and playback one handle-coordinate contract. A parameter's unit metadata must replace scattered naming heuristics.

**Soft selection.** The hook captures initial frame/value pairs and uses the maximum falloff from selected keys on the same track, measured by initial time distance. This avoids repeatedly adding movement to the last preview and gives a useful local-editing mechanism. However, direct keys snap to integral frames while influenced keys round to hundredths, and this branch emits only frame/value patches without the ordinary branch's handle adjustments. Define snapping and tangent behavior consistently in RFF. If radius or enablement changes mid-gesture, the initially captured set and currently affected set can diverge; keys that leave the influence region need restoration rather than simply receiving no patch. Either freeze falloff parameters or rebuild every preview from a complete baseline.

The ordinary branch repeats the previously observed dope-sheet pattern: initial handles combined with current neighbors, per-key sorting, key-ID-only position lookup, and neighbor records that may omit the second handle when an unselected key lies between two selected keys. Consolidate both editors around one segment-aware retiming command. Preserve composite identities and update affected boundaries from one original topology.

**Multiple tangent edits.** Dragging a handle computes separate X/Y ratios and applies them to matching handles of selected peers. Near-zero starting components switch to additive deltas. This is a practical bulk-shaping operation but differs from applying a common angle or length, especially across different units or log/linear tracks. RFF should expose the intended operation and restrict incompatible selections. The dragged key uses its current opposite handle for Aligned length, while peers use captured opposite handles. Ctrl breaks the dragged key's handles but not the peers; once written broken, releasing Ctrl does not automatically restore linkage. Define modifier behavior and apply mode invariants consistently across the whole affected set. This branch does not call the local handle-constraint helper before forwarding patches; downstream validation remains necessary.

**Picking and gesture lifecycle.** Mouse picking prioritizes selected handles; coarse-pointer detection prioritizes keys within a larger square region. This can reduce accidental handle edits, but the media query describes the primary pointer, not necessarily the current input on a hybrid device. First matching key order decides overlaps rather than nearest distance. Use the actual pointer type, deterministic nearest-hit rules and a way to reach overlapping handles. Selected-key membership uses repeated array searches while walking keys; index selected IDs and visible time ranges for large curves if profiling warrants it.

The global handlers read a latest-data ref, which avoids stale provider callbacks. Mouse-up recomputes the final marquee from the release coordinates, an improvement over relying solely on the last rendered box. However, its additive marquee policy omits Meta despite using Meta for key selection elsewhere. Unmount removes listeners but does not itself roll back edits or end the active scrub interval in this hook. Its delayed context-menu reset is also not tied to a gesture generation. Centralize completion/cancellation and distinguish transient gesture state from committed data. Parent or shared-hook cleanup can mitigate some effects, but is not proof of full cancellation semantics.

**Proposed checks:** normalized logarithmic key and handle dragging; movement back to the starting point; soft-radius changes during editing; direct versus influenced snapping; multiple tracks with different units; near-zero peer handles; Ctrl linkage changes; overlapping keys on hybrid-pointer devices; and teardown during an edit. No RFF implementation, interactive reproduction or performance measurement is claimed.

## Modulation target selection: expose only meaningful, routable parameters

The complete 347-line [ParameterSelector.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/components/ParameterSelector.tsx) was inspected after the timeline component reads. **RFF opportunity:** a shared target catalog could connect keyframes, audio/LFO modulation and reusable material masks to palette, texture, environment and lighting controls. This is especially useful as the proposed shader features grow. Flat 2D parameters and relief-only parameters should share identification and availability rules while retaining different capabilities.

GMT builds categories from registered features and expands scalar/vector parameters into routable component targets. It imports the modulatable predicate, excluded features and virtual-light property list from a shared routing module. That is a useful defense against offering a control that no evaluator consumes. For RFF, make the target descriptor carry a stable ID, component, display label, units, domain, current availability and supported modulation operations. The same descriptor should drive the picker, animation binding, saved reference validation and the actual shader/host update. Do not infer route support from the presence of a slider alone.

The ordinary feature path applies dynamic labels/visibility and parent activation conditions, listing inactive entries as disabled and active entries first. However, per-formula grouped entries take a separate path: they expand vectors and otherwise list parameters directly without the ordinary modulatable/condition checks. Virtual lights likewise enumerate every configured light slot without slot-availability checks here, and camera entries are hardcoded 3D position/rotation targets. RFF should apply common route and availability validation after all such expansions, including synthetic targets. A 2D pan/zoom or palette-phase catalog should come from RFF capabilities, not inherit this 3D camera list.

The module supports an injected formula metadata resolver so grouped or generic formula parameters can use meaningful names. This is a useful separation of stable identity from authored presentation. Yet selected-label resolution destructures only the first two segments of a dot-separated path. For a camera path such as `camera.rotation.x`, the axis segment is discarded before building the label. Preserve the complete parsed identity and component when formatting a selected target; otherwise different axes can become indistinguishable even though their saved IDs differ. The selected-label path also does not reuse ordinary dynamicConfig label overrides, so a menu label and the closed-button label can differ.

Categories read the feature registry during rendering, and item building reads current store state when invoked, but this component subscribes only to the active formula. The formula resolver setter has no notification mechanism. Therefore current-state reads alone do not prove that an already open menu refreshes immediately when availability or registration changes. For RFF, subscribe to the relevant metadata/state revision and revalidate the target when committing a link. Keep an explicit unavailable target visible in existing saved links instead of silently retargeting it or confusing an old label with current route validity.

**Proposed checks:** each offered target reaches a real consumer; inactive formula parameters and light slots; vec4 component identity; 2D-specific camera targets; dynamic label changes; formula replacement while the picker is open; registry changes; and reopening a saved link whose target is no longer available. This section records source-supported catalog design requirements, not an implemented RFF modulation feature or a complete routing-engine audit.

## Selective look import: reuse appearance without replacing the fractal view

**RFF opportunity.** Let users import chosen appearance groups from another saved work—palette/image layers, material settings, lighting/environment or post-processing—while retaining their current location and fractal computation. The complete [LoadFilterPanel.tsx](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/components/LoadFilterPanel.tsx) and [loadFilter.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine-gmt/utils/loadFilter.ts), 513 inventory lines, establish a concrete GMT reference. This is a workflow extension around shader settings, useful for flat 2D coloring as well as relief looks. It should extend RFF's existing palette/color imports rather than duplicate them.

GMT distinguishes appearance-only application from structural loading. If formula, camera and animation are all excluded, it sends selected feature slices through the partial-preset application path. Otherwise it clones the current preset, overlays selected groups and invokes normal scene loading. Before the structural path it flushes the live camera to the store, preventing an excluded camera from being replaced by a stale stored pose. RFF should similarly capture the actual accepted high-precision location and distinguish display-only changes from computation-affecting changes. Do not reconstruct its coordinates through ordinary JSON numbers or bypass its reference/MPA validity rules.

The panel remembers group choices but applies them to the ordinary Load menu only when “Always filter” is enabled; its own Load button always uses them. The menu marks an active sticky filter. This separates remembered choices from silently changing every future load. Keep that distinction, show the concrete groups being imported, and retain a simple full-load operation. The inspected label “Gradients” actually covers both coloring and image texturing; RFF should name asset-bearing groups accurately.

**Dependency-aware groups.** GMT copies formula-associated distance-estimator parameters individually rather than importing the entire quality feature. That is a useful general principle: parameters defining the computation belong with the computation, whereas performance preferences can remain local. RFF must determine its own dependency graph; GMT's 3D estimator fields do not map directly to RFF's 2D perturbation pipeline. Appearance groups can also reference image assets, palette data, field sources and animation targets. Include or explicitly resolve these dependencies so an imported material mask or emission source does not reference a missing layer.

**Missing-field semantics.** In structural merging, an absent feature slice deletes the destination slice so loading can apply defaults. By contrast, the named formula-quality helper leaves a destination parameter unchanged when absent in the source, and legacy top-level lights are copied only when the source array is nonempty. These are distinct policies, not a universal “unchecked values stay, checked values replace” rule. For RFF, document replace, merge and reset-to-default semantics, including older files, absent assets and intentionally empty collections. Compare appearance-only and structural paths for equivalent selected groups; this caller alone does not establish identical results.

The filter is read after asynchronous file claiming and parsing rather than captured when the user starts the operation. With a nonmodal panel, choices can change while loading. Capture a load request containing source identity, selected groups and destination revision, then prepare a reviewable result and commit it atomically. Preserve the prior valid render while any necessary shader preparation completes. Concurrent imports and source errors should produce a clear accepted/failed result, not only console warnings.

Persisted filter JSON is spread over defaults without checking property names or boolean types; `isLoadFilterActive` examines every resulting key. Validate the schema and migrate known fields explicitly. RFF settings additions must remain compatible with its append-only ConfigIO rules. A selective import also needs one undoable command and stable palette recipe semantics: copying a recipe must not redefine its generator or identifier.

The file-input element is removed on change; no cancellation cleanup is defined here. File-claim handlers can consume the selection before the filtered scene path, so “use filter” is not proof that every accepted file format passes through this merge. State those format-specific boundaries rather than promising generic compatibility from this panel alone.

**Proposed verification:** palette-only and material-only imports; image dependencies; old files with missing fields; empty lights/layers; current high-precision location unchanged; animation targeting excluded groups; settings changed during parsing; concurrent loads; cancellation; failed shader preparation; and one-step undo. No RFF code or runtime import test is claimed.

## Partial application completion: batch history is not atomic acceptance

Full reads of [applyPartialPreset.ts](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/engine-gmt/utils/applyPartialPreset.ts) and its [specification/history](https://github.com/gamazama/GMT-fractals/blob/ad28b8bbca3c01b4d2cfebebd727c5bcd951a2e1/plans/partial-apply-utility.md), 274 inventory lines, clarify the appearance-only path. **RFF transfer:** one shared operation for feature reset, importing a selected look and applying a starting style, driven by declared parameter metadata. This can serve 2D palette/image settings and relief materials without replacing the fractal location.

The implementation opens a parameter transaction, iterates selected registered features, assembles declared-parameter updates and calls each feature setter. A finally block ends the transaction. This gives a common history boundary, but the function does not stage all values before mutation, roll back earlier setters if a later setter throws, or wait for shader compilation. Its result is void. For RFF, separate preparing an import, validating assets/values, preparing required pipelines and publishing the accepted state. A failed compile must not leave newly stored settings paired ambiguously with an old pipeline. Do not describe one undo transaction as proof of atomic rendering or rollback.

Missing parameters use declared defaults; extra source parameters are ignored. The actual fallback checks `sourceValue !== undefined`, so explicit null is passed through, unlike the specification's null-coalescing sketch. Values and default objects are not cloned here. Resolve null/missing/reset semantics by parameter type, validate finite values and domains, and define ownership of nested arrays before forwarding them. Unknown features or missing setters are silently skipped; a RFF import result should list skipped capabilities so a partial result is not mistaken for a complete look transfer.

Current code distinguishes `userScoped` and `preserveOnApply` from accumulation-reset behavior. This is an important reusable principle: whether a value belongs to the user's device, whether bulk application should preserve authored content, whether it resets accumulation and whether it requires compilation are separate axes. The historical spec still uses `respectNoReset`, so it is not the current API. Keep these policies separate in RFF metadata; especially avoid equating a display-only parameter with a parameter that should never reset.

The filtered-load caller explicitly sets `respectPreserve:false` for appearance-only imports. That bypasses both preservation categories, not only the light-array member mentioned in its comment. RFF should request narrowly defined overrides for the selected content rather than disabling unrelated device-preference protection globally. Likewise, `includeCompileParams:false` skips compile-flagged values but does not check whether the remaining runtime values make sense with the current shader variant. A fast appearance application still needs compatibility validation.

The utility copies declared parameters, not arbitrary feature state. Comments saying it never touches arrays or lights are therefore not a universal guarantee: an array declared as a parameter can be copied if it passes the guards, while top-level legacy light data is outside this loop. Specify actual data ownership in RFF and test each asset-bearing parameter. Repeated feature IDs can also invoke the same setter more than once; normalize the requested set before preparing changes.

The design document records an implementation commit and a proposed/historical test script. Neither was run in this audit. Its claim that stable parameter paths keep animation bindings intact concerns identity only: retained animation can still overwrite imported base values on evaluation. RFF should define whether a look import changes base values under existing animation, replaces related tracks, or offers an explicit choice.

**Proposed verification:** failure in the second feature setter; failed pipeline preparation; explicit null versus absent values; mutable default arrays; preserved device preferences; missing target features; duplicate requested groups; runtime-only import into a different shader variant; and retained animation over imported material settings. No RFF implementation or executed test is claimed.

## Shader-control composition: separate layout, availability and compilation
