For the current RFF priorities, the first validation set should include constant and sharply patterned environments across roughness values; minified/warped image layers across resolutions; and masks with narrow transitions. Add preview/video/full-frame/tile comparisons using the same accepted configuration. Measure GPU time separately from compilation and image quality. These diagnostic-source reads improve the verification plan but supply no executed result, shader speedup or proof of numerical-DE/MPA compatibility.

## Optional editor loading and surface ownership

Full reads of `components/ui/lazyWithFallback.tsx`, `layerStack.ts`, `Layer.tsx`, `layerHost.ts`, `Modal.tsx`, `zIndex.ts` and `panelStack.ts` identify supporting architecture for RFF's material/palette editors. These source-level findings are not a visual UI audit or evidence of a current RFF interface defect.

**Preserve the working scene when an optional editor cannot load.** GMT's lazy loader substitutes a local notice for rejected imports whose error message matches a small set of module-download phrases. Other rejected imports are rethrown. This is a useful failure boundary for optional RFF asset browsers or editor modules: retain the accepted renderer and unsaved settings, present a local failure, and distinguish retryable loading from an evaluator/programming failure. The source uses message matching, not a structured error type; an evaluation error with matching wording can be misclassified, and unfamiliar download wording can escape. A loader that throws synchronously before returning its promise also bypasses this attached catch. Prefer explicit failure categories where the RFF subsystem can provide them.

The substituted component is cached by the lazy mechanism and offers a full page reload, not a fresh module retry. Reload itself does not save state; this file relies on any external before-unload handling. For a desktop RFF adaptation, retain or save recoverable state before restart and do not imply a reload button guarantees recovery. The notice replaces the component and ignores its original props, so a close affordance must remain available in the owning surface. Historical smoke-test claims in the header were not rerun here.

**Separate surface classes from activation order.** GMT defines bands for panels, menus, dialogs, progress and recovery notices, then maintains independent session-local activation lists within rankable bands. Raising a panel preserves relative ownership of higher-priority surfaces; releasing it removes its ID. The panel-specific module is only an adapter to that common mechanism. RFF can apply the architectural principle to its own window system without copying browser z-index values: define owned dialogs/popups, make the actively edited material panel reachable, and preserve visible recovery/progress controls. This does not address the separately documented native Win32 menu show-before-first-paint interval.

The implementation has bounded rank capacity: ranks beyond a tier's span clamp to the same value, leaving equal-z ordering to the rendering environment. IDs are the ownership key, with no reference counting for duplicate IDs; one participant's release can unregister another if callers reuse a key. Require stable unique surface IDs and a capacity policy. Pointer activation is captured before a caller callback, while keyboard focus does not raise the layer here. Align keyboard and pointer activation with dismissal ownership rather than assuming visual order alone selects the correct Escape target.

**The layer abstraction has explicit limits.** Portal tiers resolve a shared host and shell tiers remain inline, but caller `style` is spread after computed `position` and `zIndex`, allowing both to be overridden. A caller-supplied host can itself sit within a different stacking context. The host setter is an imperative boot-time convention, not a subscription that moves already-mounted surfaces. Thus the documented guarantee depends on caller discipline and host placement. Registration checks collisions at runtime even though some comments call them development-only. It registers entries sequentially, so a later failure leaves earlier entries applied; table snapshots also shallow-copy mutable definitions. Validate extension definitions and stage a complete registration batch before committing if RFF adopts an extensible equivalent.

**A modal label does not implement complete modality.** GMT's modal supplies a backdrop, dialog semantics and delegated Escape dismissal; backdrop dismissal is opt-in in executable code despite the older broad header description. This is a useful default for preserving in-progress material edits. The file itself does not provide focus capture/restore, background inertness or transaction rollback, and accepts a raw numeric stacking value. Those behaviors may be supplied elsewhere and are not established by this component. In RFF, keep draft acceptance/cancel semantics and focus restoration explicit for nested color/image dialogs, and test that closing a child does not discard or commit its parent's settings.

These mechanisms support reliable editing of both 2D palettes and relief materials. They add no new shader effect or measured rendering benefit. No panels were opened or interaction tests run; only the report and hash-checked coverage ledger changed.

## Floating editor placement: preserve reachability and explicit gesture completion

Full reads of `components/ui/FloatingPanel.tsx`, `AnchoredMenu.tsx`, `viewportClamp.ts`, `Floating.tsx`, `DropScrim.tsx`, `stopNavKeys.ts` and the UI export index complete the following supporting checks. The transfer is reliable nonblocking palette/material editing alongside RFF's canvas; these are not new shader effects or an executed interface audit.

**Keep settings reachable without moving the artwork.** GMT supports controlled or local panel geometry, a full-viewport sheet, and content-height panels that scroll rather than reposition when expanded. Width-only left-edge resizing preserves the opposite edge through `newX = oldX + oldWidth - newWidth`. Those are useful patterns for RFF's image/environment editors: preserve a stable working position while opening advanced controls, and restore saved geometry against the current monitor work area and DPI. The source clamps position on selected geometry changes and window resize; it does not generally shrink an oversized width. Its normal mode caps height at 90vh, while auto-height uses room below the top. Define both position and size recovery when the work area becomes smaller than a stored panel.

The clamp effect omits `open` and `autoHeight` from its dependencies and has no content-size observer. A mounted closed panel can therefore open without a fresh measurement when other dependencies remain unchanged; content-driven dimension changes similarly do not guarantee reclamping. Use explicit open/reopen and size-change reconciliation where needed. Controlled geometry depends on the parent accepting callbacks; direct DOM movement followed by an unaccepted controlled value is not a completed state update. Keep persisted geometry separate from temporary drag feedback.

**Cancellation is a policy, not merely a second pointer-up.** The shared drag helper captures a pointer and treats pointer-cancel as the same commit callback as pointer-up. It stores no active pointer ID, rejects no additional active press, has no lost-capture/unmount finalization and clears its snapshot after invoking the callback rather than in an unconditional cleanup. Panel movement also excludes buttons in the handle but not other interactive descendants, and does not restrict initiating mouse buttons here. For RFF, use one gesture owner, define commit-last-valid versus rollback on cancellation, and finish exactly once. Moving a panel can reasonably keep its last position; canceling a material edit may need to restore a draft. Do not conflate those semantics when reusing gesture infrastructure.

**Anchor menus after measuring, then keep the measurement current.** `AnchoredMenu` initially hides itself, measures and applies a flip-then-clamp position in a layout effect. Its pure helper is suitable for deterministic geometry tests. However, the effect depends only on anchor/options, not opening, content changes or viewport resizing. An initially closed mounted instance can remain unmeasured when opened at the same anchor; a zero-sized first measurement also has no automatic retry. Reopened menus may retain an old measured position. RFF should remeasure after open and asynchronous content changes and when the work area changes. If the menu exceeds the viewport, clamping its origin to the gutter cannot make the whole menu fit: add a bounded scrollable size. A point anchor also lacks trigger-rectangle semantics for preferred sides and gaps.

**Rendering chrome does not establish behavior.** `Floating` only provides visual styling; it adds no portal, positioning or dismissal policy. `DropScrim` draws a file-drop hint while leaving import handling to its host. Its forwarded properties can override the default class/style, so the intended pointer transparency depends on integration. RFF should make the hint describe the actual accepted file action and resolve it in the import owner, with separate handling for internal drags. Neither a displayed hint nor the shared export index proves that an import, error handler or keyboard policy is wired at every caller.

**Keyboard isolation needs balanced input ownership.** `stopNavKeys` stops bubbling keydown/keyup/keypress and optionally allows Escape keydown through; it does not prevent browser defaults or intercept an earlier capture-phase listener. If navigation has already received a keydown and focus then enters an isolated panel, swallowing keyup can leave its held-key state stale unless the navigation owner resets on focus/scope transitions. For RFF, suspend canvas navigation while editing text, clear held actions when focus ownership changes, and let only the intended topmost surface handle Escape. This is especially relevant to numeric shader fields and Japanese text composition, but no IME behavior was exercised in this batch.

Validation candidates are saved off-screen geometry, oversized panels, reopening without remount, asynchronous menu growth, resize/DPI changes, pointer cancellation and focus changes during held navigation keys. These conditions support 2D and relief editing equally. Source hashes and documentation formatting were checked; no application code, saved layout or runtime interface was modified.

## Shared choice controls: preserve selection, preview and random-seed semantics

Full reads of `components/ui/Act.tsx`, `Segmented.tsx` and `Icon.tsx` finish the remaining shared UI primitives in this batch. The source demonstrates useful separation between a one-shot action, a selected mode and a decorative glyph. For RFF, make palette interpolation, material source selection and image mapping modes follow consistent command semantics while keeping the rendered scene's accepted state distinct from a pending choice. No visual audit or runtime interaction was performed.

**Keep disabled and missing selections explicit.** Segmented row mode uses native disabled buttons and guards selection callbacks. Cycle mode searches for the next enabled option, but when none exists it retains the current option and still invokes `hit(next,false)` from an enabled button. That can call both change and repeat on an unavailable choice. With a single enabled option, cycling also re-emits the same choice. An unknown current value is displayed as the first option in cycle mode, while row mode shows no selected option. For RFF, validate selection against capabilities, disable cycling when there is no valid action, and show unavailable saved settings honestly instead of silently depicting a replacement as active. Preserve typed IDs: the row's stringified keys collide for distinct numeric/string IDs with the same spelling.

**Make reseeding reproducible across layouts.** In row mode, clicking an already selected repeatable option triggers `onRepeat`; selecting a new one only triggers `onChange`. In cycle mode, arriving at a repeatable option invokes both, synchronously and separately. Thus entering Noise can have different seed behavior in different layouts, and the repeat callback cannot assume an asynchronous parent state change is already reflected. For RFF's decorative noise or procedural palettes, define one accepted operation that chooses mode and seed together, records both for undo/save/video, and specifies whether selecting a mode regenerates its seed. Layout changes should not silently change the mathematical operation. This proposal concerns new editable operations and does not authorize changing frozen recipe generation.

**Hover preview needs an owner and a restoration rule.** The row previews only mouse pointer entry, clears on row leave, and clears on entering a disabled option. It does not independently clear preview when unmounted, when options change or when switching to cycle layout. The caller must restore the accepted value in those paths. Keyboard buttons can select, but no focus-preview behavior is wired here; choose that behavior explicitly rather than implying input parity. A RFF simplification/material preview should hold a transient candidate, never overwrite the saved base merely because the pointer crossed it, and commit only the accepted candidate once.

**Expose state consistently.** `Act` is always a non-submit button with native disabled handling, but writes `aria-pressed` as true or absent; it cannot distinguish an inactive toggle from a regular action through that property. Its explicit attributes also override forwarded values. A RFF equivalent should represent action versus toggle as a declared control role and provide both on and off state when relevant. Icon-only actions need an accessible action name from their owning button. The icon component hides untitled SVGs from accessibility and labels titled ones, which supports decorative use but does not by itself establish that every parent action is named.

The icon file mixes authored geometry, attributed Material Symbols-derived paths and distinct stroke/filled families with explicit view boxes. Its comments describe prior small-size visual checks, but those are not current raster verification and do not establish asset licenses. Reuse RFF's own icon system where appropriate; verify actual source terms before adapting distinctive paths. Inspect at the intended DPI/size if implementing new glyphs, and preserve source attribution rather than treating all shapes in one module as having one origin. No SVG path was copied or rendered in this batch. These controls support the existing shader proposals without changing their effect ranking.

## Dither laboratory: validate the output stage, not only a numerical mirror

A full read of `debug/test-dither.mts` adds concrete conditions to the existing noise/dither recommendations. This is a CPU diagnostic script with a handwritten shader mirror, source-string assertions and a call to the production CPU `renderFieldDithered` function. It does not compile or execute the GLSL tail. It was not run in this review, and the existing montage was not inspected in this batch.

**Useful mechanism.** The mirror derives noise amplitude from the maximum channel slope in output-byte units, suppresses it near zero slope, increases its permitted amplitude toward dark values and tapers each channel near its 0/1 boundaries. The test compares quantized ramps with known continuous references, separates a box-blurred error component from the residual, and compares column-average reconstruction with CPU error diffusion. For RFF, keep this as an output-quantization experiment distinct from fractal sampling noise, image-footprint filtering and material roughness. Apply any adopted technique at a declared color/quantization stage, with the appropriate output bit depth and alpha treatment; do not copy calibrated thresholds into a different transfer function without measuring their effect.

**Channel construction is not proof of independence.** Noise outputs use `(R+G-1, B+A-1, A+R-1)`. Distinct pairs share input channels. Even if the four source channels were independent with equal variance v, the first and third sums would have covariance v, while each has variance 2v. Their correlation would therefore be 1/2, not zero. The regex assertion verifies this particular expression, not the comment's stronger implication of independent RGB output noise. Triangular marginal distributions likewise require assumptions about the source channels that this file does not test. For RFF, inspect per-channel histograms, spatial spectra, means and cross-channel covariance of the actual asset and generated output; choose deliberate chromatic versus luminance noise rather than infer it from pair spelling.

**Do not optimize a plateau count without a fidelity check.** The plateau metric treats successive column averages within 0.1 byte level as one flat run. For the 1440-pixel 5-to-15-percent reference, the ideal slope is approximately 0.0177 byte level per column, so even the perfect continuous reference qualifies as one long plateau under that definition. Added fluctuation can shorten the reported run without improving reconstruction. Keep the script's RMS deviation from the ideal line and spatial error measurements, but do not promote plateau reduction alone to a smoothness guarantee. The acceptance comparison also uses cap 8 for plateau length and cap 2 for low-frequency banding; those are different configurations, and the comments explicitly report a banding tradeoff at cap 8. Validate all promised quality bounds on the same selected production configuration.

The printed high-frequency residual energy has no explicit upper-bound assertion. Consequently passing the existing gates does not establish an acceptable noise ceiling. The low/high split is an illustrative box-filter decomposition, not an orthogonal spectral partition or universal viewing model. Use multiple scales, display sizes and viewing conditions, and measure bias as well as local error. Most synthetic scenes are grayscale, column metrics and flat-region deltas use the red channel, and coverage is always one in the CPU-field tests. Add saturated colors, unequal channel slopes, near-black/white values, alpha edges, diagonal/radial fields and noise-tile seams before claiming general color-image quality.

**Check the production evaluator directly.** Four GLSL constants and two expression patterns are compared with the CPU mirror. This catches selected source regressions, but not changes in the remaining amplitude/taper logic, texture binding, derivatives, actual noise asset, coordinate orientation, shader assembly or later quantization. RFF needs controlled Vulkan output/readback cases in addition to an independent numerical reference. A flat region remaining unchanged must be paired with a nonflat region that demonstrably receives the intended operation; the script usefully includes both, preventing an entirely disabled dither from satisfying the flat-region gate by itself. The production CPU error-diffusion call is stronger evidence for that specific CPU path, but not evidence of GPU parity or temporal stability.

**Separate visualization from numerical ground truth.** The montage writes even its floating 'truth' values into an eight-bit `Uint8Array`, truncating them, while the no-dither column uses explicit rounding. Thus its truth column cannot display the continuous reference used by the metrics and can differ by one level simply from quantization convention. Use high-bit-depth references or clearly label a displayed reference as quantized, and compare signed error maps when useful. The one-dimensional upscale model uses endpoint-aligned interpolation; its claim of exact browser equivalence does not establish the browser's pixel-center, edge or color-space sampling convention. Verify actual displayed/exported output when judging resolution effects.

The local PNG reader is a narrow test fixture decoder: it skips the signature, does not validate CRCs or interlace, accepts selected eight-bit color types and does not establish color-profile interpretation. Use known fixture hashes/format checks or a validated decoder for trustworthy noise inputs. The loaded asset is `blueNoiseRGBA.png`, distinct from the previously reviewed `BlueNoiseData.ts` loader's `blueNoise.png`; do not assume identical distributions or sampling contracts between them.

For RFF, preserve full-output coordinates across tiles, define deterministic seed/frame behavior for video, and test any error-diffusion boundary state separately from pointwise shader noise. A good static column average does not prove absence of temporal flicker or tile seams. This batch refines the dither verification plan without claiming new measured improvement or changing the top-ten appearance ranking.

## Blend-space regression tests: separate mathematical claims from routing checks

A full read of `debug/test-palette-blendspaces.mts` clarifies the evidence behind GMT's optional polar, rectangular, CIE LCh and pigment-like interpolation modes. RFF already has rectangular Oklab and RGB-related interpolation; this review does not propose them as missing features. Optional polar interpolation with neutral handling and gamut mapping remains a distinct candidate, below the current environment/filtering priorities until an RFF comparison is performed.

**Useful test structure.** The script calls production interpolation and ramp functions, checks a near-neutral input sweep, tests endpoint behavior, warms a spectral-color cache with potentially colliding colors, verifies dispatcher routing, and checks that serialized mode IDs survive coercion. These are meaningful layers to retain in RFF: mathematical behavior, cached-versus-uncached agreement, correct mode dispatch, persistence and actual availability in controls. A mode that calculates correctly but is silently replaced on load is not a completed feature. Likewise, checking that several outputs merely differ is weaker than checking each against its intended evaluator.

**Keep each claim within its measured scope.** The hue-preservation check samples six color pairs at 41 positions, skips results with very low chroma and measures angular difference after conversion back to Oklab. An implementation that unnecessarily desaturates samples can evade this particular comparison; pair it with retained-chroma/lightness requirements and explicit finite checks. The rectangular test compares only in-gamut midpoints, with at least four eligible pairs, rather than every position on every segment. The near-grey continuity test walks one red-directed family toward one yellow target at 21 blend positions. That is a useful regression fixture, not a proof of continuity across all neutral directions, hue-wrap boundaries or gamut edges. Extend it with both endpoint orders, several neutral hues/lightnesses and sweeps around every branch threshold relevant to the RFF implementation.

The endpoint test compares `rgbToHex` strings. It proves byte-quantized endpoint agreement for its examples, not exact floating-point equality. It also omits the retired `hsv-far` mode that the serialization check still preserves. The neutral-to-vivid test asserts a maximum component difference below 1.5 byte levels despite its label saying under one step. RFF's tests and report should use the actual thresholds and representation, avoiding stronger wording than the assertions support. For CPU/GPU paths, add direct high-precision component comparisons where those are the stated contract.

**Independent oracle versus shared implementation.** The helper converts RGB to Oklab with a locally written matrix/transfer function, which provides useful separation from the production call. Its constants still need their own provenance and validated reference fixtures if adapted. The ramp-dispatch test compares texel 128 against the same production interpolation function at `128/255`; this validates routing and sample-position convention, not the interpolation mathematics independently. A shader adoption should test both: dispatch/persistence integration and independent reference values, followed by actual Vulkan output. The grayscale self-mix and cache-order cases help detect mistaken cache keys but do not exhaust fractional RGB values, eviction, cache bounds or all color-space settings that may belong in a key.

**Pigment-like appearance is an optional artistic mode.** The spectral dispatch test requires a blue/yellow midpoint to have a green hue and sufficient chroma. This establishes one intended artistic behavior if the test passes; it does not establish physical paint matching across pigments, illuminants or spectral measurements. If considered for RFF, keep it in palette authoring or cached palette generation unless runtime cost justifies shader evaluation, label the model accurately and verify the implementation's source/license before reuse. Do not infer a general performance benefit or physical accuracy from one color pair.

**Version the selectable set deliberately.** The test lists expected mode IDs manually and checks that every non-retired listed mode appears once in the chooser, while retired IDs remain recognized for saved data. This is a useful RFF migration pattern. A handwritten list can still omit a newly added type-union member without a compiler exhaustiveness guarantee, and label presence does not verify rendered menu behavior. Preserve old IDs and meanings, make new IDs append-only where the format requires it, and add actual save/load/render fixtures. No tests were executed in this batch, no external color-science reference was verified, and no interpolation code or constants were copied into RFF.

## Palette application tests: preserve dense samples and distinguish color-space tags from lighting

Full reads of `debug/test-palette-gradientseam.mts` and `debug/test-palette-gradientramp.mts` add evidence about the sampled-ramp alternative to editable stops. The scripts were not executed. They test production CPU helpers and stubbed feature setters, rather than actual shader sampling or environmental illumination.

**Transfer the two-representation policy.** GMT tests a small stop representation for simpler ramps and a direct 256-sample RGB representation for dense patterns. A period-two zebra and dense hard bands are valuable fixtures because a superficially smooth approximation can erase their defining structure. RFF should preserve an imported/image-derived palette's sampled source when editable-stop fitting would exceed the selected error budget. Offer approximation as an explicit reversible edit, not a silent prerequisite to use the palette. This applies to 2D coloring and the proposed gradient environment; its sampled form preserves the stored RGB samples, not arbitrary original resolution, alpha, HDR precision or between-sample reconstruction.

**A cheap fit is not necessarily accurate.** The tests exercise both a stop-count cap and a separate rule counting samples whose OKLab error exceeds 0.05. A bounded number of such misses may still be accepted, despite a nominal fit target of 0.02. Thus the source's faithfulness terminology does not mean every sample satisfies the target or that the maximum error is bounded by 0.05. For RFF, report the actual maximum error, number/locations of outliers and the source representation retained. A single bad sample can be important when the palette is repeated over a large image or used as a narrow reflective/emissive band. The unlimited-cap case asserts only that stops are returned, not that their quality is exact.

The regular band sweep compares results with a higher-budget invocation of the same fitter; the thin-band sweep derives its expectation with the same fitter and production color renderer. These are useful policy/integration checks, but do not independently establish globally minimal stops or an error-bound proof. Explicit baseline samples and end-to-end rendered comparisons remain necessary. The seeded random input makes fixtures repeatable within this implementation; its JavaScript multiply/bitwise generator should not be treated as a portable exact integer-RNG specification when porting fixtures to C++.

**One conversion boundary per consumer, with explicit units.** The application-seam test expects coloring gradients to be tagged `linear` and environment gradients to be tagged `srgb`, while preserving stop arrays and blend modes. It intercepts feature setter payloads; it does not observe texture formats, shader decoding, BRDF use or final displayed values. In particular, an environment used for illumination must not be treated as display-encoded radiance merely because this caller tags its authoring data srgb. RFF should document authoring color encoding, texture storage, sampling conversion and lighting domain separately, then verify a mid-grey and bright colored source through every consumer. Reuse source data while keeping reflection, lighting and visible backdrop consumption explicit.

**Representation equivalence tests are useful but bounded.** The ramp tests compare generated CPU texture bytes against a 256-stop RGB equivalent for srgb, linear and inverse-tone-map modes. This checks that both representations share a conversion path, not that the conversion itself is physically or numerically correct. It also does not cover texture addressing, filtering, mipmaps, GPU format decoding, export or tone-map placement. The CSS check counts color stops and selected textual positions without rendering a browser preview; fractional percentage rounding and interpolation can still differ from GPU lookup. RFF needs sampled lookup comparisons at endpoints, between samples and across cyclic seams under the actual sampler contract.

**Define precedence and mutation ownership.** Tests require authored stops to override a stale ramp, normalization to strip the stale field, and missing data to produce a greyscale fallback. That prevents ambiguous evaluation, but a fallback alone can hide a failed asset load or corrupt saved palette. In RFF, distinguish an intentional default from recovery and retain enough diagnostics to explain a substituted source. The seam explicitly tests passing the identical stop-array reference, so callers must treat shared source arrays as immutable or copy before editing; reference preservation is not deep ownership isolation. Add save/load and undo fixtures for edits after catalog selection.

Codec tests cover a deterministic RGB fixture and selected malformed lengths/characters, including the fixed 1,024-character base64 form. They do not claim arbitrary file-format compatibility. The no-feature setter cases correctly exercise a no-op/false return, which is a useful capability boundary for a standalone editor. Before exposing an Apply action in RFF, verify that its intended consumer exists and that success means the accepted render uses the new palette, not merely that a setter accepted a payload. These findings refine the palette/environment integration plan without changing the current shader ranking or asserting executed validation.

## Curve-space and easing tests: preserve authored channels while changing their presentation

Full reads of `debug/test-palette-curvespaces.mts` and `debug/test-palette-easings.mts` refine the optional channel-curve authoring proposal. Neither harness was executed. The useful transfer to RFF is independent editing of palette channels and reusable scalar remaps for material masks, with explicit units, bounded parameter domains and preserved original data.

**Changing editing space can be destructive even without a visible change.** The curve-space harness round-trips a 256-sample fixture through each supported space and compares the reconstructed displayed colors with a two-byte-level tolerance. Its comparison maps both channel sets back through the same safe Oklab-to-RGB function; different out-of-gamut channel data can therefore look equivalent after mapping. The separate high-chroma fixture checks only the maximum retained chroma, which does not prove per-sample lightness, hue or chroma preservation. For RFF, maintain a canonical authored representation and treat switching the curve view as presentation unless the user accepts a conversion. Test raw channel preservation separately from displayed-color fidelity and document when a chosen space clips or maps gamut.

The fixture itself is generated through the production safe conversion, and its nominal lightness expression ranges below zero before that conversion. It therefore tests a particular mapped RGB fixture, not an unrestricted independent color-space reference. Add explicit known in-gamut, near-neutral and out-of-gamut cases before making broad round-trip claims. The existing identity check on OkLCh L/C is useful for preventing needless changes in the pipeline's own space; preserve an analogous no-edit invariant in RFF.

**Unwrap hue without inventing information.** The angular tests exercise a densely sampled two-turn path and a degree-period example, and require adjacent reconstructed angles not to jump across a seam. This supports continuous hue-curve display. It cannot recover an intended multi-turn change greater than half a period between samples, and hue remains underdetermined near zero chroma. Preserve authored unwrapped angles where available, use declared periods/units, and define a neutral-hue policy. A generic check against pi is appropriate only for radian channels; future degree-based channels need their own period-aware checks. Keep the direction of a deliberately animated hue sweep through save/load and edits.

**Scale numerical tolerance to units, then validate color error.** The registry tests compare each channel epsilon with its nominal range and relate CIE lightness's range to Oklab lightness. This is a useful starting point for avoiding disproportionate key reduction across differently scaled units. It does not establish equal perceptual error: hue error depends on chroma, and a nonlinear conversion can amplify a small channel error. In RFF, combine normalized channel tolerances with a reconstructed-palette error check. For roughness or emission masks, use the property domain and visible output rather than blindly borrowing color-channel thresholds.

**Curve libraries need domain-specific selection.** The easing harness verifies endpoint tolerances, a linear identity, sampled monotonicity/range for a named set, intentional Back overshoot and midpoint crossing for inOut names. Overshooting easing can be useful for a decorative coordinate or animation, but is not automatically suitable for a mask constrained to [0,1], positive roughness or nonnegative intensity. Define clamp/remap behavior at the consumer and preserve continuity; a clamp can introduce flat portions or derivative changes that matter for filtering and animation. This is a scalar authoring tool, not a change to the Mandelbrot recurrence or MPA precision.

**Read assertions literally.** Endpoint 'exactness' is a tolerance of 1e-9, not equality. The inOut check only verifies the midpoint, not the full symmetry relation `f(t) = 1 - f(1-t)`. Monotonicity/range is checked on 256 samples selected by the production `MONOTONIC_EASINGS` set, so omission from that set can omit coverage. Counts of 25 names and 25 entries do not independently prove unique names, complete mapping or that an unknown valid-looking name did not fall back to linear. Several greater-than comparisons also let NaN evade failure unless finiteness is checked first. RFF's validation should explicitly check finite outputs, declared set equality, dispatch and relevant boundary behavior before using these curves as saved parameter semantics.

Unknown curve-space IDs fall back to the default, and unknown easing names to linear. Such fallbacks keep an editor usable but should remain distinguishable from faithful restoration of an unsupported saved setting. Preserve stable IDs and record migration/fallback state where relevant. No new color-space or easing code was copied, and these source checks do not change the shader-effect ranking.

## Channel-curve fitting and local smoothing: validate the stored curve and both boundaries

A full read of `debug/test-palette-channelcurve.mts` refines the editable-channel proposal for RFF. Its useful mechanisms are sample-to-key reduction, fitted Bezier tangents, explicit step holds for banded palettes, and a localized smoothing brush. These can support palette lightness/chroma editing and scalar material masks without changing fractal computation. This harness was not executed.

**Fit the representation actually used.** The tests correctly distinguish a polyline approximation from a Bezier curve subsequently assigned to its keys. A small polyline error does not automatically bound a curve with independently chosen tangents. The harness compares reconstructed production tracks, includes a black-to-white regression fixture, and uses a known cubic to check the one-third-span handle parameterization. For RFF, validate the final stored control points through the actual evaluator, after tangent fitting, serialization and any monotonicity constraints. Preserve exact step boundaries when a palette intentionally contains bands; smoothing every transition is not necessarily an improvement.

The alternate knot-placement block checks fitted-span errors and compares total key counts with the default path. That does not independently prove globally minimal knot placement or full output fidelity after every subsequent transformation. Its default-placement assertion compares only key counts, not positions, values or tangents. If preserving previous appearance is a requirement in RFF, compare the actual curve and reconstructed palette rather than equal counts. Keep any new fitting mode opt-in for existing saved recipes.

**Make skipped corpus coverage visible.** Real-palette tests use two absolute external directories and skip if neither provides maps. The remaining synthetic tests can still yield an overall pass. Input selection samples filesystem listings by stride without an explicit sorted, versioned corpus. A successful run therefore need not mean the real-palette cases ran, nor that repeated runs examined the same cases. RFF validation should bundle a small representative fixture corpus with hashes, record skipped external cases separately, and include both sparse smooth curves and dense narrow bands. The script's map reader also assumes at least one parsed row in its resampling branch; malformed/empty fixtures should fail with an explicit input diagnosis.

**Do not average away a violated bound.** In the first corpus block, the value reported as `max` is the average of the individual palettes' maximum errors. The assertion compares that average with epsilon, so an individual palette can exceed its advertised bound while the aggregate passes. The smaller-epsilon checks similarly compare mean errors and mean key counts, not each palette's behavior. For RFF, assert a per-case finite maximum and report its location, alongside aggregate summaries. The later Bezier-versus-linear block does compare each case's maximum, which is a stronger regression structure to preserve.

**Local smoothing needs an explicit affected region.** The brush tests measure reduced second differences inside the edit and repeated-stroke softening. Their 'outside unchanged' test checks frames below 90 or above 166 for a nominal edit spanning 96–160, leaving a margin around the boundaries untested. This may be compatible with a deliberate transition region, but is not proof that every sample outside the nominal span remains unchanged. Declare any transition reach in RFF's editing contract and preserve the original beyond it. Verify values and derivatives at both ends of a sparse curve: dense per-sample keys can conceal boundary artifacts that become large when a connecting segment spans many pixels.

The sparse seam check uses second differences at two integer sample positions and compares them with a fixed Oklab-lightness threshold derived from a mid-grey byte step. It does not prove analytic derivative continuity, absence of between-sample overshoot or invisibility at every luminance, palette chroma, output bit depth or tone-map setting. For RFF, compare rendered color errors near both boundaries and inspect sub-sample behavior; use property-specific limits when applying the same brush to roughness/emission masks. A small lightness-curve kink can have a different effect when transformed into a normal or a specular response.

The transferable workflow is to retain the original sampled channel, preview the fitted/locally smoothed candidate, measure the reconstructed result, then commit one undoable edit. Keep fitting quality separate from shader sampling quality: a faithful curve still needs proper filtering when used at high spatial frequency. No performance, visual quality or curve-bound guarantee was measured in this audit batch.

## Editor snapshots and color transfers: retain identity without conflating payload types

Full reads of `debug/test-palette-editorconfig.mts` and `debug/test-palette-colordrag.mts` add supporting conditions for RFF palette editing. These test files were inspected, not executed; no saved configuration or drag payload was modified.

**A pure serialization round trip is one layer of persistence.** The editor-config harness exercises the production serializer/coercer with a default stop configuration and a sampled-ramp configuration, verifies snapshot mutation isolation, rejects selected malformed inputs and tests normalization and duplicate IDs. This is a useful foundation for RFF's undoable palette edits. It does not actually register an undo provider, edit a live store, save a scene container or restore a renderer. In its undo block, configuration B is only constructed and checked as distinct; it is never applied before A is restored. Therefore describe the result as serializer/coercer determinism, not end-to-end undo verification. Add a live edit/undo/redo/save/reopen sequence that checks both restored settings and the displayed palette.

**Normalization and lossless restoration are different contracts.** The tested gate can drop invalid stops, clamp positions/bias, repair IDs and select default spaces. It deliberately rejects a nonempty invalid stop list even when a well-formed ramp is also present, while an explicitly empty stop list with a valid ramp is accepted. For RFF, define such precedence deliberately and preserve the user's valid source or report the rejected document; do not silently label a repaired result as an exact restoration. Stable stop IDs matter to selection and key editing, but repairing duplicate IDs also requires a policy for any external references. The test checks uniqueness of resulting IDs, not migration of references to those stops.

The fixture with a JSON-owned prototype key checks that particular input's result and the global object prototype. It does not constitute exhaustive validation of arbitrary JavaScript objects, nested metadata, resource limits or future fields. Extend relevant file-schema tests with finite numeric limits, repeated positions, maximum stop counts and all supported interpolation/encoding modes. Match validation to RFF's actual append-only/versioned formats rather than transplanting JSON coercion into unrelated binary persistence.

**Separate a single color from an entire palette at the transfer boundary.** The drag harness uses distinct custom MIME types for color and saved-gradient payloads, plus a text/plain hex fallback for external targets. This supports an RFF workflow where dropping a swatch changes one intended color, while dropping a palette applies or imports an entire palette. Decide the target and show its effect before acceptance; accept data only through the matching validator and commit one undoable operation. The fake DataTransfer exposes values at all times, so this test does not simulate a browser's restricted dragover data access or prove actual pointer/OS drag behavior. Add integration cases for mixed advertised types, malformed payloads, canceled drops and target changes; for native Windows use the corresponding clipboard/drop format contract.

The drag validator's accepted six-digit hex form is narrower than the configuration coercer's tested support for three-digit hex. Different boundary formats can be intentional, but document and normalize them explicitly rather than claiming a universal color parser. Retain color-space meaning when transferring colors into a linear-light material or environment consumer; a hex string alone supplies no separate HDR range or asset profile.

**Group color edits should preserve per-color differences until constraints intervene.** The nudge tests demonstrate adding the same red-channel delta to two different colors while preserving their other RGB bytes, and separately check endpoint clamping. This is useful for RFF multi-stop editing, but clamping can collapse differences at a boundary; the preservation claim is conditional on remaining inside range. Hue and value probes are weaker: they check a pattern/change, not exact target hue, unchanged saturation/value or behavior near neutral colors. For RFF, declare RGB-byte, HSV or perceptual-channel edit domains and validate them separately. Keep the original selection as the gesture baseline to avoid cumulative rounding, and test undo of a multi-stop edit as one operation. These workflow improvements support both flat 2D coloring and relief-material authoring without changing the shader-effect ranking.

## Palette facet validation: useful search descriptors are not saved identities

Source evidence: `debug/test-palette-facets.mts` (112 lines) and `debug/test-palette-facetname.mts` (72 lines), read in full. This is static inspection; neither harness was executed for this review.

**Transfer to RFF.** Faceted palette search can help users find warm, cool, muted, vivid, dark or multihue candidates without remembering catalog names. It supports both flat 2D and relief workflows but is an authoring improvement, not a shader speedup or an additional lighting effect. Keep computed descriptors separate from user names, frozen recipe identifiers and seeds. A coarse label can describe many palettes and must never serve as a unique saved identifier.

**What the metric harness establishes by construction.** Six 256-sample synthetic controls exercise grayscale, a hue sweep, fixed-HSV-hue brightness variation, alternating gray bands, warm colors and cool colors. Assertions distinguish several expected chroma, hue-order, complexity and warmth relationships. Filter checks cover only a rainbow-axis interval and an empty filter; they do not establish combined-axis behavior, every boundary, reversed intervals or nonfinite inputs. Fixed HSV hue is not an independent guarantee of fixed perceptual hue.

**Catalog coverage is conditional.** Three machine-specific external directories are optional; with none present, the real-catalog section skips and the harness can still report success. Directory listings are not explicitly sorted, and stepping by `floor(length / 40)` does not define an exactly forty-item, versioned corpus. The parser accepts finite numeric triples without checking channel range and has no explicit empty-ramp guard before resampling. A percentile spread exceeding 0.15 measures descriptor distribution in the selected corpus, not semantic accuracy, search usefulness or perceptual quality. RFF validation should distinguish skipped corpus checks from completed ones and use a fixed, legally distributable fixture manifest.

**Naming coverage is narrower than persistence compatibility.** Eight exact examples isolate the label composer from the color mathematics. Five hundred seeded cases test immediate repeated-call equality and nonempty output, with complexity held at its default; they do not prove cross-version label stability or behavior exactly at classification thresholds. The single ramp-to-name case requires a vivid rainbow suffix pattern rather than a complete expected name. Add boundary and adjacent-value cases if these labels become user-facing, and explicitly decide whether complexity contributes to names.

**Implementation contract for RFF.** Derive descriptors from the actual sampled palette under a declared interpolation and color-space policy. Cache by source content plus evaluator/descriptor revision, while preserving recipe regeneration and saved identities. Do not silently rename user palettes as metric thresholds evolve. Suppress or qualify hue-derived classifications near neutral colors where hue is unstable. Test monochrome, near-black, narrow saturated peaks and hue-wrap cases, and declare which metrics should remain invariant under reversal or cyclic shifts before asserting those properties. Classification threshold changes during editing should not repeatedly overwrite names.

A palette's sample distribution is also distinct from the distribution of its colors on a rendered fractal: field occupancy, palette mapping, lighting and tone mapping can change the visible balance. Show a palette thumbnail for catalog descriptors and use the separately proposed field histogram/render preview to judge the current image. This distinction makes palette search complementary to histogram-guided mapping rather than a substitute for it.

## Image-derived palette validation: repeatability, resampling safety and fitting fidelity

Sources read in full: `debug/test-palette-img2grad.mts` (186 lines) and `debug/test-palette-img2grad-overshoot.mts` (86 lines). These are separate static evidence for the image-derived palette proposal; no harness execution or mutation-test reproduction is claimed.

**Useful RFF behavior.** Image extraction should give stable results while users adjust controls, then produce an ordinary editable palette that works in flat 2D and relief rendering. GMT's tested modes separate representative-color extraction (`distill`), tonal extraction (`tone`) and spatial sampling (`trace`). A manual path, including a smoothed freehand path, lets users preserve a chosen sequence of image colors rather than only a global color distribution. This is palette authoring before shading; it does not require a 3D renderer or changes to orbit precision/MPA.

**Determinism evidence and its boundary.** The main harness uses one opaque 120-by-80 synthetic image with a horizontal hue sweep, vertical value variation and a warm central feature. All three modes compare exact numeric RGB arrays after re-ingestion, require 256 ramp and ribbon entries, check ramp channel bounds, and verify reversal. Those are useful within-process invariants, but the phrase “byte-identical” in its introduction is stronger than the actual assertion: it does not serialize output or require integer channels. Ingestion itself checks equal bin counts and a cloud-size limit, not equality of every bin and cloud element. Equal extraction outputs provide additional end-to-end evidence without proving every internal representation identical. No cross-platform or future-version golden result is established.

The color-count check only requires that 3-color and 16-color settings generate different 256-entry ramps. It does not count cluster nodes or prove compliance with an exact requested cluster count. Saliency extremes must differ, and one saliency setting is rechecked for determinism; warm/highlight weighting extremes are only compared for a difference. Such difference checks establish that controls affect the chosen fixture, not that changes follow the intended perceptual direction or vary smoothly during interaction.

**Trace behavior.** A two-point polyline must equal its endpoint-defined straight path, and enabling Catmull–Rom with two points must leave it unchanged. A four-point path checks repeatability and verifies that smoothing changes the result. These assertions do not establish spline bounds, arc-length-uniform sampling, repeated-point handling, out-of-image behavior or band-width behavior near image edges. The smoothed four-point output is compared for repeatability and difference but is not separately passed through the gamut check used for its unsmoothed counterpart. RFF should state the path coordinate, edge sampling and smoothing conventions explicitly before persisting them.

**The endpoint regression has distinct value.** The second harness sweeps four opaque 64-by-64 image patterns, 11 color counts, 201 warm/highlight weighting values and three spacing values: an intended 26,532 extraction cases. It requires a 256-entry finite RGB ramp and calls the stop fitter with `targetDE: 0.02, maxStops: 32` inside exception handling. This covers a cumulative-coordinate endpoint failure described in its source history. The assertion verifies finite extraction and a nonthrowing fitting call, not output gamut, fitted stop validity or reconstruction error. Passing a requested fitting tolerance is not proof that the resulting curve meets it. The source comment says removing an endpoint clamp distinguishes this harness from the main one; that historical mutation claim has not been independently reproduced in this audit.

**RFF acceptance criteria.** Keep direct boundary fixtures alongside parameter sweeps: one-color and one-pixel input, repeated/zero-weight nodes, exact final cumulative coordinate, a rounded value just beyond it, transparent pixels with nonzero RGB, and a documented empty-image response. Validate dimensions and pixel length before extraction. Define whether transparent colors are excluded or composited and which color space/profile is used during ingestion; the present opaque synthetic fixtures do not answer those questions. Use stable extraction ordering/seeding, reject stale results during asynchronous adjustments, and save the resulting palette so an algorithm update does not silently change an existing scene. If an optional extraction recipe is saved, version it independently of existing frozen palette recipe IDs.

For stop conversion, evaluate the stored, rounded stops using the actual RFF interpolation path and measure reconstruction against the extracted ramp; preserve a dense representation when the requested tolerance cannot be achieved. Check both ends and narrow color features, not merely successful fitting. New tests should separate reproducibility, numerical safety, approximation error and visual usefulness, because none of these alone proves the other three. This strengthens the existing image-derived-palette recommendation without changing the provisional shader-effect ranking.

## Image palette controls and import ownership: commit the intended image and settings together

Sources read in full: `palette/features/paletteImage.ts` (106 lines) and `palette/components/useImageDrop.ts` (187 lines). Findings are from static source inspection, not exercised browser behavior.

**Useful control separation.** The image feature exposes one mode parameter and mode-specific controls: dominant-color count/saliency for Distill, tonal bucket count/chroma for Tone, and sampling-band width/smoothing/path interpolation for Trace. Reverse is shared; spacing and shadow/highlight weighting are hidden in Trace. This is a useful RFF model for keeping extraction choices understandable while preserving each mode's settings when switching. Dynamic visibility is presentation logic, not validation: imported values and unknown mode IDs still need explicit normalization. The defaults are repeated in a separate reset object; a port should derive reset behavior from one authoritative definition or verify equivalence. The advertised Tone smoothness is descriptive copy, not a numerical guarantee established here.

The schema holds scalar controls while its header identifies separate structured image/path state. A complete RFF extraction snapshot therefore needs both, or it should simply save the accepted generated palette. Persisting only the visible scalar controls cannot reproduce a manual path or the source image. New settings must respect RFF's append-only configuration contract, and must not reinterpret existing recipe IDs. This feature is equally useful for flat and relief coloring.

**File routing worth adopting.** The hook offers all dropped files to an asynchronous content router before image extraction. This supports gradient-bearing PNG files without treating every PNG as a photograph. It then loads the first remaining image and offers all remaining non-image files to a separate handler, so a mixed drop can populate both the image slot and palette shelf. Subsequent image files are not loaded. For RFF, state that single-image policy visibly when needed, and classify supported palette containers by validated content rather than MIME alone. A failed pre-router falls back to treating the original files normally; partial success followed by rejection could therefore repeat processing unless the routing contract is atomic or returns per-file outcomes.

**Request ownership is not established by this hook.** FileReader completion starts decoding, which independently sets the global model and may reset the trace path using the mode captured by the callback. No generation check, cancellation or unmount guard appears in these asynchronous paths. Two quickly selected files can complete in reverse order; mode changes during loading can make the captured trace-reset decision obsolete. An older failing decode can also clear shared loading state while a newer request is pending. These are local code-path risks, not reproduced failures or proof that no surrounding layer mitigates them. For RFF, assign request identity when the user selects/drops the file, carry it through classification, reading, decoding and extraction, and commit only the current result with its intended settings. An old completion must not clear a new operation's busy state or switch the active panel.

`fileToImg` returns acceptance synchronously before reading/decoding succeeds; callers must not interpret that boolean as completion. FileReader has an onload callback but no local onerror/onabort handling, and the MIME check is a permissive `startsWith('image')`. The hook itself imposes no file-size or decoded-dimension limit; decoder-side limits require separate evidence. A desktop implementation should distinguish acceptance, progress, cancellation, decode failure and final commit, retaining the previous usable palette until replacement succeeds.

**One event owner per surface.** The hook supports disabling its window listeners while retaining the direct file-picker function. Its historical header discusses duplicate mounts, but current `enabled` support means actual duplication cannot be inferred without checking callers. Give the RFF host ownership of drop dispatch rather than letting multiple child panels process the same event. The hover timeout is kept in a ref so re-subscription does not cancel it; disabled listeners and completed asynchronous operations still need an explicit state policy. The global paste handler reacts to image items and otherwise emits a no-image message without checking the focused text editor or default-prevented status. RFF should route paste according to the active editing context so ordinary text paste does not trigger an unrelated extraction notification.

**Validation to add for adoption.** Test two files whose reads and decodes finish in opposite orders, cancellation/unmount, switching mode while decoding, mixed gradient/image drops, content-recognized gradient PNGs, unreadable files, multiple images, text-field paste and a pre-router failure after partial work. Verify a single final undo transaction for an accepted image/palette, deterministic extraction from that snapshot, and preservation of the old result on failure. These are integration requirements supporting image-derived palettes; no new shader benchmark or revised top-ten ranking follows from this audit.

## Generator and catalog schemas: independent color channels and stable selection semantics

Sources read in full: `palette/features/paletteGenerator.ts` (163 lines) and `palette/features/paletteFilters.ts` (156 lines). These schemas establish exposed parameters and defaults, not execution of the mathematical pipeline or proof of persistence/animation correctness.

**Transferable generator controls.** GMT exposes three authoring modes: a two-source mixer, independent OKLCh channel sweeps and direct stop editing. The mixer has separate lightness, chroma and hue blend amounts; each input also has its own hue rotation, chroma, contrast, reversal, repetition, phase and mirroring. This separation could let RFF users borrow the brightness structure of one palette and the hue structure of another. It is a more specific extension than adding another generic RGB blend. Existing RFF RGB, linear-RGB and rectangular OKLab functionality should remain intact; polar channel mixing needs a declared hue-wrap path, low-chroma hue policy and gamut mapping rather than an assumption that rectangular interpolation implements the same operation.

The sweep mode supplies start/end values and easing per channel. Hue endpoints are bounded to 0–360 in this schema; that alone does not express multiple revolutions or establish shortest-arc interpolation. Easing options are constructed from array positions in EASING_NAMES. If RFF persists such options, assign permanent identifiers rather than letting a reordered display list reinterpret saved scenes. Scalar feature state is also insufficient to reproduce the mixer: selected sources, curve tracks, authored stops and any noise seed must participate in a complete snapshot. The header's statement that parameters participate in undo/presets/animation is architectural intent; those host paths require their own evidence.

**Sampling limits and artistic noise.** The global repeat parameter is continuous, with a 0.1–16 range and logarithmic control, while per-source repeats remain integer 1–8. A fraction can show only part of a palette, so a “scale” label describes more than integer tiling. The comment that higher repeats alias identifies a finite-resolution constraint, not a proof that every value at or below 16 is safe: at 16 repeats a 256-sample output allocates only 16 samples to each complete cycle, and narrow original features can already be lost. RFF should separate the authored function from its sampled preview, consider the actual pixel footprint, and preserve old integer-repeat behavior through explicit regression cases. Do not reinterpret an existing saved repeat control merely to match GMT's range.

Noise can target lightness, chroma or hue independently, with amount and frequency controls. This is artistic palette modulation, distinct from final-output quantization dithering and from vector-noise UV deformation. Keep its seed stable while unrelated controls change, and account for hue ambiguity near neutral colors. Hidden parameters and dynamic visibility only describe presentation; they do not establish whether a dormant modifier is bypassed in the evaluator. Validate mode switching and reset as transactions, including hidden source controls. A separately maintained defaults object duplicates the generator values and needs an equivalence check or a single source of truth.

**Catalog search structure.** The filter schema actually declares six ranges: dominant hue, lightness, chroma, complexity, rainbow coverage and warmth, despite the introductory comment referring to five. It separates top-level grouping, facet-based rows and sorting within rows. This could make a large RFF palette library easier to scan while preserving both source attribution and appearance-based discovery. “Complexity” or “quality” is a descriptor, not a ranking of artistic merit. Keep the visible language tied to the measured characteristic.

Hue range controls use the same normalized pair representation as linear axes. The schema alone does not show how a window crossing the hue seam works or how achromatic palettes are treated. Specify those cases in RFF and test full-range, wrapped-range, zero-width and missing/undefined-hue behavior. The group enumeration appends collection after existing values, explicitly preserving stored indices; follow RFF's existing format rules and never renumber old choices. Stable tie-breaking is also needed so equal descriptor values do not reorder unpredictably during catalog reloads.

The state distinguishes selected themes (empty means all), hidden bundles (empty means none hidden) and a spatially selected ID set (null means no carve filter). Preserve the meaningful difference between null and an empty selection: selecting no entries should not silently restore all. A comment intends the ID set to be transient to avoid stale catalog IDs; this file does not itself implement that persistence exclusion. For RFF, either clear transient selections on a catalog generation change or reconcile stable IDs explicitly, and verify the actual serializer. These workflow improvements serve both flat 2D and relief palettes; they do not imply importing GMT's 3D rendering engine or replacing RFF's frozen recipe generation.

## Generator regression evidence: legacy equivalence is narrower than smooth animation

Source read in full: `debug/test-palette-generator.mts` (376 lines). No execution, historical checkout comparison or mutation test was performed in this audit. The source contains 22 numbered groups spanning the mixer, channel sweeps, fitting and continuous scale.

**Concrete evidence for a RFF adoption contract.** The harness compares default mixing with source A, all three blend amounts at one with source B, chroma-zero grayscale, reversed endpoints, repeated noise seeds and a five-band posterized output. This provides useful test patterns for extending RFF's palette authoring. However, the A/B checks permit maximum RGB differences below two and three channel levels respectively; they do not establish lossless identity. Moving all blend controls together also does not isolate each channel's independence. Reverse is checked at the two ends rather than across the complete ramp. RFF should separately test isolated L/C/h routing, neutral-color hue behavior and the full reversal invariant, and retain an exact bypass where its existing identity contract requires one.

The posterization assertion counts rounded RGB triples, not unrounded distinct colors. Noise checks compare two seeds at one selected configuration; they establish neither decorrelation nor compatibility with a different integer/RNG implementation. Preserve RFF's existing recipe generation sequence rather than replacing it with GMT's pipeline. Treat any new seeded generator as a distinct, versioned mode with independently recorded algorithm provenance.

**Fitting tolerance needs an honest acceptance threshold.** Both mixer-to-stops and ColorBox-to-stops examples request `targetDE: 0.02` but accept a measured maximum below `0.06`. These checks are stronger than merely requiring a nonthrowing fit, yet do not prove the requested 0.02 target is achieved. The “seam” label here refers to transfer into the stop representation, not proof that a cyclic palette's first and last colors join smoothly. Report the actual measured error and fit-limit outcome when RFF converts a dense palette into editable stops; evaluate the serialized representation with the intended interpolation space and preserve dense data when necessary.

**Channel-sweep checks.** The suite checks output dimensions, repeated-call equality, lightness endpoints, neutral chroma, one high-chroma full-hue ramp for finite bounded RGB, and a nonlinear easing that changes intermediate colors while approximately retaining endpoints. Its hue-units assertion only bounds values between -7 and 7; that range alone is not a general conversion proof. Its final-channel shape check includes a self-equality tautology and checks only final L length. Add explicit expected angle samples and all channel lengths in a RFF port. The grayscale comparisons can miss NaN because their greater-than comparisons do not reject it; finite checks should precede approximate comparisons throughout.

The wiring group obtains defaults from the real feature schema but manually reconstructs the store's channel adapter. It detects missing registered keys under that reconstruction; it cannot detect an independent future error in the actual adapter it does not invoke. Test the production adapter at the integration boundary. Similarly, fitting back to sweep parameters recovers selected easings on one deliberately low-chroma representable fixture; it does not prove arbitrary ramps can be faithfully reduced to three eased endpoint sweeps. The arbitrary-ramp assertion checks finite L/C endpoints, hue bounds, and only the L/h easing membership, not every advertised parameter range or reconstruction quality. Expose this conversion as an approximation with a preview and measured residual.

**Historical scale compatibility has valuable but finite coverage.** Eight stored digest prefixes are compared against serialized numeric ramp and final-channel arrays over 72 parameter combinations per integer scale, totaling 576 cases. These include phase, mirror, reverse, posterization and three modifier variants, using fixed input ramps, default slot modifiers, no curves and a fixed seed. The source identifies a historical revision for the digests, but this review has not verified that origin. Digest equality would establish the serialized outputs for those cases, not every preset, animation path or cross-runtime floating-point result. In RFF, use fixtures tied to the actual frozen implementation and serializer, including nondefault source modifiers, curves and old saved inputs.

**Continuous controls do not imply temporally smooth output.** Fractional scale is distinguished from rounding, the last sample at scale 2.5 is compared with source sample 128, and scale 0.5 is checked against rounded source indices. The continuity group counts RGB jumps above 12 over five small scale increments and allows up to 40 total jumps; it does not verify that each jump lies at a wrap, establish a mathematical continuity bound, or test animation at output resolution. This sampling contract can pass while fine detail still steps or shimmers. RFF should combine coordinate semantics with the footprint-aware filtering proposal and test moving narrow color features at realistic zoom/export sizes.

Mirror checks explicitly define a complete out-and-back traversal per scale unit, equivalent to alternating reversed half-cycles at twice the scale; copy that convention only as a new mode if an existing RFF control means something else. The lightness test establishes an additive 0.1 offset in internal final L for its fixture, and exact serialized equality when the new field is absent or zero. It does not establish that displayed, gamut-mapped RGB retains that exact lightness offset. Both distinctions matter for predictable flat-2D coloring and relief materials without changing their saved appearance unexpectedly.

## Image-channel recoloring and catalog position indicators: preserve the meaning of each coordinate

Sources read in full: `debug/test-palette-mapchannels.mts` (141 lines) and `debug/test-palette-lensband.mts` (136 lines). This is static examination of assertions, not a report that either suite passed.

**Image-channel recoloring for RFF.** GMT tests seven scalar drivers for applying a gradient to an image: legacy luma, individual RGB components, perceptual lightness, chroma and hue. A comparable optional RFF image-layer source could recolor a texture by its hue or saturation-related structure instead of only its brightness. This is distinct from choosing fractal-derived U/V coordinates: one chooses which image sample to read, the other maps a property of that sample through a palette. Keep these operations separately ordered and named. The transfer works in flat 2D and relief, without changing fractal computation.

**Coverage is sampled, not the entire RGB cube.** The range loop visits 32,768 triples with channel values 0,8,...,248, then adds the eight corners. It does not visit all 16,777,216 byte triples. The lattice rejects nonfinite outputs explicitly, but the added corner loop only updates extrema using comparisons, so a corner NaN can escape that portion. The separate endpoint assertions cover selected channels but are not a complete replacement. The historical luma comparison samples a step-five lattice (140,608 triples) and one fractional input; exact equality there is valuable local compatibility evidence, not a complete renderer identity proof.

The retained luma expression weights input RGB byte values directly. It preserves that encoded-domain mapping; it is not automatically scene-linear luminance merely because familiar luminance coefficients appear in it. RFF should preserve existing semantics where required, and offer a separately identified linear-light driver if desired. Decode and alpha handling, bilinear resampling and downstream palette evaluation must be included when validating the actual image pipeline.

**Channel semantics need stronger fixtures.** Index-to-ID checks mostly compare the resolver against the current enumeration, so reordering most entries together could pass. Explicitly pinned cases cover index zero and one fractional index; other stored positions need fixed historical mappings. Selected invalid indices do not prove totality for every malformed saved value. The claimed hue-invariance example compares two red-like RGB triples that are not a controlled linear-exposure pair; it establishes a bounded difference for those examples, not general exposure invariance. Circular hue comparisons should use circular distance, and neutral or near-neutral inputs need an explicit missing-hue policy rather than accidentally inheriting noise. Chroma checks show vivid red and blue both exceed a threshold, not equality of their chroma or a global maximum proof. Use an independently established normalization domain and avoid flattening all high-chroma pixels through premature clamping.

**Catalog navigation is a different coordinate system.** The lens harness tests a shared band geometry at a 56-pixel track height: top/bottom orientation, reversed bounds, out-of-range clipping and a minimum visible three-pixel band. It also tests intersection of catalog reach with a selected range, with a fallback to the selection when stale reach does not overlap. This supports a useful RFF palette-browser principle: keep a visible viewport marker synchronized with actual scroll position while selection filters define the searched domain. In grouped catalogs, scroll position must not be presented as a literal lightness measurement merely because the adjacent overview uses lightness.

The two-consumer agreement checks search source text for function names, prop syntax and an arithmetic fragment. They do not execute either rendered consumer or compare final screen pixels; comments or unused expressions could satisfy them, and harmless refactoring could fail them. Runtime validation should compare the shared inputs and displayed geometry after grouping, filtering, resize and scroll, including high-DPI rounding. Cover zero/tiny track height, nonfinite ranges and no-scroll layouts explicitly; the fixed-height fixtures do not establish those boundaries. The three-pixel minimum is a visibility affordance, not the true width of a zero-width mathematical interval. Keep that distinction out of filter arithmetic.

For adoption, test the recoloring data path separately from the browser viewport indicator. Stable saved channel IDs, color-domain definitions and neutral-hue behavior protect rendered appearance; synchronized scroll/selection state protects navigation. Neither test file establishes a shader performance gain, and these findings do not revise the current top-ten visual-effect ranking.

## Palette transitions and stop edits: test the sampled result, not just transformed records

Sources read in full: `debug/test-palette-tween.mts` (142 lines) and `debug/test-palette-stopops.mts` (160 lines). A targeted source check also confirms that `palette/core/oklab.ts:96` re-exports `lerpOklab` from `utils/colorUtils.ts`. No tests or historical mutation experiments were run for this review.

**Transfer to RFF.** Variant-to-variant palette blending can make exploratory adjustments and animated transitions easier. Batch reversal, repetition, distribution and scaling of selected color stops can complement existing palette controls. These are applicable to flat 2D and relief coloring; the incremental benefit is the editing/transition workflow, not simply adding OKLab, which RFF already supports. Preserve the existing interpolation choices and define the new operation's sampling geometry, hue behavior and identity guarantees.

**Tween assertions and limitations.** Equal-length random ramps are checked at blend endpoints with up to one RGB level of error, and at the midpoint for approximate argument-order symmetry. A separate dark/light fixture checks an interior midpoint and one red-channel quarter-step ordering. That does not establish componentwise RGB monotonicity for arbitrary perceptual-space interpolation, nor should such monotonicity automatically be required of a color-space path that does not promise it. Finite/range sweeps cover 21 blend amounts on random and primary/secondary fixtures, not every possible input or parameter.

The output length follows the first input. Therefore the equal-length midpoint symmetry test cannot be generalized to differently sampled ramps without first defining a shared output grid. Unequal-length endpoint checks inspect only red at the two ends; intermediate resampling and green/blue alignment remain unchecked there. The single-sample case asserts only output length, despite its descriptive text referring to sampling the first B color without division by zero. Empty B is more strongly tested for exact copied values and fresh storage, while source immutability during ordinary nonempty blending is not tested. Nonfinite blend factors are mapped to the A endpoint by the checked contract, including positive infinity; preserve that intentionally if adopted rather than accidentally treating it as the B endpoint via generic clamping.

For RFF, choose an explicit common sample grid for an animation, retain exact endpoint bypasses where saved appearance requires them, and test source lengths 0/1/N, nonfinite channels, source immutability, and neutral/saturated color pairs. Persist the chosen interpolation mode and source snapshots. Stable output dimensions avoid reallocations during transitions, but this file contains no GPU, frame-time or temporal-shimmer measurement.

**Shared sampling is useful integration evidence.** Six stop configurations compare individual sampling with float ramps and truncated RGB buffers at all 256 sample positions, including biased, smooth, step and linear-output cases. This detects divergence between entry points; shared implementation can also make agreement pass when a common color-conversion error affects all paths. Alpha is not compared. Two additional checks require biased/smoothed samples to differ from naive interpolation, but do not independently pin the intended numeric curve.
