Its source revision and May audit date identify a historical snapshot, earlier than the progressive-render changes reviewed above. API line numbers, consumer counts and behavior descriptions must not be taken as current implementation proof.

**Transferable architecture.** Separate render-target/history ownership, optional postprocessing and control/reporting interfaces. For RFF, this supports adding diagnostic fields or palette histograms without coupling their readback lifetime to UI widgets or duplicating shader evaluation. Run diagnostics only when a consumer needs them, but use explicit ownership/reference counting if multiple consumers can subscribe; a single global enable boolean is fragile when one consumer closes while another remains active.

**Convergence is not correctness.** The document describes a reduced-resolution difference image between successive history targets and asynchronous fence polling. For a running mean, the difference between consecutive means naturally shrinks with sample count even when appreciable variance remains. A small difference therefore does not by itself establish a low-error final image. Reduced-resolution sampling can also miss small bright features. RFF should keep a sample-budget stop, a statistical convergence estimate and a completed-field validity check distinct. A fractal boundary/precision error can be stable across frames and invisible to a temporal difference metric.

Fence completion avoids waiting for unfinished GPU work, but a subsequent synchronous readback/copy can still cost CPU time. Use generation-tagged staging resources and bounded outstanding requests for RFF; retire stale results after resize, precision changes or scene changes, and ensure old resources remain alive until their commands complete. A synchronous fallback should be explicit in the cost model. The archive's own asynchronous description conflicts with a later blanket phrase calling every periodic readback synchronous; inspect the actual path before assigning stall claims.

**Buffer naming and ping-pong semantics.** The archive warns that historical MRT names refer to single-attachment targets, while one architecture paragraph contradicts its own invariant about whether the latest output is opposite the next write index. This demonstrates why neither a field name nor an old explanatory sentence is enough. For any RFF extension, draw the before/after target ownership and verify with distinguishable frame patterns through reset, one draw, swap, partial-region update and readback. A single RGBA attachment can still encode non-color data in a component; “color target” does not prove its alpha is coverage rather than depth. Trace producers and consumers before reusing a channel.

**Preparation must match the live pipeline.** The tiny compile target is described as matching live attachment type so asynchronous preparation creates the intended shader program. The transferable RFF rule is broader: a prepared Vulkan pipeline must match its descriptor/push-constant layout, attachment formats, sample count and relevant render-pass/dynamic-rendering state. A small warm-up draw cannot prove every feature path or future format combination is compiled. Keep preparation separate from live history and replace resources atomically when ready.

**Bloom documentation is internally inconsistent.** The archive gives activeLevels=clamp(ceil(radius+0.5),2,7), then suggests rewriting a comment to say radius 5 activates all seven levels. Under the stated expression, radius 5 selects six. Do not copy that proposed correction without checking the implementation. Its description of a soft knee is also not a proof of continuity or black/threshold identity; the earlier shader audit's actual extraction analysis takes precedence. Validate intensity sweeps and radius transitions numerically and visually if adopting a new knee or multiscale filter in RFF.

Half-float readback conversion, shared fullscreen-resource lifetime, scissor application and optional diagnostic scheduling all require implementation-specific validation. This document provides useful test targets, not authorization to lower RFF precision, rename established algorithms or claim current runtime behavior from an archived API inventory.

## Shader-builder history: separate value edits from structural changes, with a checked GPU interface

Evidence: complete reads of `docs/history/audit-2026-05-20/archive/engine/shader-builder.md` (190 lines) and `docs/history/doc-audit-state/survey/e04-shader-builder.md` (91 lines), followed by current-source rereads of `engine/ShaderConfig.ts`, `engine/UniformSchema.ts` and `engine/ShaderBuilder.ts`, and a targeted inspection of the specialized GMT builder's method/assembly sites. These historical documents describe closely related snapshots, not two independent confirmations of present behavior. No shader compilation or runtime timing was performed for this section.

**The useful RFF transfer is a distinction between values and structure.** GMT's configuration describes a `pipelineRevision` for structural invalidation, whereas ordinary uniforms carry changing values. For RFF material masks, independent U/V mappings, environment controls and emission routing, classify each edit by the work it actually requires: update a value/resource binding, rerun a shading pass over existing fields, rebuild a shader/pipeline variant, or recompute the fractal field. Moving a light or changing a palette should not automatically become a fractal-field recalculation. This is a proposed invalidation contract, not a claim that RFF currently recompiles on every edit or that a counter alone makes a cache correct. The cache identity must include the actual generated program and GPU interface, relevant feature topology and pipeline state; a missed revision increment must not silently select an incompatible pipeline.

**Use the real assembler as the integration boundary.** The generic builder's default `buildFragment()` emits a minimal WebGL fragment shader with a black fallback. The specialized GMT builder instead exposes typed material, formula, shading and other insertion points with its own ordering. Improving or testing the generic fallback therefore does not prove improvement in the live GMT raymarcher. For RFF, extend the actual Vulkan shading stages and their consumers, with explicit input/output contracts for field evaluation, UV mapping, material evaluation, lighting and output transformation. Reusing an evaluated 2D field or height-derived normal does not require importing the 3D raymarching loop. Preserve operation ordering where it changes appearance; exact-string deduplication of helper code is not a dependency resolver or a semantic equivalence check.

**Current code supersedes several archived warnings.** The current `engine/UniformSchema.ts` explicitly throws for feature/base and feature/feature name collisions. Its `precision` member is gone, and its base-schema ownership comment now identifies core, tool/export and CPU-derived values. The archived claim that these schema collisions remain silent is obsolete. Builder-time `addUniform` still uses a name-keyed `Map.set`: conflicting injected declarations are outside that schema check and the last descriptor wins. Thus the transferable improvement is validation at both schema registration and final shader-interface assembly, not simply adding a duplicate-name warning already present in GMT's schema path.

For RFF, compare descriptor set/binding, descriptor type/count, shader stages, uniform/storage-buffer member offsets and strides, and push-constant offsets/ranges against the C++ configurator. A name-only comparison cannot establish Vulkan compatibility. Intentional duplicate requests may share an identical declaration; incompatible requests must be rejected before activating the candidate pipeline. Validate array lengths and resource availability as well as scalar types. GMT's `backingOnly` deliberately separates a host-side value slot from a conditionally emitted GLSL declaration; that is useful conceptual evidence for optional features, but it is not a Vulkan descriptor-layout rule and must not be copied literally.

**Precompute truly uniform work without changing precision.** The schema holds rotation matrices and other derived values so expensive expressions need not be repeated per fragment. For 2D RFF, static decoration transforms, environment rotation and compatible color conversions are candidates only where they are actually independent of pixel/field inputs. Recompute when their source settings change, preserve the established color interpretation, and measure whether the compiler already removes the work. GMT's historical `FogColorLinear` label includes an inverse filmic operation; neither that name nor its placement in a CPU cache establishes a standard color-space conversion. Do not move sensitive perturbation calculations into a lower-precision path in pursuit of this optimization.

**Do not inherit overstated type or lifetime guarantees.** Adding known fields to a TypeScript interface that retains `[key: string]: any` does not restore rejection of arbitrary misspelled field names; it only types accesses to declared fields. Likewise, `as const` is a compile-time restriction, not runtime `Object.freeze`. The current uniform factory clones recognized vectors/matrices and typed arrays but is not a recursive clone of every possible nested object. If RFF adopts shared feature metadata, use explicit ownership and validation rather than these stronger assumptions. The archived warning that every type-only import triggers registration is also too broad: emitted runtime imports determine evaluation, and the current source explicitly documents type-import elision for its configuration. This is a build-configuration concern, not a shader performance result.

Suggested acceptance evidence for a later RFF implementation: adjust continuous material controls while recording fractal recomputations and pipeline creations; change structural routing and verify the intended variant switches; rapidly supersede pending variants and verify only the latest matching state activates; compare disabled-feature output against the existing rendering path; validate descriptor layouts; and measure cold preparation, warm switching and steady-state GPU cost separately. This architecture can improve interaction in both flat 2D and relief-style shading, but these documents provide no measured RFF speedup and do not justify changing the current visual-effect ranking.

## Specialized shader-pipeline audit: preserve effect placement and distinguish logging from scheduling

Evidence: complete reads of the archived `engine-gmt/shader-pipeline.md` module audit (272 lines) and `survey/g02-shader-pipeline.md` (186 lines), with current targeted checks of `engine-gmt/engine/managers/ConfigManager.ts` and a full reread of `engine-gmt/engine/ShaderConfig.ts`. Historical line numbers and descriptions are retained as discovery aids, not treated as current runtime proof. This review adds RFF adoption constraints; it does not propose repairing GMT as the task's objective.

**Effect placement matters more than copying the 17 named slots.** GMT separates geometry evaluation, material evaluation, miss handling, ray generation, integration, post-processing and final composition. For RFF, the useful subset is existing fractal fields → mapping coordinates and filtered source samples → material-property masks → lighting and emission → existing compositing/output passes. A roughness mask must influence the lighting calculation; applying it as a final RGB multiplier cannot reproduce roughness. Emission routing must enter the chosen radiance/compositing contract before any downstream bright-pass that is intended to respond to it. Decorative UV warps alter source lookup coordinates, not the Mandelbrot iteration state. The archive's textual assembly positions alone do not establish execution order inside generated functions, so the final calls and pass dependencies must be traced when implementing each effect.

**Specialized variants need their own dependency closure.** The historical Main, Physics, Histogram and Mesh outputs intentionally omit different material and lighting stages. A feature that compiles in Main may reference a helper, uniform or resource absent from an analysis/export variant. For RFF, test the actual preview, image/video export and analysis consumers affected by a new source or mask. A histogram of a raw field and a histogram of final shaded pixels answer different questions; give each an explicit input domain. Share the coordinate/source evaluation where the intended meaning is shared, without forcing the full lighting stack into a histogram pass. A GLSL library without an entry point is not a separately validated executable shader.

**Disabled-feature stubs need mathematical identities.** The factory's documented always-inject strategy keeps dependent functions available even when a feature is disabled. RFF can adopt the dependency discipline without adopting a universal stub mechanism. Where a neutral implementation is appropriate, distinguish additive emission zero, multiplicative mask one and unchanged coordinate/normal transforms. A function that merely compiles is not necessarily an appearance-preserving disabled state. Conversely, injecting every expensive feature body can increase compiler work even when runtime controls disable it; measure a small set of actual variants before choosing static specialization versus runtime branching.

**The 50 ms timer is log batching, not evidence of fewer compilations.** Current `ConfigManager.ts` accumulates `pendingLogChanges` and schedules `flushRebuildLog()`; its comments explicitly allow synchronous shader rebuilds between updates. The archived wording about batching compile-trigger changes can therefore mislead. RFF should independently coalesce pending structural rebuild requests, discard superseded results, and measure actual pipeline creation counts if reduced compilation is an objective. A grouped console message or estimated compile duration cannot verify scheduling behavior or achieved latency.

**Do not copy the generic 1e-6 equality threshold into deep-zoom state.** The current GMT diff helper compares numbers and vector/color components with this absolute tolerance. For RFF, equality rules must follow parameter meaning and representation. High-precision centers, zoom scales and perturbation inputs cannot be collapsed by a generic absolute epsilon. Exact structural identifiers and discrete choices also need exact comparison. An appearance slider may have a defensible quantization rule, but that rule must not silently lose a meaningful edit or interfere with accumulation invalidation. This is a transfer restriction, not a diagnosis of a proven RFF defect.

**Keep editable source state separate from derived GPU data.** GMT's reverse uniform synchronization rejects tagged gradient buffers rather than storing a derived texture as gradient-stop configuration. The corresponding RFF requirement is to preserve editable source/binding state independently of palette textures, mip chains and GPU caches. Regeneration and undo should use the source representation; transient GPU data must not rewrite frozen `{presetId, seed}` recipe semantics. New persistent controls still need RFF's append-only ConfigIO handling. Avoid relying only on a loosely attached runtime tag when a typed source/resource distinction can express the contract.

**Coordinate conventions must survive preview and export.** The archived pipeline describes full-output tile coordinates, adaptive resolution, camera-relative positions and toward-light direction vectors. Transfer the explicit conventions, not their exact 3D variables: choose whether an RFF light follows the view or the image; specify normal and light spaces; use full-output coordinates for reproducible decoration/noise; and distinguish a filter's footprint from a geometry-precision epsilon. Adaptive display resolution must not change the mathematical fractal or masquerade as reduced precision. A screen-space shading radius needs a documented conversion when preview and final output have different resolutions.

Two documentation cautions affect the interpretation: a TypeScript string index signature does not by itself make explicitly required properties such as `pipelineRevision` optional, even though `any` values and unsafe assertions can bypass checks; and a once-created exported array is not runtime immutable merely because its binding is `const`. The survey's early suggestion to replace a sibling schema with a re-export was later qualified by the archive because the registration imports select different feature registries. For RFF, share pure schema/evaluation code where useful, while keeping renderer-specific registration and resource ownership explicit. None of these historical architecture notes supplies measured evidence to promote an additional visual effect above the previously ranked candidates.

## Bucket-port and output-tiling plans: preserve deep-zoom coordinates and budget actual allocations

Evidence: complete reads of `plans/bucket-render-port-handoff.md` (287 lines) and `docs/history/gmt/43_Bucket_Render_Overhaul.md` (161 lines). These are an evolving handoff and a dated draft; their build results and manual-test claims are historical reports, not tests run during this audit. Instructions to a successor in the handoff are source material, not instructions for this RFF review.

**Transfer the export contract, not the backend wrapper.** The handoff's updated section says the raw-WebGL fluid renderer bypasses a supposedly generic runner because that runner requires Three.js renderer/target/material objects. A later retained section still proposes the superseded adapter. For RFF, separate tile scheduling, progress, cancellation and output metadata from Vulkan allocations, commands and readback. A reusable UI controller is not evidence of a backend-independent GPU runner. The updated unsupported-deep-zoom caveat is especially unsuitable for RFF: turning off deep zoom for export would abandon a central capability rather than complete the transfer.

**Specify one global pixel coordinate before deriving UVs or perturbation offsets.** Let a tile's integer origin be O, its actual dimensions be T, the final image dimensions be F, and p be a local pixel-center coordinate. Then the global pixel center is O+p, and normalized full-image coordinates are (O+p)/F. If a shader starts with normalized tile coordinates, p=uvLocal*T; if it already has full-image UV, multiply that by F without adding O again. The draft's suggested noise expression `noiseCoord * uFullOutputResolution + uTilePixelOrigin` is correct only for a specifically defined `noiseCoord`; substituting local normalized UV stretches the tile to the full image, while substituting already-remapped UV double-counts the origin. Establish the domain at each producer rather than copy the expression by name.

For RFF perturbation, derive the displacement from the full-image pixel position relative to the intended reference using the existing precision-preserving representation. Avoid forming and subtracting nearly equal large world coordinates in a lower-precision shader path. Use the same global convention for decorative patterns, image lookup, jitter and export masks. A local-pixel jitter transforms into full UV by dividing by F; equivalently, jitter divided by T before the tile remap is scaled by T/F. Calling jitter global does not alone prove this normalization. Per-pixel random values additionally need a consistent global pixel identity, sample index and seed if tiled/untiled comparisons are intended to match.

**GPU subregions and smaller allocations are different optimizations.** Scissoring or rejecting fragments can bound shader work while retaining full-tile attachments. Only reducing the allocated targets, streaming/retiring them, or changing a justified storage design reduces their footprint. Budget all simultaneous color/history/composite targets, post-process pyramids, depth where used, staging/readback buffers, CPU encoded/raw buffers and temporary resize overlap. A Float32 RGBA composite costs 16 bytes per pixel before other resources. The handoff's claims of roughly 50 MB being fine on any GPU, no ping-pong, and a later roughly 225 MB ping-pong requirement describe inconsistent assumptions; neither is a reliable RFF memory model. Account for supported dimensions and allocation limits separately from total free memory.

**Cover the exact requested dimensions.** The draft floors nominal tile sizes and assigns remainder pixels to the last row/column. That requires allocating for the actual, potentially larger remainder tile, not blindly using the nominal floor-sized buffer. Another valid partition uses integer boundaries floor(i*F/n) and floor((i+1)*F/n), spreading widths that differ by at most one; either scheme needs explicit origins and exact, nonoverlapping coverage. Reject or handle grids that create zero-sized tiles. Preserve an explicitly requested export size instead of silently snapping it to a multiple of eight; internal allocation padding can be cropped. Output aspect belongs to the full image, not each remainder tile. Define orientation consistently between shader coordinates, readback row order and saved tile indices.

**Seams are not limited to bloom.** Image filtering, normal/height derivatives, AO-like neighborhood effects, distortion, chromatic aberration and diffusion can all need samples outside a tile even with bloom disabled. Render or supply an appropriate halo, perform the operation on shared full-image data, or use a deliberately documented approximation. A fixed 64-pixel skirt is not universally sufficient: derive support from all affected stages, their scales and the maximum displacement/filter footprint. Correct halo results can be cropped to their interior and stitched exactly; feathering is not inherently required and can hide mismatched computations instead of fixing them. Mip-pyramid alignment and border behavior also need to match the full-image path.

The proposed viewport-resolution bloom shared across tiles can remove discontinuity between tiles but cannot recreate missing high-resolution bright detail or guarantee the same result as full-resolution filtering. It is a quality/cost choice, not a zero-cost equivalence. Likewise, absence of bloom/CA does not prove a seam-free fluid or RFF export: coordinate precision, jitter, local derivatives, sample budgets and output transforms still matter.

**A sample cap is a budget, and a threshold is not uniform uncertainty.** The handoff calls reaching a sample count convergence; the draft suggests identical convergence thresholds leave only about one sample of variance difference. Neither establishes equal error across tiles. Content-dependent variance can differ widely, and even equal sample counts do not equalize uncertainty. Use deterministic sample sequences for reproducibility where applicable, record the stopping reason and avoid labeling a partially stopped tile as a completed final result. RFF's deterministic fractal-field validity remains separate from stochastic shading or antialiasing quality.

**Export should be a bounded session with durable output semantics.** Snapshot source settings and required simulation/animation time for the session, restore viewport state on completion, cancellation and failure, and keep the completed result available if the action promises refinement. Persist a manifest with full dimensions, tile origins/sizes, orientation, settings/seed identity, color interpretation and completion status when producing separate files. A PNG canvas path does not preserve a Float32 HDR composite; tone mapping, encoding and any quantization must be explicit. Test decoded pixels with stated tolerances when numerical equivalence is intended: the draft's phrase 'byte-compare within floating-point tolerance' conflates exact file-byte equality and image-value comparison. Include uneven grids, changed output aspect, deep zoom, all relevant spatial effects, cancellation during readback and restoration after failure. No such RFF runtime validation has been performed in this documentation batch.

## Shaped-emission specification: a spotlight proposal, not implemented material emission

Evidence: full read of `docs/specs/10_Shaped_Emission.md` (245 lines), with targeted current checks in `engine-gmt/types/graphics.ts` and `engine-gmt/engine/managers/UniformManager.ts`. The current light union is Point/Directional/Sphere and the manager assigns numeric type 2 to Sphere. The specification's proposed Spot=2 and `type > 1.5` detection therefore cannot be transplanted into current GMT or used as evidence that spotlights already ship. A search for spotlight/cone-angle spellings in RFF's shader/core directories found no matching identifiers; that narrow negative search is not a complete proof of missing equivalent functionality.

**RFF opportunity: locally directed lighting over the existing relief field.** A positional light with a cone mask can illuminate a selected part of a 2D fractal's height-derived surface, while leaving independently colored fill/rim lights available. This extends lighting control rather than fractal geometry. For a truly flat 2D image, the same angular/spatial weighting can be offered as an artistic illumination mask, with no claim that it creates physical thickness, volumetric beams or correct 3D occlusion. It is distinct from making the fractal material emit light; the existing independent emission-routing candidate remains a separate feature.

**Mechanism and direction convention.** Let L be the normalized vector from the shaded point toward the positional light, and let D be the light's normalized forward emission axis pointing outward from the light. The cone cosine is dot(D,-L), or equivalently dot(-D,L) when the stored axis uses GMT's toward-light convention. Precompute outer/inner half-angle cosines when settings change, then multiply the direct light contribution by a smooth transition from zero at cosOuter to one at cosInner. Increasing angle decreases cosine, so the ordered domain is cosOuter <= cosInner. Validate finite angles and clamp or reject reversed bounds. Handle equal inner/outer angles with an explicit hard-edge rule rather than equal-edge smoothstep; the proposed UI permits this boundary. A zero-length point-to-light vector and a degenerate direction also need defined behavior. This generic mechanism does not require copying a distinctive third-party implementation.

**Appearance and energy semantics must be explicit.** A cone multiplier at fixed peak intensity reduces total emitted energy as the cone narrows; keeping total power constant requires a different normalization. Choose and document the control meaning instead of promising both. Apply attenuation to the light's contribution in the existing linear-light computation, not to a finished tone-mapped image or indiscriminately to material emission. Cone boundaries need pixel-footprint consideration in small or distant projected regions, especially for animation and high-resolution exports. Any smoothing approximation should preserve fully unlit and fully lit limits and use the same full-image coordinate convention across tiles.

**Do not transfer the claimed performance gain uncritically.** Computing a zero cone factor saves an expensive shadow/visibility query only when the actual consumer skips that query before issuing it. The volumetric code sketch merely multiplies attenuation and does not itself demonstrate the promised early exit. An arbitrary `0.001` cutoff can remove visible HDR contribution after exposure or from a high-intensity source; it is a quality approximation, not an exact optimization. Outside-cone exact zero can be skipped when downstream behavior permits it. GPU branch coherence and the number of active lights still affect cost. RFF relief shading may have none of GMT's expensive volumetric shadow work, so the proposed volumetric speedup does not transfer automatically.

**Port only the relevant sampling model.** A point spotlight can reuse a point-light visibility direction plus angular attenuation. Extending the idea to a finite area emitter or path tracer requires consistency between the emitted radiance distribution, light selection, sampled directions/positions and their PDFs/MIS weights; the proposed simple type check is insufficient. RFF does not need a 3D volumetric/path-tracing subsystem merely to gain directed local lighting. Likewise, a projected texture or angular profile is a further feature with its own coordinates, filtering and provenance requirements, not functionality established by this spec.

If prototyped in RFF, preserve existing light identifiers and file-format semantics, append new persistent fields using the established configuration rules, and update C++/GLSL light arrays and layouts together. Verify an on-axis point, an outside-cone point, inner/outer transitions, coincident angles, a point at the light position, zero intensity, camera-relative versus image-relative lights, multiple light combinations and tiled export. Compare enabled/disabled output and measure cost before changing the current ranking. This remains an optional extension of the independent-lighting candidate, not a newly demonstrated top-priority shader improvement.

## Fractal-color redesign history: normalization must respect field meaning and skipped orbit information

Evidence: complete reads of `docs/history/plans-archive/fractal-color-accumulation-iteration-handoff.md` (107 lines) and `fractal-colour-accumulation-redesign.md` (179 lines). The redesign's status update reports phases 0–4 implemented behind an initially disabled option, while later cadence/statistics phases remain queued there. Those are dated implementation reports, not a fresh runtime verification. The embedded successor prompt and its proposed agent/sign-off workflow are historical content, not instructions for this audit.

**Prefer a useful field contract to a universal normalization promise.** The two documents identify a real design concern: different scalar fields produce very different useful palette repetition ranges. However, dividing smooth iteration count by the current iteration cap changes the color of an already escaped pixel when only that cap changes. It does not mathematically guarantee invariant spatial band density under zoom. Likewise, a common default density of one across angle, distance, iteration and trap fields is an ergonomic convention, not proof that all fields have the same spatial frequency. For RFF, expose optional, explicitly named mappings or range assistance while preserving established saved looks. Keep the mapping version, normalization parameters and any automatic range snapshot in reproducible state; do not silently reinterpret old repeat values or frozen palette recipes. A continuously recomputed view-dependent range can make colors breathe during zoom, so animation needs a fixed or deliberately controlled policy.

**Distances live in different spaces.** The redesign's later implementation note correctly retracts its initial suggestion to divide all orbit-trap distances by image pixel spacing. A trap measures orbit positions in the dynamical plane; a Mandelbrot distance estimate is related to distances in the parameter plane. They cannot share a normalization merely because both are called distances. For Julia rendering the derivative/coordinate interpretation changes again. A logarithmic mapping can expand a tiny trap-value range but cannot reconstruct precision that has already underflowed or been clamped away. RFF field metadata should state units/domain, valid pixels, scale representation and whether a quantity summarizes the whole orbit or only a selected interval.

**Log-space DE can avoid an unnecessary overflow, with limits.** If a distance estimate is represented as C*r*ln(r)/|dz| in an applicable escaping-orbit convention, its ratio to pixel spacing s can be formed through log(C)+log(r)+log(log(r))-log(|dz|)-log(s), instead of first exponentiating a large stored log derivative. The constant, derivative recurrence, bailout and formula assumptions must match RFF's estimator; this expression is not a universal estimator for every fractal. Require valid escaping r and a defined derivative, and handle interior/invalid cases separately. Compute log pixel spacing from RFF's existing high-precision/scaled representation, not by first converting an extremely small spacing to ordinary float and then taking its logarithm. The document's use of JavaScript f64 extends one range but does not establish support for RFF's deepest zooms.

**Derivative magnitude alone does not provide a directional normal.** The design calls a new normal/slope layer cheap because a derivative is already tracked, but a stored scalar log|dz| is insufficient to recover the derivative's complex direction or both screen-space derivatives. An analytic normal path needs the required directional information and correct domain conventions; a neighborhood-derived normal needs field samples, filter support and resolution handling. RFF already has relief/PBR shading, so this is a possible field-quality/input improvement only after comparing against that implementation, not evidence that lighting itself must be added. Derivative recurrence and extra orbit statistics also have per-iteration costs even if final color mapping happens after the loop. The document's blanket 'negligible per-pixel cost' claim is not a measured RFF result.

**MPA needs a separate color-statistics proof.** The documents discuss artifacts when accelerated and ordinary paths accumulate stripe/trap statistics differently. For RFF, MPA derives skip levels from periodic structure; it is not GMT's LA/AT and must not be described as BLA. A minimum trap value, the iteration where it occurs, or a nonlinear stripe average generally cannot be reconstructed from a skip endpoint alone. Before adding such a color field, establish whether each skipped interval has a valid summary, whether the approximation preserves the statistic to the required accuracy, or whether a selective unskipped evaluation is necessary. A reference-orbit statistic is not automatically the perturbed pixel's statistic. Compare accelerated and unskipped results at skip-region boundaries and across iteration budgets, preserving numerical precision. Screen-space jitter cannot repair a systematic missing-statistics boundary.

**Share kernel semantics without conflating accumulation policies.** GX and fluid-toy share color/kernel code but retain different reset hashes, sample budgets and frame sampling. This supports reusing RFF's field-to-color evaluation across preview/export while keeping each host's scheduling explicit. A high-precision center's low component, reference generation, relevant field parameters and source state must participate in validity; matching a rounded visible coordinate is insufficient. Recoloring reusable fields can avoid orbit recomputation, but RGB history already accumulated under an old palette must be reset or reconstructed from adequate samples. In general, applying a nonlinear palette to a mean field is not equal to averaging the palette applied to individual samples. Cheap recoloring therefore has a representation/quality tradeoff that must be stated rather than assumed free.

**Decorrelation is not guaranteed blue noise or anti-correlation.** Hashing pixel identity and sample round can remove a globally synchronized jitter pattern, but it does not by itself give neighboring samples an anti-correlated spectrum. Changing a stratification grid with the same total sample count does not guarantee smaller intermediate errors or the same finite-sample image. A deterministic sequence still changes while samples accumulate; determinism makes it repeatable, not inherently shimmer-free. Evaluate spatial structure, temporal stability and final error with a stable full-output pixel seed, especially across image tiles. Attribute and license-check any actual adopted hash/noise implementation before adding it to RFF/NOTICE.

The broad assertions about what all advanced renderers do, universal depth stability and 'SOTA default' status are not established by these documents and are not adopted as findings. The concrete RFF candidates are optional log-domain field mappings, explicit color-statistic validity, reproducible density/range controls and correctly invalidated reusable shading. Validate them with identical-location comparisons across iteration caps, shallow/deep representations, accelerated/unskipped paths, preview/export resolutions and old saved scenes before ranking their visual benefit. The historical green test list and byte-identical-v1 claim do not substitute for those RFF checks.

## Live fractal palette-preview scope: reuse RFF's fields and preserve the color contract

Evidence: full read of `plans/gx-live-fractal-coloring-scope.md` (342 lines), a June 6 research/design probe. Targeted current checks in `engine/fractal/FractalColorRenderer.ts` confirm `setColormap`, deep-zoom enablement, the 128-sample cap and disposal entry points exist now. The planning document's 'no code written', initial shallow-only staging and file locations must therefore not be read as a current feature inventory. No preview/export runtime comparison was performed here.

**The useful RFF feature is a live palette comparison on meaningful fractal structure.** An editable ramp is easier to judge on the current fractal field than on a horizontal strip alone. RFF can reuse its existing renderer/field data for a small preview, optionally alongside the main view or a saved comparison, instead of introducing a second shallow Mandelbrot implementation. Keep current deep-zoom precision and the existing MPA/reference machinery. A curated sample scene can be an optional comparison target, but it must be identified separately from the user's current location and use a reproducible scene identity. The plan's assertion that a shallow MVP provides 90% of value is not measured evidence and is not a reason to substitute shallow precision for RFF's main capability.

**Identical LUT bytes do not establish identical color.** The proposed 256x1 RGBA8 seam is a convenient transport representation; matching dimensions, channel count and bytes is only the start. The consuming texture format and color decode, interpolation domain, address mode, texel-center convention, cyclic endpoint handling, alpha interpretation and final output conversion all affect appearance. An encoded-color LUT sampled with linear filtering does not automatically interpolate in linear light or the selected perceptual blend space. RFF should use its established palette generator and color-space semantics, not quantize a higher-quality representation to 256 RGBA8 entries merely to match GMT's adapter. Narrow stops and high-frequency ramps need sufficient resolution or an appropriate analytic/adaptive representation; a small upload alone cannot prove fidelity.

**Live versus snapshot is an explicit relationship.** The scope identifies an overlay that originally captures configuration at open time, then proposes a live subscription. For RFF, a live preview should identify the active edit session and use the same working palette/settings as the editor. A frozen comparison should retain its own source snapshot. Undo, cancellation, switching the edited palette and closing/reopening must not leave the preview attached to an obsolete source. Preserve the source recipe/stop representation independently of GPU textures and keep recipe RNG/order stable. Saving a preview image should capture the palette, mapping parameters, location and normalization version that produced it, rather than whichever settings happen to be current when an asynchronous readback finishes.

**Cheap uploads can still trigger costly refinement.** A 1024-byte LUT replacement is small, but its frame cost includes generation, synchronization, shading and any invalidated RGB accumulation. Coalesce rapid edits to the latest state and reuse valid fractal fields; do not assume the whole preview is negligible because the texture payload is small. As discussed in the color-statistics audit, averaging fields before a nonlinear palette lookup does not reproduce averaged colored samples. Choose a representation that supports the promised preview quality, then reset or reconstruct the dependent history correctly. A downscaled buffer with temporal antialiasing does not automatically become a full-resolution final export: output resolution, spatial information and reconstruction filters remain distinct concerns.

**Lifecycle belongs to the renderer host.** The plan creates a separate WebGL context in a transient overlay. RFF's Vulkan architecture can instead share appropriate device resources while giving preview targets and pending work clear ownership. Resize and close must retire in-flight resources safely; rapid palette/location changes need generation checks so stale orbit, texture or capture work cannot overwrite the current preview. Stop refinement when its budget is reached or the preview is hidden, while allowing a real settings change to restart it. Export must read a defined completed frame and report whether it is a preview-quality capture or a newly rendered final image. A browser drawing-buffer preservation flag is not an equivalent Vulkan capture design.

**Precision and effort claims remain unverified estimates.** The scope's ranges near 1e-7, 1e-30 and 1e-300 describe proposed/practical limits without establishing accuracy across coordinates, iteration counts and hardware. A minimum allowed zoom constant, high-precision CPU reference, or uniform-controlled deep branch does not prove every GPU delta survives its representation. Turning a branch off also does not guarantee the compiler avoids its preparation cost. For RFF, validate the actual preview at deep locations against the established full renderer, and do not transplant GMT's LA/AT labels onto MPA. Sharing a kernel avoids one source of divergence, but correct host binding, reset policy and output transforms still need separate checks.

The adoption candidate is therefore a faithful live palette preview/comparison using existing RFF fields, with explicit live/snapshot behavior and reproducible capture. It complements histogram/range assistance and source-driven materials; it is not evidence of a new shading algorithm or a measured speedup, and it does not alter the visual-effect ranking by itself.

## Stop-reduction tests: useful approximation controls, with a sampled and partly shared oracle

Evidence: complete read of `debug/test-palette-reducestops.mts` (409 lines). This is a source-level assessment of its assertions, not a new test execution. The calibration and reverted-mutation outcomes in its header are historical claims. The already-reviewed reducer remains the implementation source; this section specifies what its companion test can and cannot establish for RFF adoption.

**Useful RFF transfer.** Offer stop-count alternatives with an explicit approximation tolerance, retain a preview before committing, and allow one undo operation for accepting the selected result. GMT tests an alternative at every count from two to one below the input count, four named tolerance levels, preservation of output color-space metadata, removal of a stale dense-ramp field, and a blend-space search whose named choices never use more stops than the corresponding no-search choices. This is a useful editable-palette simplification design, not a replacement for lossless map compression or RFF's frozen preset/seed recipes. Keep the original source available and save the accepted explicit approximation as a distinct editable result.

**The error contract is 256 display-sRGB samples.** The test's `worst` function rerenders both stop lists in their respective blend spaces, explicitly requests `srgb`, and measures Oklab distance at all 256 samples. It is independent of the reducer's error-aggregation helper, but shares the production `renderStopsToRamp` and `oklabDistance` implementations. It can catch incorrect reported error or mismatched blend-space labeling without independently proving those shared color conversions correct. The tests check that `linear` and `aces_inverse` metadata survive; they do not measure fidelity after those actual output transformations. Narrow features between sampled positions, HDR behavior, alpha, and the final GPU sampling path remain outside this particular error guarantee.

For RFF, define whether simplification targets the authored continuous ramp, a particular LUT, or the displayed final image. A fixed 256-point check is meaningful for a fixed 256-sample artifact but cannot establish a continuous maximum-error bound. Use additional samples around discontinuities, biased segments and narrow stops if preserving the continuous palette is the promise. A display-space error tolerance is also not an error bound on roughness masks, emission energy or other non-color data driven by that palette. Do not advertise the header's 0.02 as a universal just-noticeable threshold independent of viewing conditions and color processing.

**Some headline contracts are intentionally weaker than their wording.** 'More stops never look worse' permits an increase of 0.002 in worst sampled error between neighboring counts. That local allowance is not strict monotonicity and does not bound cumulative drift over many counts to 0.002. The blend-space fitter test requests targetDE 0.01 but accepts measured error up to 0.02 and up to four stops for its three-stop examples. Thus passing that case does not establish that every requested fit tolerance is met. The count-search benefit checks named levels and a finite corpus; it is not a proof of globally minimal stop counts or an optimal blend space. Searching a different blend space also changes future editing semantics even when the present raster is close, so expose the selected space to the RFF user.

**Corpus availability and selection matter.** External catalog packs may be skipped when absent; synthetic examples still exercise six blend spaces, bands, smooth interpolation and bias. The separate core-picks test requires more than 30 picks, so this file does not silently pass with every catalog missing, but it can run without the optional catalog families. Picks are sampled at fixed strides and first fitted into editable configurations; the reducer is compared against those configurations, not directly against every original source ramp. When assessing end-to-end import-plus-reduction error, include the first fitting stage rather than quoting only the additional reduction error. The recorded 28% reduction and the asserted at-least-15% improvement concern the chosen Light/core-pick comparison, not all palettes, memory savings or renderer speed.

**Yielding is not measured responsiveness.** The lazy-path section exhausts a generator synchronously into an array with `sliceMs: 0`, verifies null yields before the first complete plan, and checks pending/final plan structure. It does not measure how long the first plan takes, whether the caller yields to UI/GPU work, or whether canceled/obsolete searches stop. The header itself acknowledges that a lost early plan can evade some checks. For RFF, bound actual computation chunks, tag requests by edit generation and discard superseded previews; verify latency with a difficult palette rather than counting generator yields. Device-based exclusion of Spectral is an allowed-space test, not a benchmark demonstrating that all other spaces satisfy a latency budget.

**UI text pins are not interaction tests.** This file calls the menu action through a constructed context, confirming opening does not start an undo bracket. Other checks search source text for the apply/preview wiring and remembered search flag. Those checks cannot prove live preview restoration, exactly one real undo entry, cancellation, source switching or persistence in the running application. The finite-error checks reject NaN distances through Infinity, but simple position comparisons do not independently reject NaN stop positions, and the reported-error comparison alone can miss a NaN report. These are limits on the evidence, not observed rendering failures. Before using this pattern in RFF, validate finite inputs/outputs, output-space fidelity and the actual preview/apply/undo lifecycle without expanding the promise beyond the measured representation.

## Stop-fitting harness: preserve authored edges without mistaking quantization for intent

Evidence: complete read of `debug/test-palette-stopfit.mts` (367 lines). Tests were inspected, not executed. Its historical mutation results and timing observations are not fresh measurements.

**Useful RFF transfer.** When converting a sampled palette into editable stops, retain the dense original and provide a preview of the fit. Seed a repeated fit with existing positions and segment styles to reduce editing drift. Distinguish genuine step boundaries from quantization plateaus, particularly near black, and avoid uniform-stride sampling that can select only one phase of a high-frequency ramp. These are appearance-preserving editing mechanisms; they must not modify RFF's frozen recipe generation or turn lossless data into a silently approximated representation.

The test supplies valuable adversarial cases: integer-texel step boundaries, very dark shallow gradients, low-contrast bands and a period-two zebra with a phase shift. The phase shift matters because an ordinary zebra may accidentally pass even with a biased subsampling rule. For RFF, retain the idea of testing cases on both sides of a decision threshold rather than copying a threshold calibrated to GMT's 8-bit/Oklab path.

**The asserted guarantees are narrower than several comments.** Seed-position stability in section 5 compares rounded position*255 values after three rebakes, not exact floating-point positions, and does not assert unchanged stop colors, IDs, bias or interpolation. Section 8 compares positions rounded to five decimal places for one six-stop fixture. Its fidelity check uses a nonzero tolerance. The band test accepts at least 16 step stops and error below 0.001; this is not exactly one stop per band with byte-exact reconstruction. The zebra check only requires between 25% and 75% of fitted stops to be black: it demonstrates retention of both phases, not correct edge placement, ordering or low reconstruction error. Preserve these distinctions in any RFF acceptance criteria.

**Requested tolerance is not always an achieved bound.** The random-bias test requests 0.012 but allows worst error up to 0.07 for a narrow-band case. Its plain-gradient 'not worse' check compares average stop count, not maximum error; the smooth-gradient check also constrains average count only. If RFF presents a tolerance control, report achieved error and budget exhaustion separately, and offer the original ramp when an editable fit cannot meet the requested limit. Do not describe fewer control points as an improvement if the important thin band disappears.

**The real-palette fidelity pass can be absent.** Its input directories are hardcoded external H: paths, and the entire real-palette pass is skipped when none exist. Even when present, the asserted high-budget result is an average of mean errors across selected palettes, not a per-palette worst-case tolerance; maximum errors are printed but not bounded there. The 'smooth' subset is classified by changes in Oklab lightness alone, which can miss strong chromatic oscillation. Its parser interpolates non-256 inputs before fitting, so fidelity concerns the resampled data rather than every original sample. No valid empty-input handling is demonstrated by that helper. RFF evaluation should identify fixture availability, preserve original sampling semantics and include chromatic as well as luminance structure.

**Byte parity is useful, but it is CPU-path parity.** The first section compares two imported CPU texture-buffer entry points for 200 seeded configurations, using sRGB output and selected blend/interpolation combinations. Shared rendering helpers limit independence, and no GPU lookup, mip/filter behavior, HDR output or alternate output color space is exercised. The loop compares through the first buffer's length without an explicit equal-length assertion. Passing this check would be evidence for those API outputs, not proof of the full rendered image or all fitter-emitted configurations.

The performance assertion is a warmed average below 12 ms over 40 biased synthetic palettes, not a maximum latency bound and not RFF/Vulkan timing. It excludes editor work, upload and redraw. Before fitting on every slider event in RFF, measure worst-case interaction, coalesce obsolete work and make acceptance a single undoable action. Repeated fitting should be optional: retain the original editable representation whenever no conversion is needed. This candidate improves palette authoring and preservation; it does not establish a shader-speed benefit or alter the current visual-effect priority list.

## Ramp-geometry harness: useful dependency checks, not full shader or seam validation

Evidence: complete read of `debug/test-palette-rampgeometry.mts` (210 lines). No tests were executed. The harness exercises CPU palette-preview geometry, not RFF's GPU shading path.

The transferable feature is a reusable coordinate field for linear, radial, conic and radius-dependent twisted palette mappings. RFF can apply such a field to decorative palette/image lookup or material masks without changing Mandelbrot coordinates or orbit calculations. The radial wave amplitude/frequency pair is also a useful model for dependent controls: the harness explicitly checks that frequency changes output with nonzero amplitude but stays inert at zero amplitude. This is stronger than checking every control only against an all-default scene, where some correctly wired controls have no effect.

**Repeatability and compatibility are separate.** The harness compares two runs through a 32-bit hash, mostly at 64x48 with a grayscale ramp. That is useful same-process repeatability evidence, but hash equality is not a literal full-buffer equality check, an independent oracle, a cross-GPU result or a frozen-version regression baseline. It compares omitted fields with the current `GEOM_DEFAULTS`; changing both the default and its implicit fallback together could preserve that check while changing old scenes. RFF needs stable stored meanings/defaults and representative retained outputs when compatibility is promised. Four outputs from two PRNG seeds likewise do not establish distribution quality, spatial noise properties or long-run independence.

**The coverage test exercises a local copy of the blend.** Because the shipped geometries no longer create partial coverage, the harness builds a synthetic field and passes it to its own `renderGeometryFromSample`, which duplicates the intended background blend. Its assertions therefore cannot catch a regression in the production partial-coverage branch. The actual production call in this section only has its output length checked. If RFF introduces masked geometry, exercise the real mask/compositor path at zero, partial and full coverage. Define whether coverage becomes alpha or is flattened into an opaque background, and perform blending in the intended color domain. A grayscale fixture alone cannot expose swapped color channels or some color-space mistakes.

**A complete turn is not a seam-continuity proof.** Conic angle plus 2π is compared with the base field, establishing periodic parameter behavior for one sampled configuration. It does not test whether colors on either side of the angular branch cut match, whether the ramp endpoints form a cyclic palette, or whether the filtered derivatives stay stable there. RFF mirror/sector and spiral mappings need explicit wrap/branch handling, pixel-footprint filtering and full-output coordinates for tiled images. Radius-dependent mapping has separate behavior at the center and under aspect changes; include off-center, portrait and extreme-aspect fixtures rather than infer those properties from the default image.

The twist tests check two points on one ray in a 65x49 field: equal values at zero twist, unequal values at one nonzero twist, and a larger value at the farther point. This rejects a rigid rotation for that fixture but does not prove the precise log(1+r) law or global monotonicity after cyclic wrapping. Other functional radius dependences can pass it. Document the actual mapping formula from its implementation and preserve its normalization if RFF adds the option. The named non-default tests also omit some independent components (for example center Y and the second conic bias), so the comment 'all configs' is broader than the assertions.

For RFF adoption, retain the useful zero-effect and coupled-control tests, then verify actual field values and final shader output for the selected formula, wrap boundaries, degenerate dimensions, nonfinite inputs, parameter limits and preview/export scaling. Keep palette lookup filtering separate from field generation; the harness's nearest ramp-entry example is not a recommendation to reduce RFF's interpolation quality. These findings refine the existing decorative mapping candidates rather than establish a new top-ranked effect.

## Palette host entry points: bind editing to the intended shader property

Evidence: full reads of `palette/installFavients.ts` (133 lines), `palette/components/FavientsEditorEntrance.tsx` (60 lines) and `palette/components/GradientStudioEntrance.tsx` (42 lines). This source review concerns state routing and persistence boundaries, not a visual UI audit or runtime test.

**RFF transfer: one palette editor, explicit destinations.** The saved-gradient entrance matches the editor's `(featureId, paramKey)` against a registered send target before revealing the shelf or adding the current gradient through a common bridge. The floating studio entrance opens on the same parameter identity and avoids recursively offering itself inside the studio. For RFF's independent base-color, environment, emission and scalar-mask inputs, the useful pattern is a shared editor whose target is explicit and stable. Palette content and destination binding should remain separate: saving a source must not implicitly overwrite whichever material property was edited previously. Include a layer/source identity when multiple instances expose the same property name.

The shelf entrance picks the first matching target; when no target matches it leaves the prior selection intact. This file therefore does not establish unique routing or a safe fallback destination. In an RFF adaptation, validate target existence and ambiguity and make a vanished or unsupported target an explicit state. A saved palette may be reusable across properties, but a stale selection must not silently redirect a later Apply. The studio's visible 'on this target' state is keyed to both openness and identity, a useful distinction when switching between editors.

**Keep shared content separate from host window state.** The installer supplies a host-specific storage key for dock position/open state, while the favorite collection is deliberately shared. This maps well to sharing reusable RFF palettes without forcing every workspace/view to share panel placement. The stable internal panel ID is retained even though its display label changes; likewise, do not rename persistent RFF identifiers merely to improve wording. New configuration fields still follow RFF's append-only format rules and source recipes retain their frozen identifiers and generation order.

**Registration and lifetime are part of the integration contract.** `mountFavientsPanel` restores and watches panel state after manifest registration, optionally doing the same for picker filters. Its body does not itself enforce this order, provide an idempotence guard, catch restoration errors or return a subscription cleanup handle; downstream helpers may own some of those responsibilities and must be checked before diagnosing duplicate watchers. For RFF, establish registration before restoration, validate saved placement, isolate recoverable persistence failures and give subscriptions explicit lifetime ownership. A successful application boot does not demonstrate that remembered state was restored correctly. The source header's historical boot experiments are not newly reproduced evidence.

**A cross-window handoff needs completion semantics.** `openGradientExplorer` writes optional incoming data before opening a separate tab, appends an encoded trip ID and uses `noopener`. It does not locally check whether opening succeeds, clear a preexisting incoming record when no new record is supplied, or acknowledge which recipient consumed it; those details belong to the handoff implementation. For a future RFF external editor bridge, bind payload, target, source version and return route to a request ID, handle failed launches and stale returns, and commit only to a still-valid destination. Prefer an in-process shared editor when it already meets the need; a browser tab protocol is not required for shader-source reuse.

The entry buttons use contextual operations: the favorite entrance reveals a hidden shelf but adds the current gradient when it is already visible. That is an observed behavior, not evidence that clicking always saves. Likewise, optional bridge invocation can produce no addition if installation is missing. An RFF implementation should give the invoked action a verifiable result and keep saving, editing and applying distinct state transitions. The reusable architecture supports the previously proposed material-source controls; it does not independently change rendering quality or prove a performance benefit.

## Gradient Studio panel: temporary shader previews need target-scoped ownership

Evidence: full read of `palette/components/GradientStudioPanel.tsx` (260 lines). This component delegates commit/cancel semantics to the previously reviewed studio store and close/mount integration. The following findings distinguish visible component wiring from guarantees requiring those consumers; no interactive test was performed.

**Useful RFF transfer: preview derived palettes without prematurely replacing source state.** Curves and adjustments derive a preview over the stored gradient; painting creates a dense-ramp preview only after the session changes. The component sends that temporary gradient to the fractal and restores the stored gradient when the preview ends, the target changes or the panel unmounts. For RFF, temporary base-color/environment/emission previews can follow the same separation: editable source state, temporary GPU override, then one explicit committed result. Preserve the source color-space and blend semantics when deriving the preview; a shader texture alone is not the editable source.

**Unmounting and committing are distinct events.** The header explains that switching a dock tab can unmount the panel without closing the editor. Accordingly this component's cleanup restores the underlying gradient but does not itself bake the face. The close button delegates to host chrome and advertises application of a live face. RFF needs explicit transitions for hide, cancel, apply, close and target switch, so a docking action does not accidentally commit an edit. Session data may survive hiding even when its visible preview is removed. A later return should restore the intended session state, not silently treat the last temporary GPU output as the saved palette.

**Scope preview ownership beyond a boolean.** `hadPreview` tracks whether there was a preview, while cleanup captures the old target and calls `previewGradient(target,null)`. This is a useful local cleanup pattern, but the component alone does not establish arbitration if multiple editors or asynchronous producers preview the same target. RFF should associate overrides with an owner/session and generation so old cleanup cannot clear a newer preview. Restoring should resolve the current committed source, including legitimate external edits, rather than a stale source snapshot. Any pending GPU upload or shader work must also check that its destination is still the intended layer/property.

**Fallback targets depend on registration timing.** With no target, an effect selects the first registered send target that edits a parameter. Its dependency list contains `target`, while a separate subscription updates labels from the registry. A registry change alone therefore does not rerun the fallback-selection effect. This file also shows a missing-source message for an unavailable target rather than automatically retargeting it. For an RFF adaptation, define late registration, deletion and reappearance explicitly; use a stable destination ID and avoid silently redirecting an in-progress edit to the first remaining material input. This is a source-level integration condition, not a reproduced GMT failure.

**Shared stores need explicit session boundaries.** The panel reads adjustment, sampled-curve and paint state from shared stores. It synchronizes a paint base from the source and ends a paint session when the face changes away from paint, but does not locally end paint on every unmount. That supports the hide-versus-close distinction, while requiring the store/host to own eventual session completion and target switching. RFF should not infer isolation merely because each editor has its own window. Check simultaneous source editing, external palette changes, bake/cancel and reopening against the actual session owner.

The palette picker offers unique authored stop colors or eight evenly spaced ramp samples. Those eight samples are a convenience selection, not an extraction of all salient colors; narrow emission/color features can be missed. The header's 'ACES' display is also only a label for the source's alternative output mode and does not establish a complete ACES pipeline. Keep RFF's output-transform terminology precise. Finally, memoization here is not measured latency control: source/adjustment changes can still derive a ramp synchronously. Reuse valid field/shading data, coalesce rapid previews and measure the complete interaction before claiming a responsive shader editor. These mechanics support the material-source and live-preview candidates already identified.

## Palette-variant harness: compare complete edit snapshots without rolling back the library

Evidence: complete read of `debug/test-palette-variants.mts` (410 lines). These variants are named studio-state snapshots, not automatically generated color transformations. The harness uses actual feature/store code with a synthetic window/localStorage and stand-in document providers; no test was executed during this review.

**RFF opportunity: reversible A/B material and palette alternatives.** Capture a complete editable candidate, switch candidates in one undoable operation, and keep the reusable palette library outside that snapshot. The test verifies capture of generator/image/filter slices and other registered documents while excluding the shared favorite collection. This separation is valuable for RFF: comparing two material palettes should not revert newly saved library items. Specify whether an RFF variant covers only palette authoring or also source bindings, mapping, emission, lighting and output transforms. A thumbnail alone cannot encode those shader inputs, and a partial snapshot should not be presented as a complete appearance preset.

**A single added undo entry is not a demonstrated round trip.** The restore test checks representative feature values, vector rehydration, document-provider dispatch and a stack-length increase of one. It does not invoke undo/redo and compare restored documents and shader output. The already-active restore case is tested immediately after restore, not after modifying that active candidate, so it does not establish whether selecting an edited active candidate restores its saved version or intentionally does nothing. RFF should define that distinction and verify atomic restoration across both settings and structured palette/image data, including provider failure and stale asynchronous work.

**Snapshots need stronger ownership than a best-effort clone.** The clone test explicitly accepts returning a cyclic input unchanged. That behavior avoids throwing but forfeits isolation; the serializer test accepts converting a cyclic variant list to an empty array string. These fallbacks are not appropriate evidence of lossless capture. RFF can constrain snapshots to a validated serializable schema and report capture/save failure while retaining the prior durable data. Do not replace a valid collection with an empty serialization fallback. The ordinary nested-object clone tests are useful within their supported domain, not a guarantee for arbitrary resource handles or cyclic graphs.

**Validation is staged and bounded only in some dimensions.** The shape gate rejects malformed examples and an own `__proto__` key in features, but accepts a six-number ramp as a well-formed variant. The stored-thumbnail encoder separately produces 768 bounded integers, while its decoder rejects some truncated examples. This is a layered contract, not proof that every accepted variant has a fully usable thumbnail or valid nested feature values. Validate identifiers, known field types/ranges and resource references before applying imported RFF candidates. An entry-count cap does not bound individual document size, nesting or image payloads; the in-memory storage shim also does not exercise quota, persistence failure, concurrent windows or process restart.

**The ramp is an 8-bit RGB preview.** Tests verify clamping/rounding and endpoint preservation when resampling to 256 texels, with only selected decoded values checked. That thumbnail drops higher precision and has no alpha channel. Updating a snapshot without a supplied ramp deliberately retains the old thumbnail even as live feature values change, so a preview can be stale by design. For RFF, derive or mark previews from their captured source version, preserve the actual editable/HDR data separately, and never substitute the thumbnail for an environment or emission source when reproducing a saved appearance.

The cap keeps the tail of the list rather than sorting by `createdAt`; 'newest' therefore means insertion order in these checks. Silent eviction may be acceptable for explicitly temporary comparisons but should not silently delete durable user presets. Naming, rename/duplicate/remove and persistence round trips are well represented for the supplied fixtures. What remains for an RFF implementation is an end-to-end comparison of source state, undo/redo, rendered output and failure recovery. This is a workflow improvement supporting shader experimentation, not evidence of a new rendering effect or measured performance gain.

## Dense-ramp editor tests: preserve the representation before offering approximate conversion

Evidence: complete read of `debug/test-gradient-rampmode.mts` (279 lines). This source review did not execute its assertions or browser interactions.

**RFF transfer: sampled palettes and editable stop palettes should both be valid sources.** The test guards a dense-ramp mode that displays actual texels, disables inappropriate knot editing, and offers an explicit Add Stops conversion when a fitter is available. Changing output mode keeps the dense ramp; supplying real stops changes representation and removes the stale ramp. This supports preserving high-frequency imported palettes without forcing an approximate fit. RFF can retain an original sampled source plus a separately accepted editable approximation, keeping each source's resolution, color interpretation and provenance explicit. Do not silently replace its existing higher-precision palette representation with GMT's 256-sample format.

**Editor fidelity is not shader filtering fidelity.** A period-two zebra is checked across a 1536-pixel strip as six-pixel runs and through a 256-texel bar. These assertions establish that the CPU editor displays samples instead of falling back to an empty stop list. They do not establish GPU interpolation, minification, cyclic boundaries or final output transformation. Nearest-sample display can be appropriate for inspecting individual texels while the rendered fractal still needs footprint-aware filtering. Keep these two purposes separate. The fixture carries a linear-output label, but its bar expectations are the stored color values; they are not a verification of a physically linear rendered output.

**Body equality must not become full render identity.** The helper tests deliberately regard the same ramp with a different output color-space field as the same body. That is useful for deciding whether source content changed, but insufficient for a shader cache, preview-validity key or final-image deduplication. RFF's render identity must also include relevant color interpretation, mapping, filtering, target property and output transforms. Two equal sampled arrays used as emission and scalar masks do not imply equivalent rendering.

**Representation changes must respect active editing.** A Paint takeover disables actions that rewrite its underlying stops, while Add Stops remains available through the host. With an `offerStops` callback, several otherwise unavailable actions ask for conversion rather than execute directly. The harness checks menu callbacks with a synthetic context; it does not verify that a live painting is committed/canceled correctly, that conversion preserves the intended source, or that the user can undo the entire operation. For RFF, resolve the active editing session before changing representation and keep preview, conversion and commit as explicit transitions. Offer capabilities based on the actual source rather than an empty-stop-list heuristic alone.

**The static guards are intentionally incomplete.** Source-text checks require selected JSX and imperative guards to be present. The reader scan matches a specific single-line `renderStopsToRamp/Buffer(... .stops)` shape in selected trees; it can miss aliases, destructuring, multiline calls and readers outside those trees. It also constructs a filesystem path from a URL pathname with a drive-letter fix rather than a general file-URL conversion, which can matter on paths containing encoded characters. These checks help prevent familiar regressions but do not prove every consumer is representation-aware. The reverse test compares only red/green in one assertion, although a separate double-reverse identity supplies a different check; neither replaces representative asymmetric color/alpha fixtures. Before adopting dense sources in RFF, trace every primary consumer through preview, shader upload, save/load, copy/export and undo with both representations.

## Palette ground-set harness: stable source identity across browsing and cached previews

Evidence: complete read of `debug/test-palette-groundsets.mts` (234 lines), without execution. It tests pure grouping/adapter functions and a real favorites store against an in-memory storage shim, not the GPU selection/upload path.

For RFF, a common browser for recent, saved and preset palettes can feed multiple shader properties while preserving source IDs. This harness checks that entries retain favorite IDs, assign local row numbers in input order, combine split group runs, keep presets reachable after recent selections, and reuse rendered thumbnail data after a rename. The useful distinction is stable source identity versus temporary row/atlas position: sorting or selecting a subset must not redirect a material binding. Its `All` set returns no favorite members because the caller is expected to use the separate catalog; RFF should not interpret an empty result from such a sentinel as deletion or as proof that the library is empty.

**Cache correctness needs both identity and content.** A dense ramp changed under the same ID must get new preview data; the test checks that one refreshed fixture does so, while rename-only changes reuse the old buffer. Apply this pattern to RFF palette/mask previews with the full relevant representation and algorithm version in the cache key. Display thumbnails here deliberately render in sRGB and ignore the dense source's linear-output label. That is a browsing convention, not the final material's color interpretation, so do not use thumbnail-cache identity as the shader-resource identity. The stop-entry adapter also returns the source stop array by reference in the tested case; consumers need immutability/ownership discipline if this pattern is reused.

**Grouping and filing assertions do not prove persistence transactions.** `insertMany` is checked for placement at the start of an existing group, duplicate-content skipping within that group, new-group naming and last-used group. The header says 'one write', but the storage shim does not count writes and no assertion establishes that batch property. It does not test a failed save, reload, simultaneous writers or duplicate handling across every representation. RFF should preserve provenance even when visually similar entries are deduplicated, and keep library filing separate from applying a palette to the active renderer.

The day-bin fixtures use a fixed local-noon date and subtract 24-hour intervals. They do not cover local midnight, daylight-saving transitions, clock changes or timezone changes. The size policy is checked at selected count thresholds and one larger base size; it is not a viewport-fit or interaction test. The axis helper verifies nine mappings among hue/lightness/chroma and fallback arrangements, but does not validate actual color statistics, circular hue filtering or the final selection footprint. These are useful bounded tests for a palette-selection workflow, not evidence of shader fidelity or broad UI correctness.

Before connecting an analogous RFF browser to material sources, check ID-to-resource mapping after reorder/filter, same-ID content replacement, target switching, dense versus stop palettes and preview/output color differences. Reuse thumbnails for fast browsing while generating the actual shader resource from the authoritative source. This extends the existing palette-management and source-routing recommendations without asserting a new rendering effect.

## Compile-time sessions 4–5: transfer the measurement discipline, not the fxc cost model

Evidence: full reads of `docs/history/plans-archive/compile-time-initiative-session4.md` (92 lines) and `compile-time-initiative-session5.md` (100 lines). These are chronological experiment handoffs. Their embedded execution prompts are historical source material; their timings and successful checks were not reproduced here.

The later session explicitly rejects an earlier leading hypothesis: collapsing near-identical full/lean trace functions reportedly did not reduce compilation because the tested compiler already folded identical bodies. It instead reports gains from removing genuinely live expensive evaluation sites and distinct heavy bodies. This distinction is useful for RFF: count neither shader source lines nor named function calls as a substitute for measuring the generated pipeline.
