It also explicitly records that older GMT builds read a newer scene's favorites as empty. That loss must not be adopted as a harmless RFF compatibility policy: preserve existing saved data, add guarded fields under ConfigIO, and test older-format loading. File-format recognition and permission to reuse implementations remain separate; verify provenance before adapting a distinctive codec.

Finally, the triggering problem was partly destination visibility: files imported into a saved set while the browser still showed the catalog, so the user saw no result. A RFF import should report the destination and make the imported palettes accessible, with a defined merge/replace operation and undo boundary. Preserve Unicode names in metadata rather than relying on a slugged filename, distinguish exact versus sampled imports, and decide duplicate identity within the intended destination. These improvements apply directly to 2D palette workflows and palette-driven 3D-inspired shading. No new shader-speed improvement or runtime compatibility result is claimed here.
## Bucket-render audit records: distinguish historical convergence from fixed-sample export

Evidence: full reads of `docs/history/doc-audit-state/survey/g06-bucket-render.md` and `plans/overnight-audit/results/g06-bucket-render.json`. These describe different historical revisions and scopes. The later audit explicitly excludes parts of file writing, audio encoding, presentation pacing and export UI; its pass flags do not establish whole-export correctness, nor were its tests rerun here.

**Do not combine incompatible historical designs.** The survey describes asynchronous per-bucket convergence polling and a percent threshold. The later result explicitly confirms ADR-0067's fixed-sample/no-early-out behavior. Thus the survey's convergence section is not sufficient evidence for a current adaptive stopping feature. For RFF, keep “requested samples completed” separate from “an error estimate met a threshold,” and neither should imply that an MPA/perturbation result may be computed with less precision. If adaptive shading samples are later proposed, define their estimator and validation independently of the exact fractal computation.

The survey also says a raw threshold supplied where a percent was expected would silently never converge. Under its own described comparison (divide threshold by 100, then accept a smaller measured result), the demonstrated consequence is a threshold one hundred times tighter, not a proof of impossibility: a sufficiently small or zero result could still pass. RFF controls and serialized values should declare units explicitly and test conversion boundaries. This is a documentation interpretation, not a new runtime diagnosis.

**RFF transfer: describe each output coordinate system and restore every override.** Separate the final image, a memory-sized image tile and a smaller GPU work region. Keep final-image dimensions and pixel origin available to coordinate mapping, noise, palette/image sampling and screen-space shading so tile boundaries do not change the image. Scissoring limits work, not necessarily allocation. Budget all concurrently live targets and readback buffers, and include required filter halos. Restore viewport size, scissor/region, pixel footprint and temporary export state on completion, cancellation and failure. The survey's “full output resolution written once” assertion is qualified by the later record: a single-tile path rewrites it with an equal value. A useful invariant is the correct value and ownership contract, not an inaccurate claim about write count.

**Readback must match actual resources.** The later audit records changing depth readback to derive half/full-float decoding from the allocated target's type instead of the requested quality setting. For RFF/Vulkan, derive staging layout, byte count and decoding from the actual image format and copy layout, with correct synchronization and resource lifetime. A user preference or hardware tier is not that format. Tag asynchronous results with the source view/pass/job so an old diagnostic cannot be attached to a new frame. Distinguish an unfinished fence from a failed operation; release or recover failed requests without leaving a permanent “pending” flag. The record's typecheck mutation verifies that an API constant is recognized, not that real fence failure recovery was exercised; it explicitly acknowledges this limitation.

Depth stored in alpha is a pass-specific convention. The survey notes that an alpha-export pass instead writes coverage there. A RFF field-probe design should carry explicit buffer semantics and avoid interpreting coverage, accumulated color or a missing-data sentinel as depth/distance. A cached focus snapshot also belongs to one image revision. Reading the previous ping-pong target is meaningful only through the pipeline's ownership/index convention; do not infer validity from a method name alone.

**Still and video export require parity checks across separate implementations.** These records describe a bucket runner for stills and a different accumulation/encoding path for video/image sequences. Sharing a post-process material does not by itself prove matching samples, color encoding, filter support, alpha or output aspect. RFF should compare deterministic fixtures across those actual paths. Keep depth/coverage data outside beauty tone mapping and optional glow, validate sample counts before allocation/rendering, and preserve odd-sized images where the chosen output format permits them. Historical codec alignment and bitrate multipliers are not general recommendations for RFF's encoder.

The later audit confirms per-track timestamp offset fields, but subtracting each track's first timestamp does not independently prove audio/video synchronization; intended start offsets and encoder delay must remain defined and tested. Likewise, sequential file-write chains and cleanup assertions do not prove successful writes or the absence of partial files after cancellation. Preserve an explicit export result and partial-output policy. These are concrete adoption conditions for RFF's 2D image/video workflow, not grounds to import GMT's browser worker design or to claim the cited historical guard runs as present verification.
## Reflection ADRs: distinguish lobe sampling, footprint control and heuristic recovery

Evidence: full reads of ADR-0068, ADR-0094 and ADR-0095 (`docs/adr/0068-raymarched-reflection-importance-sampling.md`, `0094-faithful-reflection-march.md`, `0095-reflection-candidate-recovery-fade.md`). Targeted checks of the already audited reflection feature files confirm a current `traceReflectionRay` call, shared `getVNDFSamplerGLSL` emission and `REFL_RECOVERY_RANGE` of 6.0. This pass does not revalidate the entire estimator or execute a rendering comparison.

**RFF transfer priority remains environment/material shading before geometry reflections.** ADR-0068 replaces an arbitrary roughness cone with a distribution related to the GGX visible-normal lobe, and adds environment contribution at a reflected hit. The transferable principle is that a rough-surface lighting filter should follow the intended material response instead of merely adding random direction noise. RFF already has material shading; a shaped environment with appropriate roughness filtering can improve its relief appearance without a 3D scene tracer. VNDF sampling becomes relevant only if RFF actually introduces stochastic lobe integration. A flat 2D palette image supplies neither reflection visibility nor a reflected surface, so a raymarcher cannot be ported meaningfully by substituting iteration values for geometry.

The ADR's updates matter. The June update shares a bounded spherical-cap sampler with PT, superseding the earlier claim that PT was byte-for-byte unaffected. The July update keeps glossy sampling during motion, superseding the body text's deterministic mirror direction during motion. Its purpose is to avoid accumulating an initial sample from a different shading model. For RFF animated materials, either keep the estimator consistent or discard incompatible preview history before accumulation. A frozen per-pixel noise pattern can reduce temporal shimmer, but is not a proof of world-space stability under navigation or of independent samples.

**Sampler and weight must be reviewed together.** ADR-0068 names bounded VNDF techniques and describes an `F * G1(L)` throughput simplification. Before adopting it, verify the actual bounded sampler's density, support, normalization and material convention against the implemented weight; a named technique and a comment do not establish that every cancellation is valid. Check original sources and licenses before code reuse and add NOTICE attribution. The document's “firefly-free,” “true glossy lobe” and “no downside” language is stronger than the evidence in this record. A luminance clamp and roughness floors deliberately change the result; they are controlled approximations, not a proof of unbiased integration. Keep such choices out of RFF's precision-sensitive Mandelbrot computation.

**Footprint-aware secondary work is useful when the geometry model exists.** ADR-0094 continues the primary distance into the reflection threshold rather than letting the threshold collapse at the reflection origin. It explicitly uses total path length instead of MB3D's projected view-depth evolution: matching the origin does not make the two formulas equivalent everywhere. For RFF's existing screen-space material/image filters, the more direct transfer is to derive sampling widths from the final pixel footprint and mapping derivatives, including export scaling. Do not import its 3D DE stepping, float floor or recovery threshold as a tolerance for perturbation or MPA. MPA is not a raymarch acceleration scheme.

**Recovery fade is a visual heuristic, not measured coverage.** ADR-0095 tracks the closest ratio `DE/finalEps` and, on an exhausted/missed trace, fades a candidate using the squared fraction between one and six thresholds. This can soften abrupt switches to the environment, but the six-footprint neighborhood and quadratic curve are chosen policy. They do not integrate the actual reflection cone, prove a geometric hit, or guarantee valid normals for every distance estimator. Calling the result “confidence” does not make it a calibrated probability. If RFF ever offers a similar optional decorative approximation, separate approximate status from valid computed fields and never let it change fractal classification, location precision or saved map values.

These records also distinguish a static step-budget artifact from stochastic noise: repeatedly accumulating the same structured miss need not remove it. A future RFF validation should separate temporal noise, systematic shading bias and incorrect geometry/field data, using contact, silhouette, glossy and moving-view cases where relevant. The ADRs' compile-path isolation is a useful dependency principle, but actual emitted shaders and timings are required to prove no cost in an unrelated variant. No new convergence factor, image-quality measurement or RFF implementation is claimed by this review.
## PT reflection plan: environment importance sampling needs a consistent measure

Evidence: full read of `docs/history/plans-archive/path-trace-reflections.md` (359 lines). This is an early feature plan with a shipped-deviations header and explicitly pending visual verification. Its 4,000-to-256/512 sample goal, approximate 30% variance reduction, 10 ms table build and compile-time estimates are historical targets/claims, not measurements established in this pass or predictions for RFF.

The central mechanism is useful to understand even though full PT is not a direct RFF feature recommendation: construct a marginal distribution over environment rows and conditional distributions over columns, preferentially select bright directions, and combine these samples with material-lobe samples using densities in the same directional measure. This is different from using a blurred environment lookup for a deterministic roughness response. RFF can gain controllable environment appearance and filtering without implementing MIS. Importance sampling becomes relevant only if an actual stochastic illumination integral is added.

**The draft formulas are not a copy-ready specification.** Its CPU algorithm first calls the per-texel luminance weighted by sine, then later multiplies `L_ij` by sine again when describing the integral. Its GPU PDF expression additionally mixes a `W * H` factor, sine and an integral already containing angular cell sizes. Before adopting anything, define raw luminance, discrete cell mass, normalized cell probability and solid-angle density separately. For a latitude-longitude grid with cell probability `p_ij`, a uniform-solid-angle sample within that cell uses `p_ij / deltaOmega_ij`; uniform theta/phi sampling instead requires the corresponding sine Jacobian at the sampled direction. These are different within-cell distributions. Sampling, PDF evaluation and MIS must use the same one. Handle zero-energy rows/maps and poles explicitly, and do not infer continuous support from merely returning a texel-center direction.

The draft also calls its combination a balance heuristic while showing `misPower2`, and describes diffuse/VNDF samples in a section introduced as uniform-sphere sampling. Those are unresolved differences in this plan's prose, not proof that current GMT code has the same inconsistencies. Consult the actual sampler and contribution code together. A fixed 256-by-128 CDF cannot universally preserve arbitrarily small bright features; downsampling policy and support matter. Higher-precision CDF arithmetic cannot recover HDR values already clipped or made nonfinite in an earlier image conversion.

**Separate transform updates from distribution updates.** For a rigid environment rotation, a table in environment coordinates can be reused if sampling and PDF lookup use mutually consistent forward/inverse transforms. A brightness-pattern edit or source replacement is different and must update the table or a valid fallback atomically with the texture. A rotation inverse equals its transpose only for an orthonormal rotation, not an arbitrary UV transform. RFF's proposed decorative warps and independent U/V mappings must not inherit this shortcut without checking their Jacobians. The plan's shipped header also supersedes its body: CDF construction runs on every environment load there, rather than being skipped when its gate is off.

**Sequence indexing is part of the estimator contract.** The proposed `accumulation * 8 + bounce` packs at most eight bounce indices without overlap, but non-overlap alone does not prove desirable low-discrepancy coverage for the subsequence seen at one fixed bounce. A per-pixel shift is not the same operation as Owen scrambling. If RFF adopts stochastic shading, define dimensions, sample index, pixel/global-tile identity and reset behavior, and assess temporal convergence and spatial artifacts separately. A sequence name is not a blanket quality guarantee.

Finally, the shipped migration explicitly honors an already present new mode, including Off, while the body sketch would overwrite it whenever the legacy boolean is true. For RFF's append-only configuration evolution, give explicit new settings precedence and perform legacy interpretation once at the load boundary. The historical numeric modes and separate-feature skeleton are not a reason to renumber existing RFF options. These findings refine adoption conditions; they do not recommend copying this old plan as code or importing a general PT engine into the 2D renderer.
## Lighting-import research: preserve authored meaning rather than translating labels

Evidence: full read of `plans/mb3d/research/lighting-import-spec.md` (439 lines). It is explicitly a draft research/mapping proposal. Its VERIFIED labels refer to the author's source/byte checks, not checks independently reproduced in this pass. Its promised fixes and effort estimates are not evidence that a lighting importer has shipped or that RFF supports those formats.

**Direct RFF opportunity: configurable colored lighting and a two-color ambient environment.** The source model described here combines distinct key/fill lights, normal-dependent top/bottom ambient color, separate diffuse/specular controls and palette-driven object color. RFF can use such authored lighting ideas in its existing relief/material presentation without importing the source program's 3D geometry. A two-color or editable-gradient environment is particularly transferable: evaluate it in a declared normal/environment frame and combine it with the existing material response. A flat 2D palette image has no physical normal by default; any normal/height interpretation must be explicit. Depth fog requires an actual defined depth field, not an iteration count relabeled as distance.

**An import should report exact, approximate and unavailable semantics.** The draft usefully separates byte decoding from target-model mapping, but its “clean” roughness mapping is not physically exact. It describes the source using `RoughnessFactor/255²` internally, then proposes division by 255 plus clamping for the target, alongside a separate shininess-to-roughness heuristic. Those operations need an explicit precedence and calibration policy. Per-light Phong exponents cannot generally be represented by one GGX material roughness without loss. A single empirical intensity multiplier also cannot be assumed valid for both directional and positional lights when the source uses different scaling and falloff conventions. RFF should preserve the original parameters as provenance where practical and identify what the chosen approximation changes.

**Resolve internal contradictions before treating byte layouts as authoritative.** The draft places a 12-element Int32 `TBpos` array at offset 440, which would put indices 9 and 10 at 476 and 480, but also assigns `TBoptions` to offset 476. This may reflect an overlay, a wrong layout or imprecise prose; the document alone does not settle it. Likewise, `2 << (LFunction & 7)` evaluates to 2 through 256 for indices zero through seven, not the stated 4 through 256 unless another restriction excludes zero. Check the original packed records, versions and actual bytes before implementing a parser. Validate file lengths, endianness, finite decoded values and mode-dependent interpretations; do not copy offsets merely because the table says VERIFIED.

**Missing data and authored darkness are different states.** The suggested `lights: []` fallback inherits default lights for a headerless formula, but the same empty list could result from an authored scene with every light disabled. A RFF importer needs to distinguish absent lighting information from a valid empty/disabled rig. Otherwise a scene intended to be dark acquires a default key/fill setup. Similarly, missing external palette or environment images should produce an explicit missing-asset result or a labeled fallback, rather than a claim of matching the original scene. The draft itself first describes in-header palettes, then cautions that external maps may provide the real ramp, and finally leaves that relationship open.

Direction and position mappings must state whether vectors point toward or away from the light, their handedness, angle units and camera-relative/world-relative frame. Apply the scene-origin transformation once and preserve precision before narrowing to shader-local offsets. The draft's statements about world coordinates versus mid-relative positions need to be resolved at that boundary, not stacked as two independent translations. For RFF, do not subtract two huge deep-zoom coordinates after converting both to an insufficient-precision type. Keep color-byte decoding separate from shader linearization so the same transfer function is not applied twice.

Finally, the draft attributes an over-bright imported scene entirely to missing lighting/fog and says importing those values will fix it. Those are hypotheses to validate against controlled renders, not a basis to dismiss geometry, exposure or color-space mismatches in another renderer. Its proposed byte fixtures and matched-camera references are useful, but tests that explicitly do not exercise lighting cannot prove the lighting conversion. For RFF, compare direction, intensity, material response and palette mapping separately before judging the composite image. The most practical adoption remains richer environment/light authoring with clear units and preserved existing defaults; MB3D binary compatibility and full scene fidelity would be separate substantial features.
## Consolidated compile policy: useful experiments, with platform and equivalence limits

Evidence: complete three-part read of `docs/policy/shader-compile-optimization.md` (1,221 lines). The document combines foundation hypotheses, several later experiment logs and superseding updates. Its embedded project rules are historical material, not constraints on this RFF investigation. Referenced web research was not independently revalidated, and no timing experiment was rerun here.

**Most transferable optimization method: localize repeated expensive computations in the active shader.** The recorded wins concentrate on eliminating live, transitively inlined heavy bodies, rather than shortening source text or merely moving repeated code into a helper. Examples include a single environment image-sample site instead of duplicate branches, preserving an already computed candidate result instead of recomputing it, and removing runtime branches that keep two different normal-estimation bodies live. For RFF, inspect emitted shaders and actual compiler output where available, then investigate repeated material-field evaluation, image filtering and environment sampling. Reuse a value only when position, uniforms, source revision and all relevant inputs are unchanged. Do not change the operation order or precision of perturbation/MPA math to imitate a 3D DE optimization.

**Feature parity is weaker than numerical equivalence.** The document describes fixes with unchanged feature switches, but several alter the calculation: a large finite soft-shadow coefficient approximates hard shadows; indirect normal estimation changes from forward differences to tetrahedral sampling; and one fog evaluation is shared across reflection directions under an explicitly documented approximation. Other changes remove user controls or the entire Direct multi-bounce feature. Keep these categories separate from exact reuse. RFF should prioritize redundant-work elimination and retain existing image behavior; any optional approximation needs a stated error/appearance policy and cannot compromise the precision requirement.

The historical reflection outer-loop regression is a valuable compiler-specific example: a one-trip wrapper around a heavy body reportedly raised cold compilation from about eight seconds to forty-two, while eliminating the wrapper restored the lower cost. The later pass reduced the single-bounce case further, and Direct multi-bounce was subsequently removed. This is evidence to inspect generated structure when a small source change has a large compile effect, not a rule that nested or constant-bounded loops are inherently bad in RFF's Vulkan toolchain. The same document records other loop-bound rewrites with no measurable win and a volumetric nested loop without that pathology.

**Measure disabled-path cost rather than assuming it is zero.** The recorded volumetric case runs substantially slower even when compiled but disabled at runtime. The document attributes this to register pressure; confirming that mechanism in RFF would require relevant compiler/profiling evidence, not just the same timing pattern. The useful adoption principle is to measure whether expensive optional material features affect the baseline when switched off. Keep continuous control changes responsive, but consider separate structural variants for genuinely costly optional subsystems if RFF measurements justify them. Bound caching and variant counts; do not inherit the document's blanket ban on variant caching, which belonged to a different task scope.

**Timing claims require stronger qualification than several conclusions here provide.** A paired confidence interval spanning roughly -576 to +520 ms supports “no resolved effect in this experiment,” not proof of zero cost. Subtracting a baseline reduces some shared variation but does not guarantee cancellation of drift. A feature superset can compile faster because optimizers are non-monotonic; that ordering alone does not prove a contaminated run. The table's sum of marginals includes alternative environment modes, so comparing that sum with a maximal configuration is not sufficient proof of sub-additivity: mutually exclusive modes are not independently additive features. Use compatible configurations, repeated independent cold trials, raw data and predeclared noise/rejection rules.

The policy correctly distinguishes adaptive sample throughput from a normalized GPU-time benchmark and records in-process cache hits even with a disk cache disabled. For RFF, report source-generation time, pipeline creation, first usable frame and steady rendering separately. Identify the actual compiled variant and device/driver/cache state. A CPU timer labelled `gpu` is not GPU execution time, and a short post-swap CPU render call does not establish that all device-side work has completed. Browser-specific explanations of `compileAsync`, first-draw realization and cache behavior must not be assumed to describe Vulkan.

**Do not treat successful compilation as a complete correctness gate.** The policy calls a WebGL compile check the only fully honest automated gate, while also using image-error thresholds. Compilation can detect shader/interface failures but cannot establish correct palette interpretation, accumulation validity, geometry or deep-zoom precision. RFF needs checks appropriate to each change: resource/interface validation, deterministic output comparisons and precision-sensitive numeric checks where computation is touched. The historical image thresholds (MAE 0.5 and maximum channel error 8) are not authorization to lose fractal detail. A single canonical scene also cannot establish behavior across all feature/resource combinations.

Finally, the unread-uniform experiment measures a particular WebGL shader/upload path with unchanged active uniforms. It does not imply free enlargement of Vulkan descriptor layouts, buffer ranges or push constants. Keep C++/GLSL layouts, device limits and resource ownership explicit. The strongest RFF recommendations from this long record are targeted removal of repeated heavy shading work, measured baseline isolation for optional effects, deterministic variant identity and honest separation of exact optimizations from appearance changes. The historical claim that all remaining structural opportunities are exhausted applies only to the investigated versions and experiments, not to RFF or every future GMT shader.
## Liquify and nucleus browser smokes: image change is not image correctness

Evidence: full reads of `debug/smoke-gx-liquify-render.mts` and `debug/smoke-gx-nucleus-render.mts`. Neither browser script was executed. Their recorded historical run counts and renderer descriptions are not new device or timing measurements.

**RFF transfer: optional decorative deformation can be validated independently of fractal computation.** The Liquify smoke opens a gradient surface, applies push and grab strokes and checks sampled image changes. This supports a useful authoring idea for a separate 2D decorative UV/image layer, if desired; it is not a reason to deform the mathematical coordinates used for Mandelbrot computation or silently alter saved maps. Keep such a warp explicit, reversible and separate from the location/precision contract. Validate identity when disabled, mapping/filter behavior near folded or stretched regions and preview/export consistency before adoption.

The smoke meaningfully checks a nonempty/nonuniform initial image and changes after two pointer drags, while collecting page and console errors. It does not compare the deformation to a geometric oracle or verify the dither algorithm merely because that code is exercised. The physics section only checks that a colorful frame exists after enabling physics: the previous valid frame can satisfy that condition, so it does not prove continued motion. The comment announcing a reset step has no corresponding reset interaction/assertion. Do not report reset or physical simulation correctness as covered by this script.

Its polling is better targeted than a single fixed wait, but `settledSig` returns the latest signature on timeout without a success flag. Two matching signatures can also mean the sampled pixels did not change, rather than that all rendering is complete. A future RFF guard should expose the relevant frame/job revision and explicit completion condition. The historical HMR duplicate-store diagnosis is useful browser-test context, but a missing overlay alone does not uniquely prove that cause. Prefer a test interface belonging to the live application instance and record setup failure separately from rendering failure.

**The nucleus smoke's strongest claim exceeds its image metric.** It compares one minibrot view with periodic-reference mode on and off, checks positive versus zero period, and requires the reported nonperiodic orbit to be at least three times longer. Its image comparison is only the fraction occupied by the single largest quantized RGB bin in the central 40%-by-40% region. It neither compares the identity of that color bin nor the full histogram nor pixel positions. Two differently colored flat images both have dominant fraction one and pass the image comparison. Rearranged geometry with the same dominant fraction can pass too. The 0.18 tolerance further allows substantial differences in that statistic; it cannot establish “the same image” or precision-correct deep zoom.

The fixed wait after rebuilding does not certify that the captured canvas contains the requested completed view or matching accumulation state. Only one view is present despite the header's plural wording, and both configurations enable the same `useLA` option, so the fallback is not an independent arbitrary-precision oracle. Orbit length reduction is an observed statistic the script would check, not proof of total speedup, memory reduction or correctness. A future RFF comparison should identify the completed frame and compare spatially aligned results, including relevant raw iteration/distance/validity fields against a suitable high-precision reference and a diverse boundary/deep-zoom set.

RFF already has periodic-structure-based MPA and reference compression. GMT's periodic reference and LA flags must not be relabeled as RFF's MPA, or used to describe MPA as BLA. The transferable lesson from this test is to measure reference/storage savings while independently proving output correctness. The existing script is a coarse smoke, not evidence authorizing any precision trade in RFF.

## Render-pipeline audit history and temporal guards: preserve useful work without preserving invalid samples

Sources fully read: `docs/history/doc-audit-state/survey/e05-render-pipeline.md`, `plans/overnight-audit/results/e05-render-pipeline.json`, `debug/smoke-tsaa.mts`, and `debug/test-bucket-convergence.mts`. Relevant current sections of the already-reviewed `engine/RenderPipeline.ts` were rechecked. Historical test passes and hardware observations belong to the source authors; no test, browser run or GPU measurement was performed in this review.

**RFF transfer: separate the sampling budget, the displayed fallback image and the validity of accumulated samples.** The historical audit proposes fixing cap changes that discarded completed work. Current `setSampleCap()` simply assigns the cap, so that historical finding must not be reported as a current GMT defect. Reducing a sampling budget can stop further work while retaining the existing result; increasing it can resume only if the sampling domain and scene remain compatible. For RFF, this is useful if progressive shader sampling is introduced or extended, but does not authorize changing the mathematical iteration limit without recomputation. An iteration limit and a display-sampling budget have different correctness contracts.

Current `resize()` can copy the old displayed image into both newly allocated targets before releasing the old pair when a renderer is supplied. This suggests a smoother RFF preview during resizing. Such copied pixels must be treated as temporary presentation content until replaced by valid samples for the new footprint; a scaled old image is not a new accurately sampled Mandelbrot map. Track validity/revision and completed regions separately from the displayed fallback. This recommendation concerns application-controlled canvas transitions and does not claim to solve the documented native Win32 popup show-before-paint interval.

The temporal blend uses reciprocal sample count for ordinary full-frame rendering, while tiled rendering supplies a blend override and lets its scheduler own sample counts. A partial-band draw must not increment a global count as if every pixel received a sample. This transfers directly to both 2D image-layer antialiasing and relief/material sampling: preserve per-region sample accounting, coherent history selection and explicit invalidation when mappings, lights or relevant fields change. The survey itself contains inconsistent prose about which ping-pong target is previous; current code selects the target opposite the next-write index. Follow the actual swap and consumers rather than the field name or the inconsistent survey sentence.

**Warm-up compatibility is useful, but the historical performance explanation was corrected.** The early survey attributes compile-target matching to Three.js program hashes. The later audit explicitly retracts that mechanism for its examined Three.js version, and current `getCompileTarget()` rebuilds when texture types differ. It also documents deferred disposal to avoid freeing a target held across an asynchronous compile. For RFF/Vulkan, maintain the actual pipeline/rendering-format/layout compatibility and resource-lifetime contracts; do not import the retracted hash explanation or claim a measured compilation speedup. A matching tiny warm-up target does not by itself establish that every production pipeline variant has been prepared.

**Convergence is a diagnostic, not a correctness oracle.** A difference between successive running averages decreases partly because each new sample has weight approximately 1/n. A small frame-to-frame change is therefore not proof of a small error relative to the true image. Subsampling a diagnostic target can also miss localized defects. Preserve fixed, explicit quality budgets for reproducible exports unless a stronger error estimator is independently validated. This matters for fine 2D palette boundaries as well as noisy 3D-style highlights. The current render gate distinguishes viewport budgets from bucket rendering and tiled scheduling; the old survey's per-bucket convergence description is historical.

The bucket-convergence test executes real pipeline methods against a mock renderer and is a targeted state-transition guard: reset clears pending state, a subsequent measurement updates the lower region bound, and a supplied readback delta is returned. However, the mock draw is empty and readback injects a chosen scalar irrespective of target contents. It does not establish that GPU pixels came from the new region, test upper-bound mapping, reproduce bucket seams or exercise timeout/failure behavior. Its fake fence always signals; the old bucket-to-bucket narrative does not mean today's bucket runner uses convergence. Retain this style of focused invalidation test in RFF, supplemented by image/field checks when introducing asynchronous diagnostics. A GPU failure must not silently turn an old diagnostic into a fresh valid measurement.

The current TSAA smoke is stronger than the older audit describes: it checks console/page errors, a sized canvas, initial accumulation enabled, a finite sample cap above one, and the store setter's off transition. Nevertheless, it only captures screenshots for manual comparison and does not assert their contents, sample accumulation, subpixel reconstruction or blue-noise allocation. Its own header records earlier mutations that disabled blending or noise while the smoke still passed; those are historical observations, not mutations repeated here. For RFF, any temporal-AA adoption needs explicit scene/frame readiness and spatial output checks under subpixel motion, thin features, history reset and preview/export paths. A successful settings round-trip is not evidence that a shader implemented the setting. The script also writes tracked PNGs, so executing it would modify evidence assets; no such execution was needed for this source audit.

## Archived renderer architecture and diagnostic scripts: make shader evidence reproducible

Fully read: `docs/history/audit-2026-05-20/archive/engine-gmt/renderer.md` (421 lines), `debug/opus-dumpshader.mts` and `debug/probe-scene-de-render.mts`. The first read of the long document was truncated; it was subsequently reread in three complete contiguous chunks. Current `engine-gmt/engine/ShaderFactory.ts`, already covered in the inventory, was reread to verify the dump script's API assumptions. No scripts were executed.

**RFF transfer: publish a coherent shader configuration at a frame boundary.** The archived renderer describes keeping an old material visible while compiling its replacement, and deferring modular parameter-slot writes until the replacement is installed. That mechanism is relevant when adding configurable material masks, environment lighting or separate U/V routing to RFF: pair each pipeline with its exact descriptor/push-constant layout and parameter revision. Do not write a newly packed parameter array into the old shader's bindings while waiting for the new pipeline. Keep old GPU resources alive until in-flight work completes, and mark any simplified preview as provisional. GMT's browser scheduling strategies and dated latency measurements do not demonstrate a Vulkan speedup.

The archive also distinguishes canonical frame synchronization, display/export materials, histogram passes and texture transfer. For RFF, new shader controls need an explicit dependency map identifying which passes consume them and which changes invalidate computation, material shading, display-only post-processing or diagnostics. A uniform setter silently skipping absent keys cannot establish preview/export parity. Sharing a parameter object in JavaScript has no direct equivalence to synchronizing host writes and Vulkan GPU reads. A 2D palette histogram can deliberately analyze the scalar/color field independently of expensive lighting, provided the interface states what distribution it represents; it must not be advertised as the final illuminated image histogram.

**Keep geometric precision and display scheduling separate.** The archive's camera-offset guard uses an absolute 0.001 convergence threshold and describes split-float world coordinates. Those are not suitable replacements for RFF's high-precision location, reference orbit or perturbation contracts. Transfer the idea of associating overlays, picks and worker replies with the frame that produced them, using explicit revisions rather than a borrowed world-space tolerance. A failed or cancelled asynchronous request also needs a distinct terminal result, not an empty success that export or picking code could mistake for valid content. These principles apply equally to 2D cursor sampling and relief-light editing.

**A concrete limit in the source-dump evidence:** `opus-dumpshader.mts` constructs a `ShaderFactory` instance and looks for instance methods named `generateShader` or `build`. The current class instead exposes static `generateFragmentShader`, `generatePhysicsShader`, `generateHistogramShader` and `generateMeshSDFLibrary`. With neither tested instance method present, this script's fallback serializes the keys of an empty object and would attempt to write `[]` as a `.frag` file. Exceptions during generation are also converted into text rather than a failing diagnostic result. Its final 'wrote' message therefore cannot establish shader generation, compilation or correctness. The destination is a hard-coded external `h:/tmp` path and can fail separately; no successful write is asserted here.

For RFF's shader-adoption work, a useful diagnostic package would retain the exact shader variant/source or SPIR-V identity, relevant configuration, compiler outcome and renderer/device information alongside reference images. Treat missing APIs, empty output and compiler errors as explicit failures. Keep requested passes distinct: GMT's mesh generator intentionally returns a library without a main entry point, unlike its fragment shader. A generic nonempty-text check would not establish that the intended pass was generated. This is a proposed investigation aid, not a claim that RFF currently lacks all such facilities.

`probe-scene-de-render.mts` is a capture/logging helper for six substring-selected MB3D sample scenes. It keeps scene-derived presets and normalizes the longest image edge to 420 pixels, which can help visually review imports at a consistent viewing size. However, missing scene matches are silently skipped, page errors are ignored, evaluation exceptions are printed rather than accumulated into a failing result, and the script asserts neither nonblack fraction nor channel variation. It saves a returned image if present but does not require one or compare it with a source render. Nonblack fraction and summed channel sigma cannot prove correct geometry, distance estimation, lighting or color conversion. Reported elapsed time includes browser evaluation and harness work, so it is not isolated GPU time.

A corresponding RFF comparison should require every named case to execute, identify the completed frame/configuration and preserve spatial reference images or relevant raw fields. Include crisp 2D boundaries and thin palette features as well as relief/material examples; a low-resolution thumbnail can hide the very filtering and precision errors being investigated. The archive and these scripts supply architecture and diagnostic ideas, not measured improvements or proof of feature equivalence. Historical 'known issues' in the archive remain dated claims unless separately confirmed against current implementations.

## Bucket/export archive and followups: whole-image semantics across smaller work units

Fully read: `docs/history/audit-2026-05-20/archive/engine-gmt/bucket-render.md` and followups `q-112.md`, `q-113.md`, `q-114.md` under `docs/history/doc-audit-state/survey/_followups/`. Current histogram implementation was reread, and current bucket compositor allocation/scissor sections were rechecked. These are documentation/source observations, not export or memory benchmarks.

**RFF transfer: define output coordinates before dividing work.** The archive separates internal GPU buckets from separately saved image tiles, with full-output resolution/aspect remaining fixed while tile origins change. The corresponding 2D contract is especially useful for independent U/V maps, screen-anchored patterns, dither and procedural noise: changing bucket size or traversal order must not change the intended image. Use global output-pixel coordinates and a deliberate sample-index policy. Preserve neighboring data for filters and derivative-based footprints with overlap/halos or an equivalent cross-tile strategy; integer scissor boundaries alone prevent neither filtering seams nor independently normalized palette seams. Validate tiled and untiled output for the same settings, including odd dimensions and edge tiles.

**A smaller draw rectangle is not automatically a smaller memory allocation.** Although the archive describes GPU buckets as a VRAM safety mechanism, the current bucket compositor allocates a Float32 RGBA target at its supplied image resolution and uses scissor for the per-bucket copy. Its color attachment alone has a nominal 16 bytes per pixel, excluding accumulation, post-processing, staging and implementation overhead. Scissor reduces the affected rectangle; it does not reduce that allocation. An RFF out-of-core export design should budget the complete concurrently live resource set and bound actual tile allocations. Do not derive a maximum image size or claim VRAM savings from a bucket-size control without tracing allocation dimensions and lifetimes.

**Preview resemblance and full-resolution post-processing are different quality goals.** The historical viewport-resolution bloom path aims to retain the preview's appearance during upscaled export. It does not prove that fine bright features discovered only in the high-resolution render contribute correctly. The same distinction applies beyond bloom to roughness filtering, local contrast, image-map filtering and any neighborhood operation proposed for RFF. Specify whether a control's radius is measured in output pixels, normalized image units or preview pixels, and apply that choice consistently. Preserve linear/HDR data until the appropriate final display transform; normal/depth/coverage outputs require their own semantic handling rather than beauty-pass tone mapping.

The archive's old convergence-based bucket termination has been superseded by the fixed-sample design documented elsewhere in this review. Its claim that a fractional threshold divided by 100 would 'never converge' is also too strong: this produces a stricter threshold, and an exactly zero delta can still satisfy a positive threshold. These historical assertions do not justify adaptive early-out in RFF's precision-sensitive computation. Likewise, separate still/video exporters sharing a material name do not establish identical sampling, scaling or output encoding.

**Depth and validity should be distinct concepts.** Followup q-112 documents a historical mismatch between automatic depth probing and focus picking. A shared cutoff can make those consumers consistent, but any finite world-distance threshold can also reject a valid distant surface if the supported scene scale expands. For RFF's possible relief/depth tools, explicitly represent valid sample, background/miss and unavailable/stale result, and define whether depth is linear or transformed. Do not borrow GMT's 50-unit convention for Mandelbrot distance fields. Preserve the frame revision when caching an entire picking buffer, and avoid interpreting coverage alpha as depth. A single shared constant is useful only when the underlying meaning and supported range are correct.

**Do not infer a histogram race merely from shared resources.** The archive warns about two side-by-side histograms; followup q-113 correctly narrows that claim. Current `handleHistogramReadback()` has no asynchronous yield: it selects the material, renders, reads back synchronously, restores the target and transfers a fresh buffer copy. Ordinary sequential worker-message dispatch does not interleave those operations simply because two UI consumers requested data. The request/response Promise is not itself a global single-flight lock; the synchronous handler is the relevant serialization mechanism. RFF need not duplicate every histogram resource as a speculative fix. If asynchronous readback is introduced to avoid a stall, then give each in-flight request an identified slot, resource lifetime and completion state. The current 128-by-128 sampled luminance pass is a distribution aid, not an exhaustive image histogram; rare thin features and extrema can be missed.

**Do not copy content-specific encoder compensation as a shader-quality improvement.** Followup q-114 distinguishes Mbps-to-bps conversion from a historical 2.5 multiplier intended to counter encoder undershoot on smooth GMT content. It supplies no evidence that the same factor improves RFF output, especially dense moving fractal detail. Keep nominal bitrate, actual encoder configuration and measured output quality distinct. A capability probe at a different bitrate than the final request is not proof that the final configuration is accepted; validate the actual configuration and report failure clearly. The archived browser cap and timing claims are historical observations, not current cross-platform guarantees. These export considerations support preserving shader detail in deliverables without changing RFF's fractal precision or adopting unverified performance constants.

## Uniform contribution policy and headroom probe: extend controls without assuming spare capacity is free

Fully read: `docs/policy/uniform-plugin-contract.md` and `debug/probe-uniform-headroom.mts`. The initially combined output was truncated; the policy was reread in two complete chunks and the script separately. The policy contains dated source verification by its authors; those statements are not new runtime verification in this audit. The probe was not executed.

**RFF transfer: give each proposed control a complete data contract.** GMT's policy distinguishes schema declarations, feature-owned arrays/samplers, ordinary parameter bindings and CPU-derived writes. This is useful for new environment rotation, independent UV fields and material masks: identify the authored value, its saved representation, derived GPU value, binding/type/length, consuming passes and invalidation rule. An uploaded value alone does not make a feature animatable, undoable or persistent. For RFF, preserve append-only ConfigIO ordering and frozen palette recipe IDs/RNG behavior; do not serialize an internal GPU layout as a new file-format contract merely because a schema can generate it.

A parameter-linked declaration can reduce duplicated plumbing, but GMT's automatic UI/undo/animation behavior comes from additional consumers, not from a GLSL declaration itself. The policy's fourth path writes values; it does not independently declare the GLSL slot. Similarly, `backingOnly` creates a host-side value while intentionally omitting the normal declaration, requiring a feature to supply the shader declaration when needed. RFF's corresponding acceptance check is end-to-end agreement among C++ data, descriptor sets, buffer offsets/strides or push constants, shader declarations and shader variants. Duplicate-name rejection catches one class of integration mistake; it does not prove compatible binary layout or valid textures.

**Precompute shared shader inputs only with explicit equivalence and dependencies.** GMT describes computing environment rotation matrices and fog-color linearization on the CPU once per frame instead of repeatedly in fragments. The transferable opportunity is to cache uniform transformations used by many pixels: environment/image rotations, authored color conversion and light packing. Compute on the relevant input change where practical, include animation and export updates, and verify orientation, units and color-space conventions. This is not permission to reduce Mandelbrot arithmetic precision or replace perturbation/reference-orbit operations. CPU and GPU formulas, especially angle reduction and transcendental evaluation, need equivalence appropriate to the visual control rather than an assumption of bitwise identity.

Default values also need ownership. The policy suggests an array filled with one mutable vector; its described `createUniforms()` then clones each element, breaking that alias for that factory's consumers. Copying the initializer alone into another system would leave every element referring to the same vector. Initialize independent light/parameter records or verify the clone boundary. A null sampler default is likewise a host convention, not proof of a valid Vulkan sampled-image binding; use valid resources and defined disabled-feature behavior consistent with the actual pipeline.

**The headroom experiment measures a narrow case.** It adds 24 float plus 6 vec4 declarations, or 96 float plus 24 vec4 declarations, to one saved fragment shader, then compiles/links with a synthetic fullscreen vertex shader. None of the added uniforms is read. That can investigate front-end/link overhead for dead declarations, but not the register, bandwidth, upload or branch costs of controls that are actually used. It does not measure rendering, first-draw realization, image equivalence or frame rate. Reported active-uniform counts are recorded rather than asserted equal, and only the final round's count is retained. No numerical benchmark result was obtained in this review.

The warm-up and rotated variant order help reduce some order effects, but the script does not verify its stated hardware/backend assumption: headed Chrome and a high-performance preference do not by themselves establish ANGLE/D3D11 or exclude software rendering. It logs the renderer string without rejecting an unexpected one. Comment suffixes differ within the run, but repeat across runs, and the script does not demonstrate that all compiler/driver cache layers are cold. Link-status synchronization is a meaningful validation point, yet does not prove that all production driver work that could occur on first use is included. Recompiling the vertex shader also contributes to the measured interval.

The probe depends on an external saved shader snapshot and does not verify that it matches current production generation. Its insertion helper assumes a newline followed by `uniform`; when absent, index -1 causes injection at the beginning, potentially preceding a required version directive. Round counts are not validated as positive, and the median helper uses the upper middle sample for even counts. These limits matter when using the script as evidence, not as reasons to spend the RFF improvement effort repairing this GMT scratch tool.

For RFF, a bounded, stable parameter layout may reduce pipeline churn during ordinary editing, but measure the actual used shader paths and device limits before reserving large banks. Distinguish unused source declarations from allocated descriptor/buffer capacity, and distinguish ordinary parameter edits from topology/layout changes. Compare cold preparation, warm reuse, first display and steady rendering separately while keeping the rendered result and fractal precision fixed. This applies to flat 2D palette/image controls just as much as 3D-style lighting, without importing an unsupported claim that extra Vulkan shader parameters are cost-free.

## Vector requirements, axis-animation smoke and rotation registry: preserve semantic types across editing

Fully read: `docs/history/archive/12_Vector_Uniform_Requirements.md`, `debug/smoke-anim-vec2.mts`, and `engine-gmt/store/rotationGizmoStore.ts`. Source review only; no browser smoke or visual interaction was executed.

**RFF transfer: expose meaningful grouped controls without conflating their interpolation rules.** GMT's older requirements motivate vectors for translation, folding and color rather than spending three unrelated scalar slots. For RFF, paired 2D UV scale/offset and grouped light/environment orientation are useful applications. Preserve stable component identity across editing, saved settings and animation, including updates to one component that retain all other components. A vec3 can represent a direction, Euler angles, translation or color; the storage shape alone does not define correct interpolation. Direction normalization, angle wrap/order/units and the chosen color interpolation space need separate contracts. Adding a grouped control must not silently change existing scalar animation or palette semantics.

The historical document's capacity claims are inconsistent: its introductory 18-value statement conflicts with its listed six scalars, three vec2 and three vec3, which total 21 scalar components; the proposed slot layout later omits two of the listed vec2 entries. The header says implemented while phase/success checkboxes remain unchecked, and the history date differs from the implementation year. Treat it as design history, not proof of current capacity, full integration or performance. In particular, the claim that vector uniforms are more efficient than scalars is not supported by a benchmark here. RFF must account for the actual shader layout/alignment and device behavior, not equate fewer symbolic parameters with fewer bytes or faster execution.

**The vec2 smoke checks routing, but not full animation correctness.** It uses the fluid-toy application, creates an underscore-suffixed `julia.juliaC_x` track, seeks to zero, plays briefly, and checks that x changed, stayed in the endpoint range and left y unchanged. This is a useful regression scenario for component-path binding. However, `currentFrame` is only logged; there is no assertion that playback advanced. The initial seek could set a new x and satisfy the checks even if subsequent playback stalls. The smoke does not check a value at a known frame, the y-writing route, other vector sizes, serialization, undo or the rendered shader result. Its range checks also do not explicitly reject NaN: comparisons against NaN are false, and inequality with the baseline is true. A corresponding RFF test should require finite components and check deterministic frames plus preservation of untouched components, then verify the relevant rendered mapping or light orientation when integrating a shader feature.

**The rotation-gizmo registry offers a useful state boundary.** It stores open controls by parameter route, carrying a rotation descriptor and viewport-local position, independently of authored feature state. RFF could use this separation for temporary direction/rotation tools without adding overlay positions to saved fractal settings. The actual edited orientation belongs in the normal authored/undo path; which editing tool is open is session state. The registry alone does not prove that serialization elsewhere excludes it or that gizmo edits correctly reach shaders.

The implementation replaces an entry with the same supplied key and preserves its prior position unless a new position is supplied. It does not validate that the key matches `feature.paramId`, so uniqueness depends on caller consistency. Its default position is derived from the current entry count, not occupied positions: after closing a middle entry, a new entry can land on an existing entry's original position. This qualifies the comment that fresh controls never stack exactly; no actual overlap was measured. For an RFF adaptation, use stable parameter identifiers, resolve their continued existence after formula/scene changes, and choose available viewport positions if simultaneous controls are supported. The store itself neither clamps positions nor removes stale routes automatically. These are integration requirements for the proposed tool, not grounds to claim a present RFF defect.

## Color-authoring ADRs and pipette smoke: distinguish authored colors from interface presentation

Fully read: ADR-0008 (`activelightpopup-singleton-bypassing-store`), ADR-0080 (`runtime-color-scheme-system`), ADR-0116 (`the-colour-picker-on-a-phone-and-without-a-pipette`), and `debug/smoke-ge-pagepick.mts`. These readings concern documented architecture and test scope. No current visual audit, browser capability check or interactive smoke was performed; the ADRs' browser-support and visual-equivalence statements remain dated source claims.

**RFF transfer: keep interface themes separate from fractal/material color.** ADR-0080 explicitly excludes rendered fractals, gradients, palette swatches and functional axis colors from interface theming. That is the useful invariant for RFF's shader editing: changing panel brightness or accent hue must not rewrite material values, regenerate palette recipes or alter exported pixels. A neutral editing surround could be offered as a presentation preference, but its perceptual benefit is not measured by this document. Theme brightness is not scene exposure. The July update replaces preset CSS blocks with generated brightness/tint/contrast axes and cached startup variables; the unrevised body still describes the former data-theme switch. Do not implement both historical mechanisms as if they were simultaneously required, or cite the document's 'imperceptible' translucency change as verified visual equivalence.

**Local color sampling is a useful 2D authoring addition, with an explicit color-space contract.** ADR-0116 describes a page-local fallback for a missing system pipette: preview the sampled color, click to commit, Escape to cancel, and accurately label the sampling scope. RFF could apply the interaction to palette strips, imported image layers and the rendered canvas, while deciding whether a sample means displayed/tone-mapped RGB or underlying linear/HDR material data. Those are different operations. Sampling a GPU render should use a supported readback path tied to the displayed frame; a background color returned when actual render pixels are unavailable must not be presented as the fractal's color. Preserve high-precision scalar/map data independently of this color-authoring operation.

The ADR's treatment of pointer-transparent decorative canvases highlights a general picking issue: the event target need not be the visible pixel source. Likewise, searching descendants that geometrically cover a point is not by itself a complete raster-compositing oracle for transformed, clipped, translucent or overlapping content. RFF's adoption should define which surfaces are supported and return unavailable when their pixels cannot be sampled accurately, rather than silently fabricating a result. The host-declared roomy/compact behavior also provides a modest reusable-control idea: a narrow tool dock and a tall narrow panel need not share the same default collapsed state. Respect an explicit saved user choice over automatic defaults. No RFF layout change is proposed as a verified need from this source-only reading.

**The page-pick smoke contains a meaningful but narrow image assertion.** It removes the native API for the fallback case, reads a pixel from a 2D gradient canvas, clicks that horizontal location, and compares the resulting hex field exactly. It also checks overlay removal and Escape preserving the selected color. This is stronger than merely detecting a nonempty canvas. However, the expected pixel comes from row zero while the click is at mid-height, relying on a vertically uniform ramp; it does not validate general two-dimensional image coordinates. Only one sampled horizontal position, an opaque ramp and one viewport size are exercised. Image/video sources, scaling variants, alpha compositing, unavailable GPU pixels and overlapping surfaces are not proven by this test.

Its native-API branch checks a label and absence of the fallback overlay after clicking; it does not confirm a successful native color selection or cancellation. Page errors are collected only on the first page, and console errors are not collected. The Firefox branch is optional, controlled by an environment variable; reading the script does not establish a Firefox run, and it contains no Safari run. The assertion of end-to-end fallback behavior should therefore remain scoped to the tested ramp interaction when executed, not to all pixel sources or browser combinations.

**High-frequency hover feedback should remain transient, with stable light identity.** ADR-0008 records a mutable active-light index bypassing the store and a second mirrored field for tutorial consumption. The transferable RFF idea is to avoid sending every hover through expensive authored-state updates, undo or persistence. The dual-write singleton itself is not a recommended architecture: select an owner for transient hover/selection, notify the consumers that need it, and distinguish that from changing the actual light. If lights can be reordered or removed, use stable light identity or validate the index before applying edits. In RFF's native rendering architecture, any cross-thread handoff must have explicit synchronization; the ADR's React-specific motivation does not establish that an unsynchronized global is safe or faster.

## Thumbnail preparation, picker measurement and timeline-cache tests: separate presentation artifacts from verification

Fully read: `debug/mb3d-thumbs-from-renders.mts`, `debug/shot-ge-picker.mts`, and `debug/test-dopesheet-renderer-cache.mts`. None was executed; existing thumbnails and screenshots were not overwritten or visually verified in this batch.

**RFF transfer: useful preset thumbnails should have traceable origins.** The MB3D helper maps PNG filenames to bundled scene identifiers, center-crops each image to a square and writes a 176-pixel JPEG at requested quality 0.85. Using a good authored render for a browser thumbnail can represent an intended lighting appearance better than a simplified harness render, but that is a selection choice, not a shader-correctness comparison. Center cropping can remove important composition, and downsampling/JPEG can conceal boundary, noise and palette-banding defects. For RFF's 2D locations or relief/material presets, retain the source preset/configuration and full-size render separately; use thumbnails for recognition, not quality acceptance or reconstruction of shader settings.

The filename-based association has no embedded configuration verification. Different filenames with browser deduplication suffixes can map to the same output and overwrite it in enumeration order, and normalized scene-name collisions would overwrite entries in the mapping. The matched counter counts writes, not distinct scenes, while unmatched inputs only log and continue. Image loading has no rejection handler, so a decode failure can leave the awaited promise unresolved. Any adapted RFF batch preview workflow should validate unique identities, explicitly select the intended source when multiple renders exist, report missing/failed items and retain source metadata. The script's 'high' browser smoothing request does not identify a reproducible resampling kernel or certify color-managed fidelity.

**The picker tool measures a layout, but does not enforce a pass.** `shot-ge-picker.mts` captures the shell and optionally the tray at a requested viewport and DPR 2, and logs picker bounds, up to six descendants beyond the right edge, and the nearest vertical scroller. Those observations can help test a constrained material editor. They do not assert that the picker exists, that overflow is absent or that controls can be reached. A missing swatch skips the opening click, page errors are logged without failure, and a tray capture failure is swallowed before the unconditional 'wrote' message. The scan omits left/bottom clipping and truncates overflow descriptions; finding a scrollable ancestor does not prove that keyboard/touch interaction reaches every control. Use the output as diagnostic evidence rather than a green regression gate. The browser's small-viewport/touch emulation is not a physical-device test, and no such run was performed here.

**Timeline drawing caches can improve editing responsiveness without touching fractal precision.** The dope-sheet harness tests track/group cache lookup, replacement, stale-entry eviction, view-key differences and some statistics using fake canvas objects. It deliberately treats keyframe-array identity as a change token: structurally equal new arrays miss. Group storage snapshots the outer child-token array, but that test does not establish deep immutability of child keyframes. Mutating a keyframe inside an unchanged array is outside the tested invalidation contract. For RFF, an equivalent timeline cache should be keyed by a reliable data revision plus all relevant display dependencies rather than assuming mutable C++ containers acquire new identity when edited.

The view-key tests cover pan, row height, a track display flag and scale rounding. They do not render pixels, establish an error bound for rounding, or verify caller inclusion of theme, selection, device scale and viewport dimensions. Rounding zoom to four decimal places may be appropriate for a UI cache only after bounding the resulting screen-space displacement over the visible frame range. It must never become an approximate identity rule for RFF's deep-zoom location, perturbation reference, computed map or shader-result cache. These are responsiveness ideas for authoring tools, not evidence of a measured rendering speedup or permission to reduce numerical precision.

## MB3D lighting and camera mappers: adopt authoring capabilities, not empirical conversion constants

Fully read: `engine-gmt/utils/mb3d/mapLighting.ts` and `engine-gmt/utils/mb3d/mapCamera.ts`. These are current mapper implementations, unlike the earlier research-plan review. Source comments cite MB3D Pascal files; those external originals and their licensing were not independently verified in this batch. No imported scene was rendered. Their 'verified' and 'exactly' wording does not establish measured equivalence here.

**Strong RFF transfer: independently colored environment fill and independently controlled background.** `mapMaterial()` turns the two ambient colors into bottom/top gradient stops, sets the environment source to a procedural gradient, and scales its strength while setting background strength to zero. This separates light affecting the subject from visible sky/background. RFF's relief/material shading could use a comparable authored environment gradient, with rotation and roughness-dependent filtering as discussed earlier. The mapping is explicitly an approximation of diffuse ambient using an environment source, not a physically equivalent conversion. A flat 2D image without normals does not acquire meaningful hemispherical lighting merely by adding this control; use it for explicit relief/normals or as a separately named decorative color treatment.

The mapper preserves per-light color, shadow flag and viewer-relative versus world-fixed intent. Positional lights use the decoded mid-relative position, while directional lights construct a normalized toward-light vector, negate it to match GMT's forward convention and convert to YXZ Euler angles. For RFF, define light direction, anchoring space and angle units once and test rotated views; do not borrow the ambiguous word 'fixed' without defining whether it follows the camera. These are useful light-rig authoring capabilities even without MB3D file support.

**The import is intentionally interpretive.** Light amplitude is multiplied by 1.1 after discarding the source's width-dependent factors; radius, softness and falloff are set to zero. Material roughness is clamped to [0.02,1], diffuse/specular to [0,2], and ambient strength is halved and capped. None is evidence of an exact BRDF or radiometric match. The diffuse expression uses `(tb(5) || 50)`, so an explicit zero becomes the default diffuse value rather than remaining zero. With no active lights, the public mapper returns only an empty light list and skips material, palette and fog mapping altogether; its documented caller convention treats that as inheritance of default lights. For any RFF compatibility feature, distinguish absent data from an authored zero or deliberately unlit rig, and label aesthetic approximations. These observations identify transfer constraints, not a request to repair GMT.

**Palette import heuristics must not silently replace authored 2D colors.** `mapColoring()` normalizes/sorts ten decoded anchors, removes same-color anchors within 0.004 of the preceding retained position, rejects fewer than two stops and discards the entire palette if every stop's HSV-style saturation is below 0.22. It extends endpoints and chooses one or two repeats from a cycle bit. The saturation heuristic aims to avoid missing external-map placeholders, but cannot distinguish a placeholder from an intentional grayscale or low-saturation palette. A single solid color is also meaningful authored content. RFF should preserve such palettes or explicitly report an unavailable external source; keep editable anchors and exact sampled ramps distinguishable. An import adapter must not redefine existing RFF palette recipes or turn a heuristic repeat count into a claimed exact cycle mapping.

**Fog mapping is a compositional approximation, not a distance formula to transplant.** It combines depth-cue and dynamic-fog evidence, treats white dynamic fog as an unset default, attenuates bright fog and uses target-distance-scaled near/far bands. The actual final factors are 0.79 and 5.8; earlier comments describing 1.3 and 5 are superseded within the same function. The helper named `hexLuminance` weights encoded 8-bit channels by 0.299/0.587/0.114 without linearization, so this is a brightness heuristic rather than linear relative luminance. The fixed fog intensity cap and fallback colors change authored meaning. For RFF's 2D transfer, a field-driven haze/color mask may be useful, but iteration count or an escape-distance field is not automatically camera depth. Name the selected field and preserve sharp boundaries intentionally; do not claim physical atmospheric perspective without an appropriate geometric depth.

**Camera mapping illustrates why storage shape and coordinate meaning need separate validation.** The mapper derives orientation from stored navigation basis rows (or an expanded quaternion), negates screen-down Y, and builds a camera basis from right/up/back. It derives eye position from a recomputed step width and view-plane offset, then reports an orbit distance. This does not justify reusing those formulas for RFF's high-precision complex-plane location. If adding a 3D view or importing orientation-only presets, keep projection, basis conventions and mathematical location separate.

The camera header promises rejection of non-orthonormal bases, but the implementation normalizes rows and checks their size/finite condition without testing mutual orthogonality or handedness. Final finite quaternion components do not prove a valid orthonormal source basis. FOV is sanitized for the returned value while eye-offset computation uses the raw FOV, so fallback/clamped cases need separate consistency checks. Default returns shallow-copy an object containing nested position/rotation objects; consumers should not assume independent nested ownership. These are reasons to require explicit validation and fallback reporting in an RFF adapter, rather than treating a finite, centered result as successful faithful import. Before adapting distinctive source-derived formulas or constants, resolve provenance and licenses and update RFF's NOTICE as required.

## Preset field adapters and modular state: distinguish requested, saved and successfully rendered configurations

Fully read: `engine-gmt/store/gmtPresetFields.ts`, `engine-gmt/store/modularSlice.ts`, and `engine-gmt/utils/BenchProfiler.tsx`. The modular-update branch of the already-reviewed `ConfigManager.ts` was also rechecked. No preset round-trip, compilation or performance test was run.

**RFF transfer: keep ordinary shader editing cheap through explicit change categories.** `setGraph()` compares a structural fingerprint with a recorded key. When structure differs, it updates the editable graph only; when structure matches but parameter content differs, it publishes the new pipeline without advancing the revision. `refreshPipeline()` sorts the graph, increments the revision and emits the structural configuration. The downstream ConfigManager treats a changed revision as a rebuild request for the Modular formula, whereas a bare pipeline update requests uniform changes and accumulation reset. This is a concrete model for separating RFF's material-mask/UV numeric edits from shader topology or descriptor-layout changes. Reuse computed fractal fields only when the changed control truly does not affect their mathematical meaning; shader-only edits may still invalidate shaded samples.

**A variable called compiled is not proof of successful compilation.** Both `setPipeline()` and `refreshPipeline()` assign `compiledStructureKey` before emitting CONFIG, and the preset adapter does the same. At this layer the key represents the structure submitted for compilation, not a confirmed successful GPU pipeline. Other layers may provide additional gates, but these setters alone do not prove readiness or failure recovery. For RFF, track edited, requested and successfully installed revisions separately where their distinction matters. Bind parameter data to the active layout until the new layout is installed, and retain the last valid render or expose failure without treating the requested structure as complete.

The modular store holds an editable graph separately from the active pipeline while structural edits await an explicit compile. The preset serializers save both for Modular scenes, so an uncompiled edit can leave those representations different unless higher-level saving resolves the state. The loader accepts a pipeline array and either trusts a supplied graph or derives one, without checking that graph topology and pipeline describe the same program in this file. An RFF node/material preset should deliberately save the authored graph and derive the executable representation, or record/validate both with an explicit version. Do not silently reconstruct a different appearance from inconsistent representations.

The loader also stores a synthesized graph locally when `p.graph` is absent, but emits `graph: p.graph` rather than that synthesized value. Current ConfigManager only replaces its graph when the incoming field is truthy. Thus this adapter alone does not ensure that an old worker graph is replaced by the new fallback graph; whether a later full configuration sync resolves it depends on the wider load path. The transferable requirement is to publish one normalized load result consistently to storage, editing and rendering consumers, not to infer atomic loading merely from an explicit CONFIG event.

**Legacy adaptation needs defined precedence and zero/empty semantics.** The light handler normalizes a nonempty legacy top-level array in preference to the current feature array; an empty legacy array is treated as absent. Its serializer returns undefined because modern feature serialization owns the value. The render-mode adapter likewise reads the lighting feature's numeric flag and calls the central string-mode setter so the control and shader share a route. These bridges demonstrate why old representations need deliberate reconciliation. For RFF, an explicitly empty light rig and an omitted field need not mean the same thing, and conflicting old/new fields need documented precedence. Validate the loaded value types instead of relying solely on permissive numeric comparison. Preserve RFF's append-only binary configuration requirements; these JavaScript object adapters are not a binary-format migration recipe.

Registration order is part of this design: preset handlers must exist before store/load consumers are constructed, and `installGmtModularSlice()` initializes state when called. The installer has no idempotence guard and would replace live modular state if invoked again.
