## Adaptive interaction: model tests are not input-to-display measurements (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/interaction-latency-harness.mts` (289 lines). It was not executed. The script is a deterministic simulation around the adaptive-resolution decision module; it does not drive an actual store, renderer, input event or presented frame, despite some introductory store/frame wording.

The useful RFF design question is whether all expensive interactive edits participate in a coherent interaction policy, rather than only camera motion. A material/lighting slider in 3D or a relief/mask control in 2D can create comparable redraw pressure. Declare interaction start/update/end explicitly, coalesce redundant updates and restore final-quality output after release. If RFF supports temporary preview-resolution reduction, preserve full precision in the numerical computation and ensure export/final output returns to the requested detail without stale accumulation. This is a possible responsiveness policy, not authorization to reduce calculation precision or leave pixelated final results.

The simulation assumes frame cost equals 66 ms divided by scale squared, fixes the target at 30 FPS, omits accumulation and sets pointer-over-canvas true. The legacy/session distinction is hardcoded: sliders are invisible in legacy and visible in session. Thus the comparison can validate the decision model under those injected assumptions, but it cannot prove the application actually wires slider events into that model. Fixed CPU overhead, pipeline compilation, memory bandwidth, readback, nonlinear shader cost and scheduling delays are absent. Do not interpret its synthetic milliseconds as measured user latency or its target-FPS success as a hardware result.

There is also a model consistency limitation: the next frame cost uses the latest requested scale immediately, while the simulated store quality fraction updates only after a 5% threshold. The model can therefore reduce cost before its own thresholded output value reflects the same resolution. It records first reduction after a tick, not completion/presentation of a newly rendered reduced-resolution frame. Its target-reached predicate uses FPS derived from the latest scale rather than the smoothed value described by the interface comment. Sixty idle ticks are assumed to restore the starting condition but no such postcondition is asserted.

The script mixes one cold camera gesture with warmed camera gestures, then runs all slider gestures after them. Percentiles include only gestures that reduced quality; failures are omitted from the latency distribution and appear separately in success rates. Reporting both is useful, but p95 over five successful samples is effectively a maximum, not robust tail-latency evidence. For RFF, report cold/warm state separately, include failure rates, and measure event time, applied resource revision and completed/presented output when claiming actual responsiveness.

The baseline comparison does fail on modeled regressions, unlike many logging-only probes. However, session success requires merely positive engagement/target rates rather than every gesture succeeding; the printed legacy-slider-invisible condition is not part of the final pass expression. Cross-mode comparison does not verify identical model parameters before comparing, and the reverse unsupported mode comparison exits successfully. Same-mode comparison reserializes parsed JSON objects, so it checks the generated report's structured representation rather than literal file-byte identity. Running without check overwrites the baseline, including in session mode.

For RFF, keep a pure decision-model test for repeatable policy checks, add an integration test proving that each relevant control reaches it, and measure real render completion separately. Version baseline inputs and require compatible scenarios before comparing. Use the model to explain a hypothesis; use observed output and timing to claim that a shader editing improvement actually works. No measured latency reduction is established by this source review.

## Three-way visual review needs immutable image identity (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/mb3d-contact-sheet.mjs` (156 lines), without generating or opening its report. The script builds a useful three-way layout: original application image, previous GMT result and current GMT result, with notes and issue flags. When old images are unavailable it falls back to two columns. This pattern transfers to RFF shader evaluation: retain the current RFF baseline, candidate output and an appropriate reference, then judge the specific intended change. Geometry, material response and final color need separate criteria; a reference whose colors intentionally differ cannot certify palette fidelity. The same applies to 2D boundary detail, relief normals and color mapping.

The implementation enumerates only current GMT PNGs. A case that produced no current image disappears rather than appearing as a failed/missing result. Pairing strips all non-ASCII alphanumeric characters and uses maps that overwrite collisions, with no source/settings hashes or dimension/camera verification. Old-directory presence enables the third column for all cards but does not prove a matching baseline exists. RFF should enumerate an expected fixture manifest and explicitly display missing, stale or mismatched outputs.

Human notes are keyed by a prettified scene name under one fixed localStorage key, so changed renders can inherit earlier decisions. The displayed count includes stored entries absent from the current page, while export includes current cards only. There is no explicit reviewed-pass state: zero flags cannot distinguish approved from unreviewed. Bind review decisions to image/settings hashes and record reviewed/unreviewed separately. A new render should not inherit approval automatically.

The green outline and faithful wording describe intended behavior, not verified fidelity. Neutral labels are preferable while evaluating a candidate. URL path segments are encoded, but displayed names and attribute content are not comprehensively HTML-escaped. Storage parsing/writes lack failure handling, and clipboard failure is swallowed despite an unconditional copied message. These are limitations of this report generator, not evidence of RFF UI defects. Preserve notes in an explicit exportable artifact and report actual save/copy status if adopting a similar review tool. No visual sign-off is inferred from this source read.

Full source review: `debug/geSmokeBoot.mts`, `debug/capture-ge-trays.mts`, and `app-gmt.html`. No screenshot capture or interactive UI review was performed.

The smoke initializer seeds the returning-visitor theme flag through a context initialization script before application code executes. This makes the intended test state explicit rather than accidentally clicking through a first-run modal. It does not test onboarding, and storage errors are swallowed without verifying the seed took effect. Keep separate first-run and returning-user fixtures when validating RFF controls or a future preview browser; do not call a bypassed flow covered.

The tray-capture script uses a fresh context but does not call that initializer or dismiss the first-run dialogue. Combined with the initializer's documented modal behavior, this is a plausible capture blocker requiring runtime confirmation, not evidence that the script currently succeeds. It captures five interaction states after fixed waits, uses a fixed viewport/crop and selects some targets by CSS class fragments and coordinates. It explicitly asserts no visual properties and does not verify that each requested tray is open before saving. An image file existing therefore does not prove the intended state was captured. For RFF shader/effect comparisons, identify the precise scene and controls, verify state before capture and associate screenshots with the rendered revision.

The application HTML restores cached theme CSS before mounting, sets dark color-scheme and supplies different overflow/scroll behavior for fine-pointer desktop and mobile-style input. It also requests disabled user scaling in the viewport metadata. These are browser-shell policies, not shader improvements to transplant into RFF's native renderer. Keep those conditions recorded and keep exported pixels governed by explicit rendering settings rather than UI theme.

The useful cross-dimensional transfer is a clear startup/readiness contract. A booted application, available controls, compiled shader, completed image and visually reviewed result are different milestones. ## Semantic migrations and the limits of lexical guards (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/codemod-theme.mjs` and `debug/check-zindex.mjs`. Neither script was executed; no theme migration or UI modification was performed. These files inform validation practices for adopting shader controls, not an additional rendering effect or a measured performance improvement.

The theme codemod defaults to a dry run and applies an ordered list of regular-expression replacements across selected TypeScript trees. That preview-first approach is useful for RFF maintenance, but its actual scope exceeds its introductory claim that surfaces and raw hexadecimal colors are untouched. The rules replace multiple hexadecimal surface colors, gray backgrounds, black-alpha surfaces and lighter gray fills. Different original values converge on the same semantic token; some opacity values are discarded or normalized, such as gray-800 backgrounds and gray borders. Pixel identity therefore requires checking the resolved tokens and rendered results, not trusting the header. Replacements operate on whole source text, including comments and strings, without identifying whether a color denotes application chrome, a palette sample or rendered content. The printed counts describe ordered replacement events and show at most four examples per rule, not a complete reviewed diff. Missing directories and stat failures can silently reduce scan coverage; sequential writes are not transactional.

For RFF, keep application theme colors independent from fractal palette, material, emission and export colors. A semantic migration should identify intended usage, preserve meaningful alpha, and compare actual output in both themes. This matters equally for 3D material controls and 2D palette/mask editors: a UI cleanup must not silently alter the user's image. Do not import these replacement rules as a shader or palette conversion algorithm.

The z-index checker does exit unsuccessfully for recognized unallowlisted literals, making it stronger than a diagnostic that merely prints failures. However, its claimed ratchet is a whole-file allowlist: newly added literals inside an allowed file remain allowed. Its expressions recognize selected positive decimal forms, not every equivalent expression, stylesheet or dynamic value. The leading-comment filter is lexical rather than syntax-aware, so its absolute claim of no false negatives is not established for arbitrary source text, including multiline strings. The portal report independently searches for `createPortal` and a `document.body` argument-like suffix in the same file; it does not prove they belong to the same call and does not fail the check. The historical mutation-test account in comments was not rerun during this audit.

The transferable principle is explicit ownership of floating controls and checks with accurately bounded claims. If RFF adds layered shader editors, masks or lighting pickers, test their actual visibility, focus and interaction with the viewport using the native UI architecture. Web z-index numbers do not directly map to Win32 behavior. Likewise, use occurrence-specific baselines or syntax-aware checks when a policy truly intends to reject every new exception. A passing lexical guard establishes only its recognized source policy, not correct stacking, visible controls or accurate rendered pixels.

## Separate rendered-image evidence from interaction profiling (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/opus-shot.mts` and `debug/prof-ge-drag.mts`. Neither tool was run. Historical timings in comments are not new measurements from this audit.

The single-shot wrapper explicitly requests ANGLE SwiftShader, waits for the render harness readiness flag, and delegates a square image render to `runRenderTest`. It propagates a failed render through a nonzero exit and saves the returned PNG on success. This is useful diagnostic infrastructure, but the launch request is not a recorded backend identity or evidence of native Vulkan performance. Formula overrides and camera overrides are supported; an orbit argument replaces the entire supplied camera override rather than merging it. Path-tracing mode forces two lighting settings but does not itself specify or verify convergence or sample count. Its printed summary contains brightness-related statistics and timing, not a persisted manifest of resolved settings, source revision, camera, device and samples. Console/page errors are collected but reported only on the failed-result branch. Saving a successful thumbnail therefore does not establish an error-free run, physical fidelity or convergence. For RFF image comparisons, preserve the exact effective scene beside each image, identify software versus hardware execution, and distinguish a single sample preview from the intended final render.

The drag profiler seeds a returning-user boot state, opens a gradient tray, synthesizes forty mouse moves with 16 ms waits, and samples JavaScript through CDP on Chromium. It aggregates the time deltas attached to sampled nodes into self-time by function, URL and line, with URL query strings removed. This is a useful way to investigate CPU-side repeated sorting, ramp fitting and allocations while adjusting a palette. It is a sampled attribution, not GPU duration, total inclusive function cost or a complete accounting of every interval; missing deltas contribute zero and only the top entries are printed. The historical improvement reported in its header needs a reproducible before/after run before being used as an RFF performance estimate.

The accompanying requestAnimationFrame watcher reports frame-gap percentiles after dropping the first two observations. A long-task observer may be unsupported and silently ignored, while an empty frame list is reported with zero-valued timing statistics. The watcher is not stopped at mouse-up and the measurement includes profiler start/stop and readback boundaries around the gesture. Browser automation pacing and profiling overhead also affect the result. These observations can reveal scheduling stalls but do not directly measure pointer-event-to-presented-pixel latency or shader execution. Firefox omits CPU profiling, so the two browser modes do not provide identical measurements.

Target selection is heuristic: the widest horizontal-resize element in Adjust, or the center of the first curve canvas with optional coordinate overrides. There is no assertion that the intended parameter or curve knot changed. A missing target prints a message and returns normally; page errors are logged without making the run fail. Production builds are recommended in the header but not enforced or identified in output. Consequently, a completed script is not sufficient evidence that a representative edit was profiled.

For both 3D material editing and 2D palette/field editing in RFF, adopt the separation of CPU attribution and frame scheduling, then add verified parameter changes, fixed scene identity, repeat runs and distinct GPU timestamps/presentation measurements where available. Preserve numerical precision while optimizing redundant preview work, such as rebuilding unchanged palette data. A fast control that never changes the intended shader input must be counted as an invalid measurement, not a successful optimization.

## Import reachability is a prerequisite, not shader test coverage (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/check-rule-guards.mjs` and `plans/context-protocol/scripts/reachability.mjs`. This is source analysis; the checker and historical mutation experiments were not executed. The useful RFF transfer is checking whether a cited test can plausibly exercise the implementation it claims to protect, then separately proving that its assertions detect relevant failures.

GMT's checker resolves package scripts to test entries or browser application entries, expands several composite forms, and compares their reachable source files with documentation path scopes. Table rows can narrow a multi-application rule to a particular subtree. These mechanisms can catch a test that opens an unrelated application, a missing script or a scope with no tracked files. They address a real distinction for RFF adoption: a palette test, a generic application startup test and a material-rendering test do not establish the same property.

The current implementation nevertheless accepts any nonempty intersection, not coverage of every scoped file or execution of every imported branch. Importing a shader emitter does not prove that a particular generated shader compiles, that a Vulkan binding matches its C++ layout, or that output pixels are correct. Whole-tree exemptions are selected by script name, without validating what that script actually does. Opaque commands are counted as live and are not individually reported by this code, despite the header describing opaque acceptance as a historical blind spot. Composite expansion can retain reachable entries while discarding unresolved or missing members, and any whole-tree member exempts the composite. Scripts with both nested npm commands and direct commands are handled by the nested-command branch first, which does not also union the direct files. Treat a passing result as a limited citation check, not a complete test inventory.

Additional classification limits matter. A node entry whose reachable files all lie under debug, plans or scripts is presumed to be a text scanner and accepted with a manual-review message; the absence of product imports does not itself establish that it scans the relevant files. URL inference uses command/source regular expressions and a fixed entry map, not the actual browser navigation or HTML module resolution. Markdown/frontmatter parsing supports selected formats, scans mentions beyond a formally isolated Guards section, and removes a script from rule-wide checks if the same name occurs in a scoped row. Glob conversion is simplified: consuming the slash after a double star and emitting an unrestricted wildcard does not preserve every path-boundary constraint of a conventional glob. Git filenames are read as newline-separated, trimmed text rather than NUL-delimited paths. These are boundaries on the evidence, not proof that every current citation is wrong.

The graph walker follows recognized literal imports, re-exports and URL constructions, resolves relative paths and the root alias against tracked files, and avoids revisiting nodes. Query suffix removal and JavaScript-to-TypeScript fallback are helpful for this repository. Its own header correctly calls it an estimate. Type-only imports and unreachable dynamic branches can overstate runtime reach. Computed imports, require calls, glob imports and transitive dependencies inside CSS/GLSL/JSON are not traversed. Comment removal is not string-aware, so comment-like text inside literals can affect extraction; import-like text inside strings can also create misleading edges. Missing reads are skipped, missing entries contribute nothing, and unresolved imports are returned by the helper but discarded by the guard checker's reach cache. Do not label unreached files dead code solely from this graph.

For RFF, maintain a feature-to-evidence map with distinct checks for CPU math, shader generation/compilation, descriptor and push-constant compatibility, image correctness and execution cost. For a 3D feature adapted to 2D, explicitly test the 2D field representation and its discontinuities rather than relying on a shared material module's import path. Add deliberate failures for each claimed invariant to verify that the appropriate test actually rejects them. This complements the previously identified shader opportunities; it neither changes their measured performance ranking nor proves any feature has been implemented.

## Typed binary interchange and deterministic export boundaries (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/out/fbx2json.py` and `debug/out/encode_bin.py`. These are binary FBX utilities, not camera interpolation implementations. No conversion, generated-file validation or DCC import was executed. The source headers attribute the decoder to the assimp team and Blender Foundation and the encoder to Campbell Barton, with GPL-2.0-or-later identifiers. Preserve those notices if adapting their code; the public file-format name alone is not permission to copy an implementation. No third-party code was copied into RFF by this review.

The decoder preserves each element's identifier, ordered typed properties and ordered children. A list representation avoids losing repeated identifiers through dictionary-key replacement. Scalar numeric reads explicitly use little-endian formats; array reads support raw or zlib-compressed payloads. Version selection switches element metadata and nested sentinels at version 7500. This typed structural view is useful for inspecting exported animation fixtures, but it does not interpret coordinate systems, units, animation connections, interpolation or material meaning. Successful decoding cannot establish that an imported camera follows the intended path.

Important boundaries prevent treating its JSON output as a canonical lossless interchange. String conversion replaces the NUL/SOH pair with two colons; bytes use a representation-derived textual form rather than an explicit standard binary encoding. Element identifiers are interpolated into JSON without JSON string escaping. Floating-point values and arrays use Python representations, so nonfinite values can produce text that strict JSON does not accept. ASCII output with XML character replacement does not preserve arbitrary non-ASCII element identifiers as JSON Unicode escapes. Integer text can represent 64-bit values, but a downstream JavaScript Number consumer would still need protection against integer precision loss.

Parser checks also have limits: property-list byte length is read but not validated independently; array size uses an assertion, unknown compression encodings are not explicitly rejected, and there are no explicit resource/decompression/depth limits. On big-endian hosts, float/double array paths do not request the byte swap used by integer arrays. The version initializer asserts a previously uninitialized global state and never resets it, so a second parse in the same normal Python process fails that assertion, including the advertised multi-file command-line loop. The command-line exception handler prints errors and continues without aggregating a failing exit status. These observations concern this utility's source behavior, not a demonstrated defect in GMT's production importer.

The encoder first constructs typed property byte buffers, optionally compresses arrays, calculates absolute offsets, and checks actual write positions against those offsets. Compression uses level 1 when the raw array exceeds 128 bytes, without testing whether the compressed result is smaller. Its optional worker context reserves each property's original slot and fills it after compression, preserving ordering despite asynchronous completion. The context waits for workers before returning; it temporarily prevents element writes during the active construction phase. That ordering/barrier design is a useful general export principle. However, it patches class methods and uses module-global version state, so it should not be assumed safe for unrelated concurrent writers or overlapping contexts without further analysis.

The writer modifies FileId and CreationTime to fixed values, warns rather than fails if they are absent, and stores calculated offsets in the element objects. Reusing the same constructed tree for another write encounters assertions on those cached offsets. It opens the destination directly before validation finishes, so exceptions can leave a truncated or partial file. Deterministic metadata is useful for fixtures, but should not be confused with preserving original provenance or providing transactional export.

For RFF's 3D interchange, distinguish typed binary validity from coordinate, camera and animation semantics, and verify both with independent consumers. For 2D zoom movies, reuse the idea of ordered typed data and explicit completion barriers, not ordinary float camera coordinates as the authoritative fractal center. Retain high-precision centers and an explicit zoom representation; test exact time/key identity and endpoint behavior separately from container parsing. Keep RFF's existing map format lossless and version-stable, and use temporary output plus final replacement for completed exports. Neither binary utility adds a shader effect or establishes a rendering speedup.

## Benchmark summaries need validated inputs and identified execution targets (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/pt-bench-summary.mjs`, `debug/runWithServer.mts` and `debug/run-smokes.mts`. No benchmark, server or smoke suite was launched. These utilities support evidence collection; they do not themselves demonstrate a shader speedup.

The path-tracing summary separates convergence, seam measurements, seam convergence and timing. This separation is worth retaining for RFF: visual error, tile-boundary artifacts and execution cost answer different questions. However, the formatter trusts the supplied rows and metadata without schema, compatibility or finiteness validation. Its REAL GPU heading depends only on the backend string in extras. It cannot establish the actual adapter or distinguish GPU timestamps from harness wall time. Timing is normalized by nominal samples and image area; actual per-pixel sample counts and workload differences still matter. Grouping by scene or suite is not sufficient to exclude mixed revisions, devices or settings. A corrected PSNR column merely prints a previously computed value; it does not validate that estimator's assumptions.

Missing and nonfinite values require particular care. The display helper renders null as a dash, but convergence filtering admits null PSNR values because it only excludes undefined. Taking the square root of a null MSE produces zero through JavaScript coercion. A nonfinite statistic serialized to JSON null therefore cannot safely be interpreted as either missing data or zero error without an explicit validity field. Seam-convergence output only recognizes the two named case prefixes, and other suite/case forms can be absent from the report. For RFF comparisons, preserve invalid/unmeasured status, record effective sample counts and exact color/error domains, and identify the source measurement method beside timing numbers.

The server wrapper starts Vite on one selected strict port and waits for a TCP connection. Despite the introductory description, it does not search for a free port or increment on collision. Readiness is not tied to the owned process: its stdout readiness flag only affects a diagnostic, while an unrelated listener can satisfy the TCP probe. The header acknowledges that race. The child receives a root ENGINE_URL override, so individual harnesses must still select their intended application route. There is no explicit per-socket timeout inside the nominal readiness deadline, and no overall smoke-command timeout. Windows command construction quotes selected characters but is not a general argument-preserving shell encoder; embedded quotes, expansion syntax and empty arguments need separate treatment if generalized. The wrapper attempts cleanup of Vite and forwards the inner exit code, but its cleanup scope is not a verified lifecycle contract for every descendant process or signal path.

The smoke driver improves reporting by collecting each selected member's result and continuing after failures unless bail is requested. Missing files count as failures, and the final summary identifies how many selected members ran. Its explicit member list is useful for repeatability but is not automatic proof that every relevant smoke exists in the list. Invalid or over-restrictive selection can produce an empty set and a successful all-zero-passed result; there is no minimum-coverage gate. Each child has no driver-level timeout, so a hung member can prevent the promised final aggregate. Success is the child's exit status, making a member that only prints errors indistinguishable from a real pass. The preliminary port warning probes IPv4 port 3400 regardless of ENGINE_URL and does not verify the application; a warning can be misleading when the wrapper supplied another port or the listener uses IPv6.

For RFF feature adoption, retain independent correctness, artifact and performance suites with a manifest of selected and completed checks. Reject empty required selections, distinguish skipped checks from successful checks, and bind results to the executable/source revision and effective scene. For 3D shading and its 2D adaptations, measure the same intended output and quality conditions before comparing time. A launched server, a completed child process and a formatted table are useful steps toward that evidence, but none substitutes for verified rendering behavior.

## Deep-zoom diagnostics: preserve coordinates and distinguish missing work from interior (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/repro-gx-blacksections.mts`, `debug/repro-gx-check.mts`, `debug/repro-gx-deepiter.mts` and `debug/repro-gx-epsilon.mts`. These are diagnostic fixtures, not newly executed tests. Their comments describe historical symptoms or hypotheses; this review does not establish that those defects remain in the current renderer.

The strongest transferable fixture is the black-sections pair: both views retain identical high coordinate words and zoom while changing only the low words. At approximately 1.17e-17 scale, this explicitly preserves a pan that would disappear if the high and low components were prematurely combined into one ordinary number. Each case requests a deep-zoom rebuild and records orbit length, GPU iteration limit and relocation status beside an image. For RFF, keep equivalent high-precision adjacent-view fixtures across reference rebuilds. They can reveal an abrupt numerical transition that a large zoom or pan would hide. Expected pixels need not be identical because the coordinates differ; the relevant question is whether each view agrees with an independent accurate computation.

The fixture's header attributes historical black regions to coupling the per-pixel iteration cap to an early-escaping reference orbit. That is a valuable invariant to check, not a diagnosis proven by the script alone. Reference exhaustion, invalid perturbation, unfinished computation and a pixel that did not escape within the requested limit must remain distinguishable. Nor does reaching the iteration limit prove mathematical membership of the set. For RFF, validate rebasing/reference replacement and the requested iteration budget before turning such states into interior colors. Its MPA derives skips from periodic structure; GMT's useLA/calibrateLA switches are not interchangeable with RFF's MPA and do not justify changing RFF's precision policy.

The LA-on/off checker holds its explicit view and palette fixed, renders the two settings sequentially and compares the largest quantized-RGB bin fraction in the central 40 percent of each image dimension. A difference over 0.15 prints a square warning. This statistic can flag a suspicious flat region but does not test square geometry or per-pixel agreement: it discards spatial arrangement, and legitimate palette plateaus or interior regions can dominate. The warning does not cause a failing exit. LA-off is also not automatically an independent high-precision oracle; both paths can share perturbation or coloring errors. For RFF, compare escape status, iteration/smoothing data and validity masks before color mapping, then compare the displayed result separately.

The deeper-iteration fixture changes center, low words and zoom across its three cases, and increases iterMul only in the third. It is a useful collection of reported problem views, but not a controlled experiment isolating iteration count from location or zoom. The suggested long-run float drift remains a hypothesis until isolated. Its escaped field prints a question mark on both sides of the conditional and conveys no actual escape classification. Near-black fraction and distinct quantized colors are presentation-dependent observations, not evidence of recovered fractal detail. A separate matched-view iteration sweep with an accurate reference would support that claim.

The epsilon probe records rebuild wall time and reported orbit/calibration statistics at four fixed coordinates, with an environment toggle for calibration. It deliberately does not wait for a rendered image or compare results. Successful calibration statistics therefore establish neither image correctness nor shader execution speed; a low construction time can coexist with an invalid approximation. RFF should validate accuracy and fallback behavior before considering any approximation-tolerance adjustment, retaining the existing prohibition on sacrificing precision for speed.

All four scripts rely on fixed startup delays and direct renderer handles; the image probes additionally wait a fixed interval rather than verify a particular completed render revision. Some missing canvases skip image output, and collected browser errors are printed without making the diagnostic fail. They do not consistently force every relevant renderer option, so inherited defaults remain part of the experiment. The RFF adaptation is a deterministic fixture contract: exact coordinates, effective options, completed revision, raw numerical outputs and explicit failures for missing results. This is directly useful for 2D deep zoom and for any 3D-to-2D shading feature consuming iteration, distance or normal fields; a visually sophisticated shader cannot repair invalid source fields.

## Orbit-dependent coloring and an independent zoom-anchor oracle (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/repro-gx-glitch.mts`, `debug/repro-gx-stripe-square.mts` and `debug/repro-gx-zoomanchor.mts`. No browser render was executed. Historical defect descriptions and the stripe accumulator explanation in comments remain context or hypotheses, not current-runtime findings from this review.

The stripe fixture makes an important feature-compatibility question concrete: it fixes a very deep coordinate, stripe/trap color mapping and a high palette repeat, then compares useLA enabled and disabled. Its hypothesis is that skipped iterations contribute differently to an orbit-dependent color accumulator. The general RFF adoption requirement is broader than GMT's particular approximation: a skip that preserves an endpoint or escape estimate does not automatically preserve every statistic accumulated along the orbit. A sum, minimum orbit-trap distance, angular stripe statistic and derivative each have different composition requirements. If a new shader consumes such a field, define whether every skipped segment provides a valid equivalent contribution. Where it cannot, use a correct computation path or clearly separate the feature's semantics; do not silently supply an incomplete accumulator. RFF's periodic-structure MPA must be analyzed on its own terms and must not be renamed or treated as GMT's LA.

This is a direct 3D-to-2D transfer issue for orbit-trap material masks, emission masks and stripe-based coloring: attractive shading does not make the underlying field valid. Compare the raw accumulator, its normalization/count, validity and final palette coordinate across acceleration boundaries. High gradient repeat amplifies small coordinate errors, so retain both low-repeat and high-repeat fixtures. A displayed LA-on/off difference alone cannot distinguish an accumulator mismatch from sampling, palette aliasing or shared perturbation errors. The stripe script saves images and prints stats but computes no numeric difference, asserts no expected equivalence and does not fail for a missing canvas or merely logged browser errors. Its comment about another renderer's policy was not independently verified and should not be treated as an adoption authority.

The multi-view glitch harness extends the same central dominant-color statistic to four locations with explicit zero low words and LA-on/off pairs. Its claimed square detector still contains no spatial shape test. Its warning is one-sided: only an increase over 0.15 in the dominant-color fraction is flagged, unlike the absolute difference used by the separate single-view checker. If both probes lack a canvas, each substitutes dominance 1, their difference becomes zero and the line can print ok despite missing images. A declared fail helper is never called. The nominal control's expected relocation behavior is described in a comment but not asserted. For RFF, preserve missing-result status explicitly and validate the specific invariant rather than infer correctness from a low color-count metric.

The zoom-anchor fixture has a real failing exit condition, but its header overstates the reference calculation. Both before and after positions add center high and low components using ordinary JavaScript Number arithmetic; this is not double-double addition, despite the DD truth description. It starts at zoom 1e-6 and applies forty factors of 0.8, ending near 1.33e-10, not the approximately 8e-10 stated in the comment. This is a useful moderate-depth regression case, but cannot establish arbitrary deep-zoom accuracy. At much smaller scales, collapsing the coordinate words can hide motion by rounding both positions to the same value.

For RFF, compute cursor offsets in local image coordinates and update the high-precision center by the difference between old and new offsets, preserving the coordinate representation throughout. Validate with an independent high-precision oracle, expressing residual error in final output pixels. Cover nonzero low components, both zoom directions, repeated inverse operations, varied aspect ratios and display scales, and actual input-event routing. The reviewed fixture calls zoomAt directly, uses one off-center location and accepts less than five pixels of drift; it neither validates the event path nor establishes a subpixel guarantee. Keep preview interaction, mathematical anchor preservation and rendered-image completion as separate checks. This navigation improvement is useful in both 2D exploration and 3D view controls, while the exact coordinate model and precision requirements differ.

## Import candidate reports must separate acceptance from fidelity (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/scan-frag-parse.mts` and `debug/scan-mb3d-scenes.mts`. Neither inventory scan was executed; counts mentioned in source comments are historical, not results from this audit.

The Fragmentarium report recursively inventories sorted .frag paths and calls V3 detection and V4 processing independently. Keeping route-specific acceptance and exceptions is useful when selecting formulas for further investigation. It explicitly fails on an empty corpus, while ordinary per-formula failures only enter the printed report. Its startup message that it always exits zero is thus broader than its actual empty-corpus and uncaught-error behavior. Conversely, a normal zero exit does not establish importer correctness. Relative paths identify reported files, but the processing calls use basenames as identifiers; that does not by itself establish collision-free registration when different folders contain the same name.

The report does not drive Workshop selection or verify its current auto-routing policy. Phrases in its output such as unrenderable, should be hidden or a route would work go beyond the observed detect/process results. No GPU shader compilation, pixel comparison, camera setup or user-defined parameter evaluation occurs here. A rejected 3D distance-estimator route also does not imply that the source lacks useful 2D coloring or coordinate transforms. For RFF adoption, preserve separate statuses for parsed structure, supported semantics, generated shader, compiled pipeline and validated image. Keep potential 2D color-field candidates even when they do not satisfy a 3D geometry contract.

The MB3D scanner reads only immediate .m3p children of its selected directory, parses each and requests fused-hybrid emission after registering AmazingBox. A returned definition is placed directly in the FAITHFUL category; a substitute is separately marked best effort. The separation of substitutions is valuable, but the first label is not proved by this script: it does not compile, render or compare the emitted definition, and it does not independently assert the heading's intern/mode-zero conditions. Parser acceptance and emitter availability cannot establish equivalent iterations, transforms, materials, camera framing or lighting. Its registry context should also be recorded when interpreting substitution availability rather than assumed identical to a fully booted application.

Unsupported results retain only their first reason for grouping, normalize parts of that reason and truncate it; only the first eight caught errors are printed. The final totals line omits the best-effort count even though that category is printed earlier. An empty existing directory or a corpus containing only caught failures can still finish without a failing exit. This is a triage report with incomplete diagnostic detail, not a fidelity gate or proof that an entire source library was covered.

For RFF, the useful addition is an import/adoption inventory whose records retain full relative identity, source hash and provenance, effective formula parameters, substitution status and all unresolved semantic requirements. Evaluate promising 3D mechanisms for their mathematical contribution to 2D rendering: a transform, orbit statistic or color mapping may be independently reusable even when the complete scene is not. Validate that contribution in isolation and then in the actual RFF pipeline, including its precision and MPA requirements. Do not promise external-format or image fidelity solely because the source parses or an emitter returns code. These files add evidence-management ideas, not a newly verified shader effect.

## Numerical distance experiments require an independent reference (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/sim-numeric-de.mts` and `debug/sim-numeric-de2.mts`. These are standalone CPU experiments with local formula copies, not imports of the current shader implementation. Neither was executed. Their printed comparisons and explanatory comments do not establish current GPU behavior or an accepted numerical tolerance.

The first experiment implements a power-eight Mandelbulb and compares three probe constructions: differences of squared terminal radius at the center's iteration count, differences of its logarithm, and differences of independently smoothed escape counts. Fixing the count attempts to keep neighboring probes on the same iterate rather than differentiating a change of stopping iteration. However, the terminal-radius helper can stop early and clamp at an inflated radius cap, so nominally equal counts do not guarantee equal actual iterations or an unclipped differentiated field. Clipping can flatten probe differences, while a small probe can lose differences to rounding. Taking logarithms changes scale but cannot recover information already discarded by saturation or rounding.

The experiment is labeled float32, but Math.fround is applied only at selected intermediate operations. Input offsets, some products and sums, and camera positions still use JavaScript Number arithmetic; transcendental operations are not a simulation of a particular GPU's instructions. Nor is its analytic-DE function an independent high-precision geometric oracle: it shares the same local bulb step and approximate arithmetic. Candidate formulas use different normalization factors, so matching order of magnitude alone cannot validate their constants. The ray advances using the reference estimate, not each candidate's own steps; consequently the output does not test whether a candidate would overshoot a surface or converge during its own ray march. Only one ray and two probe sizes are printed, with no assertions or nonfinite-value gate.

The second experiment uses a fold-based Mandelbox with an inflated cap and three manually supplied scale values. Despite the calibration comment, it does not solve a scale from a measured sample; it simply sweeps the listed values. More importantly, its reference derivative chooses the sphere-fold factor from the radius before box folding, whereas the actual step chooses that factor after box folding. Those factors need not agree. This internal mismatch prevents using the printed ratio as validation of the numeric estimator without first repairing or independently validating the reference. Its final distance expression also requires its own justification for the particular recurrence; the label analytic alone is insufficient. Like the bulb experiment, it follows a reference-driven ray, uses selected rounding and has no pass/fail assertions.

For RFF's 3D shading, distinguish a visually useful scalar field from a distance estimate suitable for traversal. A gradient used for normals needs stable direction; a distance used to advance a ray additionally needs validated step behavior. Probe size, caps, iteration count and fallback policy belong in the field's contract, with explicit invalid-state handling. Test multiple spatial scales, axes, fold boundaries, nonescaping points and near-zero gradients against an independently justified reference. Do not copy the experiments' regularization constants or scale sweeps as established defaults.

For 2D adaptation, numerical gradients can support relief-like shading, contour emphasis or masks, but the differentiated quantity must be stated: escape count, smooth potential and an actual distance field are not interchangeable. Prefer derivatives available from the fractal computation where valid, or probe a well-defined scalar field at a scale appropriate to the displayed pixel footprint. Preserve high-precision coordinates when constructing probes and test palette-independent data before visual effects. Reusing a cached field for several shading passes is a candidate optimization; its cache validity must include every input that changes the field. These experiments suggest useful comparisons, not permission to lower RFF precision or evidence of a measured improvement.

## Distance floors, logarithmic probes and temporal stability are separate contracts (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/sim-numeric-de3.mts` and `debug/sim-numeric-de4.mts`. Neither experiment was executed. Both contain local copies and historical constants rather than importing the current shader; their EXACT/faithful labels are not current source-equivalence or GPU-execution evidence.

The third experiment makes pixel/world units explicit: its MB3D-style path perturbs the seed by a base offset multiplied by StepWidth, calculates a pixel-unit estimate and converts the result to world units. This is a useful dimensional-accounting pattern for RFF. However, it compares selected float32 rounding against JavaScript double arithmetic, not GPU hardware against x87 execution. The copies differ in probe sizes, caps, floors and stopping behavior as well as precision. Any observed disagreement would therefore require controlled isolation before assigning a cause. The PseudoXDB copy also divides by the XY radius without a zero-denominator policy, and nonfinite values can propagate through comparisons until a step-budget result is printed. Its sumSq return field is always zero, so that diagnostic cannot verify the accumulated squared differences.

The logarithmic candidate is motivated by the first-order relation between radius differences and log-radius differences. That relation is not exact at a finite probe displacement, and the regularization term must be transformed consistently before claiming equivalence. The code retains a fixed additive regularizer in the log denominator; simply cancelling a radius factor in the unregularized expression does not prove the two regularized formulas equivalent. The log path still caps the terminal squared radius and can terminate probes early at overflow, so it cannot guarantee absence of saturation or cancellation. Clamping infinity before the logarithm does not repair NaN or recover the lost field variation.

Unlike the earlier two experiments, sim-numeric-de3 runs separate candidate-driven marches, which is a useful additional observation. They still use a shared simplified marcher and threshold, so the MB3D-labeled estimator is not a complete execution of that application's traversal. The scale sweep prints hit positions and step counts without validating them against an independently computed surface. Its fixed approximate surface value is only a display reference, and the comment describing a smaller ray parameter as having stepped through the surface reverses the usual ordering for a ray advancing from the camera. There is no assertion resolving that interpretation. Hit counts and speed alone cannot select a safe estimator.

The fourth experiment contains march and ray-fan functions but never calls them in its current top-level execution. Despite the opening description, it reports only coefficient-of-variation measurements at selected points near one axis. The actual comparisons are forward probes, three-times-wider forward probes and iteration-count-adaptive forward probes. The central-difference branch exists but all invoked measurements pass false. Returned field names cvCen and cvWide store the wide and adaptive results respectively; the printed column headings match those actual values, but programmatic consumers of the names could misread them.

A concrete invariant follows from its local equations: for the plain marcher at positive distance, if the enforced distance floor is at least the hit threshold, the strict DE-less-than-threshold condition cannot accept a floored value. Floor, footprint and detail controls must therefore be designed together. The alternative marcher can clamp the distance again, so the same conclusion must not be generalized without following that path. At the camera origin, its hit footprint is zero while the estimator has a minimum footprint, which is another distinct boundary condition. This reasoning identifies a parameter contract, not a measured current GMT rendering failure.

Lower coefficient of variation is not proof of less visible flicker: samples are different spatial positions, whose true distances may legitimately differ, and flooring can reduce variation by hiding structure. No temporal frames, accurate reference distances or corresponding hit transitions are evaluated. The helper can return zero when its mean is nonfinite or too small, and an empty sample set yields an invalid average without a failing assertion. The claimed sharpness of adaptive widening is not tested.

For RFF, evaluate numerical fields along three independent axes: accuracy against an appropriate reference, stability under controlled sample motion, and cost in the actual pipeline. In 3D, add verified traversal and hit-threshold behavior. In 2D relief shading or distance-based masks, measure contour displacement and retained detail while varying footprint/probe width; do not accept apparent stability achieved by blurring or clamping away information. Preserve numerical precision and treat these scripts as experiment designs to improve, not validated constants or ready-to-port shader implementations.

## Reusable parameter modulation: quadrature motion and frame-bound playback (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/smoke-anim-orbit.mts` and `debug/smoke-anim-play.mts`. Both target fluid-toy by default and operate on Julia parameters; the orbit test is not a 3D camera-orbit test. Neither browser smoke was executed during this review.

A useful RFF feature pattern is expressing a circular parameter motion through two ordinary sinusoidal modulators with equal amplitude and period and a quarter-cycle phase offset. GMT's fixture targets the two Julia-constant components and expects modulation to add to the authored base value. Conceptually, x(t) = baseX + R sin(theta) and y(t) = baseY + R cos(theta). This can provide a shared modulation mechanism for 2D Julia exploration, texture coordinates or paired effect controls, and can drive 3D parameters where their semantics permit it. It does not directly create a camera orbit, whose target, orientation and distance require a separate mapping. Keep authored values and transient effective values distinct so animation does not overwrite the saved starting point.

The orbit smoke injects the two modulators through the store, checks target registration, then samples their effective offsets six times. Radius and pairwise spread assertions are stronger than checking merely that a value exists or stays inside a box: they reject a frozen zero offset and a stationary point on the circle. Its radius assertion uses a negated less-than-or-equal comparison, so NaN radii are rejected there despite the earlier typeof check accepting NaN. Browser errors also fail the smoke. The actual inter-sample waits span five intervals, or 600 ms before automation overhead, rather than the 720 ms stated in one comment.

The test still establishes only limited store-level behavior. It neither observes renderer consumption nor verifies the phase at an exact time, frequency, direction, full-cycle coverage, modulation-panel authoring or preset loading. Different motion on the same circle can meet its radius and spread bounds. Its early heuristic against values near zero can also reject a legitimate relative offset if a nonzero authored base lies within the orbit's reach of zero; that condition is not a universal proof of incorrect composition. For RFF, test the analytic values at controlled timestamps as well as live integration, and verify the final effective shader inputs and displayed output.

The playback smoke creates a two-key scalar track, starts playback and checks that frame position advances and Julia power changes from its first key while staying within the endpoint range. It explicitly skips scrubbing despite the broader opening description. isPlaying is collected but not asserted, pause is invoked without testing that time then stays fixed, and the sample is not compared with the value expected at its actual frame. The range checks also allow NaN through JavaScript comparisons; subsequent toFixed calls on numeric NaN do not reject it. This limits the claim to the particular assertions rather than a complete playback/scrub contract. Invalid or stale values should fail explicitly, not masquerade as movement.

For RFF's 2D zoom movies and 3D material animation, adopt generic parameter tracks with explicit units, interpolation and composition order. Use an authoritative frame/time input for export so identical frame requests produce identical effective settings regardless of preview timing. Keep deep-zoom centers in their high-precision representation and animate zoom in an explicitly defined scale domain rather than placing ordinary floating-point coordinates in a generic scalar channel. Test playback, pause, seek, scrub, endpoint behavior, save/load and rendering separately. The two reviewed fixtures motivate this reusable architecture; they do not prove deterministic export or authorize changing RFF's existing serialized track/config formats incompatibly.

## Timeline retiming and explicit parameter-writer ownership (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/smoke-audio-fps-remap.mts` and `debug/smoke-binder-registry.mts`. These browser tests were not executed. They describe useful contracts for RFF animation features but do not establish audio export or GPU binding correctness.

The retiming test distinguishes keeping integer frame positions from preserving approximate wall-clock positions when the frame rate changes. It checks both a parameter key and two synthetic audio-clip start positions through a 60-to-30 change, undo, redo, return to 60 and a keep-frames change to 24. The distinct odd clip position is valuable: 91 maps to 46 by nearest rounding, whereas floor would produce 45. Undo restores 91 from history; converting 46 back at twice the rate produces 92. Thus undo and inverse rate conversion are deliberately different operations. RFF should make that distinction explicit if it adds synchronized audio or richer timeline editing, and snapshot the whole affected state for a single reversible retiming operation.

The test does not load audio, measure audible synchronization or inspect encoded output. It does not check trim fields, clip duration, other metadata, key collisions, sequence limits or the playhead after retiming. Its keep-mode checks cover audio starts and fps, not keyframes. Only ratios one-half and two exercise match-mode rounding, so ceil and nearest remain indistinguishable in these cases; the source explicitly acknowledges this limitation. Historical mutation results in comments were not repeated. For RFF, use non-half ratios as well, define collision and rounding policy, and consider an authoritative time representation that avoids cumulative rounding during repeated rate changes. Any representation change must preserve existing saved-format compatibility rather than silently reinterpret old integer frames.

The binder test exercises a complementary animation contract: an explicitly registered parameter writer should override an automatic writer, unregistering should restore automatic behavior, and a late registration should take precedence over a cached automatic writer. It scrubs fixed frames and compares the custom sink with the store, including a known linear interpolation value of 35 at frame two. This is stronger than merely counting calls because it checks that the competing sink is not updated at the same time. The pattern is relevant to RFF if a generic animator needs specialized writers for high-precision coordinates, coupled material parameters or values requiring renderer invalidation.

The fixture still has limits. Its first custom-write check compares the store after custom and automatic scrubs rather than recording the original store value, so it does not prove the custom phase left every relevant state unchanged. Several numeric comparisons omit explicit finiteness checks; NaN can evade typeof-plus-range checks and absolute-difference tolerances. It tests one scalar id, direct scrub calls and one override lifecycle, not vector components, duplicate registrations, teardown ordering, save/load or shader consumption. A passing registry test cannot demonstrate that a Vulkan descriptor or push constant receives the intended value.

For both 3D material animation and 2D palette/zoom animation, define one authoritative effective value per parameter, an explicit composition order for tracks and modulators, and a clear owner for writing coupled or precision-sensitive state. Validate timing independently from parameter routing, then verify rendered frames and export synchronization. The practical adoption opportunity is a reusable animation layer with specialized precise bindings, rather than separate ad hoc oscillators for each shader effect. These files support that design direction without proving it is already implemented or measured in RFF.

## Camera bookmarks and gesture commits need complete state checks (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/smoke-camera.mts` and `debug/smoke-canvas-pan-zoom.mts`. Both exercise the fluid-toy 2D camera by default, not the full GMT 3D camera. Neither was executed during this audit.

The bookmark fixture demonstrates an adapter-based camera slot: save an application-specific view, change it, recall it, serialize a preset, clear the slot and reload. Checking that clearing actually empties the slot is a useful nonvacuous round-trip pattern. RFF can use camera/location bookmarks for repeated shader comparisons as well as navigation, provided the saved state identifies the intended view precisely. A shared bookmark interface can support 3D position/orientation and 2D center/scale without pretending their payloads are interchangeable.

The assertions here do not establish the printed claim that the round trip is all exact. They compare only center.x and zoom with a 1e-6 tolerance; center.y and low coordinate components are not checked. Missing nested payload values become undefined, and subtracting them produces NaN, which evades the greater-than-tolerance checks. The preset is JSON-serialized in memory, not written to and read from a file. Loading is checked for the slot label and selected fields, but the restored slot is not subsequently recalled into a deliberately changed live view. For RFF, validate payload types and finiteness, all coordinate components and the actual post-load recall. Deep-zoom equality must use its high-precision representation, with pixel-relative comparisons where approximate behavior is intended. Preserve existing location/config formats when extending bookmarks.

The gesture smoke separates a centered wheel input, an off-center wheel input, a right-button drag and a right click. The off-center case is valuable because a center-only fixture makes the anchor correction zero and cannot detect its removal. However, this test checks only that the center moves in the expected directions, not that the world point under the pointer remains fixed. Incorrect displacement magnitude can pass. It resets the low components to zero, uses one viewport and zoom scale, and does not test transpose, varied display scale or deep-coordinate precision. Its wheel event is dispatched directly to the canvas, so it checks handler behavior rather than the complete native input route.

The pan portion observes committed state after pointer release; it logs but does not assert behavior during the drag. Both coordinate components must move, but neither expected sign nor magnitude is checked. Menu suppression and menu opening are checked as store flags, not visible rendered surfaces. Thus it cannot prove smooth intermediate display, a single commit, one undo entry, pointer-capture recovery or correct menu placement. Browser errors do fail the test, which is useful but separate from those omitted properties.

A practical RFF adoption pattern is a transient interaction state for immediate preview followed by a coherent final commit for history and persistence. Validate that the final committed view matches the last preview, including cancellation and focus-loss paths, and that expensive recalculation is invalidated at the right time. For both 3D camera moves and 2D pans, assert the full coordinate transform and final rendered revision; for 2D cursor zoom, check the high-precision under-pointer point directly. These tests suggest feature and verification patterns, not proof that RFF needs a new bookmark system or that a particular interaction optimization already improves performance. Keep native Win32 menu show-before-first-paint behavior separate from application-controlled gesture/menu state.

## Catalog identity and direct manipulation are distinct from successful rendering (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/smoke-catalog-browse.mts`, `debug/smoke-catalog-load.mts` and `debug/smoke-bc-drag.mts`. No browser interaction or visual review was performed. The first two exercise formula-source browsing/loading, not complete rendered-scene preset restoration.

The browse smoke opens Workshop through the store, clicks a matching browse button through DOM evaluation, and checks the picker shell, a particular source-repository link and at least one image element. Source provenance alongside candidates is useful for RFF's shader/effect library. However, an image element count does not establish successful image decoding, correct thumbnail identity or a representative render. The test never selects a card despite its header promising selection into the editor. DOM presence and programmatic clicking also do not prove the visible picker is accessible through the intended interaction path.

The load smoke directly supplies catalog keys to openWorkshop, covering a cached DEC source path and an asynchronously fetched Fragmentarium path. It checks the first editor element for a short DEC token, then checks only length and generic shader syntax for the named frag. A different source, including stale prior editor contents, could meet those predicates. Falling back from the named DEC entry to the first entry changes the fixture identity without making the test fail. No source hash, selected-key assertion, completed detection result, compilation or image is checked. For RFF, associate each preview and editor state with an immutable source identity and verify the requested revision has arrived before enabling an apply operation. Preserve author/license metadata separately from a repository hyperlink; the latter is not sufficient permission to reuse source.

The gesture smoke demonstrates direct manipulation of brush size and Julia c through modifier-plus-drag gestures. It usefully validates type and finiteness before numeric comparisons, avoiding the NaN/undefined loopholes found in other fixtures. It checks a meaningful increase in brush size and a nontrivial change in the two-component Julia constant. These are useful patterns for responsive 2D exploration and, with an appropriate mapping, 3D material or field controls. The specific default brush and dye values are application choices, not defaults to copy into RFF.

Its asserted scope is narrower than the introductory description: there is no middle-click zoom test. The Julia check only requires some vector displacement, not correct motion in both axes or the expected coordinate under the pointer. Brush growth has no upper-bound or inverse-drag check. It does not verify rendered brush coverage, Julia-image updates, undo grouping, modifier cancellation or that typing in an editor leaves the canvas unaffected. Collected errors fail only when they match a small JavaScript-error pattern; shader compilation or other console errors can remain non-failing. Fixed startup waits and selection of the first canvas further limit its portability.

For RFF's 3D-to-2D feature adoption, separate four outcomes: the correct candidate is selected, the intended parameters are committed, the renderer consumes them, and the resulting image is validated. A 2D palette, orbit mask or coordinate warp can share browsing and direct-manipulation infrastructure with 3D effects, while retaining its own numerical and licensing requirements. Match thumbnail/source identity and parameter units explicitly, and add deterministic state assertions alongside actual rendered-output checks. These scripts support that workflow; they do not establish that any particular effect is visually correct or that a preset round trip preserves all scene state.

## Startup health, compile recovery and contextual actions need separate evidence (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/smoke-boot.mts` and `debug/smoke-canvas-menu.mts`. The already reviewed `debug/smoke-compile-failed.mts` was reread for comparison and is not counted again. No browser tests were executed.

The startup smoke collects JavaScript exceptions, console errors and failed requests, and explicitly reads the application's error-boundary channel. Including caught render exceptions is valuable: a fallback screen can prevent an uncaught exception without making startup successful. It seeds returning-user state, waits for network idle plus two seconds, and prints title/body text for diagnosis. Its final pass condition excludes requestFailures, however, and the HTTP status and page identity are only printed. Thus a transport failure without a console error, or an unexpected error-free page, is not necessarily rejected. The fixed observation window cannot establish completed shader compilation or a correct first image. RFF should define those milestones independently when validating startup with newly added effects.

The compile-failure smoke provides a stronger negative test for its stated subsystem: it registers an intentionally invalid shader, requires the unique marker in the proxy error and visible-state element text, then switches back and checks error clearing and frame-count progress. That is useful evidence design for RFF's shader/pipeline error reporting. Even here, frame-count advancement does not prove restored pixels, and the sampled formula field is printed rather than asserted. A complete recovery check should associate success with the requested shader revision and verify a known valid image. A failed compile, a cleared error indicator and a successfully rendered replacement are different events. The test's browser flags are harness settings, not renderer requirements to transplant into a native Vulkan application.

The context-menu smoke adds an event-level assertion beyond store visibility: a window listener observes whether the contextmenu event was default-prevented after canvas handling. It also checks labels for copy, simulation pause/resume, recenter and reset, and treats browser errors as failures. This establishes expected event cancellation and selected menu-state contents. It does not inspect actual menu placement, clipping, focus, enabled status or the result of selecting any action. The observer depends on the event reaching the window, and matching either Pause or Resume does not establish that the label agrees with simulation state. These limits matter when citing it as interaction coverage rather than as a state smoke.

For RFF, contextual actions such as copying a precise location or returning to a saved view can be useful in 2D exploration and 3D editing, but must be checked through their results, not labels alone. Verify full-precision copied data, correct recenter semantics and coherent render invalidation. Keep the native Win32 menu show-before-first-paint interval separate from this browser event-cancellation test; it is not evidence for changing native-menu painting. Overall, pair startup/error-channel checks with explicit rendered-output and action checks so an apparently healthy UI cannot hide a failed or stale shader. These are validation improvements supporting feature adoption, not new visual effects or runtime findings from this audit.

## Periodic-reference fixtures should validate precision before packing (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/smoke-deep-zoom-nucleus.mts` and `debug/smoke-deep-zoom-orbit.mts`. Targeted source checks also confirmed that HPComplex.toFloat32Pair returns two ordinary Number conversions, while the reference-orbit output is a Float32Array. Those helper files are not newly credited here. No tests were executed.

The nucleus smoke imports the actual period detector, Newton refinement and reference builder, making it more directly connected to production arithmetic than the standalone distance experiments. It checks four shallow nuclei with expected periods, the critical-orbit residual after refinement, an exterior negative control, adoption of a three-sample periodic reference and a shallow-view exclusion. The RFF transfer is a useful test structure: independently check period selection, refined-center residual, reference convention and the integration decision to use the reference. RFF already has FPG and periodic-structure MPA; this is a validation opportunity, not evidence that it lacks periodic acceleration, and it must not be described as BLA.

The numerical assertions do not prove the full 160-bit working accuracy. Expected centers are ordinary Number literals; converting the result to Number and adding the double-double high/low parts in Number arithmetic discards the low-word information the round-trip claim is meant to protect. The residual is evaluated using the same HPComplex implementation under test, so a shared arithmetic defect may affect both solver and verifier. A small period-P residual alone also does not prove minimal period, since lower-period roots can satisfy a multiple-period equation. The separate expected-period checks help for the chosen cases, but do not cover high periods, ambiguous detection balls, failed Newton convergence or deep sub-ulp centers.

The orbit smoke checks explicit low-iteration values, escape-sample placement, bounded examples, a precision-selection threshold, cubic Mandelbrot and Julia initial-state conventions. Disabling automatic reference relocation in raw escaping-orbit cases correctly separates recurrence checks from reference selection. For RFF, retain that separation and verify both the original-coordinate and relocated-reference paths. Julia tests also highlight that changing the initial point and changing the recurrence constant are different operations, relevant to any proposed formula generalization.

Coverage boundaries remain. A precisionBits value above a threshold proves a selected setting, not achieved numerical error. Comparisons to packed Float32Array samples include output quantization; they cannot attribute observed differences exclusively to high-precision or ordinary-double recurrence arithmetic. A maximum-norm loop ignores NaN values because greater-than comparisons with NaN are false, so its boundedness check alone is insufficient. The timed 10,000-iteration case checks elapsed time and buffer-length consistency but not that the requested number of iterations was actually returned. Several zero-orbit cases are useful regressions but weak precision stress tests. No GPU perturbation, periodic wraparound, per-pixel escape result or final image is evaluated.

For RFF, compare high-precision values before packing against independently generated reference data, then validate the packed/compressed representation and consumer separately. Include exact residual/low-word checks, finite-state checks, nontrivial complex coordinates, long periods, reference changes and iteration budgets crossing multiple periods. Retain memory-efficiency requirements when constructing fixtures; a test should not require uncompressed billion-iteration tables. For 2D relief, contour and orbit-based shader features, validate their source fields after the reference/MPA path as well as the final color mapping. These checks protect the numerical foundation on which visually effective 3D-to-2D shading depends.

## Approximation tests must exercise both arithmetic and applicability (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/smoke-deep-zoom-la.mts`. The test was not executed. Its LA mechanism is distinct from RFF's periodic-structure MPA; the transferable contribution is the validation design, not an interchangeable acceleration algorithm.

The test combines table-structure checks, stage-zero predictions and exact small complex-arithmetic fixtures. Its evaluated LA first forms dz times (2 Ref plus dz), then multiplies by ZCoeff and adds dc times CCoeff. It compares this segment prediction with direct perturbation over the same reference samples. Nonzero complex fixtures are especially useful: real-axis-only or zero-input tests cannot expose many imaginary-sign and operand mistakes. The hand-computed coefficient results supplement the aggregate tolerance, which the source records as having allowed a sign mutation previously. Coverage floors for evaluated nodes and stage count prevent a destroyed or empty table from passing with a zero initial error statistic. These are concrete patterns worth applying to RFF's own MPA equations and compressed-table invariants.

The direct comparator is still not an independent high-precision pixel oracle. It uses packed Float32Array reference samples and imports complex addition/multiplication from the same module as the approximation. Each segment starts with a directly recomputed dz rather than the preceding segment's approximate result, so this tests local segment prediction without measuring accumulated error along a real sequence of skips. Its claim that the fixed dc lies within thresholds is not asserted against LAThreshold or LAThresholdC, and runtime eligibility/rejection logic is not exercised. The maximum-error update ignores NaN because NaN is not greater than the current maximum; node-count floors alone cannot close that gap. Explicit finite checks and input-domain checks are needed before interpreting the reported bound.

The stage-one check verifies that a larger-stage table exists and contains fewer nodes, but it does not evaluate its predictions, verify complete interval coverage or show that the rendering consumer selects those skips correctly. A malformed zero-node higher stage can meet the fewer-nodes comparison and only print an infinite average skip. Exact coefficient cases do not inspect threshold propagation or every structural field. Historical measured errors and stage counts in comments are not current measurements from this audit, and the 1e-3 local bound is not an acceptable precision target to import into RFF by analogy.

For RFF, pair nondegenerate exact arithmetic fixtures with independent high-precision end-to-end results. Check valid skip domains, rejection just outside those domains, cumulative skips across period levels, fallback steps, period wraparound and agreement between compressed and uncompressed representations. Require nonempty, finite, structurally complete test coverage before accepting small reported errors. Evaluate the actual consumer as well as table construction. For 2D shading adapted from 3D, include derived distance, gradient and orbit-statistic fields in those comparisons: matching an endpoint does not establish every quantity used by a material or mask. The useful improvement is stronger evidence that acceleration preserves the requested output, without changing RFF's precision policy or conflating MPA with LA/BLA.

## Feature switching: verify the consumer and preserve stored identities (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/smoke-formula-switch.mts` and `debug/smoke-fractal-kind.mts`. No browser tests were executed. These fixtures cover fractal-toy's Mandelbulb/Mandelbox switch and fluid-toy's Julia/Mandelbrot mode routing, respectively.

The formula-switch smoke goes beyond a store write by querying active uniforms on the currently bound WebGL program. RFF can use an analogous pipeline/variant identity check when adding shader features, together with explicit validation of descriptor and push-constant compatibility. WebGL active-uniform introspection itself is not the Vulkan implementation to transplant.

CURRENT_PROGRAM represents the program most recently bound at the probe, which would need more precise identification in a multipass renderer. Fixed waits replace revision-specific completion, and switching directly through setState bypasses user interaction and any specialized selection action. The kind-switch smoke usefully separates three owners: declared parameter defaults, a startup preset's effective state, and the engine's received mode.
