A startup preset can hide a wrong schema default, so checking only the live store would miss it. The fixture also pins the persisted index mapping for Julia and Mandelbrot before checking both transitions at the engine handle. This directly supports RFF's existing stability requirements: never reinterpret saved identifiers or palette recipe ids by reordering an enum or recycling an id. Additive modes need explicit stable identities and compatible loading behavior.

The test does not actually operate a dropdown, validate its option metadata, serialize a save file or inspect rendered mode differences. It asserts only the first two mode mappings, not the complete enumerated domain. Its diagnostic mentions agreement with the engine's default parameters without directly reading that separate declaration. An engine params field changing is stronger evidence than store echo, but still does not prove the shader received the mode, reset temporal history or rebuilt the correct deep-zoom reference. Those are separate invalidation paths to verify.

For both 3D material variants and 2D palette/field modes in RFF, define a complete transition contract: stable saved identity, effective defaults, parameter transfer, required pipeline changes, reference/cache invalidation and a newly completed image. Test A-to-B-to-A transitions with distinguishable parameters so stale state cannot pass by coincidence. Preserve deliberately shared settings while verifying which settings are formula-specific. The adoption benefit is reliable composition and switching of the previously identified visual features; these smokes do not establish new speedups or justify rebuilding a pipeline when a uniform update alone is sufficient.

## Feature-state persistence and worker liveness do not prove rendered state (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/smoke-fractal-toy.mts` and `debug/smoke-engine-gmt.mts`. Neither browser test was executed.

The fractal-toy test groups formula, camera and lighting settings into independently named feature slices and serializes them under feature ids. It changes values, captures a preset, changes them again and reloads the captured JSON. That modular persistence pattern can support reusable 3D material settings and 2D shader effects in RFF, provided stable identities and explicit defaults are maintained. The test's strict equality comparisons for selected restored values reject missing or NaN values more reliably than tolerance comparisons without finite checks.

Its restoration claim is nevertheless partial. It mutates twist, field of view and ambient-occlusion amount but never verifies those fields in the saved or restored state. It does not assert the second mutation took effect before loading, so a setter that accepts the first change but ignores subsequent changes could make a no-op load appear successful. Only selected values from each feature are checked in the serialized object, and the round trip is in-memory JSON rather than file I/O. No renderer parameters, shader bindings, image or dependent cache invalidation are examined. For RFF, use a deliberately different, verified intermediate state, compare the complete intended payload and then verify the rendered revision. Preserve the existing binary configuration ordering and palette-recipe semantics rather than importing the web application's serialization format wholesale.

The main-engine smoke inspects worker boot state, a compile-issued latch, frame-count feedback, default formula and six feature-slice presence flags. It also records canvas ancestry, feature-registry contents and several parameter values for diagnosis. Contrary to one comment that every collected value feeds an assertion, many of those diagnostic fields are not checked, including registry membership, canvas visibility/dimensions and detailed parameter values. Frame feedback proves some communication occurred, not that the requested scene was rendered correctly. The screenshot is saved for human inspection and is not compared by the test.

The source itself explains why hasCompiledShader is not a success signal: it can become true before an asynchronous shader failure. This smoke adds console-error rejection, but filters messages containing deprecation or DevTools anywhere, potentially excluding unrelated errors with those words. It does not explicitly check the later-added compile-failure state exercised by smoke-compile-failed. Its statement that console errors are the only main-thread failure signal is therefore historical context, not a complete description of the reviewed test suite. A fixed eight-second wait is not a completion contract, and no adapter identity is captured despite the header discussing headless SwiftShader limitations. The final success banner's shader-compiled claim is stronger than the directly asserted latch and log conditions.

For RFF, model startup and feature application with explicit requested, compiled, submitted and completed revisions. Verify errors through a structured channel and validate the image independently of frame counters. Persist each effect's full intended state, and test that restoration updates both the CPU configuration and the Vulkan resources consuming it. These requirements apply equally to a 3D lighting feature and its 2D relief/mask adaptation: a healthy worker and a correct settings object can coexist with a stale or invalid image. The opportunity is reliable reuse of effects and reproducible comparison, not a demonstrated performance gain from these tests.

## Binary export smoke: offset traversal is not full container validation (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/smoke-fbx-writer.mts`. It was not executed and no FBX file was generated or imported. The fixture imports the actual binary writer and constructs a small version-7400 scene with nested records, scalar/string properties, long/double arrays and a childless animation-stack record. This is useful focused coverage of several output shapes, but not a full exported scene or every possible writer path.

Its local reader traverses records using their declared end offsets and property byte lengths. It checks that end offsets move forward within the supplied list limit and separately checks the trailing magic and footer version. It never decodes the property payloads or checks their values and type encodings against the input. A wrong scalar, array content or property count can therefore remain undetected if structural offsets still agree. The header magic and version are printed rather than asserted.

The comment that the walk proves it lands exactly on the top-level sentinel and footer is stronger than the implementation. The walk returns no final position, accepts a zero record anywhere in a list, and uses the whole file length as its top-level bound. It does not compare the sentinel location with the footer start or assert that all expected nodes were visited. It also does not reject a property-derived child start beyond the node end when the recursion condition is false. Required childless sentinels, footer identifier and padding are not explicitly validated. These are limits of this checker, not evidence that the writer currently emits malformed files.

The output artifact is written before the final status exit even if accumulated structural checks failed. Its existence is therefore not a pass signal. The suggestion to import it in external applications is a remaining manual step, not a completed interoperability result. The minimal camera Model and debug arrays do not establish camera optical semantics, animation connections, unit/axis conversion or shader/material fidelity.

For RFF, use layered export evidence: compare decoded typed values with the intended scene, check exact structural boundaries, then validate semantics through an independent consumer. Maintain distinguishable failure status alongside any diagnostic output. For 3D camera exchange, verify framing and motion in addition to successful file opening. For 2D zoom-video metadata or location exchange, retain authoritative high-precision centers and explicit time/scale units; an ordinary 3D camera container cannot be assumed to preserve them. The useful transfer is stronger validation of exported data, not a reason to adopt FBX for RFF's native lossless maps or to copy this writer without its own provenance review.

## Capability fallback and gesture feedback need outcome checks (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/smoke-ge-floor.mts` and `debug/smoke-ge-cursors.mts`. These concern the gradient editor shell, not GPU shader arithmetic. Neither was executed and no interface screenshots were reviewed.

The capability-floor test removes roundRect before page code runs and subsequently verifies that the removal took effect. It checks that a wall canvas contains nontransparent pixels, tapping creates a hero element without a page error, and the viewport shell contains both a fallback height class and a modern inline height. Deliberately removing a capability and verifying that the fallback runs is a useful pattern for RFF hardware/resource fallback tests, provided the injected condition corresponds to an actual supported alternative. Browser emulation with one deleted method does not reproduce all behavior of an older browser or physical device; the version claims and historical device reports in the comments were not independently revalidated here.

The pixel probe accepts any positive alpha in the first 64 canvas rows, including partially transparent pixels despite the opaque wording in its log. It does not establish correct gradients, populated tiles or the selected ring's appearance. Hero presence and absence of page errors do not prove that ring was drawn; caught error-boundary state and console errors are not explicitly checked. The height assertions pin declaration shape and computed height on the modern test browser, not actual parsing of unsupported viewport units on the historical browser. Separate behavioral coverage from source-shape checks when adapting this approach to RFF.

The cursor smoke uses elementFromPoint and computed cursor style to distinguish a range edge from its interior, selection from insertion, and an active drag from idle hover. Keeping the gesture's meaning stable while crossing another control is a useful interaction pattern for palette stops, mask handles and 3D material controls. The test checks several points during a drag and restoration over the insertion track after release, which is stronger than checking a single CSS class on the editor root.

Its result is nevertheless cursor feedback, not editing correctness. It never verifies selected knots, inserted stops, range movement or resizing. A cursor-only implementation with broken editing could pass. It covers one edge, one gesture and release inside the page, not cancellation, capture loss, release outside, keyboard interaction or different scaling. Only page errors are collected, and timing relies on fixed waits. An accurate cursor is useful feedback but cannot substitute for asserting the changed model and resulting palette pixels.

For RFF, apply these patterns to deliberate, bounded failures and interactions: verify the fallback actually activates, preserves required precision and produces valid output; verify an active gesture retains ownership and commits the intended values. For both 2D palette/mask editing and 3D shader controls, test feedback, state changes and rendered consequences separately. Native cursor and device-capability handling should use RFF's own architecture; these browser-specific APIs and CSS fallbacks are not direct rendering improvements to port. The reviewed tests add validation ideas around the visual features, without changing the shader-priority ranking or proving measured performance.

## Shared-scene loading: use distinguishing fixtures and verify full provenance (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/smoke-gallery-link.mts`. No server, browser or external gallery was accessed. This is a mocked gallery-loading test, not verification of live service availability or shared-scene image fidelity.

The test uses a real bundled GMF as the scene payload and intercepts gallery-item REST requests with a canned item. It follows a URL query into a lightbox, clicks Open & Remix, and checks that the editor's iteration count changes to a value different from its startup default. That distinguishing-state assertion is a valuable RFF test pattern: a load that leaves the application untouched should not pass simply because the fixture and startup use the same formula. The fixture additionally checks the expected formula, title, fetch occurrence, button disappearance and browser errors.

The mock accepts any URL containing a slug filter and returns the same item; it does not verify the requested slug value or the approval/status filter. Thus the fetch assertion does not prove correct item lookup. Expected formula and iterations are extracted through regular expressions rather than the scene's structural path: the first formula and last integer-looking iteration occurrence determine expectations. A reordered or extended payload can change that interpretation. The discriminating-value assertion rejects some accidental fixture collapse but does not prove the matched value came from the intended scene field.

Only formula and iteration count are examined after loading. Materials, palette, camera, lights, animation tracks, sky references and rendered output are not compared, despite the broad end-to-end description. Removing one button does not independently prove both overlays closed. The canned image is a one-pixel placeholder, so it cannot establish thumbnail-to-scene correspondence. The interception covers the gallery-items endpoint, not a blanket denial of all external network traffic; the documented offline claim should be understood within that mocked path rather than as verified network isolation.

The test explicitly exits successfully without assertions when the gallery is disabled by missing build configuration. That is a documented optional skip, but a suite that treats every zero exit as a pass loses the distinction. Its readiness call also supplies the timeout-shaped object as waitForFunction's second argument, which is the page-function argument, rather than the options position used elsewhere in these scripts. The requested 20-second timeout is therefore not set by that call. No historical mutation claim in the header was rerun here.

For RFF, a reusable scene/effect library should retain stable source identity, schema/version and provenance, with separate evidence for selection, deserialization, parameter application and completed rendering. Use fixtures with distinctive camera, color and material values, verify the pre-load state differs, and compare the complete intended payload through the actual load path. Report skipped external-service coverage separately from verified passes. For 2D adaptations of 3D shader ideas, share appropriate color/mask/effect settings while preserving high-precision locations and explicit compatibility limits; do not imply that a loaded 3D scene has a faithful 2D equivalent. These are adoption and reproducibility opportunities, not evidence that RFF requires a network gallery or that any live sharing feature was tested.

## Editable palette documents versus sampled-ramp interchange (2026-10-08)

Full source review: all 725 lines of `debug/smoke-ge-gradientfile.mts`. No export, import, browser interaction or visual inspection was executed. This substantial browser fixture checks downloads and file entrances with the application's PNG reader, supplementing the separate format tests mentioned in its header.

A useful RFF feature candidate is a palette document that carries both a visible ramp and editable metadata. The test exports a catalog gradient, checks its name and origin credit, edits a stop to step interpolation and changes a bias, then checks the downloaded configuration and imports it through a file chooser. Deliberately testing nondefault interpolation and bias is valuable: a default-only fixture would not detect their omission. For RFF, this could support portable 2D palettes and 3D material ramps, with explicit metadata for color/blend spaces, stop behavior and provenance. It should complement existing stable palette recipes, not alter their ids, seeds or generation order.

The metadata-stripped PNG path intentionally recovers sampled ramp data rather than editable stops. The fixture compares displayRampBytes outputs and rejects routing that same gradient image into ordinary image extraction. This distinction is important: equality of sampled display texels is not equivalence of editable definitions, unlimited-resolution evaluation, HDR precision or continuous interpolation. The comparison uses shared application sampling/decoding code, so common defects can cancel. Its loops inspect expected-length bytes without an explicit equal-length assertion; shorter actual arrays induce a failing NaN result, but extra actual data is ignored. Keep exact document restoration and sampled appearance preservation as separate compatibility claims.

The signature used for configuration comparison covers stop positions rounded to nine decimals, case-normalized color strings, bias, interpolation, color space, blend space and ramp data. It deliberately omits stop ids and normalizes some defaults. It is therefore a semantic subset comparator with finite positional precision, not a byte-exact or every-field comparison. The collection round trip checks count and sorted group/name strings after a verified clear, but not each restored configuration, origin or identity. The CSS import checks addition, naming and reveal in the selected collection, without checking the expected stop colors/positions. The session test verifies the working gradient changes and one undo restores a distinguishable prior gradient, not every session field. Scope these success claims accordingly.

The test also covers useful workflow boundaries: a normal image routes to extraction, a file dropped on a child swatch reaches the intended loader, removed export kinds are cleaned from recents, repeated actions are deduplicated, size edits affect actual downloaded dimensions, and imports become visible in the destination collection. Its phone context checks button bounds and downloads, but is browser device emulation, not physical-device coverage. Synthetic DataTransfer events exercise handlers without proving native OS drag delivery. Confirmation dialogs are automatically accepted within the disposable test context. The script catches page errors but does not gate on console errors, and many steps depend on fixed waits or canvas coordinates.

Delayed image decoding is injected by postponing data-image src assignments. The desktop case verifies that the delay actually occurred and checks reading indicators for both empty and populated slots. This is a useful way to test transient states, but the completion predicate only requires the indicator to disappear and the working kind to be extract; it does not identify the newly decoded image or compare its pixels. Sequential drops do not test out-of-order completion, cancellation or stale-image replacement. Similarly, an explicit z-index value does not establish that an overlay is unobscured in every stacking context.

For RFF, retain the functional ideas: editable palette exports with provenance, a clearly distinct sampled-ramp fallback, consistent import routing, visible imported results and reversible session replacement. Validate metadata with an independent reader where practical and compare actual shader sampling at discontinuities, biases and color-space transitions. Include malformed metadata, profile/alpha behavior, large inputs and concurrent-load identity before treating interchange as robust. For a 3D-to-2D adaptation, share the color definition while keeping its field-to-palette mapping explicit; a material ramp and an escape-time palette may use the same colors but different coordinates. This file provides substantial interaction coverage patterns, not evidence that RFF currently lacks all these capabilities or that the proposed export is already implemented.

## Save feedback is useful only when tied to a verified save (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/smoke-ge-setsave.mts`. This is a gradient-editor feedback-animation test, not a fractal shader or post-processing bloom test. It was not executed.

The test selects a gradient, invokes Keep and inspects a temporary gradient fill on a collection chip. It samples the computed transform twice and requires finite values and a falling vertical scale before checking that the temporary element disappears. This is stronger evidence of animation progress than an animation-name declaration alone: a declared name can exist even when its keyframes are absent. The same principle applies to RFF preview tests: inspect the resulting change rather than only the requested setting.

Several reported properties are not actually established. The background check only recognizes a linear-gradient prefix, not the colors of the saved item. The destination set id and transform origin are printed but never compared with expected values. The label check only requires an animation name, while the bloom check only requires an element with a class. Duration is checked as greater than 600 ms, not against the stated slow constant. The test checks neither collection data nor persistence, so an animation detached from a failed save could pass. Its matrix-component interpretation assumes a simple scale transform; combined rotation or a matrix3d representation would need a different probe. Fixed-time sampling also depends on scheduling and motion settings, neither of which is explicitly normalized here.

For RFF's 2D palette and 3D material libraries, modest destination feedback can help confirm where an item went, but should follow verified data insertion and identify the actual saved item. Test persistence separately, and provide equivalent confirmation when motion is reduced. Keep this as an optional interaction refinement beneath image quality, precision and reliable export priorities. The CSS bloom element here is not evidence for a rendering bloom algorithm and does not affect the non-bloom shader opportunity ranking.

## Palette painting as an explicit, reversible document operation (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/smoke-ge-paint.mts` (299 lines). This desktop browser integration test exercises palette painting, not general canvas repaint invalidation. Brush mathematics are delegated to another suite. It was not executed during this review.

The useful adoption pattern is a local painting buffer with scoped stroke undo, followed by an explicit document commit. A deterministic two-stop palette is opened, real mouse strokes modify the displayed ramp, and Apply converts the document to a sampled ramp with one application undo entry. A second Apply is separately tested: undo removes that second painting while retaining the first. This repeated-commit case is valuable because an initial editor transaction can conceal missing grouping in later operations. When local strokes are exhausted, undo falls through to application history without closing the painting tool; redo restores the painting. Escape discards local work, whereas switching to another editor tab commits it. These are distinct behavioral contracts worth deciding explicitly in RFF rather than inheriting accidentally from widget focus.

The assertions establish less than some success messages imply. Before Apply, the working-document probe checks only stop count and history depth; it does not compare stop colors, positions, bias or the complete original payload. Thus it cannot prove that the working gradient remained untouched. Ramp checks establish a string representation and zero stops, not the complete committed ramp contents. Pixel checks use isolated RGB texels with a threshold of 12 code values, assuming a 256-sample painting surface. The `far` helper classifies missing pixels as different, so a positive change assertion can succeed on missing data; restore assertions using the same helper instead fail. Require valid pixels first and compare the complete relevant document independently of its preview.

Endpoint and wrap coverage should also be interpreted narrowly. The right gutter must match the final painted texel, but the left gutter is not similarly tested. Wrap is checked through alpha coverage in the brush-hover overlay at the opposite end. That demonstrates an overhanging guide, not an actual wrapped stroke or seamless cyclic texture sampling. Switching to Clone only verifies picker visibility; clone-source capture and cloned color output are outside this file's coverage.

Converting a painting back to stops is a particularly useful but lossy operation. The test requires separate history entries for applying pending paint and fitting stops, closes the paint tool, and checks that knots reappear. It compares only one fitted RGB pixel with a tolerance of 30 code values. This is not a global approximation bound and can miss narrow bands, endpoint errors or discontinuities. The Double Stops path checks that a prompt appears and that some stops result, not that the count doubles correctly or that declining preserves the original. Fixed waits, one desktop context and page-error collection provide no GPU image, persistence, console-error or concurrent-update guarantees.

For RFF, a one-dimensional paintable palette could serve both 2D escape-time coloring and 3D material ramps. Keep sampled ramps distinct from editable stop documents, retain the original when fitting stops, and measure whole-ramp error in an explicitly selected color metric with extra sampling around discontinuities. Align wrapping with the shader's palette-coordinate and texture-filtering rules. Connect preview and committed palette revisions to GPU uploads so undo restores both data and displayed output; validate this with actual rendered frames. Preserve existing recipe IDs and generator order, storing painted results as explicit documents rather than silently changing recipe regeneration. This adds artistic control without changing perturbation arithmetic or MPA semantics. It is an adoption opportunity, not an implemented RFF feature or a measured shader-performance improvement.

## Live palette output and deferred stop fitting are separate contracts (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/smoke-ge-livedrag.mts` (367 lines), without execution. The strongest transferable idea is to update the actual sampled color result during a gesture while deferring the expensive reconstruction of editable stops. Freezing the fitted stop layout must not freeze the displayed ramp. Updating colors at old stop positions is also insufficient when an operation moves features along the ramp: it can visibly redraw while displaying the wrong interpolation between displaced features.

The test distinguishes the result canvas from a deliberately frozen source canvas. It watches both color signatures and knot positions during the same mouse gesture, then requires the held positions to differ from a fresh fit before release and agree afterward. That discriminating precondition is useful: if a trivial two-endpoint palette never needs different fitted positions, unchanged positions cannot prove that release performed any work. It also exercises a baked stop document separately from a live input. Baked-document knots must disappear at least once, while any visible layouts remain identical; an identity transform may legitimately reveal current knots again. These cases suggest a clear RFF distinction between the authoritative color preview, the editable representation and whether that representation currently describes the preview.

The strongest color comparison samples 24 output-canvas positions against the pipeline's live ramp during a phase-like drag and after release. It additionally requires at least three distinct ramp signatures, preventing a vacuous comparison of two frozen results. The one-code-value RGB tolerance is justified here by nearest-neighbor expansion of the same samples and differing float-to-byte tie rounding. It should not be copied as a universal tolerance for filtered, HDR or color-managed shader output. In RFF, define the palette texture format, interpolation, transfer function and rounding path first, then compare the expected sampled output under that contract.

There are important limits. The header's claim of repainting on every move is stronger than the executable condition: only three distinct signatures across eight moves are required, with 90 ms waits between moves. Six later comparisons wait 120 ms each. This tests periodic progress, not frame-by-frame responsiveness or pointer-to-present latency. Sixteen RGB samples summarize the bar and eight summarize the ramp; unsampled narrow features, alpha and high-frequency errors can be missed. The final comparison still samples 24 positions, not every texel. Its expected values come from the production working-pipeline debug accessor, so agreement validates presentation consistency rather than independent correctness of the color operations.

Additional acceptance weaknesses matter when adapting the test. Non-finite ramp values can turn the worst error into NaN, which passes both the negative-sentinel and greater-than-tolerance checks; require finite components and error statistics before comparing them. Empty final knot and fit arrays satisfy the matching helper, despite the separate nonempty check made before release. Knot positions are rounded and accepted within 0.01 of the normalized track, not verified against exact stop data. Selecting the widest slider and later the fourth slider is fragile: a different operation can still change the ramp while no longer exercising movement of features along its coordinate. Use stable parameter identity and verify that the intended phase actually changes. The collection tile is selected geometrically rather than by a fixed palette identity. Page errors are collected, but this does not verify Vulkan uploads, a fractal framebuffer, undo grouping, gesture cancellation or performance. Sampling a debug accessor that itself derives a fresh fit may also perturb the work being observed; it cannot establish that no fitting ran during interaction.

For RFF's 2D palette and 3D material-ramp editors, adopt the separation where fitting or other expensive derived representations exist: publish the current ramp promptly, label or hide stale handles, and settle the editable representation on commit. Use revision-aware GPU texture updates and verify the corresponding rendered frame, including a rapid sequence ending in release or cancellation. Benchmark input-to-present latency separately from fitting cost. This is a responsiveness and correctness opportunity shared across 3D and 2D, without reducing fractal precision or changing MPA. It does not establish that RFF currently uses the same fitting pipeline or has GMT's historical regression.

## Session recovery, explicit imports and palette-state fidelity (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/smoke-ge-session.mts` (369 lines). This browser integration suite was read, not executed. Its useful design distinction is between restoring a startup baseline and importing a document during editing. Startup recovery should not create an undo action that immediately removes the recovered work; an explicit file replacement should be reversible. The suite tests these separately, along with independent autosave preferences for the main app and Gradient Explorer. RFF could apply the same distinction to palette/material editing and scene recovery, while retaining its existing configuration-format compatibility rules.

The opt-in checks are deliberately discriminating. Another app's autosave preference is seeded on, while the Explorer preference is unset. Editing and reloading must leave neither a restored editor nor a stored session. Enabling the actual settings row must write only the Explorer preference. Disabling removes its stored session, and a valid session manually reinserted while disabled must still be ignored and removed at the next boot. This last case tests the restore decision itself rather than merely observing that there was nothing to restore. For RFF, decide and document whether disabling recovery also deletes recovery data; GMT's deletion policy is a product choice, not an automatic requirement to copy.

A live Mix input must reopen its owning editor after reload, avoiding accidental reinitialization when entering that editor again. However, the assertions compare only the input kind and open face, not the mix sources, weights or output colors. More generally, the working-document signature concatenates stop positions rounded to three decimals and uppercase colors. It omits bias, interpolation, color/blend spaces, IDs, names, sampled ramps and other working parameters. Equality of this signature does not establish complete session fidelity, and sub-0.001 coordinate changes may be invisible. The knot-track edit helper proves that the signature changes, but does not require the stop count to increase as its insertion description suggests.

The share-link case checks that recognizable linked colors appear and that undo does not reveal the previously stored live input underneath. That is stronger than checking the displayed link alone. Its subsequent claim that a reload occurs without the link needs additional evidence: this test calls `page.reload()` without explicitly navigating to a clean URL or asserting that application code removed the query. If the application retains the query, reapplying it could conceal failed session persistence. Likewise, a 600-second autosave interval reduces periodic-save interference but does not by itself prove that `pagehide` was the unique write path; event or storage instrumentation would distinguish immediate saves, hidden-tab flushing and pagehide. Waiting for the hero and then settling for 900 ms cannot prove the header's first-paint claim. Recorded historical mutation tests are useful context, not fresh execution evidence.

The file path uses an actual browser download and chooser. It checks a versioned envelope, the presence of a working document and exclusion of the favorites shelf. A different palette is constructed from the downloaded body and passed through the production session encoder before import. One undo must restore the previous stop signature. This establishes a useful interaction pattern, but the saved working payload is never independently compared with the original complete state, and the replacement uses the same production encoding conventions. Invalid-JSON storage and a plain-text invalid file exercise graceful refusal; syntactically valid but malformed bodies, unsupported versions, truncated valid envelopes, storage quota failures and interrupted native file writes are separate cases. Invalid-file rejection compares the limited signature, not all state or history depth.

The phone portion is Chromium device emulation. It checks horizontal button bounds and loads through a chooser, without testing vertical visibility of both rows, a phone save/download flow or physical mobile lifecycle behavior. Console errors are not collected. No assertion inspects a rendered fractal frame, GPU palette contents or deep-coordinate preservation.

For RFF, reuse the architectural ideas: explicit precedence among startup recovery and requested imports, separate recovery settings where applications truly differ, an undoable file import, and recovery of the live editor's actual parameters. Validate complete palette/material documents and corresponding shader output, not only stop counts or an approximate signature. Keep 2D escape-time coordinates and 3D material mappings separate from the shared color document. Preserve high-precision view data exactly, recipe identity and generator order, and the append-only ConfigIO contract if settings are added. This is reliable editing and recovery functionality supporting shader work; it is not a new shader effect or evidence of a current RFF recovery defect.

## Stop reduction can search representations, but needs a separate fidelity bound (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/smoke-ge-reduce.mts` (498 lines), without execution. The adoption opportunity is interactive simplification of a color document: preview several reductions, choose a target stop count, optionally search alternative blend spaces, then commit the selected representation as one undoable operation. Searching blend spaces can express a ramp with fewer stops than merely deleting points in its current space. The fixture demonstrates the intended case by rendering a blue/yellow Spectral blend, fitting that result into RGB stops, and expecting the desktop search to recover a compact Spectral representation. This is palette interpolation behavior, not proof of spectral light transport or a physically complete material model.

Several integration checks are particularly useful. Hover and touch previews change the result strip while replacing real knots with preview knots. Leaving the hover, Cancel and Escape must restore every RGBA sample across the strip's first row. The slider is traversed with real mouse input, and every count from 2 to 15 must be observed with a corresponding preview-knot count. Apply must use the preview's count and named blend mode while preserving output color space. Undo compares stop positions, colors, bias, interpolation and both spaces; this is stronger than the approximate signatures in the session smoke. A second reduction on an already edited document checks undo grouping independently of the initial document bake. These are good RFF acceptance patterns for reversible palette simplification shared by 2D coloring and 3D material ramps.

Those checks do not establish fidelity of the reduced result. The suite requires the preview to change, not to stay within a measured color-error bound. No independent renderer compares original and simplified ramps over the full domain, sharp edges or cyclic endpoints. Apply checks count and spaces without requiring the committed pixels to equal the chosen preview. The supposedly inert preview knots are counted, not dragged to verify inertness. The working projection excludes IDs, names, provenance and ramp payloads; normalization also equates missing bias/interpolation with defaults. Exact undo is therefore exact only for those projected fields. Full-row cancellation is useful but still tests the editor's canvas rather than GPU palette sampling or the fractal image.

The fixtures intentionally include nondefault RGB blending and linear output, which helps catch accidental space resets. However, bumpy-fixture stops have default bias and linear interpolation, so that branch would not reveal a reset of nondefault values. The Spectral fixture and expected compactness are generated using production sampling/fitting code; correlated errors can survive. Its numeric assertion allows any count at most three, rather than explicitly requiring two or three. The phone branch only verifies that no displayed candidate names Spectral; all amounts being disabled, or absence of a mode label, can satisfy it without proving what the search evaluated. Do not infer computational savings or output quality from that exclusion test.

Other coverage limits are concrete. Declining ramp-to-stops conversion checks that no reduction popup or stop-count element appears, but does not compare the ramp bytes or document history. The pending-state helper can succeed when the popup is absent because optional chaining yields no pending attribute. The second page used for preference persistence and the ramp/Spectral pages collect page errors but never gate their own results on those arrays. Setting both ONLY_PHONE and ONLY_DESKTOP skips both suites while still printing success. Preference persistence is tested in a new page of the same context, not a restarted browser; live cross-page synchronization is deliberately not required. Desktop/mobile layout checks establish bounding rectangles and touch access in emulation, not physical-device performance. Fixed waits and screenshots, when requested, do not constitute latency measurements or visual inspection results.

For RFF, treat stop reduction as an explicitly lossy editing operation with a reversible original. Evaluate each candidate under a defined color metric and the actual shader sampling contract, retaining sharp transitions and wrap behavior. Offer target count and preview without implying that fewer stops necessarily accelerate rendering: if RFF uploads a fixed-size palette texture, stop reduction principally simplifies editing and storage, while texture lookup cost remains largely unchanged. Cache or defer expensive candidate searches as needed, measure them separately, and preserve the selected blend mode in the document. Verify licenses and provenance before adapting any distinctive pigment-mixing implementation. Keep recipe regeneration stable and use explicit edited documents for derived palettes.

Cross-check with the preceding session review: this file comments that the shell removes `?g=` after reading it. That supports the intended clean-reload behavior, but is still a comment rather than an executable URL assertion in the session test. It does not close that test's evidence gap by itself.

## Palette-library interaction must preserve pending material edits (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/smoke-ge-wall.mts` (319 lines), without execution. This tests the relationship between a palette library and its active editor, rather than thumbnail color fidelity. Its most relevant RFF pattern is preservation of pending local work when choosing another palette. A stroke is made, the library is activated, and a different palette is chosen. The expected history contains two operations: commit the painting, then select the replacement. One undo must recover the painted ramp. This makes exploratory palette browsing reversible for both 2D coloring and 3D material editing. It should be considered alongside explicit Apply/Cancel semantics, not copied without deciding RFF's intended behavior when changing documents.

The other useful pattern is a library state dependent on the active tool. Mix needs the library as its picker; other tools can dim or hide it. Clicking the dimmed library activates it without selecting a tile or adding history, and a subsequent click selects. The visibility preference survives a fresh navigation, but Mix and the absence of an active editor override it to expose the picker. A persistent, reachable show button provides a return path. RFF could offer an optional collapsible palette/material browser during detailed edits, while avoiding accidental palette replacement. The web-specific veil and two-click activation are possible interaction choices, not requirements for native RFF.

The test uses actual hit testing to require that the toggle is above the veil and that chosen points reach a library canvas. This is stronger than checking a z-index declaration. It also opens the image editor through a synthetic paste event, bypassing the usual tab press. That distinguishes a per-tool state reset from a reset that only happens incidentally when the user clicks inside the editor. For RFF, test equivalent non-panel entry routes such as import commands as well as button-driven transitions. A synthetic ClipboardEvent proves routing of supplied data, not operating-system clipboard permissions or native image formats.

Coverage remains narrower than the success messages. Dimming is inferred from a state attribute and pointer-event interception; veil strength and visible contrast are explicitly not asserted. The current-input comparison uses only the first 400 characters of serialized input, so changes beyond that prefix can be missed and distinct palettes can be treated as identical. The selection helper tries multiple geometrically located tiles and may undo unsuccessful candidates; it does not establish a deterministic palette identity or compare the chosen tile's colors with rendered output. Curves remaining open is checked, but refitted curve values are not. The tucked toolbar corner check has upper bounds only; separate center-point reachability helps but does not prove its full rectangle stays on screen. A 1440-by-1100 desktop viewport leaves generous room and does not establish behavior on smaller windows or high-DPI layouts.

The pending-paint case compares one RGB texel, assumes a 256-sample surface and allows a difference of 12 code values. Its change helper treats missing pixels as different, weakening the initial stroke setup; the later restore comparison rejects missing values, but still does not compare the whole painted ramp. The representation check establishes zero stops and a ramp string, not complete document identity. The activation-only check compares history depth and the truncated input rather than all edit state. Keyboard accessibility, pointer cancellation, persisted document content and GPU uploads are outside this suite. Page errors are gated at the end, while console errors and measured latency are not covered.

For RFF, prioritize the transaction guarantee over visual dimming: a new palette choice should not silently discard local paint or material edits, and undo should restore the actual color document and the corresponding GPU-visible revision. Validate complete payloads plus a rendered result, including sharp palette features away from the single probe. If a browser is hidden, separately determine whether thumbnail rendering work is suspended; CSS visibility in this test is not evidence of CPU or GPU savings. This is an editing-reliability improvement transferable between 3D and 2D, not a shader-quality or performance result.

## Fullscreen previews need an explicit live source and fallback identity (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/smoke-ge-wallpaper.mts` (215 lines), without execution. This is a fullscreen gradient-preview integration test, not a wallpaper shader benchmark. Its architectural contribution is a host-registered live color source: a reusable preview resolves the current working palette through a registration point rather than assuming one editor's internal store layout. The overlay is initially opened with a snapshot, then edits to the working document should update it. If the live source cannot produce a gradient, a snapshot fallback keeps the preview usable. A comparable RFF preview could serve a 2D palette editor and a 3D material editor through explicit document identity and revision, avoiding a stale opening snapshot.

The test verifies a registered hook exists, creates a known navy/amber palette, opens the overlay and switches to a very different neon palette. It downsamples the canvas to eight RGBA pixels and requires a changed signature. This demonstrates a broad visible response if the canvas remains valid, but does not verify the expected neon colors or the correctness of interpolation. Only the initial sample rejects the NO_CANVAS sentinel: a missing canvas after editing produces a different string and passes the immediate change assertion. A later canvas check provides another constraint but does not prove that the change step rendered correctly. Downsampling also removes narrow spatial features and depends on canvas filtering; it is unsuitable as a precision oracle for palette texels or shader output.

The empty-input test sets an image-extraction input without an image and requires a nonuniform RGB result. It does not assert that the registered resolver returns null or compare against the opening snapshot or last valid live result. Any nonuniform stale output could pass. The source comments alternate between an opening-snapshot fallback and leaving the last gradient visible; these are different identities after the neon edit. RFF should define which fallback is intended, retain that exact revision, and compare the fallback output to it. A uniform gradient can be legitimate, so nonuniformity should not be the general validity criterion.

The split-preview keyboard case is stronger: it tests both directions. A real mouse press in a control-free application area followed by Escape must preserve the overlay; a press in the preview followed by Escape must close it. Hit-tested points avoid accidentally activating a toolbar control. However, this does not test whether the application's own Escape action actually occurred, keyboard-only focus movement, other shortcuts or native window focus. The split-state accessor is used only in failure diagnostics, not as an affirmative setup assertion. For RFF, route preview shortcuts by the intended focus/interaction contract and test the main editor action as well as preview survival.

The harness mutates production stores through bare-URL dynamic imports. The file documents that development hot reload can create a second module instance, making registration appear absent or edits affect an unrendered store. This is a known harness ambiguity in the source, not evidence that a failure should automatically be dismissed. Prefer a deliberate test interface attached to the running application instance, and verify instance identity before interpreting results. Console filtering is also broader than its comment: any message containing net::ERR_FAILED is discarded, even without the catalog CDN hostname. Noncatalog failures can therefore be hidden. Fixed waits of hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, direct store mutation and one desktop viewport provide no interaction-latency, native input or GPU-frame guarantees.

For RFF, the useful adoption is a preview that explicitly follows the active color document, supports a well-defined fallback, and remains usable beside the editor. Verify the full expected palette result and actual rendered frame with matching revision IDs. A 3D material preview must retain its lighting and field-to-color mapping; a 2D fractal preview must retain its escape-time mapping. Sharing the color source does not make those images interchangeable. This improves preview reliability and comparison workflows, without establishing a new lighting effect, shader speedup or existing RFF defect.

## Undo scope and editor context are different design decisions (2026-10-08)

Full document review: `docs/adr/0023-undo-per-scope-stacks.md` (33 lines) and `docs/adr/0120-the-interface-rides-the-undo-entry.md` (152 lines). These are design records, not runtime verification. Together they offer a useful distinction for RFF: which history owns an action is separate from which editor context accompanies that action.

ADR-0023 records separate parameter and camera stacks, with animation history handled separately, typed camera entry points and a 50-entry limit per lane. The motivation is preventing an ordinary parameter undo from unexpectedly reverting camera motion. RFF could preserve distinct histories for color/material edits and navigation if that matches its established controls, with explicit commands and understandable labels. The same principle extends to 2D pan/zoom and 3D camera movement. Separate stacks do not by themselves make incorrect routing structurally impossible, despite the record's broad consequence claim: controls can still call the wrong lane, and cross-scope actions require a deliberate atomicity policy. The recorded animation deferral remains a design caveat, not proof of a current runtime defect.

ADR-0120 is specifically scoped to Gradient Explorer v2 and explicitly excludes the main GMT application. Its latest update makes interface providers contextual snapshots that accompany data history entries without creating entries merely for navigation. Undo restores the interface from gesture start; redo uses the interface state captured when undo was invoked. Thus redo is not necessarily a replay of the exact original post-gesture panel arrangement. This policy can help RFF return a user to the palette or material controls responsible for an edit, while keeping ordinary panel opening off the data history stack. It should remain a consciously chosen RFF behavior rather than a wholesale transplant of a host-specific decision.

Read the document chronologically: the September 24 update supersedes the original change-only provider mechanism and removes the reliance on flushSync described in sections 2–3. Those older sections and several consequence bullets remain as history. Copying their synchronous-flush prescription as the current design would misread the record. The newer mechanism carries context even when a surface changes outside the data bracket; tab switching is grouped with its fit operation. Inspected-stop selection, armed Mix slot and filter/fold ownership are added to the contextual state. This also makes the older statement that only four fields are captured stale; capture cost must be measured for the actual providers rather than called free.

The strongest invariant is that a document-dependent editor must not remain open after history returns to no document. The record places that rule at the shell level because independent history providers may restore in different orders. It deliberately distinguishes an absent document from a valid but incomplete operation, such as an image-extraction editor waiting for an image or a Mix with no inputs. For RFF, validate editor context after the complete restoration transaction, preserve legitimate incomplete editing states, and avoid rejecting them merely because no preview can yet be rendered. Restore selection by stable identity where possible and handle selections whose target no longer exists.

The later Escape policy is also explicit: Escape cancels the current face, an untouched visit adds no data entry, and undo after an edited cancellation can recover that editing context. Leaving through other routes may commit. These are interaction semantics to specify and test, especially when adding palette painting, stop reduction or material controls. They do not establish that every cancellation should create history or that RFF must change its existing Escape behavior.

For RFF, adopt only the useful guarantees: consistent scope routing, one transaction for a user-visible edit, lightweight optional context captured with that transaction, and valid editor state after all providers restore. Verify parameter values, palette bytes, selection, open controls and the resulting GPU frame together. Do not put high-precision orbit buffers or full render targets into every context snapshot; retain precise document parameters and manage heavyweight resources separately. Preserve numerical precision and the existing palette/configuration contracts. Neither design record proves implementation completeness, memory cost, shader quality or performance; cited historical falsification runs need current execution before being treated as present test results.

## Parameter snapshots must precede the first input mutation (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `debug/smoke-undo.mts` (290 lines), without execution. This main-application smoke complements the separate Gradient Explorer history design. Its strongest directly exercised mechanism is transaction ordering at pointer-down: a real registered scalar control must capture its pre-interaction value before a track click changes it. The test seeds a value of five, presses the actual slider, checks the active snapshot, drags, and requires undo to return to five. This is a useful RFF acceptance case for material roughness, palette controls and post-processing sliders, where capturing the first changed value would make quick undo restore an intermediate state.

Other sections validate store contracts more narrowly. A roughness transaction checks one entry, change to zero, undo and redo. An LFO fixture changes period from five to twelve and tests restoration, but has an empty target and does not exercise a connected LFO slider or time-dependent shader output. Histogram coverage directly brackets a levelsMax update; it does not drag a histogram handle and therefore cannot prove that the handle opens a transaction. An absent color-grading slice is reported as a successful skip. Camera coverage starts the camera interaction route and writes a synthetic quaternion directly into the store, then checks only its x and w components after undo. It does not verify y/z, camera position, redo, interpolation state or rendered viewpoint. The synthetic quaternion is not normalized, so this case should not be interpreted as a camera-math validation.

The scope-isolation section's heading describes parameter undo ignoring camera history, but the executed case is the reverse: one parameter entry exists, camera history is empty, and camera undo must return false while leaving the parameter entry available. That is valuable but does not cover both populated lanes, both undo directions or unchanged parameter values. Mixed edits and redo invalidation need their own discriminating fixtures before claiming complete scope isolation.

Shortcut coverage exercises both registration orders for equal-priority bindings and requires the first registration to win. It also replaces the real camera-undo and parameter-redo handlers with recording stubs, dispatches a synthetic Ctrl+Shift+Z event and checks which binding wins. This proves resolver selection under that setup, not that the actual handler restores the camera. RFF should test its established shortcuts with real resulting state and native focus conditions; GMT's choice to assign Ctrl+Shift+Z to camera undo is a product-specific convention, not a recommendation to replace RFF bindings. Text inputs, modal controls and timeline focus can change routing and are not covered here.

There are additional harness limits. The initial wait passes its timeout object as the page-function argument rather than Playwright's options argument, so the stated 20-second limit is not applied by that call. No deterministic returning-user or feature-state seed is installed here. The negative assertion that a dragged value differs from five accepts NaN because the near helper returns false; positive restore comparisons reject it, but a broken transient value could still escape detection. Require finite values throughout. A missing pointer interaction is labeled a positioning miss without evidence that rules out an application handler failure. Page and console errors are collected without the broad exclusions seen in some other smokes, which is useful, but no GPU-frame or device validation occurs.

For RFF, adopt the transaction ordering test and extend it across real histogram, palette, material and navigation controls. Verify a changed value, one coherent undo step, exact restored document data, redo, and the corresponding displayed result. Shared 2D/3D color controls benefit directly; camera tests must use each mode's actual representation and preserve deep-zoom precision. History success at the store level alone does not prove that Vulkan uniforms, textures or accumulated frames were invalidated correctly. This is reliability support for shader features, not evidence of an implemented RFF regression or a rendering-speed improvement.

## Historical transaction design: sparse history and render invalidation (2026-10-08)

Full document review: `docs/history/engine/06_Undo_Transactions.md` (184 lines). This historical guide is useful architectural evidence, not an authoritative statement of every current host's behavior. Its central transferable mechanism is recording pre-gesture parameters, retaining only changed keys at commit, restoring through normal setters where possible, and explicitly invalidating accumulated rendering after restoration. For RFF, undoing a material, palette or post-processing change must update the rendered result as well as the displayed control. The exact invalidation scope should follow actual dependencies: a palette-only change need not discard reusable high-precision fractal computation, while any cached image depending on the palette must be refreshed.

The document describes feature-registry-driven parameter capture plus selected scene fields. This highlights an integration requirement for new shader features: registering a visible control is not enough unless its parameters also participate in history, persistence and render updates. A no-op gesture should leave no history entry. Sparse entries reduce retained history data but do not eliminate the cost of taking a full pre-gesture snapshot or comparing its keys. The stated 50-entry cap is an entry count, not a byte budget; large palette arrays or nested feature state can still dominate memory. RFF should avoid storing orbit tables, GPU resources and transient framebuffer data in these snapshots, while preserving exact high-precision document values.

Several historical details require qualification. JSON-stringification comparison is described as the change detector; that is not a general numerical equality contract and should not be transplanted to GMP-backed or binary state. Camera recordings are described as suppressed within a 1500 ms window when the stack is nonempty. Such time grouping can combine distinct quick gestures and needs tests across interleaved edits, undo, redo and cancelled interaction. Prefer explicit gesture boundaries unless a documented product behavior calls for merging. The statement that a five-knob multi-touch gesture produces one entry is an asserted behavior, not proof of correct nested-transaction or overlapping-pointer handling in this document.

The redo prose is temporally imprecise: it says current values are captured before applying undo, but then calls them the post-undo state. The described capture would preserve the values immediately before undo. The actual implementation and tests must decide the contract, especially for independently changing values. Likewise, a fallback to direct state assignment can bypass setter side effects even when a global accumulation reset occurs; palette uploads, derived coefficients and uniform bindings require their own dependency updates. RFF should restore a coherent transaction and schedule a frame from that completed state rather than expose a partially restored mixture of parameters.

This guide's no-UI-history and no-grouping limitations must not be read as current universal GMT limitations. The later, separately reviewed ADR-0120 adds contextual interface history and grouping for Gradient Explorer v2 without requiring a new public UI scope. The historical claim that non-feature UI state is not snapshotted also does not describe those later providers. Its preset-load policy clears history, whereas the Explorer session-import tests deliberately require an undoable replacement. These are different host/workflow contracts. Neither policy is logically mandatory: a complete atomic replacement can support undo, while a deliberate document boundary may clear history. Specify the RFF policy before adopting either.

For shared 3D and 2D editing, keep navigation history routing explicit, use typed parameter snapshots, and verify that each newly added shader setting survives undo/redo with the correct render revision. Distinguish animation keyframe history from live modulation parameters: separate timeline history does not mean every animation-related value is absent from parameter snapshots, as the reviewed LFO smoke demonstrates. Add precision-preserving camera state for 2D deep zoom rather than copying the three-field 3D pose record. This document contributes integration criteria and historical tradeoffs; it does not establish a current RFF defect, measured memory saving or shader speedup.

## Renderer-comparison briefs define questions, not verified equivalence (2026-10-08)

Full document review: `plans/mb3d/sessions/S-render-pipeline-spec.md` (107 lines) and `engine-gmt/features/fragmentarium_import/reference/Examples/Kashaders/README.md` (3 lines). The first is a historical task brief; its commands to delegate, create specifications and commit are source material, not instructions for this RFF review. The second only identifies a Fragmentarium shader collection, mainly fractals. It provides no shader mechanism, license grant or compatibility guarantee by itself.

The render-pipeline brief contributes a useful comparison structure for RFF: follow camera-ray construction, distance-estimator dispatch, iteration scheduling, march advancement and termination, surface-hit threshold, refinement, normal sampling and imported parameter conversion separately. A correctly translated formula does not by itself establish equivalent rendered geometry or shading. The brief's claim of 279 decoded formulas with zero cross-check mismatches is a recorded assertion; this file contains neither the fixtures nor execution evidence needed to reproduce it. Its proposed equivalence work must not be treated as already completed merely because the brief calls the intended specification definitive.

Several hypotheses identify meaningful failure boundaries. Distance termination and a maximum step count are different reasons for a ray to stop; exhausting a work budget must not silently acquire the same meaning as finding empty space. Post-hit refinement cannot recover a surface that the primary march never reached. Normal-probe distance, hit tolerance and the scale factor applied to a numeric distance estimate are different quantities and need distinct units and mappings. Per-slot iteration counts and the scene's overall cap are also separate contracts. The brief explicitly warns that earlier explanations confused these mechanisms. Its source coordinates and historical paths are starting points for verification, not current line-level evidence for the equations listed there.

For RFF's 3D rendering, these distinctions suggest explicit termination diagnostics and precision-preserving comparisons of estimator output, hit position and normal before judging a material or lighting change. Do not simply remove a GPU work cap to mimic a CPU renderer: evaluate bounded work scheduling, cancellation and resumable rendering if a fidelity requirement exceeds an interactive budget. The brief alone provides no measurements establishing a safe cap or performance benefit. Likewise, translating an imported scene's visual settings should distinguish an exact supported mapping from an approximation whose resulting image must be checked.

For 2D, transfer the validation structure rather than a 3D ray marcher. Distinguish escape, interior classification, reference exhaustion and work-budget exhaustion; verify palette coordinates and derivative-based shading independently of the orbit computation. Preserve high-precision coordinates and RFF's MPA periodic-structure semantics. A 3D distance-estimator scale or normal-probe constant is not automatically appropriate for a 2D perturbation path. The useful adoption is explicit numerical contracts and observable failure modes supporting the already identified shader opportunities, not an unsupported proposal to replace RFF's computation core.

The short Kashaders README does not authorize copying distinctive shader formulas or constants. Any later adaptation must retain the implementation-specific provenance and verified license recorded elsewhere or establish them from the actual source. Collection naming alone is insufficient. Neither of these two documents changes the shader-effect ranking or supplies new runtime evidence.

## Detailed renderer specification: useful mechanisms and internal qualifications (2026-10-08)

Full document review: `plans/mb3d/research/gmt-render-pipeline-spec.md` (805 lines). Its historical VERIFIED tags and line references are source claims, not fresh verification by this review. The opening correction is significant: MB3D comparisons were re-anchored from an uncalled RayMarch body to the live CalcThread loop. This supersedes the older session brief's source map. RFF comparisons must trace reachable dispatch, including formula and quality variants, rather than infer behavior from a plausibly named function.

The specification describes several useful 3D mechanisms: screen-footprint-dependent hit tolerance with a numerical floor, short-biased step jitter during accumulation, tracking the best near-miss relative to local tolerance, optional post-hit refinement, and distinct normal estimators. It separates compile-time feature inclusion from runtime controls. These are independent choices: refinement improves a found intersection, candidate recovery changes which misses are accepted, and stochastic stepping changes sampling. They do not repair an incorrect distance field merely by being enabled. In RFF, classify their intended effect and validate thin structures, grazing surfaces, sharp color changes and temporal stability separately.

Two internal numerical discrepancies are directly resolvable from the printed formulas. The recovery condition is ratio <= 1 + tolerance, so tolerance 2 accepts a candidate up to three times finalEps, not the two times stated in the prose. In the estimator table, 0.34657359 times log2(r squared) is approximately ln(r), not 0.5 times ln(r). Thus the displayed dampened estimator numerator is approximately r*ln(r), whereas the default coefficient 0.17328679 gives approximately 0.5*r*ln(r). Do not erase that factor-of-two difference when translating the table. These are specification inconsistencies, not newly verified runtime bugs.

Other equivalence claims need narrower wording. Preserving trap/color data from the coarse hit avoids another expensive evaluation, but after moving the intersection that data is not necessarily equal to evaluation at the refined point. Subpixel geometric motion can cross a discontinuous palette or orbit-trap boundary. Reusing a snapshot at exactly the same point is a different claim and additionally assumes a deterministic evaluation context. A binary search needs an appropriate bracket and field behavior; the shown loop does not prove these conditions at an initial hit or a recovered near-miss. Likewise, a positive step floor guarantees forward progress only when its inputs and direction remain finite and the effective multiplier is positive.

The numeric estimator's extra probe factor cancels the leading finite-difference scaling only where differences are approximately proportional to probe size. It does not make the finite estimate exactly probe-invariant near folds, clamped orbit radii, precision loss or changing iteration counts. The described shared center count is valuable because independent escape counts introduce another discontinuity, but the radius cap and rounding still matter. Calling a footprint-dependent, clamped probe zoom-invariant is too broad: the probe itself varies with footprint until a clamp binds. A wider probe for secondary distance calls can yield a different effective field from the primary call, requiring shadow/AO consistency checks rather than an assumption of geometric equivalence.

The document also contains historical tensions to resolve at source before adoption. Section 8 calls the header RStop radius-squared while section 9 calls it linear and explicitly squares it. The coarse-step importer floor and forced recovery are calibrated compromises, not guarantees of faithful geometry. The suggested low fudge factor for deep views differs from the importer's minimum, reflecting budget tradeoffs. Compile-time loop ceilings are repeatedly called unrolled while another passage says ANGLE does not unroll them; actual driver behavior needs compiler or timing evidence. Claimed 5-percent mapDist regression, numeric-DE cost, compile delays and visual equivalence between two box estimators depend on historical fixtures and hardware, not universal algebraic equivalence. The coefficient and threshold discrepancies above are enough to show that line-tagged prose still needs inspection.

For RFF's 3D shading, consider footprint-aware normals, optional refinement and precisely defined termination diagnostics as independent experiments; retain sharp detail and numerical correctness as acceptance criteria. Preserve orbit/color semantics when optimizing geometry-only evaluations. For 2D, transfer screen-footprint filtering, separation of geometry/computation from coloring controls, and independent validation of derivative shading. Do not transfer 3D march caps, numeric-DE calibration constants or low-precision modes into deep perturbation computation. RFF's MPA is a distinct periodic-structure approximation and must not be recast as the iteration machinery described here. This specification adds implementation questions and mechanisms to the adoption report; it does not supply new benchmark results or justify changing the current shader-priority ranking on its own.

## Archived path-tracing switch timings measure compilation, not image benefit (2026-10-08)

Full artifact review: `debug/measure-pt-switches.out.txt` (39 lines). The already reviewed producer `debug/measure-pt-switches.mts` was selectively rechecked for measurement labels and parsing; no additional full-file credit is assigned to it. The output records historical compile-switch observations for Mandelbulb and GreatStellatedDodecahedron. It is not a new benchmark run.

The archived baseline values are 10341 ms and 15140 ms respectively. The combined environment MIS plus importance-sampling variant adds 2579 ms and 7274 ms; area-light variants add 2027 ms and 4381 ms. Sobol's recorded difference is only 23 ms in one scene but 2865 ms in the other. These figures show why feature cost cannot be inferred from one formula or a small source-code change. They are single observations with no repeated trials, spread, hardware identity, driver version, source revision or image-quality results in this artifact. They do not establish stable marginal costs, statistical significance, interaction costs between arbitrary features or a ranking of visual improvements.

The gpu label must be interpreted through the producer. Its parser can use a compile log's gpu field, fall back to the total field, or use an observed compiling-state window when parsing fails. This output does not disclose which path supplied every value. It therefore must not be presented as GPU timestamp-query duration, shader frame time or path-tracing throughput. The zero values explicitly marked NO recompile represent no observed recompilation, not free rendering. Disabling one disk cache and requesting distinct variants is not independent proof that every driver/cache layer was cold.

There is also an artifact-version boundary: the present producer prints firstDraw and accumulation-fps information, while this archived output does not. It cannot be used to fill those missing metrics or assumed to represent the current script revision. Its observations may remain useful historical context, but a source hash and execution manifest are needed to reproduce them. The source's current fallback logic explains potential ambiguity; it does not prove the exact historical producer used that identical logic.

For RFF, the useful improvement is to evaluate compile-time shader specialization and interactive uniform controls separately. Optional costly paths may warrant cached pipeline variants, but the choice must account for first-use latency, steady-state render cost and equal-quality output. A 3D environment-lighting improvement should be judged by reflection fidelity and convergence as well as compilation delay. For 2D, the transferable practice is the same measurement separation for palette, filtering and post-processing variants; the path-tracing effects themselves are not direct 2D equivalents. These historical numbers do not change the current source-informed shader ranking and do not justify lowering numerical precision for speed.

## Reference images: visual coverage and embedded benchmark provenance (2026-10-08)

Reviewed both complete images visually and inspected their PNG chunk structure and all text metadata: `debug/bench-shader-refs/DsyneGrafix-numericDE-rings.png` and `debug/bench-shader-refs/GMT_Mandelbulb_v1.png`. Binary-asset coverage here means visual and metadata review, not source-code reading or independent render reproduction. The chunk walk reached each file's end; it was not a CRC conformance test.

The rings image shows multiple curved, nested bands with dense fine grain across both forms and background. Its chunks contain no text metadata. The filename associates it with numeric DE, but the pixels alone cannot identify whether the grain comes from estimator instability, normal variation, stochastic sampling, intended texture or another stage. It is useful as a difficult visual case, not a numerical oracle or proof of a specific cause. A corresponding scene, camera, estimator configuration and converged comparison are needed before claiming an RFF technique fixes that appearance.

The Mandelbulb image shows a compact detailed object against a largely dark background, with bright left/front relief, dark cavities and warmer upper/right surfaces. Unlike the rings image, it carries substantial metadata: a May 2 timestamp, 1280-by-720 viewport, an ANGLE/D3D11 RTX 2070 adapter string, shader hash/size, 240 timing draws, 60 warmup draws and timing statistics. The recorded p50 is 8985.95 microseconds and p95 is 10809.34 microseconds. Its comment says the image accumulated 256 Halton-jittered frames, used three point lights, a three-tap forward-difference normal optimization, and a named tone-mapping plus transfer-function post-pass. These are embedded historical claims, not a new measured result. The Software field calls the hexadecimal identifier a commit while GMT.frag.hash uses the identical value as a shader hash; do not assume it resolves to a repository revision without checking. All three embedded image-difference metrics are n/a, so the file supplies no measured error against an independent reference.

The already reviewed benchmark's reference-diff path was selectively checked: it draws both images into the benchmark dimensions before comparing them. Resampling changes the comparison domain. The large dark background can also dilute whole-image average error, while normal or silhouette defects occupy a small region; quadrant summaries help but are not an object mask or a detail-specific metric. An existing optimization embedded in the reference image can become part of the accepted baseline, so comparison with this PNG establishes regression consistency rather than independent physical or numerical correctness.

For RFF, retain both types of visual case in a reproducible validation set: smooth shading and high-frequency curved detail, with crop-level checks of silhouettes, cavities, highlights and fine bands. Record source revision, shader identity, complete scene parameters, color transforms, sample count and timing methodology separately. Compare linear data where appropriate before display conversion, and use matched display-space images for appearance review. For 2D, transfer the same reference discipline to thin escape-time bands and deep-zoom boundaries; a Mandelbulb image does not validate a 2D perturbation result. These assets help define coverage for proposed shader changes, but do not establish a new effect ranking or a current RFF performance improvement.

## Small renderer feature schemas expose integration contracts clearly (2026-10-08)
