Full source review of five Fractal Toy files: `features/camera.ts` (44 lines), `features/lighting.ts` (45), `registerFeatures.ts` (32), `setup.ts` (12) and `panels.ts` (15), all beneath `fractal-toy/`. These are the minimal demonstration host's declarations and registration, not GMT's full material or lighting implementation. No code was executed.

Camera parameters expose yaw, pitch, distance, FOV and a target vector. Injection declares five uniforms but supplies neither values nor ray construction; the latter belongs to the renderer assembler. Lighting similarly declares directional light, color, intensity, ambient amount, AO amount and three albedo channels, then declares shader uniforms. The albedo channels must be combined into one vec3, color must be converted under an explicit transfer-function contract, and direction must be handled as a direction rather than an arbitrary magnitude. These files alone do not prove any of those upload operations. In particular, the direction range admits the zero vector; the consuming shader or validation layer needs a defined result for it. A declared control is not evidence that its uniform is bound correctly.

The lighting comment identifies step-count AO and Lambertian diffuse as the intended simplified shading. Step count is affected by the marcher and its budget, so such darkening must not be presented as a full ambient-occlusion estimate. This toy is useful for inspecting data flow, but its lighting should not replace RFF's already reviewed richer shading. A 2D adaptation could use controlled directional shading over a defined scalar field and a palette-based color source; it should not claim 3D visibility from a 2D iteration-count darkening heuristic.

Registration explicitly adds Mandelbulb and Mandelbox before camera and lighting. Formula registration is described as lifting parameters into the shared feature system; static panels cover only Camera and Lighting, while formula panels are registered separately. This makes ordering a concrete dependency: defaults, history and preset enumeration must see the required definitions before the store is constructed. However, claims in comments about freezing registries and automatic preset round trips are not independently proven by these five files. The panels comment says formula tabs are not known at boot, while registerFeatures explicitly registers two formulas before store construction; interpret the actual distinction as formula-owned registration versus the static manifest, not necessarily late discovery after boot.

For RFF, the transferable improvement is a coherent feature contract connecting parameter defaults, controls, persistence, history, uniform packing and shader consumption. Verify the C++/GLSL descriptor and layout agreement explicitly; TypeScript declaration patterns do not enforce Vulkan binary layout. Keep camera math outside individual fractal formulas, while preserving formula-specific parameters and stable identities. Orbit controls can help a 3D preview, but the toy's bounded ordinary-precision target and distance ranges are unsuitable for RFF's 2D deep-zoom coordinates. Use the shared architecture where useful and retain mode-specific numerical representations. These files add integration guidance, not a new shader-effect recommendation or a measured speed improvement.

## Development hooks provide limited reminders, not shader verification (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `.claude/hooks/guard.mjs` (126 lines) and `.claude/hooks/stale.mjs` (44 lines). These files were read as repository tooling, not executed or adopted as instructions for this task. Their useful contribution is preserving decision history, keeping low-level UI primitives separate from application stores, and resurfacing unresolved source annotations when a file is touched.

The guard reads a tool payload and considers only Edit/Write operations with file_path. History edits are allowed when replacement text starts with the old text; existing-file writes must preserve the entire prior content as a prefix. This protects retained text under the covered operation shapes, but Edit can insert within the file rather than strictly at EOF. ADR edits permit a replacement containing the old substring, while full writes permit the original lines to survive as an ordered subsequence. The UI restriction scans proposed text for a particular store-import pattern or two hook names. Shell writes, patches using other tool names and malformed payloads are outside its coverage; read/parse failures defer. The stale reminder checks a fixed set of source extensions and finds markers only when they begin after a recognized comment leader. For RFF, the applicable ideas are lightweight source-linked reminders and clear separation between reusable controls and rendering state. Any adaptation should use the existing project rules, understand native file types and verify actual dependencies where enforcement matters. Preserve correction history while providing an unambiguous current statement for shader equations, color spaces and uniform layouts. ## Coverage percentages and source hashes prove different things (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `docs/history/doc-audit-state/scripts/blob-sha.mjs` (49 lines) and `coverage-check.mjs` (87 lines) in the same directory. These historical audit utilities were not executed. The useful idea for RFF shader work is attaching findings to a precise source identity while separately tracking which files were actually reviewed. A content hash establishes identity; it does not prove that a shader was understood, compiled, rendered or tested.

The hash helper resolves each supplied path against the invoking process's working directory, checks existence, and invokes git hash-object with an argument array and an option terminator. This avoids shell interpolation of filenames. Its REPO_ROOT calculation walks three levels up from the present scripts directory, landing under docs/history rather than the repository root; Git can still discover a parent repository, so the name mismatch does not by itself establish failure. The helper does not constrain inputs to repository members, distinguish regular files from directories up front, or verify output shape. Existing directories fail later in Git. Multiple-file hashing can also emit earlier results before a later read fails. The coverage checker counts membership in path sets. Its percentage includes entries marked partial because partial is only reported in a separate list, not subtracted from covered. It checks neither recorded hashes against current files nor the underlying evidence. Duplicate paths collapse silently in sets, missing paths can introduce undefined entries, and orphan claims are reported without making the process fail. An empty inventory produces zero percent but still a normal successful return. Thus a successful command means that a report was produced, not that the review is complete or consistent.

Its small YAML reader handles a constrained line shape, not general YAML. It strips outer quote characters without proper escape decoding, does not implement inline comments or multiline values, and can interpret deeper list items as top-level entries. That may be adequate for a tightly controlled generated format, but validation must reject unsupported shapes instead of silently changing the coverage denominator. No schema or uniqueness checks are present here. These limits are relevant when interpreting historical percentages produced by this utility; they do not establish that any particular stored report actually encountered malformed input.

For the current RFF adoption audit, retain the stricter distinction already used: selective or truncated reads do not receive full-file credit, reviewed binary images are identified as visual/metadata inspection, and source hashes are checked before recording completion. File-count coverage remains a measure of inventory progress, not a percentage of shader correctness, engineering effort or runtime verification. For future RFF shader changes, keep source identity, test execution, rendered-image comparison and performance measurements as separate evidence fields. This applies equally to 3D lighting and 2D coloring; these utilities themselves add no rendering feature or numerical improvement.

For RFF shader work, retain explicit links among source hashes, reviewed ranges, findings and actual test results, but validate those fields independently before presenting completion. ## OSL Mandelbulb: useful material outputs, but proxy shading is not geometry (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `plans/c4d-redshift-osl/mandelbulb.osl` (318 lines), without compilation or execution in Redshift. This planned port marches a Mandelbulb inside an assumed object-space [-1,1] cube, then outputs albedo, opacity, an object-space normal and a step-based darkening term. Keeping unlit color separate from normal and occlusion is useful for RFF material composition: lighting can be changed without embedding it into the palette. The optional self-lit branch instead multiplies albedo by ambient plus Lambert diffuse and the darkening term. A consumer must distinguish these modes to avoid applying lighting or AO twice.

The proxy limitation is fundamental to interpreting this file. Its local pHit is used for DE normals and color, but no hit-position or depth output relocates the renderer's surface interaction from P. Thus the header's claim of responding like real geometry is broader than the implementation establishes. A shading normal and opacity mask can affect appearance, but do not themselves supply the renderer with the marched hit position, correct secondary-ray origins or full fractal visibility. This is an approximation requiring host-specific testing. No current OSL/Redshift support, normal-port encoding or closure-compatibility claims from the header were independently verified in this local-source review.

The distance estimator starts z and c at the sampled point, updates a scalar derivative and performs spherical exponentiation. A notable finite-iteration detail is that r is measured before each iteration, while dr and z are updated afterward. When the loop ends by exhausting iterations, the returned expression uses the previous radius with the updated derivative; when it ends through the early bailout, those stages differ. The trap is updated after the orbit step and can retain its 1e10 sentinel if the initial point bails out immediately. These paths need explicit reference cases before calling the port verbatim or numerically equivalent. The log expression may return negative values for radii below one, which the marcher immediately accepts as a hit; no explicit escaped/interior classification accompanies the estimate.

Ray reconstruction transforms P and I into object space and normalizes the direction. The cube code computes only far slab intersections, assuming P is already an appropriate entry point. It has no full slab interval or explicit parallel-outside rejection. If tFar is nonpositive, it retains maxDist rather than immediately rejecting that ray; outgoing, back-face or secondary-ray cases therefore require separate validation. March distance t begins at the proxy surface, so eps = minDist*(1+t) is neither camera-distance precision control nor a pixel-footprint estimate. Moving the camera or changing output resolution does not appear in that expression. Declared UI ranges are not runtime clamps, and invalid scale, step counts or non-finite values are not comprehensively handled.

The normal is a four-sample tetrahedral gradient with offsets scaled by the hit epsilon. A near-zero squared length gets a fallback, but NaN does not satisfy that comparison and is not explicitly rejected. Normal space and any required encoding must match the receiving node; simply labeling a port object-space does not verify that integration. The AO output is clamp(1-strength*stepsTaken/maxSteps), so changing the allowed step budget changes brightness even if the same surface is reached after the same number of steps. It is a traversal heuristic, not independent visibility sampling. The palette blend uses min-orbit-radius divided by scale; adjusting scale can affect tint normalization in addition to geometry framing. These couplings should be intentional controls, not hidden consequences of a quality setting.

For RFF 3D, adopt the separation of albedo, normals and optional occlusion as a material contract while retaining real hit depth in the rendering pipeline. Evaluate footprint-aware normals and actual occlusion independently of this proxy demonstration. For 2D, transfer orbit-field-to-palette mapping and separate lighting/compositing controls; a derived height-field normal can provide a deliberate relief effect, but is not the geometry of a Mandelbulb. Preserve high-precision orbit evaluation and MPA semantics. The header names GMT and a named DE provenance but provides no explicit license grant in this file; confirm the applicable license and NOTICE attribution before adapting recognizable implementation details. This review does not establish a new measured shader benefit or justify copying the proxy architecture into RFF.

## OSL Apollonian: distinguish orbit-constant parameters from ray-constant parameters (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `plans/c4d-redshift-osl/apollonian.osl` (340 lines), without compilation or rendering. The already reviewed production Apollonian definition was reread, and loopInit placement in `engine-gmt/shaders/chunks/de.ts` was selectively checked. These checks expose a concrete semantic difference behind the port's fidelity claim: production computes the modulation from the initial point of each distance evaluation, before that point's orbit loop; the OSL file computes it once at the proxy entry point and reuses it along the entire march and all normal probes. Constant during an orbit is not constant along a viewing ray.

The mechanism is modular folding followed by sphere inversion. Each orbit step scales coordinates by cc = foldScale + 1, folds each axis into [-1,1], divides back by cc, and applies k = tMod/max(dot(z,z),1e-10). The derivative accumulator multiplies by abs(k), the color trap tracks the minimum squared orbit radius, and the estimate is deCoef*abs(z.y)/dscale. The OSL adds signed near-zero guards for cc components. These keep division finite near foldScale=-1 but alter the formula in that region; they are not evidence of a verbatim port. Spatial modulation is tMod = scale*(foam2 + 0.25*cos(pi*modAmt*(z-x))). With modulation enabled, freezing this at each proxy entry can make the effective field depend on the view ray. Normal probes then differentiate a constant-modulation field rather than the production spatially varying field. Recompute modulation per evaluated point if production equivalence is the goal, then validate both geometry and normals.

The port also omits production twist, Julia-offset behavior and optional spherical inversion pre-transform with its distance correction. Its defaults do not reproduce the production default preset, which enables that pre-transform and uses different parameters. The shared kernel remains useful as a limited demonstration, but comparing default renders would mix multiple differences. The source's label ray-constant is itself misleading in the production comments; actual loopInit placement inside map and related evaluators resolves the scope. This is precisely why code reachability and evaluation lifetime matter when adapting shader optimizations.

Placement has another documentation mismatch: fitScale help says it divides coordinates, while the code multiplies them. For positive uniform scaling, multiplying coordinates and multiplying the resulting distance by 1/fitScale is coherent, but zero/negative external values are not fully validated by UI metadata. Normal epsilon is measured in fractal space yet derived directly from an object-space hit threshold; changing fitScale therefore changes their relative smoothing scales. The outer loop checks the exit distance only after advancing, allowing an initial sample even when the clipped interval has zero length. It lacks a complete parallel-outside slab rejection and comprehensive non-finite handling. These require dedicated camera, transform and singularity cases before use as a geometry reference.

The orbit-trap gamma provides a useful independent artistic control: clamp a scalar trap to [0,1], raise it to a positive exponent, then blend two colors. For RFF, a richer palette lookup can replace the two-color blend while preserving explicit scalar mapping. The AO remains a hit-step/maxSteps heuristic, so increasing the work budget alone can brighten a surface; it is not a geometry-only occlusion result. Self-lit output already contains that factor and emission gain, so downstream AO or lighting must not be duplicated. The header mixes old emission instructions with newer raw-albedo wiring and overstates native-shadow/GI equivalence; as with the Mandelbulb proxy, no actual hit-position replacement is supplied. Host compatibility and closure claims are unverified here.

For RFF 3D, the useful mechanisms are modular coordinates, inversion-based structure and independently mapped orbit fields, with parameters evaluated at the correct spatial scope. For 2D, folding and circle inversion can generate separate procedural patterns, masks or palette-coordinate transforms; they are not a precision-preserving replacement for Mandelbrot perturbation or MPA. Filter high-frequency folds at the pixel footprint and retain the distinction between a stylized mask and geometric visibility. The kosalos attribution in comments is a provenance lead, not a license determination. This review adds concrete transfer constraints and a source-confirmed scope mismatch, without claiming measured visual improvement or executing the port.

## OSL Tetrix: folding, distance normalization and view-dependent color (2026-10-08)

Full source review: `plans/c4d-redshift-osl/sierpinski-tetrahedron.osl` (344 lines), without host compilation or rendering. The production Sierpinski formula's kernel and parameter declarations were selectively rechecked. The port repeatedly reflects coordinates across x+y=0, x+z=0 and y+z=0, then applies a uniform scale about foldOffset. Conditional swap-and-negate operations are the relevant fold mechanism. The comment describing these planes as mutually perpendicular is incorrect: their normals have nonzero pairwise dot products. The fold implementation does not depend on that descriptive claim.

The port returns length(p)*scale^(-n). That is not algebraically equivalent to the documented production linear estimator (r-1)/dr: even with dr=scale^n their difference is 1/scale^n. With a finite iteration budget, this changes the implicit surface reached by a fixed hit threshold. The port also always runs its clamped fold count, whereas equivalence with the production wrapper requires matching bailout behavior. Production supports per-axis scaling, rotation, shift, Julia offsets and a cutting-plane accumulator; this port implements a narrower uniform-scale path plus twist. Its verbatim/production-quality wording must therefore be treated as a claim requiring tests, not a fidelity result.

Twist rotates the XY coordinates by an angle depending on Z at every fold. A position-dependent rotation is not globally an isometry, yet the distance compensation includes only scale^n. Consequently the simple untwisted distance rationale does not establish conservative stepping for nonzero twist. Test grazing and thin features or account for the deformation's derivative bound before relying on full-distance advancement. UI metadata restricts nominal scale values, but runtime code clamps only iteration and march counts. Invalid scale or non-finite inputs can still invalidate pow, normals or marching. Large repeated scales can overflow intermediate coordinates before the inverse-scale factor is applied; a final normalization cannot undo that loss.

This file improves on the other two OSL examples by computing a complete slab interval, including parallel-outside rejection, and checking t against the clipped interval before sampling. However, fractalFit changes only the bounding interval, not the DE coordinates or scale compensation. It crops the visible domain rather than scaling the fractal to fit. A proxy mesh of a different extent is not automatically inferred despite the header's broad wording. Normal epsilon grows with distance traveled from the proxy surface, not with camera pixel footprint, and the near-zero gradient fallback still does not explicitly handle NaN.

The coloring field is also different from the production orbit trap. The OSL accumulates minimum length(p) along the viewing ray's march, while production updates the trap inside the fractal orbit. The OSL tint can therefore change with view direction, entry position and step sampling even for a similar hit. If RFF wants stable material color, evaluate an orbit or spatial field at the hit and map it independently of traversal. The step-ratio AO again depends on the allowed budget, and its zero-based usedSteps makes the first sampled hit receive no darkening. As in the other proxies, outputs provide no relocated hit depth; albedo, opacity and a normal do not establish native geometric visibility for external lights and secondary rays.

For RFF 3D, the useful building blocks are explicit symmetry folds, scale compensation with a stated estimator contract, complete ray bounds and separated color/normal outputs. For 2D, use dimension-appropriate triangle folds or coordinate transforms to construct independent patterns and masks, with pixel-footprint filtering at fold boundaries. Do not transplant a three-dimensional Tetrix formula as a Mandelbrot optimization or alter MPA/perturbation precision. A shader improvement should keep color fields independent of traversal quality unless view-dependent coloring is an intentional effect. This review records those mechanisms and adaptation limits, not measured image fidelity, host support or rendering speed.

## Shared interaction helpers: recovery and state lifetime (2026-10-08)

Full source review of `hooks/useClipboardCopy.ts` (56 lines), `useDismiss.ts` (108), `useDragEndSafetyNet.ts` (28), `useGlobalContextMenu.ts` (28) and `useHelpContextMenu.ts` (24). These helpers were not executed. Their relevance to RFF is reliable interaction around palette/material controls, not shader mathematics.

The clipboard helper centralizes success/failure feedback and cancels an existing reset timer when a copy starts, resets or unmounts. It does not cancel or identify outstanding clipboard promises. Two overlapping writes can resolve out of order and install multiple reset timers; reset or unmount during an outstanding write can be followed by a late completion that updates state and creates another timer. For RFF's copy-location or copy-palette feedback, associate asynchronous completion with the current operation/item and ensure cleanup covers outstanding work as well as timers. Copy completion should report the actual requested operation rather than a previous item's delayed result.

The dismissal helper keeps callbacks and surface references current without reattaching listeners on every render. It defers outside-pointer registration to avoid immediately closing a newly opened surface, and routes Escape through an instance-specific shortcut scope with cleanup. This is useful separation of event ownership from panel code. The ignore selector is captured when the effect attaches and intentionally omitted from dependencies, so changing it while open does not update behavior. Nested outside-click listeners are not automatically limited to one surface; multiple containing/ref relationships can dismiss more than one. The topmost Escape claim depends on shortcut-scope ordering, not actual visual stacking alone. Event-target containment also needs care for portals and shadow boundaries. It supplies no native-focus or accessibility guarantee by itself.

The drag safety net assumes mousemove is suppressed during a native HTML drag and uses the first observed move while active as evidence that the drag ended. That is a fallback heuristic, not a general pointer-drag lifecycle. It captures onEnd only when active changes, so callers must honor the stated stable-callback assumption. Until active becomes false, multiple moves can call onEnd repeatedly. It does not independently handle pointer cancellation, touch, capture loss or an inactive window. For native RFF controls, use the appropriate capture-loss/cancel events and an idempotent transaction-end operation; a stale interaction flag can otherwise leave adaptive preview or editing history in the wrong state.

The global help-menu listener respects defaultPrevented, collects help IDs from the event target and opens only when IDs exist. The local helper instead collects from currentTarget, prepends supplied IDs and stops propagation. These differences affect which contextual help is offered for nested controls. Extra IDs are not deduplicated here, and the local helper does not first honor an already-prevented event. Both paths open an empty action list with help IDs; neither proves that help content exists or is correct. A RFF adaptation can associate shader controls with precise contextual explanations while keeping ordinary component actions authoritative.

For 2D and 3D editing alike, the useful improvements are operation-aware feedback, scoped dismissal, idempotent drag completion and contextual documentation tied to the actual parameter. Test cancellation during active edits, rapidly repeated actions and unmount/close transitions, then confirm the resulting palette/material state and rendered revision. These browser hooks should inform native behavior rather than be copied directly, and they do not change the shader-priority ranking or establish a measured performance gain.

## Entry points and update recovery: scope and readiness (2026-10-08)

Full source review of `index.html` (46 lines) and `launcher.html` (302 lines); no update/reset script was executed. The root entry loads `/app-gmt/main.tsx` and applies cached theme variables before mounting. Its mobile layout retains scroll capacity while fine-pointer desktop layouts lock to the viewport. The source comment describes an alias and offline fallback intent, not a tested deployment guarantee. The comment calls the launcher a six-app menu, while the inspected launcher exposes five app links. This is minor navigation documentation drift, not a rendering defect.

The launcher's service-worker recovery separates checking, applying, ready and manual-reset feedback. Existing waiting workers receive SKIP_WAITING, and newly observed updatefound events attach installation listeners. However, a worker already installing when the initial scan occurs is not directly subscribed to; its earlier updatefound event may already have passed. The five-second reset offer measures elapsed time since script startup, not five seconds without progress as the comment says. A slow but advancing installation can therefore receive a stuck label. The initially hidden reset button is made visible on timeout and is not explicitly hidden again by subsequent state changes. The controller-change reload guard lasts for this page instance only, not across reloads.

Registration enumeration and manual reset cover all registrations and cache names accessible on the origin, with no app-scope/name filter. Reset catches failures and reloads anyway; it does not verify successful unregister/delete results. It does not clear localStorage. Individual update failures are swallowed, while the initial getRegistrations promise lacks a rejection handler. None of these states verifies successful rendering, a first completed frame or graphics-device readiness. The static launcher's automatic reload is not a suitable default for a document editor with unsaved material or palette changes.

For native RFF, adopt explicit progress and recovery states, with separate evidence for resource loading, shader compilation, GPU readiness and presentation of the requested render revision. Tie stale-work rejection and cache invalidation to the relevant application, device, shader/source revision and resource identity; preserve or restore the editing transaction before a disruptive restart. A progress-aware timeout should offer diagnosis/retry without declaring every slow operation failed. Apply this consistently to 3D material setup and 2D palette/filter setup. This is a reliability improvement around shader work, not a new shading algorithm or measured speedup, and it does not justify copying browser service-worker logic into Vulkan.

## Deep-zoom shader smoke tests: what their evidence can establish (2026-10-08)

Full source review of `debug/smoke-gx-fractal-cycle.mts` (82 lines), `smoke-gx-fractal-deepzoom.mts` (97) and `smoke-gx-fractal-glitch.mts` (177). These scripts were inspected, not run. Historical measurements in comments remain historical, and their success messages are stronger than the assertions alone support.

The cycle test changes fractal/linear mode 24 times with fixed 120/60 ms delays, then requires a final canvas with at least 50 quantized RGB colors and no captured runtime errors. This is useful end-to-end survival coverage. It does not count context creation/destruction, prove every intermediate mount completed, monitor memory or detect browser warnings about forced context eviction. A final working image cannot prove absence of a resource leak; quantized color diversity also does not establish spatial structure or correct fractal geometry. For RFF, exercise 2D/3D or preview/export resource transitions with explicit completion markers and bounded resource-allocation measurements, while checking a known final image. Do not transplant the comment's browser context cap into a Vulkan resource budget.

The deep-zoom test requests a fixed coordinate at zoom 1e-9, rebuilds the reference, waits three seconds and checks at least 50 quantized colors. Disabling deep zoom is checked only through the resulting zoom parameter being at least 1e-4. Contrary to its introductory description, it does not capture or compare deep-off color diversity at the same coordinate/scale; the off path deliberately changes scale. Its observable result is a nonflat capture plus parameter-floor behavior, not independent proof of accurate iteration values or complete worker/upload/kernel routing. Parameter comparisons do not explicitly reject NaN. Fixed sleeps and a generic first-canvas query do not establish that the captured image corresponds to the requested render revision. A RFF verification should compare numerical escape/iteration or field values against an independent high-precision reference before relying on display color, and associate each capture with completed state and accumulation samples.

The glitch test adds a useful positive check before its negative comparison: both LA-on and LA-off captures must keep their dominant quantized color below a view-specific ceiling. Its own historical comments explain why comparing only their difference allowed shared wrong blocks or two blank images to pass. It also checks relocation and a positive period for selected views. These are useful, separate observables. However, the image statistic is only the largest color-bin fraction inside the central 40 percent of width and height (16 percent of image area). It discards pixel locations, other histogram bins and the surrounding image. Scrambling pixels, moving an artifact outside the box, or producing different structured errors can preserve that statistic. Even the phrase 'distribution comparison' overstates comparison of one histogram statistic. The absolute ceilings reject simple flat failures but do not make pure perturbation an independent correctness oracle. A positive period does not validate the nucleus, residual, orbit closure or correct image; reference statistics are not a fence proving a matching GPU frame was presented. The empty-region case would leave maxFrac at zero, so explicit dimensions and nonzero sampled-pixel count belong in any adaptation.

The strongest shader-related lesson for RFF is the compatibility contract between iteration skipping and coloring. A stripe average, orbit minimum or other per-iteration field cannot generally be recovered from the final skipped endpoint alone. When adding GMT-inspired field masks or orbit coloring to RFF, either derive a valid aggregate for the skipped segment, compute the required field through a compatible path, or explicitly disable the incompatible skip for that mode. Never silently present endpoint-only coloring as the full per-iteration definition. GMT's LA/AT terminology and tests are not evidence that RFF's MPA has the same implementation or defect: MPA derives skips from periodic structure and is not BLA. Preserve its precision requirements and validate each proposed field against a direct high-precision calculation.

This transfers most directly to 2D Mandelbrot coloring, but the same principle applies to 3D iterative orbit traps and to any cached/accelerated field evaluation. Pair accelerated/unaccelerated comparisons with an independent reference and spatially localized error checks across the full image, including interior/exterior boundaries, escaped references, periodic references and mode transitions. For new material masks, verify the underlying scalar/vector field separately from palette, lighting and postprocessing, since those can hide or amplify numerical errors. These findings improve the validation and feasibility assessment of shader additions; they do not establish a new measured performance ranking or prove a current RFF rendering bug.

## Procedural geometry parity and live-color control evidence (2026-10-08)

Full source review of `debug/smoke-gx-geom-gpu.mts` (136 lines) and `debug/smoke-gx-fractal.mts` (127); selective cross-check of the already-reviewed compositor presentation methods and geometry-mode registration. No browser test was executed. The geometry test actually covers three geometries (linear, radial and conic) in ten parameter cases, despite its header saying four. Cases include angle, bias, center, scale, sinusoidal modulation, mirror and twist controls. At 320 by 220 it compares every RGB component, requiring maximum error at most 12 and mean error at most 1.5 in 8-bit levels. Mean error is rounded to three decimals before evaluation, so the effective boundary has a small rounding tolerance. Alpha is excluded.

This is stronger spatial evidence than color-count-only checks: one misplaced contour can contribute a large maximum error. It still tests one palette, aspect ratio, resolution and output encoding, not all parameter ranges or high-frequency aliasing. Dithering is explicitly disabled, so it does not compare the still-image error-diffusion quality to the live shader's noise tail. Both paths share compositor infrastructure and ramp-generation dependencies; the CPU field is presented through the same compositor, not an independent end-to-end color oracle. Correlated LUT/output defects can survive this comparison. The script does not independently assert nonflat output, record page/console errors or measure speed, and historical timing/quality statements in comments are not fresh results. A missing case or a wrong shared output path could escape the intended protection.

For RFF's proposed coordinate transforms and masks, use this CPU/GPU parity pattern with deterministic fixtures but compare the raw coordinate/coverage field as well as final color. Include negative coordinates, centers, seams, near-zero scales, high frequencies, different aspect ratios and pixel footprints. Then separately test palette encoding, filtering, dithering and alpha/compositing. A shared mathematical specification can drive native CPU and GLSL implementations without assuming identical floating-point execution. Keep tolerances tied to the represented field and output precision; these 8-bit display thresholds do not justify relaxed Mandelbrot perturbation precision. This applies directly to 2D procedural backgrounds and palette mappings, and to the same mappings evaluated on 3D material coordinates.

The live-fractal smoke has useful positive checks for a nonzero canvas, at least 50 quantized RGB colors, a 30 percent nonblack fraction and a 10 percent colored fraction. These reject several blank/grayscale failures but cannot identify the Mandelbrot geometry or establish correct escape values. Its control step sets mapping mode and repeat count together, waits, logs the before/after color counts, and only asserts that the final count is still at least 50. It never asserts that the image or even color count changed. Phase is mentioned in the header but is not changed. An ignored setter with the original image intact can therefore pass; two changed setters also cannot isolate which one works. Store calls bypass the visible controls, and elapsed waits do not identify a completed requested render revision.

For RFF, test mapping, repeat and phase independently using a known nondegenerate field/palette, assert the expected parameter value and a matching presented revision, and compare spatial outputs against the expected transformation. Keep a control case for palette periodicity where certain shifts intentionally produce the same image. Separate parameter plumbing from the mathematical mapping and from temporal accumulation reset. These checks support the adoption of richer live shader controls in both 2D and 3D; they do not establish that a current RFF control is broken or rank a speed improvement.
