## Spline extension and synchronized shader previews (2026-10-08)

Full source review of `debug/smoke-gx-spline.mts` (235 lines), without execution. Its valuable behavioral fixture is a straight, horizontal path confined to the middle third of a black-to-white image: extension should carry endpoint colors into the margins. Later comments and actual assertions describe endpoint-color clamping, whereas the opening explanation describes spreading the ramp over an extended span. These are different mappings; RFF should specify which is intended rather than deriving implementation behavior from that opening paragraph.

The test checks averages of six samples at each end of a 48-sample center row. It does not check monotonicity, the interior ramp shape or the full image, despite introductory claims about a continuously rising ramp. Black-to-white interpolation in Oklab does not make the sampled 8-bit red channel an exact linear along-path coordinate or physical luminance. The actual margin thresholds are useful endpoint behavior tests, not an analytic coordinate oracle. Resampling the canvas to 48 pixels can hide thin discontinuities, and the off-state condition only rejects the simultaneous presence of both expected endpoint margins. It is not a detailed characterization of extension-off behavior.

Omitting splineExtend is compared with explicitly setting the current GEOM_DEFAULTS value, using a three-level tolerance. This verifies present default equivalence, not historical preset-image compatibility. The document explicitly records an intentional default change. RFF's frozen palette recipes must not inherit such a change implicitly: persist/version a new mode or parameter when an omitted field previously meant another image, preserving existing recipe identity and generation order.

The preview synchronization checks are particularly relevant to an RFF material editor with multiple views. They inspect all canvases, including the editor's visible preview instead of only the first underlying canvas. However, each full image is reduced to six red-channel values and compared exactly. That can miss color-only or localized spatial disagreements, and one-level resampling/dither differences can also cause false mismatches. The palette-change test checks at least two canvases before the edit but does not require the same count or identities afterward. If one disappears and the remaining sample changes, its checks can still pass. The edit replaces a whole palette configuration, not an isolated spline-point drag or individual knot update. Fixed waits and bare module imports introduce timing/module-instance assumptions; the test comments acknowledge a historical development-server duplicate-instance hazard, but that is a possible cause rather than proof of the cause of any new failure.

For RFF, resolve the working palette/material and render revision once and pass that same state to the main view, spline editor preview and export path. Verify stable surface identity and count, RGB/alpha where relevant, and completed revision rather than only aggregate red samples. For a 2D spline field, independently validate along-curve coordinates, endpoint extension and lateral falloff, including curved ends, coincident points and self-intersections. For a 3D material, explicitly select object/UV/world coordinates and define continuity at seams before reusing the field. These checks support curve-directed coloring as an expressive feature; this smoke test alone does not establish its GPU cost or numerical correctness over general curves.

## Minimal 3D demo documentation and archived DE-lighting proposal (2026-10-08)

Full review of `docs/modules/fractal-toy/index.md` (43 lines) and `docs/history/plans-archive/fractal-de-and-compositing.md` (84). The module overview describes the already-reviewed minimal 3D Mandelbulb/Mandelbox app, formula-driven parameter registration, camera/lighting features, its own animation loop and a viewport frame-end hook. Its statement that there is no 2D Mandelbrot or Julia path must be read in the scope of this sibling app, not the whole GMT repository, which contains the separate deep-zoom path reviewed above. The recorded main-source line count is 162 while the reviewed current file has 178 lines; historical verification metadata is not proof of current whole-file agreement. Separate renderer ownership and common viewport feedback can inform RFF modularity, but copying an extra scheduling loop is not itself an improvement.

The archived compositing document explicitly labels itself design/research, not implemented behavior. Its useful architectural separation is a distance-derived scalar used for palette mapping versus derivative-direction lighting applied independently to base color. It proposes pixel-scaled distance in log space, edge falloff, logarithmic bands, separate lighting controls and later layer compositing. RFF already has lighting and layer facilities identified earlier in this report, so this is evidence for assessing missing field inputs or controls within that system, not justification for adding a duplicate stack or claiming all listed features are absent.

The proposed slopeShade normalizes the complex quotient z/dz to a 2D direction, takes its dot product with a light azimuth and uses an artist-controlled offset/divisor before clamping. That is an illustrative directional relief shader; its stated optional power of this response is not by itself a full Blinn half-vector specular model. Normalizing z/dz discards its magnitude, so the example is not a metric slope field for a specified surface height. The unguarded complex division and normalize need a defined result for zero, tiny, nonfinite or overflowing derivative/quotient values. Avoid copying the literal squared-magnitude division into a deep-zoom path without scaled arithmetic and precision analysis. The archived phrase 'analytic and free' does not account for derivative propagation, GPU storage/bandwidth, extra shader work or compatibility with skipped iteration segments. Its superlative visual-impact and cross-product prevalence claims are not new findings from this audit.

For 2D RFF, a derivative-direction field could support controllable relief independent of palette choice if the current computation retains enough reliable information. A stored log derivative magnitude alone cannot reconstruct complex direction. Audit that data contract and the MPA-compatible propagation before proposing new buffers or recomputation, and retain an unlit base-field view for correctness checks. Pixel-space widths require a stated coordinate-to-pixel scale and robust log-domain handling near zero. For 3D, use actual geometric normals for geometric lighting and treat this 2D direction as an optional texture/relief input with an explicit tangent basis; do not substitute it for a 3D surface normal.

The proposal's instruction to shade each sample before temporal averaging is a meaningful ordering choice: averaging already shaded samples generally differs from shading an averaged normal or scalar. Shader-state changes must invalidate the appropriate accumulation, and parameter layouts/bindings must agree across all RFF consumers. Its external-source list is a research lead, not a verified license or correctness certificate for the supplied code/defaults. Recheck original derivations and provenance before adapting distinctive implementations. No performance, visual ranking or implementation-completion claim follows from this archived design alone.

## Parameter identity, scene application and camera-state portability (2026-10-08)

Full document review of ADR-0011 (31 lines), ADR-0012 (32), ADR-0021 (36), ADR-0025 (28), ADR-0029 (33) and ADR-0030 (27), all dated 2026-05-20 as retrospective decisions. The enum helper was reread and scene/camera entry points selectively cross-checked; these cross-checks do not add coverage credit for already-reviewed implementation files. The decisions explain architecture, not fresh runtime evidence.

ADR-0011 represents enumerations as numeric indices with a string resolver at the boundary. This can keep parameter editing and shader routing compact, but tuple position becomes serialized meaning. The actual helper floors fractional values and falls back for out-of-range or NaN indices; it does not round to the nearest integer or clamp to the nearest endpoint. A valid default and nonempty tuple are caller responsibilities. The trailing extra config spread can override the generated default/options while the resolver still closes over defaultIndex and values, so declaration consistency is not automatic. For RFF shader modes, use explicit stable identifiers and validate finite integer values at the loading boundary. Never reorder existing palette recipe identities or imply that UI option order is a harmless implementation detail. Append-only configuration rules and existing Vulkan numeric layouts remain authoritative.

ADR-0012 centralizes non-feature preset fields and freezes both field registries during store construction. It reduces scattered save/load field lists, but the decision itself notes that a missing registrar import silently loses fields. A useful RFF adaptation is a declarative inventory linking each persistent material parameter to its default, stable encoding, validation and render invalidation behavior, with round-trip coverage. Freezing registrations proves that the set stops changing, not that it is complete or that all corresponding shader bindings exist. Keep transient viewport/device resources out of the serialized scene inventory.

ADR-0021 distinguishes decoding a scene from applying it through the complete rendering transition, including compilation and worker configuration. The inspected SceneIO call sites retain a decode-then-loadScene pattern. That separation is useful for previewing or validating imported data, but two independent calls allow a new import entry point to omit the apply phase. RFF can retain a reusable pure decoder while providing one application-level operation that validates, prepares required resources and publishes a complete render revision, with explicit failure behavior and preservation of the previous usable scene. Do not equate a successful parse or updated controls with a successfully rendered scene. The ADR also narrows plugin idempotence: registry replacement does not make all captured dependencies or side effects idempotent.

ADR-0025 separates viewport subscriptions by quality, size, FPS, interaction and mode, and supplies an imperative reporting/control facade. For RFF, this supports decoupling frequent performance telemetry from expensive parameter/pipeline updates. It does not make rendering cheaper by itself, prove that adaptive resolution preserves final detail, or justify relaxing numerical precision. Distinguish temporary interactive quality from completed still/export quality, and ensure resizing or interaction-end transitions actually publish the intended resolution. The document explicitly says an older planned unified viewport API was not built; recommendations should use the implemented responsibilities rather than resurrect that historical API as an existing feature.

ADR-0029 deliberately retains both lightweight camera slots and a richer state library. In dual-install apps it assigns shortcuts to one owner and does not register the lightweight camera adapter, while retaining its persistence path. Thus an installed camera plugin alone does not establish active save/recall behavior. For RFF, quick camera bookmarks and a labeled preset library can be useful distinct workflows, but avoid duplicate shortcut ownership, divergent copies of the same snapshot, or presenting a saved state that cannot be recalled. A shared validated snapshot payload can support both interfaces without adopting GMT's two-store arrangement verbatim.

ADR-0030 makes camera payloads opaque to the generic plugin so 2D center/zoom, 3D orbit and six-degree-of-freedom cameras can share the storage interface. The useful transfer is an adapter boundary, not an untyped universal camera schema. In RFF, include camera-kind and schema/version metadata, validate payloads before application, and preserve high-precision 2D coordinates without conversion through ordinary floating-point JSON numbers. A 3D pose is not automatically convertible to a 2D deep-zoom location. Labels, thumbnails and library operations can be shared while each adapter owns precision, orientation conventions and valid ranges. These changes support shader/material experimentation and reproducible comparisons in both dimensions; they are workflow and state-integrity improvements rather than new shader algorithms or measured performance gains.

## Boot signals, worker contracts and shader-feature registration (2026-10-08)

Full review of ADR-0005 (35 lines), ADR-0033 (34), ADR-0034 (28), ADR-0035 (47), ADR-0036 (54) and ADR-0037 (51). These are architectural records rather than new runtime verification. Later updates embedded in a record take precedence over its historical description; no source implementation coverage is inferred from reading the records.

ADR-0005 moves worker boot behind a producer/consumer readiness signal instead of a top-level arbitrary delay. Its May 23 update is essential: the signal means that the startup mount effect ran, not that scene hydration or rendering completed. The update also replaces the historical silent timeout with worker boot/compile events and an explicit failure surface. Therefore the old frozen-splash consequence must not be reported as an established current GMT defect. For RFF, model device/resource preparation, shader compilation and first completed image separately; a short scheduling yield is not a completion fence. A one-shot boot latch also needs a deliberate retry/reinitialization policy after failure or device recreation rather than being mistaken for proof of successful initialization.

ADR-0033 preserves a worker-shaped stub during engine extraction and replaces it through a shared proxy registry. Its null picks, rejecting exports and stub GPU label are intentional unsupported behaviors, not successful rendering. A reference captured before replacement can continue referring to the stub. ADR-0034 leaves render-state and camera/offset payloads opaque at the generic boundary. This supports engine separation but does not validate message layout, semantic version or successful delivery. For RFF, explicit capabilities, validated payloads and request/render-generation identity would make worker/background operations easier to extend safely. Installation order should be a checked dependency, and unsupported operations should produce an explicit result. Generic transport need not understand every fractal field, but typed/versioned application boundaries must still verify precision-bearing coordinates and ownership of large buffers. These documents do not demonstrate a current RFF worker fault.

ADR-0035 keeps pointer-over-canvas in a mutable reference rather than reactive store state. Its July update says adaptive engagement is activity-driven and no longer reads this input; the remaining live display reader chooses an Auto/Always label, while a reporting path still polls it. Thus the original claim that hover drives adaptive rendering is superseded within the same file. A nonreactive reference trades immediate display updates for reduced subscription coupling; it is not universally faster, and changing a value on pointer crossings is not the same as updating it every frame. For RFF, separate high-frequency render telemetry from semantic editing transitions, but keep visible mode indicators synchronized through the appropriate low-frequency event. End-of-interaction quality recovery must be driven by actual activity/cancellation, not merely pointer position.

ADR-0036 uses an identity helper to retain inferred parameter keys/types that a broad feature annotation would erase. It improves static access to authored features, not runtime validation of imported configuration or proof that GLSL bindings match. The record notes legacy declarations outside that typed path, so its safety guarantee is not universal. For RFF, the transferable idea is one authoritative parameter declaration feeding typed access, validation, persistence and shader binding checks where practical. C++/GLSL size, alignment, offsets and descriptor layouts still require explicit verification; a type-safe setter alone cannot establish binary compatibility.

ADR-0037 separates engine feature registration (state, shader chunks and parameter schemas) from component/style registration. This can enable reusable headless computation and shared 2D/3D features without imposing a particular UI. However, the record's proposed headless scenarios are not proof that all transitive dependencies execute without a DOM or GPU context. Registration is only one dependency boundary. For RFF, keep reusable palette, field/mask and material math independent of panels, then register the corresponding controls separately. Validate both a headless calculation path and the application's full rendering path when such separation is implemented. Missing controls or missing feature state should be diagnosed explicitly rather than accepted as silent partial initialization. This is a maintainability and testability direction supporting shader expansion, with no measured speedup implied.

## Editing contracts for shader controls, guided lessons and preset libraries (2026-10-08)

Full document review of ADR-0009 (27 lines), ADR-0010 (32), ADR-0013 (29), ADR-0014 (63), ADR-0022 (51) and ADR-0032 (31). These findings concern documented architecture and its adaptation to RFF; no live interface or rendering test was performed.

ADR-0009 replaces runtime mutation of store actions with named tutorial events. That separates lesson advancement from the action implementation but leaves string-name mismatches as silent failures. For RFF, optional guided explanations of roughness, field masks, lighting or 2D palette mapping could subscribe to stable semantic action identifiers. Distinguish an attempted command, accepted state change and completed render: a tutorial should not claim an effect is visible merely because a button event fired. Subscription cleanup and event ownership should remain independent of the underlying numerical operation. This is a documentation/learning opportunity rather than a shader-speed improvement.

ADR-0010 registers live tutorial anchors through component reference callbacks, selecting visible entries when multiple controls share an identifier. Its own consequence records incomplete resize tracking for anchors registered late. That is a documented limitation, not a newly reproduced current defect. For RFF's dynamically appearing light/material panels, an equivalent control-location service would need lifecycle cleanup and layout/visibility updates, with an explicit choice when multiple views expose the same parameter. A shared identifier can connect 2D and 3D explanations, but the content should distinguish a scalar palette mapping from a geometric or tangent-space lighting effect.

ADR-0013 intentionally widens the component registry to arbitrary component props to accommodate heterogeneous panels. Typed construction of ordinary feature props is useful but does not ensure that a selected component identifier accepts those props. For native RFF, keep heterogeneous panel registration possible while validating each adapter's parameter contract, required services and lifetime. This decision is not evidence that untyped Vulkan uniforms or descriptor layouts are safe; the UI flexibility and GPU data interface are separate concerns.

ADR-0014 records an incremental migration from direct global-store reads to injected callbacks. Its July and September updates explicitly supersede the original 'only Slider' claim, note mixed consumers and replace a retired Gradient Explorer host. Do not turn these historical migration stages into a blanket current defect. The useful RFF lesson is to centralize interaction-start/end and context actions without creating a second state source, and test each host/preview that consumes the controls. Memoizing a callback container can reduce unwanted updates but cannot by itself prove correct lifetime, transaction grouping or scene routing. Apply changes within the relevant panel boundary rather than assuming a broad architectural rewrite is necessary to add one shader control.

ADR-0022 contains a crucial correction: at equal score, first registration wins, not last registration. Its described score combines scope position times 10000 with priority. Such an arithmetic encoding only guarantees that scope outranks priority when priority differences are bounded; a new implementation should compare scope and priority explicitly or enforce the bound. The record identifies a specific priority needed to distinguish camera undo from parameter redo, illustrating why action meaning must not depend accidentally on installation order. For RFF, resolve modal/panel/timeline/global ownership deterministically, preserve native text editing, and test both chosen action and resulting state. Scope-stack order is not automatically visual z-order. This applies equally to 2D location edits and 3D camera/material edits, without implying that RFF should copy GMT's particular key assignments.

ADR-0032 keeps library data in the state owner and makes library panels consume supplied data/handlers, with only transient rename/drag state local. This is useful for shared camera, palette and material libraries because undo, load and multiple panes then observe one authoritative collection. It does not remove the need to cancel or revalidate an in-progress rename/drag if its item is deleted, replaced or changed by undo. Validate referenced IDs and adapters so a missing binding cannot leave feedback silently disconnected. RFF could reuse library presentation while each snapshot type preserves its own stable schema, high-precision coordinates and shader settings. None of these documents proves current cross-pane synchronization, accessibility, image quality or performance; they inform bounded workflow improvements around the already identified shader opportunities.

## Time-dependent shader parameters: transport, mapping and audio assets (2026-10-08)

Full document review of ADR-0027 (28 lines), ADR-0028 (30), ADR-0107 (114) and ADR-0108 (105). Historical bug descriptions and performance assertions are not fresh measurements. These records supply design evidence for optional RFF animation/modulation improvements, not proof that RFF needs a replacement animation system.

ADR-0027 avoids repeatedly seeking a playing audio deck, reserving synchronization for resume, large timeline jumps and range exit. This separates continuous playback from transport transitions. Its half-second jump threshold is a heuristic: elapsed frame jumps can reflect a stall as well as an intentional seek, and a smaller intentional scrub need not cross that threshold. The statement that clocks reconverge on the next tick depends on the actual master-clock design; suppressing seeks alone cannot establish convergence. For RFF, explicit play/pause/seek/loop events and a defined master time would be more reliable than interpreting every time delta as intent. Offline video should evaluate modulation at output-frame/sample time, independently of live device playback and machine rendering speed.

ADR-0028 keeps raw audio Files outside history/store snapshots, with only metadata and peaks serialized. This reduces repeated binary storage but intentionally loses the source file across sessions. Its cache is keyed by deck index rather than a durable asset identity; the record does not establish restoration of the same bytes after undo, replacement or reopening. Export decode failures and beauty-pass-only dispatch are documented risks, not newly reproduced failures. A RFF extension should give external media a stable identity and explicit availability state, resolve it before export and distinguish missing audio from an intentionally silent video. Avoid copying large immutable assets into each edit snapshot, while preserving a reproducible link from saved modulation settings to the source data.

ADR-0107 identifies four modulation destinations: direct uniforms, composed engine values, render-state feature blocks and display-only values. Its recorded failure is instructive: controls and exported frames could change while the live worker never received rotation/camera/light offsets. The adopted transport sends a complete modulation dictionary on every render tick, including empty state, and replaces the worker copy before frame synchronization. This gives removed targets a clearing path. Resolving the proxy inside the tick also avoids retaining an earlier stub. For RFF, make the destination and clearing behavior of every animatable shader parameter explicit, including values packed into matrices/arrays rather than individual uniforms. Carry render-generation identity so late updates cannot affect a different loaded scene; a transport message alone is not proof of a presented frame.

The shared target classifier reduces divergence between what a picker offers and what dispatch can handle. However, the ADR expressly acknowledges a trusted list of merged feature blocks that can mark a dead route healthy. Its coverage gate tests classifications, not actual GPU output for every target. The claim that preview now matches export for every target therefore requires stronger end-to-end evidence than the described gate alone. For RFF, compare evaluated values and selected rendered frames at identical time, base state and modulation inputs, covering target removal, scene change and both direct and packed bindings. A retained zero-valued dictionary entry can be semantically harmless without demonstrating bounded memory or serialized-message size over arbitrarily many distinct targets.

ADR-0108 centralizes parameter display mappings and composes a modulation offset as travel in the mapped slider domain. In its notation, with value span R and display span L, the result is f^-1(f(base) + offset * L/R). For an affine mapping this reduces algebraically to base + offset; for a curved mapping it intentionally changes the value-space response. Thus preserving the offset's input units does not preserve the old numerical or physical effect on curved parameters. The record's bit-identical linear claim depends on its implementation and tests, not algebra alone. Constant travel is also limited by endpoint clamping, special zero bands and changes in the mapping itself.

This is a useful optional control model for RFF color repeats, material parameters and light intensity: an artist can tune motion in a domain matching the control's response. Define whether a rule uses physical-value addition, multiplication/exposure, or normalized control travel, and persist that choice so older animations remain stable. A logarithmic or log1p curve needs explicit domain and exact-zero behavior. The ADR's EV-light caveat is substantive: applying a display curve and then exponentiating an exposure parameter composes two nonlinear mappings. Choose the intended physical or artistic quantity before adding such a mode. Do not inherit a widget's arbitrary scale as an undocumented rendering law.

The strongest reusable architecture is a single parameter-mapping/composition function shared by live updates, ordinary setters and export, with one routing definition. The document still records duplicated export dispatch structures, so shared arithmetic does not guarantee identical destination selection. Memoized mapping construction must account for parameter range, light type and schema changes. Apply these principles to 2D palette/mask animation and 3D camera/material/light animation, while keeping deep-zoom coordinates and MPA precision out of low-precision generic modulation routes. No source-only finding here establishes a current RFF defect, a measured speedup or a reason to reprioritize these workflow features above the previously identified image-quality shader improvements.

## Formula fidelity: bit-level ports, fourth coordinates and estimator contracts (2026-10-08)

Full review of ADR-0101 (66 lines) and ADR-0102 (51). These records describe previously implemented importer decisions and historical checks; their reported counts, image statistics and owner confirmations are not new measurements in this audit.

ADR-0101 separates a manual formula overlay from generated decompiler output for Amazing Surf 2's exponent/sign manipulation. This preserves generated output and a separately maintained reference interpreter, while allowing the manual entry to override generated entries. The reusable idea is an explicit, traceable exception layer with collision policy and independent validation, not weakening a general equivalence gate until an exceptional formula passes. The record's phrase 'byte-exact' sits alongside a nonzero maximum absolute numerical error of 1.9e-7; those are not equivalent claims of output identity. A float32 transliteration and a double-semantics oracle need an explicitly stated input domain, rounding convention and error criterion. Exact integer bit operations do not make surrounding floating-point arithmetic exact, particularly at exponent transitions, subnormal values and signed zero.

The same ADR records an empirical estimator override from r/dr to (r-2)/dr. This changes estimated surface location and step sizes, rather than merely adjusting appearance. A coherent image, nonblack fraction, variance and absence of NaNs do not prove a conservative distance bound or faithful geometry. For RFF's possible 3D formula extensions, treat the iteration, initialization, derivative update, bailout and final estimator as one versioned contract. Keep formula-specific overrides explicit and validate grazing rays, thin features, camera scale and iteration limits against independent evidence. Do not generalize one aesthetic/empirical correction to other formula families or to Mandelbrot perturbation math. A manual override must survive regeneration and remain attributable, but the architecture itself does not grant permission to copy another implementation.

ADR-0102 distinguishes a genuine fourth spatial coordinate from a derivative accumulator packed into the fourth component. It records separate fixes for the Julia constant c.w and the distance/bailout radius: seed all intended coordinates, and enable the 4D radius only for the identified IFS estimator family. It deliberately excludes another 4D family whose estimator behavior differs. Thus 'use length(z) whenever w is spatial' is not a safe universal rule derived from this document. Coordinate dimension, derivative storage, seed dimension and estimator dimension are independent pieces of metadata; coloring and orbit traps are explicitly left 3D in this decision.

The important RFF opportunity is stronger formula capability metadata and diagnostic field views: show or inspect initial state, Julia constant, derivative state, bailout radius and final DE separately when validating a new formula. Per-iteration agreement cannot detect a wrong initial constant or a correctly computed radius passed to the wrong estimator. For 2D, preserve the same separation for complex coordinates, auxiliary orbit fields and derivative values; optional 4D slices could be a distinct visualization feature, not a modification of existing Mandelbrot/MPA semantics. Specify the slice plane and whether coloring observes projected or full-dimensional state. Source records alone do not establish a safe new ray-step bound or a performance advantage.

## Deferred renderer construction and stale camera acknowledgements (2026-10-08)

Full review of ADR-0041 (57 lines) and ADR-0042 (45). ADR-0041 distinguishes an initialization acknowledgement that only stores parameters from a later boot that constructs the renderer and compiles. It buffers resize before boot and describes teardown/recreation as a recovery path for a stalled browser worker compile. For RFF, staging resource construction until a formula/configuration is ready can improve startup control, but a READY message at the first stage must not be presented as GPU readiness or a completed image. Every message accepted before construction needs a defined policy: queue, latest-value replacement, explicit rejection or deferred execution. Browser canvas transfer rules and worker termination behavior should not be copied as Vulkan device-lifetime rules. Cancellation of a host worker is not proof that GPU work has already stopped or resources are safe to free.

ADR-0042 avoids accepting stale camera-offset echoes after a new offset is set. It removes a time-based release and instead waits for numerical convergence within 0.001, with teardown/crash cleanup. This is better evidence of application than merely waiting two seconds, but a fixed absolute tolerance is scale-dependent and equality of position does not identify which request or scene produced the acknowledgement. An old frame at the same location can satisfy a position comparison without being the new frame. A worker that never acknowledges leaves the guard engaged, as the record itself notes.

For RFF's 2D deep zoom and 3D camera changes, carry a monotonically changing scene/camera revision with submitted and presented state, associate overlays/picking with the frame's revision, and use numerical tolerance only for the specific geometric comparison that needs it. Preserve exact/high-precision location data rather than using a fixed world-unit epsilon as a synchronization token. Define reset and failure recovery so the interface can report a pending or failed transition without silently snapping back or waiting indefinitely. These are rendering-consistency improvements that complement shader work; no current RFF failure or timing gain is asserted here.

## Scene ownership, modulation writers and a unified palette input (2026-10-08)

Full review of ADR-0103 (184 lines) and ADR-0111 (126). Both contain amendments that materially change the original decisions. Reading only their Decision/Consequences sections would produce incorrect current recommendations. No live behavior or listed historical test result was reproduced here.

ADR-0103's leading amendment explicitly reverses preservation of modulation rules across scene loads: the audio input is live equipment state, while rules are scene content and must load with the scene. The older two-holder predicate table and consequence are superseded. A scene without modulation data resets rules rather than inheriting the previous look. For RFF, distinguish device/session configuration, saved artwork parameters, transient evaluated values and accumulated render buffers. Preservation during scene load, preservation during partial copy and suppression of accumulation reset are separate decisions; no single 'persistent' flag should imply all three. A consistent pre-load snapshot avoids application order changing conditional preservation. The historical LFO/stale-cache limitation needs current code evidence before being presented as an unresolved defect.

The same record describes durable target retargeting after formula-slot changes. Recomputed transient modulation values do not repair durable links pointing at a retired parameter. Disabling an unresolved link can preserve its band/envelope/gain for reassignment, whereas silently attaching it to another formula's same numeric slot changes the artwork. RFF could use stable parameter/formula identities and an explicit retarget report for future formula or layer restructuring. Collision policy should reflect semantics: several audio inputs may intentionally add to one parameter, while two exclusive track owners may conflict.

Its successive writer-conflict addenda are directly relevant to shader control architecture. A slider setter, animation tick and full-config synchronization can all write the same GPU uniform. Composing base plus live modulation in only one path leaves another writer able to overwrite it. Persisting the already-modulated result as the base instead can apply the offset twice after recompilation. The record therefore keeps base state separate, publishes uniform ownership, batches multiple axes into one vector result and reasserts evaluated values. For RFF, compute each frame's final parameter block from authoritative base state and time inputs, then publish it consistently across direct and packed bindings. If configuration is restored before modulation after a compile, gate presentation or initialize the final values before the first visible frame; 'the next tick corrects it' is not itself a no-flash guarantee. This applies to 2D palette vectors and 3D material/light vectors alike.

ADR-0111 routes multiple gradient sources into one working pipeline: source channels, optional curve replacement, global adjustments and an output representation. Its amendments refine representation fidelity: an identity operation must retain an existing stop configuration or dense ramp, and merely opening an untouched curve fit must not silently refit the saved gradient. A fit can be lossy even when its preview looks close. For RFF, imported ramps, fixed palettes and generated recipes should share adjustment behavior without forcing every source into a lossy stop representation. Preserve the source representation until an explicit edit or conversion requires a new one, and keep frozen recipe generation semantics intact. JavaScript object identity is a useful implementation guard in this record, but RFF's user-facing requirement is preserved data and appearance, not an identical pointer value.

The bake/fold design commits the current result as a new input and resets already-applied modifiers, preventing the transform from being applied twice. It also retains enough prior structure for return-to-source and one-step undo. The later amendment distinguishes choosing a fresh source (discard pending dials in one transaction) from restoring a saved session (retain its dials). Those operations should remain explicit in any RFF palette/material workflow; loading a session through an ordinary 'use palette' command could otherwise destroy intended pending edits.

The final amendment separates the snapshot restored by undo from the subset used to decide whether to record an undo step. The tracksEdited flag is restored with curves, while changing that flag alone should not manufacture a history entry. This preserves semantics without spurious steps. The document still identifies load/return/cancel paths that do not carry the flag; their desired behavior must be specified rather than inferred from the undo fix. Its historical 'old shell untouched' statement and original visibility-predicate limitation are context, not proof of the current source state.

A unified input pipeline is a strong reusable workflow for 2D palette editing and 3D albedo/emission/material ramps. Keep base color transformations distinct from geometric normal or lighting computations, resolve one authoritative result for all previews/exports, and compare untouched pass-through, explicit bake, source replacement, session restore and undo at both data and image levels. These records explain mechanisms and compatibility requirements; they do not demonstrate that RFF lacks equivalent functionality or establish a measured visual-quality gain.

## Blend-space semantics, gamut handling and bounded stop reduction (2026-10-08)

Full review of ADR-0113 (103 lines) and ADR-0127 (64). Their historical color measurements, timing figures and dependency-license statements are recorded research claims, not newly reproduced measurements or a fresh dependency license audit.

ADR-0113 distinguishes rectangular Oklab from polar OkLCh, retains the old serialized key for compatibility and changes the visible label. This is an important RFF interoperability lesson: a familiar string need not identify the algorithm its spelling suggests. Import/export adapters should map documented semantics, not labels alone. Preserving a key does not preserve the rendered image when the underlying gamut handling changes; the ADR explicitly acknowledges changed older gradients. RFF's stable recipes require retaining old behavior or introducing an explicit version/new mode rather than silently applying this migration policy.

The useful color mechanism is reducing chroma at fixed lightness and hue for polar interpolation instead of clipping channels independently. Near neutral colors, the design fades between polar and rectangular paths to avoid a hard threshold discontinuity where hue is poorly defined. Such a fade is an intentional artistic interpolation rule, not evidence of full color-standard conformance. Validate endpoints, hue wrap/tie conventions, continuity near neutral, output gamut and the case where fixed lightness itself is outside the representable range. The proposed ordering of blend modes and example chroma/lightness numbers depend on the sampled colors and chosen metrics; a rectangular straight line having zero deviation from itself does not establish a universal pigment-to-tint ranking for every endpoint pair.

The record describes CPU-side ramp baking as a way to make richer blending available without changing the fragment shader. This is directly useful for RFF's 2D palettes and 3D albedo/emission ramps: compute/cache the selected interpolation when its inputs change, then upload a stable LUT. It does not guarantee that every export format, precision level or interpolating consumer reproduces the baked ramp exactly. Cache identity must include stops or source ramp, interpolation mode, color encoding, relevant algorithm version and other applied transforms. The quoted spectral cost and memoization gain are historical, not expected RFF timings. Pigment-style palette mixing should be labeled as a color tool; it does not by itself simulate spectral light transport or layered physical materials in the 3D renderer. Verify the actual dependency/version and original implementation provenance before adopting code.

ADR-0127's amendment replaces the original four-only reduction choices with a stop-count axis and optional search across blend modes. Consequently, retaining the original mode is conditional on search being off; the superseded API names and original UI description should not guide an implementation. The useful underlying contract remains preview without mutation, then one undoable commit or cancellation. If a blend-mode search changes the interpretation, persist the chosen mode along with the reduced stops and show that choice before applying it.

The tolerances are maximum rendered Oklab differences sampled at 256 texels, not a bound over the continuous gradient or over all future output resolutions. Narrow transitions between samples, later LUT filtering and different output encodings can expose errors outside that sampled guarantee. Greedy removal plus a fresh fit is a search heuristic, not proof of the globally smallest stop set. Monotonic stop counts across tolerance choices do not alone prove monotonic image error; inspect and measure the final candidate for both properties when that is the intended contract. The phrase 'one amount per macrotask, so ... never blocks a frame' is stronger than scheduling guarantees: one long task can still block a frame, even if work yields between amounts.

For RFF, offer stop reduction as an explicit lossy editing operation with a preview and a stated measurement domain. Preserve the original on cancel and avoid automatic reduction when opening or saving an unchanged palette. Use denser or adaptive error sampling around sharp transitions if exported high-resolution or analytically sampled palettes need stronger fidelity. Reducing editable stops can lower editing and ramp-rebuild work, but does not reduce the per-pixel cost of sampling an unchanged-size GPU LUT. For 3D, evaluate the resulting base-color/emission field separately from lighting; specular contrast or emissive postprocessing can make a small palette error more visible. For 2D, inspect repeated palette seams and high-frequency bands. These are concrete palette-quality and editing opportunities, with no newly measured shader speedup implied.

## Stable entry aliases and explicit palette-editor handoff (2026-10-08)

Full review of ADR-0125 (48 lines) and ADR-0126 (79). Their deployment and cross-browser success statements are historical claims, not new browser verification. The alias HTML files were separately inspected earlier; this document review adds design rationale, not another coverage count for those files.

ADR-0125 preserves an older preview entry as the same application while generating new links on the canonical path in the same deployment directory. This is useful compatibility design: old serialized references continue to identify the same functionality after an interface replacement. Identical HTML avoids redirect-specific query handling but does not by itself prove server routing, offline availability, payload-decoder compatibility or correct application of the encoded gradient. The statement that only pre-swap links reach the alias is an intention, not a guarantee: visitors can still copy its address manually. For RFF, retain stable preset/file identifiers and compatible import entry points through feature renames, while validating decoded payloads and preserving their semantics. This is compatibility around 2D palettes and 3D material workflows, not a rendering optimization.

ADR-0126 separates three operations: sending the currently relevant gradient to the editor, returning to the originating application instance, and recovering a scene if that instance is unavailable. It explicitly does not automatically send the edited gradient back; shared Recent supplies discovery instead. Thus 'round trip' here means scene continuity, not automatic palette replacement. Any RFF adaptation should state whether closing the editor commits to a specific material/palette destination, merely saves a reusable palette, or cancels. A stable destination identifier plus a scene/material revision is safer than assuming whichever layer is currently selected remains the intended recipient.

The described input selection prefers a still-applied favorite, then the panel destination, then gradient 1, treating a flat single color as no useful candidate. That last rule is a product choice, not a universal property of palettes: a constant albedo or emission color can be a valid RFF 3D material, and a deliberately flat 2D palette should not be silently discarded. Preserve the selected source and its data even when the editor offers little variation. The amendment keeps theme onboarding from changing the caller's shared theme during an editor visit; analogous session settings should remain separate from the imported artwork.

The record uses a two-minute one-shot incoming key, a BroadcastChannel return handshake and a reason-specific recovery stash. One-shot consumption, expiry and caller identity are distinct concerns. A shared key alone does not demonstrate isolation for two concurrent senders, reliable delivery, or matching an acknowledgement to the correct source instance; inspect those guarantees in implementation before claiming them. For native RFF, associate each editor session with an explicit request ID and owner document. Resolve whether stale replies are discarded, offered for import or applied after validation, and preserve recovery data until the receiving operation has succeeded.

The scene stash deliberately excludes shared gradient documents to avoid resurrecting items deleted in the editor, flushes current camera state and retains the unsaved flag. This illustrates selective ownership in recovery snapshots: save document state needed to restore the view without overwriting independently edited shared libraries. A failure to save the stash is reported while navigation continues, so the trip is not equivalent to guaranteed recovery. Its 24-hour retention and opt-in autosave have different scopes; ordinary reload/crash recovery is not established by this path. For RFF, verify that recovery includes high-precision 2D location or full 3D camera state, shader settings and unsaved status, while respecting stable ConfigIO and palette formats. Test two simultaneous documents, deleted/replaced destination layers, failed writes and return after the original document closes. These are concrete reliability requirements for reusing a palette editor across dimensions, without asserting a current RFF handoff bug.

## Camera interaction evidence versus actual rendered output (2026-10-08)

Full source review of `debug/smoke-orbit.mts` (149 lines) and `debug/smoke-interact.mts` (120). Neither script was executed. Historical deliberate-break experiments in their comments are informative descriptions, not fresh reproductions.

The orbit smoke drives a real mouse drag, reads the main-thread shadow offset before/after and requires a movement magnitude of at least 0.5. It then waits up to 45 seconds for an accumulation counter to increase. Its own documented blind spot is decisive: the band scheduler can advance that counter outside the render operation, so a stopped render pipeline can still pass. Worker tick counts and a convergence label are not independent pixel evidence either. Historical PNG file sizes differ in the recorded failure experiment, but compressed file size itself is not a reliable correctness metric.

Additional limits are visible in the assertions. The drag is placed relative to the whole viewport rather than a verified canvas hit target. The scalar movement threshold is scene-scale dependent and cannot verify orbit orientation, pivot, radius or the expected final camera. Adding the high and low offset components into one ordinary number discards the extended representation's benefit for sufficiently large coordinates. A NaN delta does not fail the less-than comparison. The error gate rejects only messages matching TypeError, ReferenceError or 'is not a function', so many graphics/worker failures can be logged without failing. The timeout reflects historical software-renderer observations and is not a native RFF performance target.

For RFF, distinguish input handling, camera-state update, interaction-quality release and completed GPU presentation. Check all numerical fields for finiteness and compare high-precision locations without collapsing their representation. In 3D, validate the intended orbit transform and a rendered frame at the resulting camera revision; in 2D, validate the pan/zoom transform and preservation of the reference/precision contract. After interaction ends, verify the target resolution and actual sample/image progress instead of relying solely on a scheduler counter. Include cancellation or capture loss as well as ordinary mouse-up. These tests would substantiate improvements to adaptive preview and camera responsiveness without conflating 'scheduled' with 'rendered'.

The interaction smoke directly calls a generated store setter with distinctive scalar, vector and color values, then checks state and serialized preset fields. Asymmetric vector components make axis swaps visible; endpoint red/green channels avoid ambiguity from color transfer, while the final hex string checks the whole serialized color. However, despite one comment claiming either a string or RGB object is accepted, the actual immediate color assertion requires object r/g fields. The blue channel is not checked in the live state. Several expected scalars remain hardcoded despite the fixture's stated single-literal intent.

The captured screenshot has no image assertion. The script never verifies overlay geometry/color pixels, user-control wiring, a GPU uniform, or loading the saved preset into a fresh state. Its 'roundtrip' is getPreset followed by JSON serialization and parsing, not a file decoder/application roundtrip. Absence of console/page errors is useful but cannot prove that an absent or inert overlay rendered correctly. For RFF, retain this kind of parameter-type fixture as a serialization check, then add a separate restore-into-clean-state test and render-field/image assertion for new shader controls. A mixed-channel color is useful for detecting color-space conversion errors, but test its expected linear/encoded values explicitly rather than skipping the sensitive channel. Apply the same discipline to 2D palette/mask parameters and 3D material/light vectors. These source findings refine evidence requirements; they do not assert a current RFF rendering defect.

## Mask-driven particle reflection: useful effect, limited collision evidence (2026-10-08)

Full review of `debug/smoke-particle-bounce.mts` (233 lines), with a selective symbol cross-check in the previously reviewed `fluid-toy/brush/particles.ts`. No simulation was executed. This path uses a scalar collision mask and its sampled gradient, not a proven signed distance field. The distinction matters when considering reuse in RFF.

The smoke installs a stepped collision gradient, finds a high-mask point and a nearby low-mask point, injects sixteen particles toward the former and snapshots initial velocity in the same operation. That last detail avoids measuring an already-decayed velocity after a separate asynchronous call. It waits 1.2 seconds, then checks final positions against the mask, slowdown and projected displacement toward the selected wall point. The header correctly notes that drag alone can satisfy the slowdown assertion and that a particle can cross a wall before the final capture. Its historical deliberately-disabled-bounce runs justify adding a displacement bound, but do not make that bound a universal proof of reflection.

The reported 'max penetration' is the maximum across particles at the final instant, not each particle's maximum over its trajectory. It is measured from the common nominal spawn point, not each randomized initial position, and the gap is to an interior high-mask sample rather than the true first boundary intersection. A particle that crosses and later returns can pass; a particle stopped by unrelated drag can also pass if it slows and remains outside. The final success message claims velocities reverse, but no assertion checks a reflected direction or incoming/outgoing normal components. An oblique ideal reflection preserves speed; any speed loss belongs to restitution/drag, not obliqueness itself. The source's corresponding explanatory comment should not become a physics assumption in an RFF adaptation.

Random spawn jitter has no fixed seed, and wall/free anchors are selected by scanning the current mask rather than from an independently specified analytic wall. The test does not prove each jittered spawn begins outside, that every particle reaches the wall, or that real elapsed time equals simulated time. It relies on runtime array order for velocity pairing rather than particle identity. Empty output is caught by the zero-slowed check, but particle-count preservation and finite coordinates/velocities/mask samples are not explicitly enforced. Slow speed and a broad band are deliberate fixture choices that leave fast traversal, thin obstacles and large time steps uncovered. Only selected error-message patterns fail the test. These are source-level scope limits, not newly observed simulation failures.

The implementation cross-check identifies finite-difference mask gradients with a fallback wider stencil, reflection scaled by restitution and a fixed normal nudge from the previous position. A gradient of a thresholded/downsampled mask can give an approximate boundary normal, but the mask magnitude is not a distance-to-surface bound. It cannot safely be used as a ray-march step or a penetration depth. A fixed UV stencil/nudge is also resolution/aspect dependent in physical or screen coordinates. Distinguish the mask's sampling footprint, its geometric coordinate system and the simulation step length.

For RFF, this suggests an optional 2D flow/particle overlay following or colliding with fractal-derived masks, with the underlying fractal computation left intact. In 3D, surface-following particles or similar effects need an actual geometric field, consistent normals and a collision method appropriate to fast motion; projecting this UV mask test into 3D is insufficient. Use deterministic analytic fixtures, fixed simulation steps, recorded trajectories and particle IDs to validate reflection and nonpenetration. Compare collision on/off with the same drag and initial state, verify normal/tangential velocity behavior, and cover thin boundaries and finite-value failures. Such effects are feature-expansion candidates, not evidence of a shader-quality improvement or performance gain in the existing RFF renderer.

## Optional editor load failure: containment versus rendering recovery (2026-10-08)

Full source review of `debug/smoke-lazy-fallback.mts` (89 lines); no browser run. The test deliberately aborts requests matching AdvancedGradientEditor, opens the Gradient tab with a real click and checks for a local failure notice, no root-boundary error and continued proxy frame-count advancement. It then boots a separate fresh context without blocking and checks that a matching successful response occurs and no failure/crash notice appears. This is a useful positive/negative pair for isolating an optional editor-load failure from the whole application.

Its observable scope is narrower than successful rendering or recovery. Proxy frameCount is a tick count, as the separately reviewed orbit smoke documents, so an increase does not establish GPU presentation or a responsive camera image. The drag is not checked against camera state or output pixels. The success case records a response URL/status, not successful module evaluation, presence of working editor controls or a palette edit reaching the renderer. The notice is searched across body text, so its existence alone does not verify its placement. The successful second boot does not test retrying a failed import in the same application instance, preserving unsaved editor state, or recovery after a shader compile failure. The two-second post-click wait can produce timing-dependent observations. Page errors are checked, but there is no general console-error gate, and no counter explicitly proves which blocked request was exercised.

For RFF, isolate failure of optional palette/material editors or external resources so the existing scene remains usable, while presenting a specific recoverable state for the unavailable feature. Verify a completed image at the current scene revision, successful interactions in unaffected controls and preservation of unsaved state. If retry is offered, test it in the failed instance rather than only on a fresh launch. Keep CPU-side panel construction failures, missing resources, shader compilation failures and graphics-device loss as separate recovery cases: this browser module-fetch test cannot establish a common recovery mechanism for them. The same containment principle applies to 2D palette editors and 3D material tools, but no startup-speed benefit or current RFF fault is demonstrated by this source review.

## Contextual help and quality indicators: test scope (2026-10-08)

Full source review of `debug/smoke-help-menu.mts` (111 lines) and `debug/smoke-hud-hint.mts` (83), without execution. These are interaction-test sources, not a visual/accessibility audit or shader performance measurement.

The help-menu test locates one Help button, clicks it, finds expected text among all page buttons, toggles a store flag by click and keyboard, and requests the Getting Started view. It deliberately pins Fluid Toy's use of GMT-default support/topic content. That demonstrates a shared default contract, not correctness or relevance of the help for every sibling app. The expected separator is described but not asserted; menu item text is not scoped to the actual popover. The two flag comparisons require inequality rather than boolean negation, and the forced Getting Started click bypasses ordinary actionability checks. A state-visible flag plus body text does not prove focus placement, correct overlay ownership or that every topic's content matches the live parameter. The comment about body.dispatchEvent no longer describes the actual keyboard.press call. Only selected error patterns fail the final error gate.

The HUD test checks an initial hotkey panel and a quality-badge text pattern, collapses the panel, hides hints through a direct setter and re-enables them by keyboard. It records that remount resets the local expansion state; RFF should choose deliberately whether global hide/show preserves a user's collapsed preference. At the global-off step it only asserts absence of the pill, not both pill and expanded panel as the header claims. The first button whose title contains Hide is force-clicked without scope to the panel, and CSS classes are part of the title selector. These can make test behavior depend on unrelated layout/style changes. Short fixed delays and visibility reads are weaker than waiting for the specific expected transition.

For RFF, contextual explanations can make field masks, roughness, palette mapping and interactive-quality controls easier to use, but topics should identify the actual 2D/3D mode and parameter semantics rather than inheriting another app's defaults. Tie documentation identifiers to supported controls, verify visible content and keyboard ownership, and keep editing text from triggering global hotkeys. A quality badge should reflect the actual rendered resolution/sample state and requested final quality; text such as q50% alone is no evidence of GPU quality or convergence. Use stable control identities and normal-actionability interactions in tests, with separate data/pixel checks for the rendering claim. This is a supporting usability and evidence improvement around shader features, not a new shader algorithm or proof of a current RFF issue.

## Vector animation bindings and screenshot evidence (2026-10-08)

Full source review of `debug/smoke-track-binding.mts` (110 lines) and `debug/smoke-screenshot.mts` (23). Neither was run. The first is a deterministic helper-level test, while the second is a capture utility with no image assertions; they establish different kinds of evidence.

The binding test checks scalar keys, underscore-suffixed vector-axis keys, labels and an explicit composition mapping from a displayed orbit vector to three scalar camera parameters. Its useful regression fixture supplies nonzero base values while modulating only one axis: unmodified components must retain their bases instead of snapping to zero. A separate additive case distinguishes an offset from an absolute evaluated value and verifies that the untouched axis is not doubled. These are good local invariants for RFF's 2D coordinate/palette vectors and 3D camera/material vectors. Explicitly label the representation at each boundary so an already-composed value is not added to the base again.

Coverage remains local. Vec4 is checked for key construction, not readLiveVec values/type; composeFrom is checked for output names, not actual live reads or animation delivery. The test does not cover zero-valued live updates with nonzero bases, nonfinite values, missing/extra composition entries, colliding identifiers, input mutation, binding removal or the shader/export route. JSON-string equality is adequate for these simple fixture arrays but is not a general numerical/schema validator. The test's success message should not be treated as proof that every rendered parameter type or all four vector components reach the GPU. For RFF, add boundary checks where the feature actually consumes a new vector type and retain the relevant precision for 2D deep-zoom coordinates rather than passing them through ordinary low-precision vector controls.

The screenshot utility waits a fixed 2.5 seconds after DOM content load and writes a viewport PNG to a fixed scratch path. It does not require renderer readiness, a completed scene revision, any canvas pixels, a specific camera or absence of application errors. A loading screen or error page can be saved successfully. Its destination also matches the separately reviewed interaction smoke's output, so the filename alone does not identify which test or state produced it. For RFF comparisons, capture after an explicit rendering milestone and record scene/settings, output dimensions, device, revision, accumulation state and capture purpose beside uniquely identified images. Pair visual inspection with field or image comparisons appropriate to the proposed change. A successful PNG write is an artifact-generation result, not a correctness or performance result for either 2D or 3D rendering.

## Adaptive viewport checks: forced quality is not natural recovery (2026-10-08)

Full review of `debug/smoke-viewport.mts` (120 lines), with a selective cross-check of suppression and manual-mode branches in the previously reviewed `engine/AdaptiveResolution.ts`. No browser run. The test checks installed target FPS and interaction downsample settings, forces a full-quality baseline through suppression plus synthetic FPS reports, switches to manual mode for interaction, and finally re-enables suppression to obtain full quality again.

The opening description says quality naturally recovers over two to three seconds, but the actual code deliberately does not test that behavior. Its later comments acknowledge that the interaction sample observes the reportFps-driven manual branch, not necessarily the immediate interaction-start subscription. A fixed 100 ms delay cannot establish immediate response latency. The final suppression step is even narrower than the claimed release check: the inspected adaptive code hard-forces full resolution when suppressed before reaching later active/manual handling. Therefore full quality under suppression does not independently prove that handleInteractionEnd cleared the interaction state. A still-active interaction can be masked by this override.

Assertions also leave invalid values uncovered: the during-interaction check has only an upper bound, so zero or negative quality can pass, and comparison-only checks do not explicitly reject NaN. The initial/final checks only require values above 0.99, without an upper bound. No canvas backing dimensions, actual render-target size, completed image, export resolution or precision are examined. Synthetic 60 FPS reports and a forced manual mode cannot demonstrate automatic load response under real shader pressure. Captured page and console errors do fail this smoke, which is useful but does not close these semantic gaps.

For RFF, separate four tests: immediate interaction-state transition, adaptive quality decision, propagation to allocated render dimensions, and natural full-quality recovery after activity ends. Inspect the actual interaction flag before enabling an override, require finite in-range quality, and capture the requested revision at the restored dimensions. Add a distinct export override test rather than using export-like suppression as a proxy for release. Controlled timing and recorded frame costs can validate the decision logic, while a real workload verifies the render path. Include cancellation, window deactivation and resizing as well as normal end events. The same mechanism can support responsive 2D palette previews and 3D camera/material edits, but it must not lower Mandelbrot numerical precision or leave the final image permanently downsampled. This review establishes test-scope limits and an RFF validation approach, not a current RFF adaptive-resolution bug or a measured speed gain.

## Formula-adoption prioritization: blockers versus verified scene support (2026-10-08)

Full source review of `debug/survey-mb3d-blockers.mts` (61 lines). It was not executed: it uses an external hardcoded H: corpus and writes its result to another H: path. This review does not claim access to that corpus or any current survey counts.

The survey parses top-level .m3p files, derives a weave sequence, deduplicates used slot indices and classifies each transpiler result as supported whenever its tier is not unsupported. It separates mode-0 scenes without missing formulas, mode-0 formula blockers, other modes and no-addon/errors. This is a useful dependency inventory, but its 'renderable' label means only mode 0 plus no unsupported used slot according to this check. It neither assembles/compiles the complete shader nor verifies seeds, hybrid semantics, DE selection, camera, color or rendered output. An empty used-slot set can also have no missing entries without proving meaningful geometry. The parametric choice is based on the number of distinct used slots, not full end-to-end scene validation.

The blocker ranking counts how many scenes mention each missing formula, not how many scenes that single port would actually unlock. A scene requiring several missing formulas contributes to each count. The separate one-away list is closer to marginal benefit under this narrow classifier, while multi-blocker groups require joint work. Formula names are used as identifiers, so aliases or name collisions can distort the ranking. Modes greater than or equal to one are grouped under a label for modes 1-3 without explicit range validation; those scenes can also have unsupported formulas, so resolving blend semantics alone need not make them usable. Exceptions from parsing, sequence construction or transpilation are all labeled PARSE_ERR, losing the failure stage.

For RFF, prioritize possible 3D formula additions with a capability matrix that distinguishes decoding, iteration support, hybrid composition, shader compilation and verified scene fidelity. Record sample-corpus identity and representativeness, not just a headline count. Estimate marginal benefit after prerequisite sets, provenance checks and precision/estimator validation, and keep manual approximations separate from faithful ports. If a 3D formula's coordinate folds or orbit fields are useful as 2D patterns/masks, track that as an independent feature candidate rather than claiming 2D Mandelbrot compatibility. This technique can guide effort allocation, but the script supplies no basis for ranking current RFF visual improvements by measured benefit or declaring imported scenes correct.

## Performance-log comparison: missing measurements must not count as gains (2026-10-08)

Full source review of `debug/spike-diff.mts` (173 lines). This compares timeline benchmark JSON, not rendered images. It was not run against benchmark data. Historical experiment criteria and the printed recommendations are source content, not instructions or new findings about RFF.

The utility joins scenarios by name, prints notification counts, converted FPS metrics, long-task totals and top profiler totals, then accepts two of three improvement criteria. Duplicate scenario names overwrite earlier entries without validation. There is no schema, finite-value, matching-workload, run-duration, device/build or seed-equality gate. Keyframe seed counts are printed only after the verdict. Aggregated medians provide no variance or confidence interval here, so the report cannot distinguish a stable improvement from run-to-run noise by itself.

A concrete false-gain route is visible: frameTimeMs maps nonpositive FPS to zero milliseconds. A post-run zero FPS can therefore look like a 100 percent frame-time improvement rather than no progress or invalid data. Separately, the profiler criterion substitutes zero for a missing post-run scenario or profiler. A disappeared measurement can satisfy the 50 percent reduction requirement. Missing data should be reported as unavailable and block the affected comparison, not be treated as free work. The printed 'frameDt p5' is the reciprocal of low-percentile FPS; for reciprocal instantaneous samples it corresponds approximately to the opposite, high frame-time percentile, not frame-time p5. Its exact interpretation also depends on how the producer aggregates FPS.

The first two criteria pick the best reduction among four scenarios, while their displayed labels still name only two. Thus different favorable scenarios can satisfy different criteria despite regressions elsewhere. The third scans all pre-run scenarios and broadly named slider/track profilers rather than proving the specific useTrackAnimation work improved. Raw profiler totals are not normalized for event count or duration. Its percentage formatter also negates the positive reduction for the 'improve' detail, producing misleading negative-improvement wording. The utility prints failed/partial verdicts without setting a failure exit code, so process success is not a performance gate. Two favorable metrics alone cannot establish the causal diagnosis claimed by the success banner.

For RFF shader or preview optimization, pair identical scenes, camera, dimensions, sample budget, precision, driver/device and interaction workload; verify image/field fidelity and actual rendered work before interpreting speed. Reject invalid or missing samples, distinguish CPU UI cost from GPU rendering time, and report both targeted gains and regressions across the selected workload set. Use repeated measurements with variability, separate startup/compile costs from steady-state frame cost, and document percentile definitions. Notification-count reductions may help UI responsiveness but do not demonstrate faster 2D fractal computation or 3D shading. This source review strengthens the measurement plan for the previously identified improvements without supplying any new RFF performance result.

## Preset-library drag ownership and import passthrough (2026-10-08)

Full source review of `debug/smoke-statelibrary-drop.mts` (152 lines), without execution. The useful contract is that an internal row reorder must work without consuming unrelated external file drops. This can inform RFF camera, palette and material libraries, where a list may occupy the same area that accepts scene imports.

The test injects two camera entries with empty state, dispatches synthetic dragstart/dragover/drop events and checks the resulting label order. This validates one in-list reorder route, not a real OS drag gesture, camera recall or preservation of meaningful snapshot payloads. It locates drag handles globally by a title and assumes their parents are the intended rows; another library with matching handles would change the fixture. The internal sequence omits dragend, so it does not independently demonstrate normal native cleanup, cancellation or capture-loss behavior. Helper error returns and its recorded defaultPrevented observation are not asserted by the caller.

For external drops, the script first proves that an invalid text-file drop on the body produces a warning, waits for that warning to disappear, then requires a new warning after dropping the same invalid file on a row. Clearing the control notice is useful evidence that the second result is not simply old feedback. However, this only proves the warning route for that synthetic invalid file; it neither loads a valid scene nor verifies that the row's order, active ID and saved payload remain unchanged. Page errors are logged rather than made test failures. Fixed waits assume toast and application timing, and the warning is searched across the whole page rather than tied to a particular import request.

For RFF, give internal reorder operations explicit ownership and payload identity, leave supported external imports to the intended handler, and reject foreign or stale reorder payloads without mutating the library. Verify reorder plus undo with stable IDs and real camera/material data, then verify an external valid import and invalid-file feedback separately. Include cancellation and simultaneous library surfaces. Preserve high-precision 2D locations and complete 3D camera/material snapshots when moving entries; reordering must not regenerate a palette recipe or alter shader parameters. This supports organizing visual experiments, but is not a shader rendering improvement or evidence of an existing RFF drag/drop failure.

Full source review of `debug/smoke-workshop-state.mts` (78 lines), without execution. This specifically tests a Formula Workshop's in-session source draft, not a saved scene/material roundtrip. A second test reloads the page to clear module-scoped state, then closes/reopens an untouched editor.

The first assertion proves only that some editor contains the marker. It does not compare the full source, require the intended editable source pane, verify active formula identity, or compile/render the snippet. The expandSource helper's comment says it clicks only if collapsed, but its implementation always clicks the first button with matching text when present; it does not check expansion state. Global first-editor selection and fixed waits can obscure which pane is being edited. For the second case, beforeClose2 is captured but never compared with the reopened content. Any nonempty text without the marker passes, so exact default-template preservation is not established. Page errors are printed but do not affect the final success decision. Reload intentionally discards the draft; this test is not evidence of crash/restart recovery or disk persistence.

For RFF, an optional custom shader/formula workspace could preserve unsaved draft text across panel closure while keeping it separate from the last successfully compiled and active renderer state. Define close, cancel, apply, reload and scene-change semantics explicitly. Store the document/formula identity with the draft so reopening another scene cannot accidentally reuse it. Validate exact source restoration and editor identity, then separately validate diagnostics, successful compilation and the intended rendered revision. Failed compilation should leave a clear distinction between the editable draft and the active formula. The historical mutation results in comments are not newly reproduced evidence. This is a supporting interaction improvement for both 2D and 3D controls; it has no shader-quality or performance implication. Runtime page/console errors are not collected as assertions.

A reusable RFF test harness should confine paths structurally, bind locally and reliably release resources even when launch/setup fails; here browser launch occurs before the cleanup try block.

After Escape disables the tool, it dispatches a vertical swipe and requires scrolling. Checking behavior as well as the declared touch-action value is a useful pattern: a style string alone does not prove input routing.
